title: The world’s 50 best restaurants for 2026 are revealed
text:
The world’s 50 best restaurants for 2026 are revealed
The best restaurant in the world this year is Asador Etxebarri, an eatery in Atxondo, Spain, that’s nestled in the Basque region and which has become a revered destination restaurant known for a revelatory grilling technique.
That’s according to The 50, which announced its global list of The 50 Best Restaurants 2026 at an awards ceremony Wednesday night in Lima, Peru.
In remarks given in Spanish after winning, Chef Bittor Arguinzoniz said the prize was “a real honor,” and he cited as inspiration “our mothers and grandmothers,” who, he said, were accomplished cooks.
Coming in at No. 2, according to The 50, was Gaggan, located in Bangkok.
Formerly known as 50 Best, the company bestows awards for the best restaurants across the globe. The list is compiled based on the votes of the 50 Best Restaurants Academy, which is comprised of more than 1,100 international restaurant industry experts, representing 28 regions around the world. The panel of experts includes food writers and chefs.
In addition to restaurants, The 50 also ranks the top bars, hotels and vineyards in the world.
The third best restaurant in the world for 2026 was Alchemist, in Copenhagen, Denmark, which was cited for “extraordinary craftsmanship” and where diners should be “prepared for a meal unlike anywhere else.”
Rounding out the top five were Quintonil in Mexico City, Mexico, which placed fourth, and Wing in Hong Kong, at No. 5, cited for taking pride in its Chinese heritage and offering diners the “untold stories of Chinese culinary history.”
Quintonil was also named the Best Restaurant in Latin America.
For anyone interested in fine dining, the awards are akin to the film industry’s Academy Awards (and included almost as much fanfare).
Restaurants are eligible for the top prize only once from The 50. Winners are then entered into a separate “Best of the Best” program.
The top American entry on the 2026 list was Atomix in New York City, which placed eleventh. The Korean restaurant was named the Best Restaurant in North America, while Chef Junghyun Park was honored with the Chef’s Choice Award and praised for providing a “window into a culture.”
Last year, the ceremony was held in Turin, Italy, where Lima’s Maido won the top prize.
The 50 is one of several organizations that rank high-end restaurants. Other groups include Michelin and LaListe.
The top 50
The academy says it aims to spotlight not just fine dining but cuisine that’s truly innovative. Last year’s winner Maido, for example, was a Peruvian restaurant run by Mitsuharu ‘Micha’ Tsumura, who is a descendant of Japanese immigrants to Peru and uses Japanese cooking techniques.
Four out of the five top restaurants in the ranking last year were in Spanish-speaking countries, but other restaurants honored included Piazza Duomo in Alba, Italy, and Steirereck in Vienna, Austria.
This year, the top five included restaurants in Asia, North America and Europe.
“For the past 25 years, we’ve celebrated the people and places shaping hospitality,” said Rikki Tidball, who heads up the awards program at The 50, in remarks that kicked off the gala event.

title: A Maine peninsula’s towns keep saying no to marijuana stores
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Residents of a Blue Hill peninsula town voted for the third time in one year on Tuesday not to allow recreational marijuana sales, putting an end to a local’s goal of opening the area’s first such store — for now.
Sedgwick residents voted 428 to 294 on Tuesday against the measure, their second ‘no’ on the question this year. The decision follows a similar vote in neighboring Blue Hill in 2025.
All three bids were brought forth by Brian Sherwell of Sedgwick, who said he and wife, Abril, saw a missed opportunity in the area’s lack of a recreational store.
“The community has spoken, and that’s how they see it right now,” he said Wednesday. “It’s clear at this point that the peninsula just isn’t ready for a store of this kind.”
The votes contrast the peninsula with some other Maine communities that embraced recreational marijuana establishments in the five years since they were legalized, though some later tried to limit their number of stores. Most of Hancock County has not opted in to allowing them, according to state data. The nearest recreational shops are in Bucksport and Ellsworth.
Opponents mostly seemed concerned about negative impacts on the community, which he pushed back on as misconceptions, Sherwell said.
Nearby Penobscot also faces a substance question later this month with a vote on whether to allow on-premise liquor sales in the semi-dry town. Some residents there have similarly worried that would change their quiet community for the worse.
To allow adult-use, or recreational, marijuana stores — separate from medical establishments — towns have to vote to “opt in” under state law.
An opt-in vote doesn’t automatically open the door to a store, as a town then needs to develop and approve an ordinance for regulating and licensing them.
Sherwell, who grew up on the peninsula and returned several years ago, said he feels Maine has benefited from job growth in its successful cannabis industry, which reduces black market demand.
He chose to pursue adult use because of exhaustive state safety standards, especially compared to Maine’s looser tracking rules for medical marijuana.
It was also a philosophical decision for Sherwell, who said he doesn’t think people should need a medical card to buy a product that’s been grown agriculturally for thousands of years.
“A lot of what it comes down to, it seems like, is the perception of stores being places for stoners and attracting the wrong kind of people and the wrong kind of business to town,” Sherwell said of the opposition. “Which I think is clearly a misconception.”
Sherwell added that he doesn’t think of cannabis users as “stoners,” and people who consume it live “healthy, productive lives.”
If he did get the go-ahead, Sherwell wanted to spotlight interesting, small Maine farms that are farther from the busy Portland market, he said.
Blue Hill, a service center for peninsula towns, voted down his opt-in initiative last November. Sedgwick did the same initially in March. Sherwell brought the question back Tuesday to hear from more voters with higher turnout for the midterms.
Sherwell expects to try again at some point, saying it’s a matter of time until public sentiment changes, but he has ‘no desire’ to bring opting in before local voters again in the immediate future.
“There is a very positive attitude for a lot of people on this peninsula, especially the under 50 crowd,” he said. “… I know it will come with time, but just not today.”

title: Letter: Congress should protect family farms
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
Providence Farm in Wilton is a family farm rooted in the belief that good food comes from careful stewardship of animals, land, and the community. Like many small farms across Maine, we rely on state and local laws that support responsible farming, food safety, and transparency for consumers.
We are concerned about the Save Our Bacon Act (SOBA) because this federal bill would weaken agricultural standards by overriding state laws that reflect local needs and values. States play an essential role in protecting animal welfare, encouraging sustainable practices, and allowing farmers to meet consumer demand for healthy food raised with care. Removing that authority replaces local decisionmaking with a one-size-fits-all approach that does not work for diverse farming communities.
SOBA would also tilt the playing field even further toward large, industrialized corporations. Small family farms depend on state and local policies to remain competitive. Stripping away those protections could push many independent farms out of business, reducing consumer choice and further consolidating food production in the hands of a few corporations.
Family farms already face challenges. Policies that undermine local control only add to those challenges and threaten the long-term viability of farms that prioritize healthy food over maximizing profit.
We believe the future of agriculture depends on diverse, locally rooted farms and strong community connections. We urge Sens. Susan Collins and Angus King and Rep. Jared Golden to reject the Save Our Bacon Act and stand up for family farmers, fair markets, and the rights of states to support responsible agriculture.
David Soule
Wilton

title: 3 executions scheduled for the same day in Indiana, Florida and Alabama
text:
3 executions scheduled for the same day in Indiana, Florida and Alabama
An Indiana man who admitted killing two children in a house fire was set to be executed in the first of three lethal injections scheduled for Thursday in the U.S.
Florida and Alabama were also set to carry out executions, which would mark the second time this year that three people would be put to death on the same day. The death penalty has faced renewed scrutiny following Tennessee's failed execution of Christa Pike, although courts have rejected efforts to halt other executions since she survived two lethal doses of pentobarbital last month.
Related video above: Christa Pike's attorneys speak after court hearing
It will be Florida's 19th execution this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis — matching a record set by the state in 2025 — but the first this year in Indiana, where the death penalty is not as common.
Lawyers had asked for life sentence for Indiana man
Jeffrey Weisheit was convicted of setting a fire that killed his girlfriend's two children, ages 8 and 5, at a home in the Evansville area in 2010, murders apparently related to the couple's deteriorating relationship.
Lawyers wanted Republican Gov. Mike Braun to allow Weisheit, 50, to undergo brain scans in an effort to reinforce their argument that he has a history of head injuries and mental health problems. Braun declined, and he also turned down a request to reduce the sentence to life in prison.
Weisheit's latest objection centered on the state's planned use of lethal drugs purchased from a pharmacy that is facing a disciplinary hearing next week at the Indiana Pharmacy Board. The Indiana Department of Correction said it's confident “in our ability to humanely carry out” the execution.
Florida on the verge of tying last year's execution record
In Florida, Jesse Guardado confessed and quickly pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing a 75-year-old woman inside her Walton County home in 2004 before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other valuables to support his drug habit. She had helped him get a job and housing.
A federal appeals court in 2024 said Guardado, now 64, had received a “full and fair” hearing during the death penalty phase of his case.
Florida has carried out more than half the 32 total executions in the U.S. so far this year. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said his goal is to bring justice to families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out.
Alabama man convicted for killings when he was 19
Michael Taylor, 54, faces execution in Alabama, 35 years after fatally beating an older couple with a metal bar during a robbery in their Gadsden home. Police arrested the 19-year-old with the victims' Cadillac, an hour away in Birmingham. The execution would be the state's third this year.
Death penalty opponents had urged Republican Gov. Kay Ivey to reduce Taylor's sentence to life in prison, noting his age and immaturity at the time of the killings. She declined.
“If the state kills Michael, it is not the 19-year-old who made the worst mistake of his life [whom] it kills. But the mature, well-respected, God-fearing man sitting in that cell today,” said Esther Brown of Project Hope to Abolish the Death Penalty.
The state plans to execute Taylor by lethal injection after a judge declared a nitrogen gas method unconstitutional. His attorneys objected to the last-minute switch to lethal injection since he selected nitrogen gas as his method several years ago, but a judge ruled against Taylor.

title: A brutal sell-off for AI stocks sends Wall Street reeling; S&P 500 sees worst day since 2025 ‘Liberation Day’ tariffs
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A brutal sell-off swept through Wall Street Thursday, led by stocks tied to the buildout of AI data centers. The wipeout more than erased the U.S. stock market’s gain from the day before, which was its best in three months.
The S&P 500 fell 4.4% for its worst day since President Donald Trump shook markets worldwide in April 2025 with his “Liberation Day” tariffs. The Dow Jones Industrial Average sank 1,833 points, or 3.4%, while the Nasdaq composite tumbled 5.5%.
The Nasdaq, which is full of AI-related and other tech stocks, sank 11.9% below its all-time high set last month. Stock geeks call a loss of more than 10% a “correction.”
Stock markets around the world felt pressure from continued drops for companies that had benefited from the boom in the artificial-intelligence technology industry, and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbled 5.3%. Such stocks have been swinging for months on worries that the construction of further AI data centers may slow because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money. Critics also said AI stock prices had shot too high and were in a bubble.
Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections added another challenge. The nationwide victories for Democrats raised the possibility that governments could force pauses in construction of more data centers. Voters across political parties say they’re wary about AI and don’t like the increases to power bills caused by data centers.
Any slowdown in construction of AI data centers would mean fewer purchases of AI chips, not to mention electricity and other products and services that are getting vacuumed up in the AI frenzy, which is driving much of the U.S. economy’s growth.
Nvidia, the chip company that quickly became the face of the AI boom, fell 9.3% and was by far the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. It’s now down 2.6% for the year so far following annual gains of roughly 39%, 171% and 239% in the last three years.
Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 17.3%. CoreWeave, a company that rents access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, fell 9.8%. GE Vernova, which has been helping to power data centers, sank 7.5%.
Compounding the pain for investors, AI chip stocks are some of Wall Street’s most influential because they’ve become some of the largest. A 1% move for Nvidia, for example, has more effect on the S&P 500 than a 1% move for nearly any other U.S. stock.
Thursday’s losses were broad after gains for the majority of stocks on Wall Street during the morning quickly evaporated.
Among the handful of winners was AppLovin, which jumped 31% after the marketing platform reported both revenue and profit that topped analysts’ expectations. The company’s board also approved a program to send up to $3.2 billion to investors by buying back its own stock, bringing the program’s total potential value to $3.6 billion.
Tapestry rallied 7.1% after the company behind the Coach and Kate Spade brands likewise delivered a stronger profit than expected. It also raised its forecasts for revenue and earnings this fiscal year.
Stock prices tend to follow where corporate profits and interest rates go over the long term, depending on them much more than on who controls what in Washington.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 334.89 points to 7,353.73. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,833.06 to 51,523.06, and the Nasdaq composite sank 1,421.52 to 24,315.00.
In other financial markets, the initial knee-jerk reaction to the U.S. midterm election results faded a bit. The price of a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 3.9% to $98.29 and recovered a chunk of its nearly 9% drop from the day before. Uncertainty still reigns about what will happen in the war with Iran and when the global energy industry can return to normal.
In the bond market, Treasury yields continued to tumble. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.84% from 4.90% late Wednesday. It had been at 4.95% on election night and above 5.30% last month. That could be a signal that investors are herding into U.S. Treasury bonds in search of something that’s safer to own as stock prices tumble.
The drop in yields came despite some encouraging reports on the U.S. economy. Fewer U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week. A separate report, meanwhile, suggested overall productivity for U.S. workers improved by more during the summer than economists expected. That could help the economy grow without adding pressure to the nation’s high inflation.
In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. Besides South Korea, Japan’s Nikkei 225 also felt the sting of drops for tech and AI-related stocks and sank 1.8%.
London’s FTSE 100 dipped 0.4% after the Bank of England increased its main interest rate for the first time in three years to help limit high inflation.
The bank said its next moves on interest rates will largely hinge on what happens with the Iran war, which sent oil prices and inflation higher worldwide.
“We’ve seen encouraging news in the past 48 hours,” Bank Gov. Andrew Bailey said at a press briefing. “The best thing that can happen is to resolve the conflict in the Middle East; there’s no question about it.”

title: Multiple flights in Europe diverted because of bomb threats after ‘malicious’ hoaxes
text:
MILAN (AP) — Bomb threats targeted more than a dozen flights in Europe on Thursday, leading to a slew of emergency landings and military escorts in some cases, authorities said. No hazardous or suspicious materials have been found in what a British official called “malicious” hoaxes.
Several similar threats targeted planes earlier this week, prompting searches and diversions, with at least 25 flights targeted, officials said. Europe has experienced a slew of other disruptions recently, such as attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems, drone incursions and mysterious triggers to alert apps.
While fake bomb threats are relatively common, it is unusual to see so many in a single day. They come at a time of increased geopolitical tensions and warnings from authorities that Russia may be ramping up so-called hybrid threats in Europe.
It wasn’t known whether this week’s threats were linked, who sent them or what they hoped to achieve.
An email containing the threat to Rome-bound planes was sent on behalf of a group that described itself as anti-feminist, according to a copy provided by an airport official and reviewed by The Associated Press. An official from another European airport said the threat they received also came from a group calling itself anti-feminist, and used some of the same language. It wasn’t clear if the same group sent the two threats. Both officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to share the information.
Travelers weren’t too frightened
At Rome’s airport, travelers whose flights weren’t affected seemed to take the threats in stride.
“As of now, I am not scared of being in an airport or getting on board a plane,” said Alessia Strada, a 19-year-old Italian returning from Kenya. ”Probably this idea I have about traveling in Europe will change in the near future, but let’s see how it goes.”
Alex Langenkamper, a 38-year-old German headed to Munich, said “crazy people” exist and will in the future.
Meanwhile, Michael Romano, a 54-year-old traveler headed to Colombia, expressed concern about the world moving toward war.
“These things never used to happen here in Europe,” he said. “This is all new, so it is a little bit scary.”
‘Stress-testing’ governments and driving up costs
Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, senior fellow at the Bruegel think tank in Brussels, said the threats were “stress-testing” how European governments and airport officials respond, and whether their responses were coordinated.
The idea behind the threats “appears to be to sow chaos, uncertainty, about the reliability of air traffic across Europe” and could have “cascading effects” — like economic damage and costs related to inspection, investigation and cleaning aircraft.
Joji Waites, who heads flight safety at the British Airline Pilots’ Association, said the industry has put in place “proved mechanisms” for dealing with such threats, including a team of assessors to grade the level of threat in a red-amber-green color-coding system, quick notification of flight crews, and the evacuation of planes on the ground.
Each flight disruption could cost airlines as much as $250,000, on a par with the possible costs of dealing with an unruly passenger, said Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England.
“And that’s because you might end up with the crew going out of hours. You might need replacement crew. You have got passengers that miss their flight connections,” Baum said. ”It knocks everything out of sync for the rest of the day for the airline in question.”
Military escorts cost money, too, which would be borne by governments rather than airlines, he added.
Officials decry the hoaxes
Britain’s transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, told British broadcasters that flights across Europe have been hit by “malicious hoax threats.”
European Union Transport Commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas told reporters in Dublin that it was “too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked.”
“National investigations remain ongoing,” he said, adding that an EU information-sharing mechanism on aviation security had been activated.
French air base goes on high alert
An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a military air base in France after receiving a threat, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s office said. The flight landed safely at the base in Evreux, which was under high alert, and military bomb disposal teams were examining the plane, the office said.
Lecornu ordered warplanes to intercept the plane because the pilot “didn’t cooperate as expected with the authorities,” his office said. It declined to comment further.
Hours after the flight landed, the plane was sitting on the tarmac with a Red Cross vehicle nearby while explosive experts with dogs examined it.
An investigation was opened by French aviation security authorities. The regional prosecutor, Remi Coutin, said in a statement that the pilot and co-pilot were questioned about what happened.
Aer Lingus later said its pilots fully cooperated with the French authorities and “the engagement of the pilots with the authorities has now concluded.”
Italian and Croatian air force jets escort a Finnair flight
Italian air force fighter jets escorted a Finnair flight that departed Helsinki bound for Rome after a threat was received by email, the air force said in a statement. Croatia’s defense ministry said one of its fighter planes first intercepted the commercial jet in Croatian airspace before handing it off to the Italians.
Finnair said that two of its flights, including the one that received the military escort and landed safely in Rome, “faced unfounded hoax bomb scares.” The other flight, operated by Jettime from Helsinki to Vienna, landed safely at its destination, and was expected to return to service after an inspection, Finnair said.
Three Ryanair flights bound for Sofia, Bulgaria, meanwhile, also received military escorts and made emergency landings after bomb threats, officials said. Two of the flights — one from Copenhagen, Denmark, and the other from Madrid — landed safely in Sofia, airport officials said. The third, from London, was diverted and landed safely in Plovdiv, Bulgaria’s Plovdiv Airport, CEO Krassimir Peshev said.
Hoaxes prompted similar searches earlier this week
Several flights across Europe received bomb threats earlier this week, officials said.
The flights included ones operated by Polish airline LOT, Scandinavian Airlines, Wizz Air and Ryanair. The hoax threats came after a plane headed for Bulgaria was diverted to Hungary upon receiving a similar bomb threat while in the air. No one was injured.
A slew of other flights were disrupted Thursday. Among those incidents:
— Czech police said searches of four planes that landed in Prague after being targeted by bomb threats turned up nothing. They haven’t given details on where the flights originated, and said they took precautions despite not finding the threats credible.
— A LOT Polish Airlines flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed at its destination, where inspections found no hazardous or suspicious items, the airline said.
— A Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest landed safely in the Romanian capital following a bomb threat, airport spokesman Teo Postelnicu said. Checks turned up no bomb.
— A flight to Warsaw landed in Vienna after Polish authorities received a threatening email, said Stefan Loidl, a police spokesperson in the Lower Austria province. Nothing was found and the plane continued to Warsaw. He said there was also an abstract threat to Vienna Airport concerning four other flights, which he declined to identify, but operations weren’t disrupted.
——-
Charlton reported from Paris and Biller from Rome. Associated Press writers throughout Europe contributed.

title: GOP House member says he will trigger impeachment vote against Defense Secretary Hegseth
text:
GOP Rep. Thomas Massie says he will reintroduce articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Hegseth
President Donald Trump may have made the decision to launch the war that tanked voters’ support for the GOP and dealt them a historic midterm loss. But the significant losses are accelerating a push for someone else to take the fall: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
And the House could vote as soon as next week to impeach the Pentagon’s top leader.
Many Republican lawmakers and allies alarmed by Tuesday’s wipeout are moving swiftly to pin blame for the election results on Hegseth, arguing behind the scenes that he played a chief role in convincing Trump to attack Iran with no exit strategy — and no plan for managing the inevitable political fallout.
The knives-out campaign comes despite private acknowledgement from House and Senate GOP strategists that the party’s problems extended far beyond the war, triggering 2008-level losses that will take years to reverse. But for now, party leaders – and many in their ranks – remain unwilling to directly blame Trump for their woes.
Even among House Republicans who survived Tuesday’s onslaught, there’s zero expectation they will suddenly break from the president with two years left in his term. Yet that fealty does not extend to Hegseth, the combative defense secretary who has made few friends on Capitol Hill since taking over command of the Pentagon.
House Republicans are expected to vote to directly repudiate the defense secretary in a matter of days. Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, the famously anti-Trump GOP lawmaker, told CNN he plans to trigger a vote to impeach Hegseth when Congress returns next week — and multiple GOP sources said they expect it to pass.
Hegseth, a vocal cheerleader for the war, oversold the U.S.’ ability to win the conflict quickly and easily, multiple Republicans argued to CNN, describing on condition of anonymity why many in their party are now turning against the defense secretary. They accused him of continuing to advocate for escalation despite little sign that continued bombing has brought Iran closer to surrender.
The conflict has since turned into a quagmire, they said, entangling the U.S. in the Middle East indefinitely, worsening the affordability crisis, and triggering voters’ midterm revolt against the GOP. On Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance issued an extraordinary statement that “the reason we lost is the war,” though he did not assign any specific blame for the conflict.
“The pivot is starting” on the war and Hegseth, a former senior Pentagon official said. “This has been primarily a Department of War-led effort because you chose to take military action to resolve a foreign policy matter.”
Still, despite efforts around him to turn up the heat on Hegseth, Trump’s own confidence in his defense secretary hasn’t yet wavered even as he’s continued to survey allies about his performance, multiple White House officials told CNN.
Trump personally likes Hegseth, and has told aides that he believes he should fight back against efforts to impeach him or launch investigations into his decision-making.
“Just two days ago the president was in the room with him, telling him, ‘You’re my best guy. You’re the best guy I have,’” one of the officials said.
Trump may also feel an additional need to keep Hegseth around if he chooses to move forward with additional strikes against Iran, another source familiar with his thinking told CNN, especially with Democrats’ new majority in the Senate likely to complicate any administration efforts to confirm new Cabinet appointees.
Pressed Wednesday on Hegseth’s job status, Trump defended the war effort and denied any plans to fire him, saying he thought the defense secretary was “doing a very good job.”
“If I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again,” Trump said of his decision to go to war.
The White House also decried the prospect of Democratic investigations into the Pentagon, with spokeswoman Lauren Bis arguing in a statement that “if Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people.”
But some Republicans feel it may be only a matter of time before Trump looks for someone to blame for the midterm losses, and they view Hegseth as an obvious target.
“If the president is serious about anyone taking responsibility for it, it’s Pete Hegseth,” one Republican close to the White House said of the electoral thrashing. “Pete has been either dishonest or incorrect — neither of which are acceptable — about timelines, goals and objectives since the beginning.”
Trump has not yet signaled plans to fire any top officials. But in the aftermath of the GOP’s midterm drubbing, allies and advisers widely expect him to eventually oversee some level of changes within the administration.
Within Trump’s orbit, some have seized on Hegseth’s likely impeachment as additional justification for making him the fall guy in the wake of an embarrassing rebuke of Trump’s presidency — contending that he’s bound to become a central target of Democrats’ ire over the war anyway.
Hegseth, for his part, has been defiant about his ability to withstand the forthcoming wave of congressional scrutiny.
While he has at times discussed his potential future ambitions with allies — including possibly running for office in Tennessee — those closest to Trump don’t believe that’s an immediate goal of his, people familiar with the discussions said. (Some Republicans on the Hill, in the meantime, privately bristle at the prospect of Hegseth serving in Congress.)
In the immediate aftermath of Tuesday’s midterm election results, one person close to Hegseth told CNN that Trump’s defense secretary still expects to stay in his role and is prepared to fight an impeachment effort.
Hegseth has also communicated to the White House that he’s prepared to own every policy decision and action taken by the Pentagon, the person said, believing that he’s well-equipped to defend those moves in public hearings that would likely grow contentious if Democrats launch them after they take control of Congress in January.
In a statement, chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said that Hegseth “will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists.”
“We will continue to drive President Trump’s agenda at the Department of War — despite threats of sham witch hunts from Democrats — and Secretary Hegseth is 100% committed to leading the Department until the end of President Trump’s term in office,” Parnell said.
Yet once that congressional scrutiny ramps up, Trump advisers and allies have questioned how long Hegseth’s resolve might last. Even before Tuesday, several White House officials, members of the president’s political operation and Trump allies candidly acknowledged the Iran war was — in their view — their biggest liability for the midterms. And Hegseth, one of the biggest proponents of military action in Iran, is intrinsically linked to that liability, they added.
“I think he probably knows he’s dead but would like an exit sufficiently dramatic that it gives him a launching pad to run for POTUS,” one administration official said.
For skeptics of the administration’s open-ended war in Iran, successfully pushing Hegseth out of the Pentagon would mark a critical victory — but only the first step in a broader effort to bring the fight to an end.
After all, Massie noted, Trump has continued to argue for continuing the war in Iran, no matter the political and economic price paid at home.
“You don’t screw up this badly an election with just one issue,” Massie said. “It was completely avoidable if they’d just broken out of the cultish following of Donald Trump.”

title: Indiana carries out the first of 3 US executions taking place on a single day
text:
3 executions carried out on same day in US, including Florida tying a record
Florida, Alabama and Indiana all carried out executions Thursday, putting to death three people on a day when California Gov. Gavin Newsom said he would commute hundreds of death sentences before leaving office.
The unusual trio of executions on a single day in the U.S., and Newsom's plans that experts say would represent the largest mass clemency in American history, underscored national divisions over capital punishment. They also come at a time of renewed attention over the death penalty following Tennessee's botched execution of Christa Pike in September.
In Florida, the state tied a record with its 19th execution this year and is on track to set a new mark in the coming weeks. Indiana executed a man for killing two children by setting a house fire in 2010, and in Alabama, a man was put to death by lethal injection over killing an older man and woman in a home robbery.
“California may let their criminals escape justice, but not Alabama," Republican Gov. Kay Ivey said. “Here, we enforce the law and always will.”
It marked the second time since August that three states had conducted executions on a single day, although it remains unusual. Previously, the last time it happened was 2010.
Florida inmate apologized to victims
Jesse Guardado was pronounced dead at 6:13 p.m. following a lethal injection at a state prison in Starke. He had pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing Jackie Malone, 75, inside her Walton County home in 2004 before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other valuables to buy drugs. The woman had helped him get a job and housing.
Florida has carried out more than half of the nation's 35 executions so far this year under outgoing Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis.
Guardado, 64, was already strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm when the death chamber curtain went up promptly at 6 p.m. Asked if he had a last statement, he replied, “I would like to once again apologize for the pain and suffering I’ve caused to the victim’s family and my own family as well.”
The drugs began flowing immediately afterward. Guardado began breathing heavily, followed by some sputtering and twitching. Soon after, a warden shook Guardado and shouted his name but got no response and a medic then pronounced him dead.
DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said he wants to bring justice to victims' families who have often waited decades for death sentences to be carried out. He signed the death warrants that led to a state record of 19 executions in 2025. The state is planning two more executions later this year.
Patrick Malone, the victim's son, told reporters that he questioned those who oppose the death penalty.
“Do such people ever think about what happened to the victim or consider the unending aftermath the victim’s family endures and relives every time that terrible event comes up?” Malone said.
Alabama man was condemned for a double killing
In Alabama, Michael Taylor, 54, was pronounced dead at 6:10 p.m. local time after a lethal injection. The execution got underway shortly before 6 p.m. as Taylor replied “no, sir” when asked if he had any final words.
He appeared to mouth “thank you” toward his attorneys seated in the witness room. Taylor’s spiritual adviser approached and prayed with him, and he closed his eyes, never opening them again.
In 1991, Taylor, then 19, fatally beat Ivan Moore, 83, and his wife Lucille, 79, with a metal bar during a robbery in their Gadsden, Alabama, home. Police arrested him in their Cadillac an hour away in Birmingham.
Death penalty opponents had urged Ivey to commute Taylor’s sentence to life in prison, noting his age and immaturity then. She declined.
The victims' family thanked the state attorney general's office for bringing closure, but they lamented having to wait 35 years for the death sentence to be imposed.
“We know that a person has the right to appeal, but there should come a time when the jury’s decision is final. For all these years, our family has had to live with the waiting, the delays, and the uncertainty," the family said in a statement. "We have never forgotten our loved ones or what was taken from us.”
The state switched Taylor's execution method after a judge declared a nitrogen gas method unconstitutional. His attorneys objected since he selected nitrogen gas as his method years ago, but a judge ruled against Taylor.
Attorneys for Taylor said in a statement that he knew the harm he had caused and that “Michael’s life was proof that God isn’t finished with any of us."
Lawyers had sought a life sentence for Indiana man
In Indiana, Jeffrey Weisheit, 50, was pronounced dead at 12:45 a.m. at the state prison in Michigan City, said Noelle Russell, a Department of Correction spokesperson. He had no final words.
Weisheit had acknowledged killing his girlfriend’s two children in a house fire in the Evansville area in 2010 but had hoped Gov. Mike Braun would grant clemency and change his sentence to life in prison. Braun declined.
The execution provided “long-awaited justice for Alyssa Lynch and her brother Caleb, two innocent children whose lives were stolen in an act of unspeakable cruelty," Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said.

title: A long tradition of greeting our troops at BGR
text:
COURTESY OF BANGOR INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT
For more than three decades, one of Bangor’s proudest traditions has begun with a simple act: showing up.
In 1991, thousands descended on Bangor International Airport to welcome home troops returning from Operation Desert Storm and support those deploying to areas of conflict. Veterans, families, students, scout groups, and neighbors filled the terminal, sometimes lining the airport access road with cars. From those extraordinary gatherings grew what would become the Maine Troop Greeters & Museum, and a tradition now known by generations of American service members.
Since formal recordkeeping began in 2003, Maine Troop Greeters have welcomed more than 1.6 million service members through BGR. For those returning from deployment, Bangor may be their first step back on American soil. For those deploying, it may be one of their last stops before heading overseas. In either direction, the mission is simple: be there. A handshake. A smile. Applause. A sincere “thank you.” A reminder that someone recognizes their service.
Continuing that tradition requires something important — the next generation of Maine Troop Greeters. The organization is entirely volunteer-driven, and preserving this uniquely Bangor tradition means welcoming new people into its ranks. You do not need to be a veteran or have a military connection. You simply need a willingness to show up and offer a few moments of gratitude to the men and women who serve our country.
And today, there is more to the mission than greeting flights. Over the years, service members have left behind thousands of challenge coins, patches, flags, photographs, letters and other pieces of military history as tokens of appreciation. Those gifts became the foundation of the Maine Troop Greeters Museum at BGR and expanded the organization’s mission from welcoming those serving today to preserving their stories for tomorrow.
The Maine Troop Greeters welcomes new members and greatly appreciates donations, which are used to purchase snacks and toiletry items for soldiers, as well as help with museum operations. If you are at the airport when a troop flight arrives, please join us in welcoming and thanking the transiting troops. Greeting these men and women who serve our country is a memorable experience and unique to Bangor, Maine.

title: Maine’s CD2 race goes to ranked choice tabulations; Dunlap concedes
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Democrat Matt Dunlap conceded to Republican Paul LePage in the race for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, which is going to ranked choice tabulations.
The Secretary of State’s Office said Thursday that no candidate has received a majority of votes and the law requires them to run the ranked choice tabulation, even if a candidate concedes.
Vote totals
According to numbers from the state, Republican Paul LePage had 170,263 votes equaling 49.9%. Democrat Matt Dunlap received 164,845 votes equaling 48.3%.
Declared write-in candidates received 123 votes, equaling 0.036%. There were more than 6,000 blank votes in the race.
Candidate responses
Wednesday afternoon, LePage declared victory in the race. Dunlap then responded saying it is too close to call.
Lepage’s campaign released this statement:
“I have spoken with Secretary of State Bellows and we are aware initial indications show a small number of blank votes and write-ins for this race may trigger Ranked Choice Voting based on their interpretation of law.
“It is very clear from our campaign team’s work yesterday talking one-on-one with local town clerks, and the publicly available numbers, that Paul LePage is the Congressman-Elect.
“Paul’s vote margin is extremely large. Decision Desk HQ alone reports Paul LePage has over 4,400 more votes than Mr. Dunlap. That is in line with our campaign’s estimate yesterday of a 4,500 vote lead as Paul declared victory.
“Paul LePage looks forward to working for all of the people in Maine’s 2nd District. He will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”
Dunlap conceded in a statement. His campaign does not currently believe ranked choice voting will change the results of the race.
“This isn’t the result we were hoping for, and I’m disappointed that we came short. Congratulations to Paul LePage, I wish him the best. I want to thank every volunteer who knocked doors, made calls, and made their voices heard. Your support inspired me, and I’m honored to have worked side by side with you over the past year,” Dunlap said.
Ranked choice required despite concession
Even with the concession, election officials say state law gives them no choice when it comes to RCV.
That means every ballot and memory stick must be brought to Augusta and verified.
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows says the process is built to give voters certainty.
“In elections, we love showing voters that our results are accurate. So, as time-consuming as the process is of bringing back the ballots and memory devices from the various towns, this allows us to go very meticulously through the results so that every voter can have confidence that at the end of the day, the winner receives 50% plus one,” Bellows said.
Tabulation schedule
The ranked-choice tabulation process will begin Monday at 10 a.m. at the Maine Department of Public Safety Headquarters in Augusta.
It is open to the public and will be livestreamed on the Secretary of State’s YouTube.
Bellows anticipates the process will take about a week to complete.

title: Bangor And Brewer Veterans Day: Pancake Breakfast, Parade, Ceremonies
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Veterans Day is coming up next Wednesday November 11th, and there are a number of way the you can help to honor veterans along with many ways in which veterans are being celebrated by businesses across Maine.
Read More: When Will Bangor-Brewer's Chamberlain Bridge Return to Two Lanes?
In the Bangor/Brewer, there's everything from a pancake breakfast and parade to discounts at local shops and eateries.
What's Happening And When?
Breakfast:
Things kick off at Jeff's Catering in Brewer with the Bangor Breakfast Rotary Club's Annual "All-You-Can-Eat Veterans Day Pancake Breakfast. Veterans eat free, but for the rest of us it's just $10 for adults and $5 for kids 12 and under. The breakfast will run from 7 AM to 10 AM, and wraps up right in time for the Veterans Day Parade (more on that in a moment.) All the proceeds they collect from the breakfast go to Bangor Breakfast Rotary Charities.
Parades and Community Observances:
The Bangor High School JROTC will once again host a Veterans Day Parade the will travel from Vista Way in Brewer across the Joshua Chamberlain Bridge into Downtown Bangor. That will kick off at 10:15 AM and go till noon.
Following the Veterans Day Parade, there will be a ceremony to commemorate Maine's Korean War Veterans featuring the playing of Taps and the Marine Color Guard. This will take place at the Korean War Memorial at the Mt. Hope Cemetery in Bangor at 12:30 PM.
After that, at 1 PM at the Cole Land Transportation Museum (405 Perry Road in Bangor) they will have another ceremony to honor veterans. That will conclude at 2:30 PM.
Folks are welcome to make their way to St. John’s Episcopal Church (225 French Street, Bangor) for another veterans commemoration called "America at War in the 21 Century." It will feature music, poetry and guest speakers, that will take place at 3 PM.
Musical Tributes/ Concerts
There will be two special tributes to honor America and her veterans this weekend.
The Bangor Symphony Orchestra is teaming up the actor/author/champion for veterans, Gary Sinise, and the Lt. Dan Band will play two shows at the Collins Center for the Arts. The shows will include music and a book sale of Sinise's new book, with the proceeds going back into his foundation to help veterans.
Read More: Bangor Symphony Orchestra Honors Veterans With Gary Sinise
The shows will be at 7 PM Saturday 11/7 night and at 1 PM on Sunday 11/8 afternoon.
There will also be a concert at the Gracie Theater on the campus of Husson University in Bangor. Veterans can get into the "Bruce in the USA" Tribute for free with their military ID. That show will start at 7 PM as well/.
Free Meals & Discounts For Veterans
Many area local and national restaurants and stores will be offering veterans and active military discounts on food and sale items on Wednesday.
It's important that you call ahead to check if the offer is a dine-in or drive through only, if it requires a membership card or coupon, and what times the offer will run. The it's usually as easy as showing a military ID and you're good to go.
Some of the businesses offering specials or discounts include Dunkin, Starbucks, McDonalds, Burger King, Wendy's, Olive Garden, Buffalo Wild Wings, Denny's, Chili's, Chick-fil-et, Texas Roadhouse, Applebee's and Taco Bell.
Other companies such as FedEx, UPS, T-Mobile, AT&T, Verizon, Home Depot, Ace Hardware, Sports Clips and the Dollar General also offer discounts to veterans on Veterans Day.
Read More: This Tiny Maine Town Is One of the Most Underrated in America
If you're looking for more information about special Veterans Day meal specials and freebies, there is a list online. You can access it through this site by clicking here.
Make sure you stop to thank a veteran next Wednesday (and whenever you see them out and about).
To our veteran listeners and readers, we appreciate you. Thank you for your service.

title: Pope Leo XIV to head to Latin America, Peru for 12-day trip weeks after lung surgery
text:
Pope Leo XIV to head to Latin America, Peru for 12-day trip weeks after lung surgery
Three weeks after lung cancer surgery, Pope Leo XIV is embarking on the longest and farthest trip of his pontificate: a 12-day, three-nation tour of Latin America that carries more personal and historic weight than any of his voyages to date.
The U.S.-born Leo is returning home to Peru, where the former Robert Prevost lived for two decades as a missionary priest and learned to be the pastor he is today. Leo holds Peruvian citizenship and is so attached to Peru’s people, he gave them a shoutout in Spanish from the balcony of St. Peter’s Basilica on the night of his election.
Leo is also going to Argentina, the home of his predecessor, Pope Francis, to whom Leo owes his pontificate. It will be a homecoming of sorts there, too, since Francis never returned to Argentina after his 2013 election, leaving a complicated legacy that Leo will now have to navigate.
Related video: Notre Dame coaches reflect on meeting Pope Leo while in Rome
Leo starts his trip Friday in Uruguay, the least Catholic, most secular country in all of Latin America, where not even the big Catholic feast days get their due: Christmas in Uruguay is officially “Family Day” and Holy Week is “Tourism Week.”
Leo is nevertheless expected to draw huge crowds throughout his trip and will likely raise issues of concern to his still-young pontificate: economic injustice, the plight of Indigenous peoples and the Amazon, and the church’s dreadful legacy of clergy sexual abuse.
But many eyes will be on Leo himself for having confirmed this grueling trip at all so soon after surgery Oct. 13 to remove a cancerous tumor from his lung.
When doctors announced that Leo required no further treatment, they also said there was no reason why he couldn't make the Nov. 6-17 trip. It includes a dozen flights and two helicopter rides covering 31,000 kilometers (19,000 miles), the longest of Leo’s pontificate.
While popes always travel with ample medical care, the Vatican said no special or additional provisions are planned for Leo, including when the 71-year-old travels to Cusco, Peru, at an altitude of 3,400 meters (11,200 feet).
“We’re not talking of a permanent condition,” said Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni. “We’re talking about something that you heal from, because it is surgery.”
A papal homecoming to Peru
No leg of the trip is more anticipated than the final stop in Peru, with Leo’s arrival in Lima, and after that Chiclayo, his beloved former diocese that he headed from 2015-2023, when Francis summoned him to Rome.
“He is so excited. He personally confirmed this trip with no changes,” said Maria Montserrat Alvarado, the Vatican’s new communications chief.
Leo told the region’s bishops in September that it was in Peru where he “came to know firsthand the faith of a people from whom I received so much, and I came to understand better what it means to be a shepherd.”
Alvarado said Peru “opened his eyes” to the diverse needs of the church and how the church encounters its flock. “This is a place that gave him his ministry and inspired who he is as a pastor,” she said.
Alvarado predicted that Leo will speak off-the-cuff in Spanish throughout the visit and will show his true feelings much in the same way he did in June during his visit to Spain, where the world saw a much more relaxed and happy Leo than the reserved, quiet one often on display in Rome.
“You will see that again but in a totally different way because he knows these streets,” she said.
Another homecoming to Argentina, with a different pope
Francis befuddled friends and foes alike for the duration of his 13-year pontificate, because he never returned home. He had plenty of opportunities, including during his first trip as pope to Rio de Janeiro, and subsequent trips to the region, including to neighboring Chile and Bolivia.
“How many times, I and other people asked him,” confided one of Francis’ closest friends at the Vatican, Guzmán Carriquiry, the former head of the Vatican’s pontifical commission for Latin America. “But it was useless, useless! He’d respond with jokes, by staying silent or getting irritated if you insisted.”
Carriquiry said Leo was coming to Argentina to “fill a void that has remained,” much in the same way Leo has undertaken trips to Spain and France — two once staunchly Christian European countries that Francis stubbornly refused to visit, preferring instead more far-flung “peripheral” places.
María Marcela Mazzini, an Argentine theologian who participated in Francis’ 2015 big meeting on the family, attributed Francis’ reluctance to return to Argentina’s complicated political polarization during his pontificate.
“We understand,” she said. “Things are contextual. I believe the people never doubted the pope’s affection. They always felt he was close to them and now we’re also watching with great joy as Pope Leo” continues his legacy.
“So we’re waiting for him with open arms,” she said.
The Argentine leg of the trip, however, is likely to be the most politically delicate, given the clear differences of priorities and styles of the reserved, pensive Leo and those of President Javier Milei, a self-described “anarcho-capitalist” who once described Francis as a “filthy leftist” and “representative of evil on Earth."
Leo Guardado, associate professor of theology at Fordham University, said he expected Milei’s push to attract AI investment and data centers to Argentina will be a point of discussion, given Leo’s concern about AI’s impact on humanity and the environment.
A visit to the most secular country in Latin America
The visit begins in Uruguay, the first country in the world to legalize marijuana for recreational use, the second country in Latin America to decriminalize abortion, and the third country in the Americas to legalize same-sex marriage.
More recently, it became the first country in the region to approve assisted dying legislation over the strong opposition of the Catholic Church, evidence of Uruguay's entrenched, church-state separation that prohibits any mention of God in oaths of office.
“Uruguay is by far the most secularized nation in Latin America. It’s pretty much like a Western European nation,” said Andrew Chesnut, chair of Catholic studies and an expert in the Latin American church at Virginia Commonwealth University.
All of which begs the question of why Leo would bother spending three days of a 12-day trip in a country of 3.5 million people, only a third of whom identify as Catholic and a fraction of whom actually goes to Mass regularly.
Alvarado had a ready reply: ”Why not?”
Leo is expected to make clear church teaching on abortion and euthanasia. But he is likely to also recall Uruguay's strong Catholic roots from the Spanish colonial era, most significantly on Sunday when he marks an important Catholic feast day that is intrinsically connected to Uruguay's 1825 declaration of independence and nationhood.
“He is going to meet people and meet hearts and hopefully inspire them to look again for the places where the church was big and now is small," Alvarado said. His message to today's religious “nones,” or nonbelievers, is: “Reconsider.”

title: InvestigateTV+: Aging and driving
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ looks at the emotional toll when seniors “hang up the keys” and offer a roadmap for families navigating that difficult conversation.
Plus, we investigate homeowners facing a costly nightmare from repeated pipe leaks in relatively new houses.
Then, an inspiring story of a local attorney using billboards to spread a little hope.
Aging & driving
As people age and their health changes, families can face the question of when a loved one should stop driving.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports older drivers are more likely than younger drivers to be involved in a car accident. They are “more likely to be seriously hurt,” according to the agency. Most older drivers do not have a plan for when they can no longer drive, which aging experts say is critical.
Defective pipes
For more than a dozen homeowners outside Atlanta their dream home came with a costly surprise.
They’re blaming one of the nation’s biggest home builders for selling them houses with defective plumbing. Homeowners say the pipes began leaking about four years after they moved in.
Beau’s Bags
Sabrina and Brenden Miller walked through the doors of Oak Lawn Hospital with 17 bags full of comfort items, a delivery they make each year on their son’s birthday.
Nurses in the birth center received the bags, which will eventually go to mothers of stillborn children.
Positive billboards
Sam Aguiar has been a personal injury lawyer since 2008.
“It’s a tough field, but it’s a rewarding field,” Aguiar said.
In December 2024, he decided to go beyond the courtroom and put up billboards around town with motivational messages. He’s up to 60 total billboards so far.

title: Woman charged with hiding income to pocket $12K in illegal SNAP funds
text:
TOWN OF ADAMS, New York (WWNY/Gray News) - A woman was arrested Wednesday on four felony charges alleging she fraudulently obtained more than $12,000 in SNAP benefits, authorities said.
According to an arrest report and felony complaints in Watertown City Court, Nicole Brown, 35, of Adams, was charged with first-degree offering a false instrument for filing, third-degree grand larceny, third-degree welfare fraud and misuse of food stamps.
The complaints allege that from Nov. 1, 2022, through Oct. 31, 2024, Brown obtained $12,037 in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits from the Jefferson County Department of Social Services under false pretenses.
Investigators said Brown failed to give the department accurate information about her income on an application and two periodic reports, which she submitted knowing they contained inaccurate information.
Brown was arrested Wednesday, processeD and held pending arraignment in Watertown City Court.

title: Tiny towns in Maine are holding up results in key races
text:
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
There still aren’t final calls on several key rural Maine races, as incredibly tight vote margins leave the result up to a handful of tiny towns.
Getting in touch with some of those towns is difficult. Several town clerks in northern Maine could not be reached on Wednesday or Thursday morning, as town offices were closed.
With some towns lagging in reporting their results, key races, including the relocation of the Penobscot County Jail and the Oxford County sheriff’s election, have yet to be called. It could take days to know the results in such cases.
Towns are not obligated to report their vote totals to the media, only to Maine’s secretary of state’s office. That office cannot share vote results until they are certified, a process which can take days.
In Penobscot County, it’s unclear whether a referendum on relocating the county jail will pass. As of 12:32 p.m. Thursday, 58 of 63 municipalities in the county had reported their results. The “yes” side was ahead by just 52 votes.
One town could swing the race.
Springfield, with about 300 residents, has yet to report its results. Nor has Maxfield, a town of about 89. Results from that town won’t be available until next Wednesday when the clerk is back in the office, a Bangor Daily News reporter was told.
Results from Kingman Township and Prentiss Township are also still unreported.
In Oxford County, a three-way race for sheriff has come down to single digits. Vote counts in a few small towns could swing the result.
The two leading candidates, the embattled Republican Sheriff Christopher Wainwright and the Democrat, Timothy Holland, are separated by just 17 votes in BDN’s count as of midday Thursday. The candidates themselves have written on Facebook that by their own calculus, Wainwright is ahead by 12 votes. They plan to ask for a recount.
“Every vote counts, and every person matters,” Holland wrote Thursday morning.
In that race, BDN is awaiting vote counts from a handful of plantations and the town of Gilead, where the town office is only open Tuesdays and Thursday afternoons.
The state’s largest race yet to be called — the winner of the 2nd Congressional District — was heading to a ranked-choice count because neither candidate secured more than 50% of first-round votes, the secretary of state’s office said.
Though Republican Paul LePage declared victory in the race Wednesday, the BDN and Decision Desk HQ have not yet made a call. As of midday Thursday, LePage was leading Democrat Matt Dunlap by 4,458 votes, with 95% of votes reported.
Dunlap conceded the race Thursday.
“This isn’t the result we were hoping for, and I’m disappointed that we came short. Congratulations to Paul LePage, I wish him the best,” the state auditor said.
Daniel O’Connor is a Report for America corps member who covers rural government as part of the partnership between the Bangor Daily News and The Maine Monitor, with additional support from BDN and Monitor readers.

title: Energy drinks linked to higher risk of cardiac arrest in young adults, study finds
text:
Energy drinks linked to higher risk of cardiac arrest in young adults, study finds
Energy drinks have been linked to a higher risk of cardiac arrest, a new study shows, particularly in younger adults.
A new study examined "adverse-events" reported to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration over eight years.
That study found that energy drinks and other caffeine-fueled beverages were linked to increased reports of cardiac arrest, heart attacks and other heart problems.
Researchers reviewed more than 28,000 reports filed from 2017 to 2025. Cardiac arrest appeared about 11 times more often in reports involving products with caffeine or other stimulants than in reports about products without them, according to new independent preliminary research to be presented at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions 2026.
Heart attacks were about 4.5 times more likely to be reported, while irregular heartbeats were about four times more likely, the study states.
Nearly half of the heart-related reports involving these products concerned adults ages 18 to 34.
The researchers say the pattern raises concern because young adults are not usually considered at high risk for heart problems.
But the findings show a link in reports, not proof that the products caused the events.
The data also does not show how many people used these products without problems, or how many heart events went unreported. Some energy drinks and workout supplements contain far more caffeine per ounce than brewed coffee, and people may consume them before intense exercise or alongside other substances.
Researchers say more study and better safety monitoring are needed. For now, they urge health professionals to ask younger patients with symptoms such as chest pain, fainting or a racing heartbeat whether they use these products.

title: Reporter forced out of Republican candidate’s election party during profane-laced speech on live television
text:
AMSTERDAM, New York (WWNY/Gray News) - Republican congressional candidate Anthony Constantino ordered a 7 News reporter and cameraman to leave his election-night party while he was thanking supporters and criticizing the news media.
Speech carried on 11 p.m. news
Constantino was leading Democratic opponent Blake Gendebien in the race for the 21st Congressional District Tuesday night.
7 News aired 15 to 16 minutes of Constantino’s live speech to lead the 11 p.m. news in which he thanked President Donald Trump “for having my back.”
Constantino also thanked former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani and political strategist and advisor Roger Stone.
However, the Republican candidate also criticized “the evil news media.”
Constantino and other people who came to the stage used inappropriate language before 7 News left live coverage to report on other election results in the region.
Reporter ordered to leave
Constantino continued to speak before randomly singling out 7 News reporter Garrett Domblewski.
He called Domblewski and 7 News anchor Jeff Cole a**holes. He also called a reporter from a different organization a “f**king a**hole.”
Constantino then ordered Domblewski to leave and led the crowd in a chant, “Kick him out. Kick him out.”
Five or six security guards escorted Domblewski out of the building.
While Domblewski was led outside, Constantino and the crowd chanted, “F**k the evil media.”
Reporter unsure of reason
Domblewski was unsure what prompted Constantino to order him to leave.
He said he conducted a cordial interview with Constantino earlier in the evening, a portion of which aired in the 10 p.m. newscast.
Live report from parking lot
After Domblewski was escorted outside, he reported live from the parking lot.

title: Key federal panel is expected to approve Trump’s arch while it’s being challenged in court
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A key federal panel has given final approval to President Donald Trump’s proposed memorial arch near downtown Washington, clearing a key hurdle on the road to breaking ground.
The National Capital Planning Commission on Thursday approved the 250-foot (76-meter) project that Trump has sought as part of his efforts to remake the capital region. The 8-4 vote Thursday gives a green light to launch construction within a day.
The arch still faces legal challenges and a judge is expected to rule soon on whether to block it.
THIS IS A BREAKING NEWS UPDATE. Check back for updates. AP’s earlier story follows below.
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal panel was expected Thursday to approve President Donald Trump’s proposed memorial arch in Washington at the end of a meeting that drew dozens of opponents to a key part of the president’s push to leave his imprint on the nation’s capital.
The approval by the National Capital Planning Commission would clear a hurdle on the road to breaking ground on the project, and the administration has said it could launch construction within a day of the vote. But the proposed 250-foot (76-meter) tall gilded arch still faces legal challenges.
The remote, call-in hearing — which crashed repeatedly and was accompanied by a nearly universally negative comment section — drew witnesses who gave impassioned, three-minute comments opposing an arch they said will destroy the solemnity of the nearby Arlington National Cemetery. As of 6:30 p.m. Washington time, there were still dozens of people waiting to give testimonials.
The Trump-appointed chairman of the commission, however, launched into a gushing appraisal of the towering monument and lauded Trump for wanting to build it.
“President Trump understands as president and a superb builder that it’s important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments,” said Mark Paoletta, the commission’s chairman.
As Trump has often remarked, “the great cities around the world have arches: Paris, Rome, London,” said Paoletta, who also serves as general counsel for the White House Office of Management and Budget. In addition to Paoletta, the arch received support during the hearing from Republican lawmakers and a veteran who praised the administration’s efforts to build the monument.
The commission oversees construction on federal land in the city and began reviewing the arch plan in June.
Trump is working to remake Washington
The arch is one of several projects around Washington that the Republican president has undertaken as he alters the capital to his tastes — from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Those projects could soon face intense scrutiny after Democrats gained control of Congress in the midterm elections this week.
Many of the plans are being challenged in the courts, and three lawsuits have been filed opposing the arch. A judge has been asked to block the construction so long as lawsuits are still being litigated, and she could rule as early as Thursday.
Rep. Jared Huffman, a California Democrat who is set to chair the House Natural Resources Committee, called the project ill-advised and illegal.
“This arch would dishonor America,” Huffman told the commission. He called the proposed arch “a tribute to Donald Trump,” not veterans as Trump administration officials claim. The monument is similar to those built for emperors or kings, Huffman said, adding that Trump was using veterans as a pretext to build a memorial to himself.
A small group of protesters joined at the proposed site to oppose the arch. Julius Spain, a member of the Arlington County Board and veteran of Operation Iraqi Freedom, told the crowd it was their moment. “I’ve seen combat. I was prepared to give my life in defense of a grateful nation,“ he said. “And now in this moment, my friends, and residents, and citizens and everyone, this is our civil rights moment.”
Virginia Democratic Rep. James Walkinshaw told the protesters that if the arch is somehow built, “I’m not going to stop until we ensure it’s a temporary arch.”
Opponents argue that the arch is too big for the skyline and would disrupt carefully designed sight lines between landmarks in and around the capital — most prominently the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery — that were meant to symbolize the reunification of the North and the South after the Civil War.
But the opposition has done little to influence the members of the commission, which is led by some of Trump’s closest allies. Trump appointed Paoletta to chair the 12-member panel. Two other commissioners are also White House aides.
At one point, Arrington Dixon, who was appointed by District of Columbia Mayor Muriel Bowser, broke in during a period of relentless criticism of the panel to foreshadow what he called “the reality” of having the majority of the commission appointed directly by Trump, members of his administration or House committees currently chaired by Republicans.
Trump wants an arch, but it faces legal challenges
Still, a federal judge on Monday complicated Trump’s efforts to move quickly on the project.
U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan, who is overseeing a lawsuit challenging the Trump administration’s plans, said she must be told of any decision by the planning commission within an hour. The order set the same time limits for any decision by the National Park Service and the Department of the Interior.
Before Thursday’s hearing began, attorneys with the Justice Department filed a notice with Chutkan informing her that a contractor had already done site preparation work on Oct. 31, with what she said appeared to be no authorization from the National Park Service.
The plaintiffs in the three lawsuits are calling for a halt to work on a monument that is set to be built on a patch of grass off a bridge that spans the Potomac River and connects Washington with Arlington National Cemetery, in Arlington, Virginia. When complete, the monument would be 100 feet (30 meters) taller than the Statue of Liberty without its pedestal.
Critics, including the plaintiffs, argue that the Trump administration must seek congressional approval. The administration maintains that Congress cleared the way for a monument at Memorial Circle decades ago.
Paoletta said it was a “national disgrace” that a memorial arch had not been placed there, despite a 1925 law that designated such a memorial, he said.
Last week, the government submitted a 106-page plan for the arch that envisions a massive structure more than 12 stories high that includes a huge bronze statue of Lady Liberty with wings and carrying a torch with an eternal flame. The structure would include an observation deck and two mezzanines.
Inside the arch would be rooms for program space, offices, a staff lounge, circular staircases, multiple elevators and a fire command center. The project proposes significant traffic changes in the area, including rerouting traffic on nearby roads. Administration officials have said the arch also will have a national security function.
In a recent hearing, Chutkan asked why the Trump administration was so keen on moving ahead quickly with the arch despite the ongoing lawsuits, aside from Trump’s “desire to bedazzle the city.”
Administration lawyer Robert Stander said the arch was “absolutely a high-priority project” and that any ruling delaying construction would impede the work of the government.
___
Associated Press videographer Nathan Ellgren contributed to this story.
