title: Penobscot County HIV outbreak reaches 50 cases
text:
The Penobscot County HIV outbreak hit the 50-case mark with a new diagnosis reported Thursday, a sobering milestone just over three years into the outbreak.
The outbreak began in October 2023. Nearly all of the people infected have reported injecting drugs or being homeless within one year of their diagnosis, according to the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention.
New diagnoses have been reported steadily in recent months, with an additional case diagnosed every month since May. The last month with no new diagnoses was August 2025. Public health officials have emphasized that the actual number of cases is likely higher than what’s been detected.
The Maine CDC now updates its public-facing dashboard tracking HIV case counts every other week instead of weekly. The agency also expanded its criteria in April for counting a case as part of the outbreak, now including cases linked to the outbreak through molecular surveillance, which allows scientists to identify particular strains of a disease and track transmission networks.
Community organizations across the state have ramped up testing and prevention efforts as the outbreak continues, and the Maine CDC identified a set of five cases in November 2025 that had been detected in Cumberland County last year among people who inject drugs.
HIV attacks a person’s immune system and interferes with their body’s ability to fight off infection and disease, according to the CDC. There is no known cure, although there is medication that can control the disease.
Penobscot County typically has two new HIV cases per year, according to the Maine CDC.
In nearly all of the reported cases in Penobscot County, the people affected also tested positive for hepatitis C, the Maine CDC reported.
Hepatitis C is a liver disease that can be a mild, short-term illness for some people but can cause more serious, long-term issues for others, including liver cancer, according to the CDC.
Seventy-eight percent of HIV patients in the Penobscot County outbreak were connected to care within 30 days of their diagnosis, and 69% of the 48 people currently living in Maine had reached viral suppression — meaning they can’t transmit HIV to others — at their most recent test, the Maine CDC reported.

title: Lockheed Martin to pay $29.5 million to settle federal claims it discriminated against white workers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Lockheed Martin to pay $29.5 million to settle federal claims it discriminated against white workers
Defense contractor Lockheed Martin has agreed to pay $29.5 million to settle claims by President Donald Trump's administration that it discriminated against white workers through its efforts to promote diversity and equity in an internal bonus program.
Lockheed Martin will pay $22 million to the U.S. government to resolve claims that it failed to comply with anti-discrimination requirements in its federal contracts, according to the settlement announced late Tuesday by the Justice Department and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.
In addition, Lockheed Martin will pay $7.5 million to more than 1,000 affected employees as part of a settlement with the EEOC, which had been investigating the company for violating Title VII of the 1964 Civil Rights Act, which prohibits employment discrimination based on race.
Related video above: Trump reopens Reflecting Pool in final midterm pitch as control of Congress hangs in balance
In a statement, Lockheed Martin denied the government’s allegations but said it “agreed to resolve this matter with the Department of Justice and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to avoid the distraction and expense of prolonged litigation.”
“We did not admit liability, determining it would be best for all involved to put these matters behind us so we can remain focused on our critical national security mission,” the company said.
The case is the latest example of the Trump administration's use of the 1863 False Claims Act to pressure federal contractors into abandoning diversity, equity and inclusion practices. The law states that contractors that make false claims to the government could be liable for extensive damages. Typically used to police fraud, the Trump administration has invoked the False Claims Act against companies it maintains have pursued discriminatory practices under the guise of promoting diversity.
The Justice Department has reached similar settlements with IBM, Deloitte and Accenture.
Civil rights groups have criticized the Trump administration's policies for taking aim at many long-established practices that are aimed at ensuring the hiring, promotion and other employment practices do not intentionally or unintentionally discriminate against traditionally marginalized groups. Several groups have filed lawsuits against the Trump administration's anti-DEI policies.
The allegations against Lockheed Martin center around a program the company introduced in 2021 to give the top 20% of employees a merit-based salary bump and promotion opportunities, according to the settlement agreement.
Managers submitted nominations for the bonuses, which the company then ran through an analysis to “flag” statistical outliers based on the race and sex composition of the list. If the nomination list raised flags, managers were asked to review their nominations and the “merit-based basis for the selections, without asking them to take any protected characteristic into account.”
But in practice, according to the Justice Department, Lockheed Martin personnel “exerted pressure on leaders in their business group to resolve race-related ‘flags’ by directing them to add or remove particular employees based on race.” The Justice Department claimed the managers were asked to remove nonminorities from the selections and add racial minorities.
The settlement with the DOJ and the EEOC stems from complaints made by Tim Booher, a former vice president at Lockheed Martin, who will be paid $4.4 million by the U.S. government under a whistleblower provision of the False Claims Act. According to a complaint he filed in federal court in October 2025, Booher resigned from Lockheed Martin in May 2023 because he "felt that he could no longer be complicit in LMC’s illegal discrimination."
In July 2024, Booher said he met with EEOC Commissioner Andrea Lucas to detail his allegations against the company. Lucas, who was elevated to EEOC chair after Trump took office in January 2025, filed a commissioner's charge against Lockheed Martin, triggering the EEOC's investigation.
Attorneys representing Booher released a statement applauding the "amicable conclusion that avoids prolonged litigation and ensures statutory compliance in federal contracting."
Lucas, a vehement critic of DEI practices, has publicly urged white men to come to the EEOC with discrimination complaints and has filed her own "commissioner's charges" against the diversity practices of companies, including Nike.
“Title VII protects every worker from employment discrimination on the basis of race — and that protection does not yield when discriminatory decisions are framed as diversity initiatives,” Lucas said in a statement announcing the settlement.

title: Dunlap concedes in Maine’s CD2 race; ranked choice tabulation to proceed
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Democrat Matt Dunlap conceded to Republican Paul LePage in the race for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, which is going to ranked choice tabulations.
The Secretary of State’s Office said Thursday that no candidate has received a majority of votes and the law requires them to run the ranked choice tabulation, even if a candidate concedes.
Vote totals
According to numbers from the state, Republican Paul LePage had 170,263 votes equaling 49.9%. Democrat Matt Dunlap received 164,845 votes equaling 48.3%.
Declared write-in candidates received 123 votes, equaling 0.036%. There were more than 6,000 blank votes in the race.
Candidate responses
Wednesday afternoon, LePage declared victory in the race. Dunlap then responded saying it is too close to call.
Lepage’s campaign released this statement:
“I have spoken with Secretary of State Bellows and we are aware initial indications show a small number of blank votes and write-ins for this race may trigger Ranked Choice Voting based on their interpretation of law.
“It is very clear from our campaign team’s work yesterday talking one-on-one with local town clerks, and the publicly available numbers, that Paul LePage is the Congressman-Elect.
“Paul’s vote margin is extremely large. Decision Desk HQ alone reports Paul LePage has over 4,400 more votes than Mr. Dunlap. That is in line with our campaign’s estimate yesterday of a 4,500 vote lead as Paul declared victory.
“Paul LePage looks forward to working for all of the people in Maine’s 2nd District. He will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”
Dunlap conceded in a statement. His campaign does not currently believe ranked choice voting will change the results of the race.
“This isn’t the result we were hoping for, and I’m disappointed that we came short. Congratulations to Paul LePage, I wish him the best. I want to thank every volunteer who knocked doors, made calls, and made their voices heard. Your support inspired me, and I’m honored to have worked side by side with you over the past year,” Dunlap said.
Ranked choice required despite concession
Even with the concession, election officials say state law gives them no choice when it comes to RCV.
That means every ballot and memory stick must be brought to Augusta and verified.
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows says the process is built to give voters certainty.
“In elections, we love showing voters that our results are accurate. So, as time-consuming as the process is of bringing back the ballots and memory devices from the various towns, this allows us to go very meticulously through the results so that every voter can have confidence that at the end of the day, the winner receives 50% plus one,” Bellows said.
Tabulation schedule
The ranked-choice tabulation process will begin Monday at 10 a.m. at the Maine Department of Public Safety Headquarters in Augusta.
It is open to the public and will be livestreamed on the Secretary of State’s YouTube.
Bellows anticipates the process will take about a week to complete.

title: The Latest: Alaskans wait for more votes in US Senate and governor’s races
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Alaskans are awaiting more results from key races on the general election ballot, including a bitterly fought U.S. Senate campaign and an open seat for governor. A ballot measure seeking to repeal Alaska’s unique system of open primaries and ranked vote general elections was also too early to call.
The midterm election blowout has set up a new era in Washington, with Democrats eager to meet voter demands for change while Republicans watched their congressional majorities evaporate in a revolt against President Donald Trump’s policies. Democrats triumphed in several surprise upsets, marking a decisive rejection of unified GOP control of the House and Senate. See the full election results.
Trump acknowledged the Iran war affected the midterms, suggesting voters were frustrated by surging gas prices that have been a byproduct of the more than 8-month-old conflict. He struck a conciliatory tone earlier, suggesting he could work with the Democrats, only to later threaten to use his veto power to strike down their agenda.
The fallout for Republicans is only beginning. Vice President JD Vance, a 2028 presidential contender, blamed the war in Iran for Republicans’ midterm wipeout. And Mike Johnson of Louisiana will not seek reelection as House speaker, according to two people familiar with the matter.
Here’s the latest:
World shares mostly gain after US midterm elections as AI-related stocks sink
World shares were mostly higher Thursday, though heavy selling of artificial intelligence-related stocks offset gains for some markets following the U.S. midterm elections.
South Korea’s Kospi sank more than 5% and the Nikkei 225 in Tokyo lost nearly 2%. Oil prices were mixed after the Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped more than 3% on Wednesday after Republicans lost control of the U.S. Congress.
In early European trading, the German DAX rose 0.6% to 26,598.03, while the CAC 40 in Paris surged 1.2% to 8,276.55. The United Kingdom’s FTSE 100 gained 1% to 10,935.08.
The future for the S&P 500 was nearly unchanged, while that for the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 0.4%. On Wednesday, the S&P 500 jumped 1.6%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average surged more than 1,500 points, and the Nasdaq composite rose 1.4%.
U.S. stocks usually climb following midterms. But technology shares have taken a hit as investors mull the potential impact on the artificial intelligence boom from a Democratic-led Congress next year.
After taking control of Congress, Democrats vow major probes into Trump’s ‘tentacles of corruption’
Corruption topped the list of concerns for voters who ousted Republicans and handed Democrats control of Congress in the midterm elections. Now, the newly empowered Democratic Party is putting the issue front and center as its leaders chart their course for investigations and policymaking.
Senior Democrats in both chambers of Congress have vowed to marshal the subpoena powers and larger investigative staffs that come with their soon-to-be majorities to probe what they say is the self-enrichment that President Donald Trump and people in his orbit have done at the public’s expense. The Republican president and his White House have long denied any wrongdoing.
House Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda to look at how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office — and Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who’s in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Trump for a third time.
‘A beautifully American story’: El-Sayed’s historic Senate victory resonates with Muslim Americans
Campaigning across Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed didn’t highlight the possibility that he could become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. But with victory in hand, he savored his triumph over the vitriol aimed at him and his fellow Muslim Americans.
“They tried to demonize people because of how they pray,” he told The Associated Press on Wednesday. “And Michigan — the whole Michigan — clapped back. People don’t want that. They’re sick of it.”
Twenty-five years after the Sept. 11 attacks and their aftermath yanked anti-Muslim sentiment into the forefront of American life, those emotions are shared by many Muslim Americans.
They saw a surge of anti-Muslim rhetoric after Zohran Mamdani was elected New York City mayor, and they saw the attacks intensify as El-Sayed became the new prime target. But after El-Sayed’s defeat of GOP rival Mike Rogers, there is a pervasive sense that a broader victory is at hand.
Inflation, tariffs and a voter revolt: The midterm verdict on Trump’s economy
Trump was publicly humbled by inflation in Tuesday’s midterm elections, as rising prices provoked a blistering set of losses for Republicans in House, Senate and gubernatorial races.
Most voters said that Trump’s own policies had smothered growth and driven costs even higher, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of roughly 100,000 midterm voters. The president’s message that the fault lay with his predecessor, Democrat Joe Biden, didn’t land. Americans saw prices start to climb with Trump’s chaotic rash of tariffs last year, and energy costs spiked after he launched a war with Iran in February.
About two-thirds of voters said Trump’s own policies had fueled inflation. By contrast, only about half of 2022 midterm voters said this about Biden’s policies, according to AP VoteCast.
The election results matched what voters had been telling pollsters for months, but Trump had campaigned with a decidedly deaf ear.
“I’ve done a great job,” Trump said at one of his final midterm rallies in Iowa.
Trump-backed Republican redistricting sought a midterm edge. It didn’t work
At the urging of President Donald Trump, Republicans in eight states redrew the boundaries of dozens of congressional districts over the past year while angling for an edge that could help them hold onto a slim House majority in a tough midterm election.
Ultimately, it didn’t work.
Republicans lost most of the Democratic-held seats they had targeted to flip, lost others they had banked on retaining and got swept out of power by a Democratic surge fueled by voter dissatisfaction with Trump, the economy and the war with Iran.
The Republican redistricting plan fell flat in Alabama, Florida and Texas. It got scuttled by courts in Missouri and then firmly defeated by its voters Tuesday. And it got offset in California, where a retaliatory Democratic redistricting flipped all five of the Republican-held seats it targeted.
“This is a catastrophic rebuke of Donald Trump’s failed effort to gerrymander the country into oblivion to save the U.S. House of Representatives for himself,” John Bisognano, president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, said Wednesday.
The 2028 election season begins as both parties navigate midterm fallout
The final midterm votes are still being counted, but make no mistake: The next election season has already begun.
Presidential prospects in both parties jockeyed for position on Wednesday, even as the political world was digesting the impact of the Democratic wave that crashed over American politics the night before. Democrats celebrated their party’s stunning success — and began promoting themselves — while dejected Republicans scrambled to distance themselves from Trump’s wreckage.
The Republican with the most at stake was likely Vice President JD Vance, who entered Tuesday night as the GOP’s leading presidential prospect and woke up on Wednesday far more vulnerable — like any Republican who is close to Trump.
Voters still processing an extraordinary midterm campaign may not welcome an immediate pivot to 2028. But for would-be candidates, there is real urgency to move toward a White House bid in what is expected to be a wide-open contest in both parties.
After midterm loss, Trump is left to weigh his next move in Iran war that contributed to GOP debacle
As he takes stock of his Republican Party’s midterm drubbing, Trump now faces the difficult question of what to do about his unpopular 8-month-old war against Iran.
For weeks, Trump has threatened to return to a full-scale bombardment of Iran once the U.S. elections were in the rearview mirror if Tehran did not come to a settlement under terms acceptable to him.
In his first comments on Wednesday after Democrats’ resounding election victory — a wave powered in part by the American electorate’s dissatisfaction with the war — Trump largely agreed with Vice President JD Vance, who publicly ruminated on the war being a catastrophe for Republicans.
The strikes, and counterstrikes, have caused tens of billions of dollars of damage in the region. And the conflict has reached into the pocketbooks of families around the globe with elevated gas prices and rising costs in just about every sector.
Now, as Trump ponders his next move, the stakes couldn’t be higher for Iran, the Middle East and the global economy writ large.
Alaskans wait for more votes in US Senate, governor’s races. Both could go to ranked tabulations
Alaskans settled in Wednesday to await more results from key races on the general election ballot, including a bitterly fought U.S. Senate campaign and an open seat for governor.
A ballot measure seeking to repeal Alaska’s unique system of open primaries and ranked vote general elections was also too early to call.
If no candidate wins more than 50% of first-choice votes, rankings will come into play. Alaska accepts ballots from overseas voters for up to 15 days after the election, making Nov. 18 the date targeted by state elections officials to tabulate under the ranked vote system.
The major candidates in the Senate race are two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola.
In the governor’s race, former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is trying to become the first Democrat elected to the office in a generation. He faces three other Republicans, including business owner Bernadette Wilson, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump.

title: The election is over, but when will all the campaign signs come down in Maine?
text:
The election is over, but when will all the campaign signs come down in Maine?
Election Day has come and gone in Maine, but political and campaign signs are still lining many streets across the state. Many people have asked when those signs must come down.
Public Right of Way
State Law
The 129th Maine Legislature updated the state law that governs the placement of temporary signs, including political signs, in 2019. Under that law, temporary signs may be placed in the public right of way for up to a total of 12 weeks each year, including no more than six weeks between January 1 and June 30 and no more than six weeks between July 1 and December 31.
This means that not all signs have to come down at the same time. The time of removal is tied to when the sign went up.
The law also says that signs that have essentially the same message must be at least 30 feet apart.
State law says that temporary signs and posters cannot be put on traffic control signs or devices, public utility poles or fixtures, a rotary traffic island, a tree in a public right-of-way, a control-of-access area, a median less than 6 feet wide, or be painted or drawn on rocks or other natural features.
Campaigns can face fines if signs are up for more than six weeks, but it is rare for those fines to be imposed.
Local Rules
Local municipalities may add their own restrictions. For instance, according to a notice on the town of Kittery's website that was updated on July 1, 2026, political signs on public property in Kittery can be placed no earlier than 30 days before the election they are related to and must be removed no later than two days after the election.
Private Property
In general, signs on private property can stay up for as long as the property owner wants, as long as the sign is outside the public right of way and is not more than 50 square feet in size. There are some other limits and rules outlined in the state law. One of the rules is that there cannot be more than 10 signs on any property, unless there is more than one business, facility or point of interest being conducted on one property, in which case each is limited to 10 signs.

Rollinsford police say the pedestrian was walking along the tracks wearing headphones when the train approached from behind
A pedestrian was killed after being struck by an Amtrak train in Rollinsford, New Hampshire, Wednesday afternoon, according to police.

title: What causes dry mouth, and what can you do about it?
text:
(Aging Untold) — Dry mouth can show up alongside soreness, bad breath and trouble with dentures.
It affects 40% of adults 80 and up and 30% of adults 65 and up, according to the American Dental Association.
What causes dry mouth?
Dry mouth happens when the salivary glands do not produce enough fluid, and there are several causes for it, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said. Finding that reason is the first step.
“Basically your salivary glands are just not producing enough fluid. And so you want to know why. You know, always find your why,” Rogers said.
Rogers listed several possible causes:
- Dehydration
“If you’re dehydrated you’re not producing fluid,” Rogers said.
- Damage to nerves
- Cancer
- Underlying autoimmune disorders
Rogers said a cause such as an autoimmune disorder might be a clue that “something else is going on.”
- Medications
Rogers also said dry mouth can be an early sign in a person who is otherwise healthy.
“That might be their clue that you have something going on in your body. And this is your early sign,” Rogers said.
Why saliva matters
“Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said saliva does more than keep the mouth wet.
“People don’t realize just how important saliva is,” she said. “Think about driving a car without any engine oil. It’s not going to last long.”
Without enough saliva, Cradduck said talking, eating and chewing are difficult.
“It is the mouthwash for your body. It really is,” she said.
Rogers added that saliva cleanses and protects the enamel.
Dentures do not make saliva less important, she said. Dry mouth can affect how dentures fit and how a person chews, and it can lead to discomfort, pain and more sores.
Ways to manage dry mouth
Cradduck said she has dealt with dry mouth for a long time because of an autoimmune condition and shared what she does.
“I keep gum in all the time. There is gum in my mouth right now. I sleep with gum in, candy, little hard drops, things like that that cause your mouth to salivate,” Cradduck said.
Cradduck also brought up mouthwash.
“A lot of mouthwash has alcohol, and alcohol is drying, so that’s counterintuitive,” she said.
“A lot of the things that will dry your mouth, you need to stop doing and avoid doing,” Cradduck said, and named drinking and smoking.
Cradduck also mentioned sticky drops that can be placed on the gums.
“It helps, for some people,” she said.
Cradduck described a person who had salivary glands removed because of cancer and uses stickers that go around the gums.
Rogers said treatments either stimulate a gland that is underproducing or provide moisture when the gland cannot produce.
Talk with your dentist
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said a regular conversation with a dentist can help.
“I think that idea of having a conversation with your dentist every year or twice a year, however often you go: How’s my mouth doing? How’s the dryness?” O’Rourke said.
She said possible signs of trouble with dry mouth include coughing a lot, having recurring infections and avoiding certain foods.
“Stay on top of it by reaching out to the professionals,” O’Rourke said.
Key takeaways
- Dry mouth means the salivary glands are not producing enough fluid. Dehydration, nerve damage, cancer, autoimmune disorders and medications can all play a role, according to Dr. Rhea Rogers.
- Dry mouth can be an early sign. Rogers said it can point to something going on in the body, even in a person who is healthy and not taking medications.
- Dentures are affected too. Dry mouth can change how dentures feel and how a person chews, and it can lead to pain and sores, Rogers said.
- Ask your dentist. Bring up dryness at regular visits, and mention coughing, recurring infections or avoiding certain foods, Amy O’Rourke said.

title: New study links energy drinks to reports of heart attacks and cardiac arrest in young adults
text:
New study links energy drinks to reports of heart attacks and cardiac arrest in young adults
A cardiologist recommends moderation as well as healthier options
New study links energy drinks to reports of heart attacks and cardiac arrest in young adults
A cardiologist recommends moderation as well as healthier options
A new study is raising concerns about the potential heart risks associated with caffeinated energy drinks and stimulant supplements, particularly among younger adults.
Researchers reviewed more than 28,000 adverse-event reports submitted to the FDA between 2017 and 2025. Products containing caffeine or other stimulants appeared disproportionately often in reports involving serious cardiovascular events, including cardiac arrest and heart attacks.
What researchers found
About 45% of reports linking caffeine- and stimulant-containing products to cardiovascular events involved adults ages 18 to 34 — a group not usually considered at high risk for heart attacks or cardiac arrest.
The analysis found cardiac arrest was reported about 11 times more often in connection with caffeine- and stimulant-containing products compared with products without those ingredients.
Reports involving energy drinks and supplements were about 4.5 times more likely to include heart attacks and four times more likely to include ventricular arrhythmias or heart palpitations.
Dr. Brian Downey, director of General Cardiology Services at Tufts Medical Center in Boston, Massachusetts, said the findings are notable.
“That’s quite a bit higher than we would expect to see,” Downey said.
He also cautioned that the FDA database is voluntary, meaning not every patient who experiences an event submits a report.
Why energy drinks may be different
Downey said the potential concern may involve a combination of the amount of caffeine and other ingredients in these products.
A 20-ounce energy drink can contain the caffeine equivalent of as many as four or five cups of coffee, he said. The study also notes that some energy drinks contain three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce than brewed coffee.
Exercise and other factors that increase heart rate may also contribute to the risk of abnormal heart rhythms or heart attacks.
Researchers said the reasons for the pattern among younger adults aren't fully understood. Possible factors include how frequently young adults consume these products; whether they use them before intense exercise or with alcohol or drugs; or whether some people have an undiagnosed heart condition.
What consumers should know
The American Heart Association says up to 400 milligrams of caffeine per day is generally safe for most adults. But some people can quickly exceed that amount with energy drinks or stimulant supplements.
Downey said moderation is key, particularly for teenagers.
“Having an occasional energy drink is probably not the end of the world, but being prudent with how much and how often is probably a good idea,” he said.
He also recommends considering more natural sources of caffeine, such as coffee or tea, and consuming them in moderation.
“A cup or two of coffee a day or something in the afternoon is probably fine,” he said.
The important caveat
The AHA acknowledges the study has not been peer-reviewed and does not prove that caffeine or stimulant products caused the reported heart events.
Its experts say more research and systematic safety monitoring are needed to better understand the relationship between these products and cardiovascular conditions.
For now, consumers can pay attention to how much caffeine they're getting, how often they're using stimulant products, and whether they experience symptoms such as chest pain, palpitations or fainting.

title: California Gov. Newsom says he will commute all death sentences in state to life without parole
text:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — California Gov. Gavin Newsom said Thursday that he’ll change all death sentences in the state to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
Newsom’s decision comes as he prepares to leave office after eight years. In 2019, he placed a moratorium on executions in the state but hundreds of people remained on death row.
“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” Newsom said in a letter.
Newsom moved to grant clemency to 548 people are currently sentenced to death in California, of which 529 are men and 19 are women, according to numbers provided by his office.
The state constitution requires the California Supreme Court’s approval to grant clemency to anyone convicted of a felony more than once, which means the court would have to approve 382 of those commutations, or roughly 70%, according to numbers provided by Newsom’s office..
Newsom said the decision was among the most difficult choices of his career because it will surface painful memories for crime victims’ families.
“As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution,” Newsom wrote.
California voters rejected a ballot measure in 2016 that would have repealed the death penalty in the state.
The American Civil Liberties Union, who has said the implementation of the death penalty reflects racial bias, applauded the announcement.
“These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long,” said executive director Anthony Romero in a statement.
The ACLU is involved in an ongoing legal challenge to California’s death penalty statute, alleging it is racially discriminatory and unconstitutional.
Newsom has said in the past that it is wrong for the government to kill its citizens and that capital punishment in practice has discriminated against mentally ill people and people of color.

title: Why this attorney has been putting up positive billboards
text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (InvestigateTV) - Sam Aguiar has been a personal injury lawyer since 2008.
“It’s a tough field, but it’s a rewarding field,” Aguiar said.
In December 2024, he decided to go beyond the courtroom and put up billboards around town with motivational messages.
“I designed them myself,” Aguiar said. He sent them to his billboard representative and told them to get the billboards up before he changed his mind.
“I know it sounds a little crazy,” he said.
Simple messages for difficult times
Aguiar said the plan was to make the messages simple so they would resonate with people.
“I remember there was ‘Believe in yourself.’ There was ‘Good vibes only today.’ There was ‘Stay strong’—very short messages, you know—hoping to speak to different people who may be going through different times,” he said.
Since December, Aguiar has put up about 60 billboards in high-traffic areas around Louisville.
The response was immediate. More than 2,000 people have reached out through phone calls, emails, texts, and social media.
“I was getting messages from trauma nurses who said they saw some by the hospitals that really braced them for what they knew was going to be another tough shift. We’d gotten a great message from a cancer patient who was driving up from E-town a few days a week to go through chemo, and she said that when those messages popped up, it gave her a little bit of a boost. We had EMTs reach out. We had some teachers reach out. We had single moms reach out. It was awesome,” Aguiar said.
Aguiar has also had fun with the campaign. One billboard near the fairgrounds references a social media trend his 13-year-old would recognize.
“I figured if you can’t beat them, join them,” he said. “Maybe Mom and Dad up front will, you know, like being reminded that they’re a 10. And then maybe their kiddos in the back will see six, seven and start doing whatever that little motion is at six, seven.”
Not about business
Aguiar said the goal was never about generating business, though some new clients have come his way.
“It’s not hard to remind people that they’re important, that they’re loved, that they’re making a difference, um, and that they make the world a better place,” he said.
Aguiar has spent more than half a million dollars on the campaign and wants to continue it.

title: Maine fisheries biologists study stocked salmon in Albany Twp.
text:
Songo Pond in Albany Township was the focus last month of a salmon-sampling program by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife.
Songo Pond is nearly 1.5 miles long and covers 2.6 square miles. It is located beside Routes 5 and 35 just south of the Bethel town line.
It is is known as a “put-and-take” winter salmon fishery, according to IFW Fisheries Resource Supervisor Jim Pellerin. That’s because it is stocked for fishing by the department with the expectation that the fish will be “harvested relatively soon after stocking. We’re not really looking or expecting to create a quality fishery with multi-age fish,” he said.
Salmon rely on rainbow smelt for food, he said, and Songo Pond is small and the population of smelt limited.
Salmon stocking in the pond became a regular program around 2008, according to Pellerin.
The Songo Pond sampling project was conducted by biologists Brian Lewis and Joel Rojas. They placed nets suspended from buoys in two locations on the pond and checked them three days a week.
“They evaluate age, growth and salmon condition,” Pellerin said, by collecting length, weight, sex, maturity and hooking wounds, and add various comments on each fish. “Based on the information, we may make changes in stocking rate, species and age class.”
Sometimes they cancel a stocking program based on the information.
IFW samples salmon in this region, designated Region A, which extends from Kittery to Bethel and the New Hampshire border to the Androscoggin River. Three of the best salmon waters, said Pellerin, are checked annually and one biannually.
“Most of the remainder (about 10) are on a five-year rotation,” he said, and another half dozen are rarely sampled because of location and lower priority.
Songo Pond has not been evaluated in a while, Pellerin said. Limited staff restricts coverage, so they do five to seven salmon waters each fall.
In a healthy salmon water, he said, “We like to see at least 15 to 30 fish of the predominant age class, typically age 11-plus. Our better waters generally meet or exceed that number.”
In others they may have difficulty getting that sample size. Pellerin said the preliminary information from Songo Pond shows that fish growth “is relatively poor compared to most of our other salmon stocking programs.”
A complete report is expected next spring, after all the data is entered and analyzed.
Alison Aloisio is a freelance writer.

title: Who speaks for you? Choosing a medical power of attorney
text:
(Aging Untold) — Staying in control as you age can mean choosing someone you trust to make health care decisions if you can’t. The key is picking a person who knows your wishes and will keep them front and center.
The Aging Untold experts are talking about what a medical power of attorney covers, how to set one up and why you should have the document with you.
What a medical power of attorney can decide
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the person you name holds a wide range of decision-making power.
“They can decide whether you’re going to have surgery,” Cradduck said. “They can decide whether or not you’re going to go into a skilled facility in a rehab after a surgery. They can decide if you’re going to go into an assisted living. They can decide if you’re going to be at home, who your caregivers are going to be.”
The person you choose needs to be someone who can set their emotions aside, she said.
“You need to make sure that this person knows you, knows your wishes, will honor your wishes, and that they’re not going to be torn by emotion if it comes down to life and death decisions,” Cradduck said. “You need to know that this person can advocate for your wishes, not for their heart’s desire.”
A medical power of attorney is a document that goes by several names, including health care surrogate, health care power of attorney and health care proxy, and those names all refer to the same thing, aging expert Amy O’Rourke said.
Why being married is not enough
Married couples should not assume a spouse can make decisions for the other, O’Rourke cautioned.
“Don’t just think because you have a family relationship that you’re going to have the power to make these decisions,” she said.
O’Rourke said a spouse who goes to the hospital without a medical power of attorney could be turned away, depending on state rules and laws.
Keep the paperwork where it can be found
Another thing Cradduck said to keep in mind is that having the physical document matters.
A hospital does not have to honor a person who says they have power of attorney without the paper, she said.
In a car accident, “That doctor can be the one making the decisions and he doesn’t know what your wishes are,” Cradduck said.
Copies of the document should be easy to grab, people involved should have duplicates and know how to produce them.
“This needs to be something that a paramedic can find. Might be on your fridge,” aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said. “It is not something to have locked away in a safe deposit box. It needs to be with you.”
Choose someone with integrity and backbone
Cradduck compared the choice of medical power of attorney to picking a designated driver.
“This is literally picking out your designated driver before you go to the party,” she said.
Ambrose said the person you choose needs to be able to stand up to others.
“Even long lost relatives will show up during a medical crisis and try to say what they think their brother would want,” Ambrose said.
You can help that person by communicating your wishes to others, she said. You could also record a video of what you’ve asked them to do.
A video might not stand up in court, but it could persuade a sister or son, Ambrose said.
Ambrose also raised the idea of naming a backup person in case the first person isn’t available.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said a medical power of attorney does not take away your rights.
“It is not taking away your rights as long as you have capacity,” she said.
Where to get the paperwork
O’Rourke pointed to FiveWishes.org as a resource.
“Medical power of attorney is not that hard to get,” O’Rourke said. “There’s a lot available online, but FiveWishes.org is a wonderful site because it’s very expansive in the topics that they talk about.”
Ambrose said local charitable organizations may also offer essential documents. For more help, she said, an estate planning attorney can help put all essential documents in place.
Check your state’s rules, including when you travel
O’Rourke said a medical power of attorney does not need to be notarized in every state, but some states require it.
“Just go back and check your state rules and regulations to make sure that you’re following the protocol that your state set out,” she said.
Cradduck said people who are traveling should make sure that they have their bases covered. Do not assume a state that doesn’t require a notary has the same rules as the state you’re visiting.
Resource
Key takeaways
- Name a specific medical power of attorney. Standard powers of attorney don’t cover medical choices.
- Don’t count on your spouse being automatic. Spouses don’t automatically get to decide.
- Pick someone who knows your wishes. Choose a person who will honor them and not be torn by emotion in life-and-death decisions.
- Pick someone who can handle pressure. Don’t just choose your closest relative. Choose someone who can handle intense medical pressure and will fight for your wishes.
- Check your state’s rules and name a backup. Notary requirements vary by state, including where you travel. A backup person can step in if the first isn’t available.

title: LePage, Dunlap still duking it out in 2nd District Congressional race
text:
Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows announced Thursday morning that the close race for the 2nd District between Republican Paul LePage and Democrat Matt Dunlap will proceed to ranked choice tabulation, despite the fact that Dunlap has conceded.
Bellows said Maine’s 487 municipalities recorded 170,263 votes (49.894%) for LePage and 164,845 votes (48.307%) for Dunlap. Another 123 votes (0.036%) went to write-in candidates.
“Since no candidate received more than 50% of the total ballots cast, the ranked choice tabulation process will begin this Monday, Nov. 9, at 10 a.m., at the Maine Department of Public Safety Headquarters in Augusta,” Bellows said.
The process will be livestreamed on the Secretary of State’s YouTube page.
“The first step in the process will to be to verify the vote totals from every municipality to ensure accuracy,” said Bellows. “Once the election night totals are verified, assuming neither candidate received a majority of the votes, which is what we are observing now, we will proceed to the ranked choice voting tabulation.”
LePage declared victory on Wednesday, saying he led Dunlap by 4,000 votes.
“There are plenty of ballots left to count,” Dunlap said Wednesday. “Maine has the most reliable elections staff in the world, and I want to thank them as they diligently finish the count.”
Cities went to Dunlap
The largest municipalities in the 2nd District — Augusta, Bangor, Lewiston and Auburn — all went blue by healthy margins, according to the Associated Press. Dunlap also carried much of the midcoast.
LePage dominated largely in central and northern communities, including Skowhegan, Houlton, Millinocket, Caribou, Fort Kent and Presque Isle.
The 2nd District delivered for Donald Trump three times, but has been divided on its representatives. Democrat Jared Golden, who did not run for reelection, had held his Congressional seat since 2019.
Lewiston native
If 78-year-old LePage wins, he would be one of the oldest freshman congressmen ever elected — sharing that title with Illinois’ James B. Bowler, who served in the 1950s. He’d also be a Republican in a House controlled by the Democrats.
LePage was the governor of Maine from 2011-19 and mayor of Waterville from 2004-11. Before becoming governor, he worked as general manager of Marden’s Surplus and Salvage stores.
He was born and raised in Lewiston and has lived in Edgecomb and Boothbay. After leaving Blaine House in 2019, he moved to Florida, where he owns a home, and now maintains a registered voting address in Augusta.

title: Indiana carries out first of 3 US executions taking place on single day
text:
(AP) - An Indiana man who admitted killing his girlfriend’s two children was executed early Thursday in the first of three lethal injections scheduled for the same day in the U.S.
Jeffrey Weisheit killed the children, ages 8 and 5, by setting fire to his girlfriend’s house in the Evansville area in 2010.
Weisheit died at the Indiana State Prison in Michigan City. The lethal injection started just after midnight and he was pronounced dead at 12:45 a.m., according to Noelle Russell, Indiana Department of Correction chief communications officer.
She said Weisheit’s final meal was barbecue ribs and he had no final words.
Florida and Alabama were also set to carry out executions Thursday, which would mark the second time this year that three people in the U.S. would be put to death on the same day.
It will be Florida’s 19th execution this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis — matching a record set by the state in 2025 — but the first this year in Indiana.
The death penalty has faced renewed scrutiny following the September failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee, although courts have rejected efforts to halt other executions since she survived two lethal doses of pentobarbital.
Lawyers had asked for a life sentence for Weisheit
Lawyers wanted Indiana Republican Gov. Mike Braun to allow Weisheit, 50, to undergo brain scans in an effort to reinforce their argument that he has a history of head injuries and mental health problems. Braun declined, and he also turned down a request to reduce the sentence to life in prison.
Weisheit’s latest objection centered on the state’s planned use of lethal drugs purchased from a pharmacy that is facing a disciplinary hearing next week at the Indiana Pharmacy Board. The Indiana Department of Correction said that it’s confident “in our ability to humanely carry out” the execution.
Following the execution, Braun issued a brief statement noting Weisheit’s case was reviewed many times by state and federal courts.
“These reviews have never resulted in an overturned sentence,” he said. “Today, Weisheit’s sentence has been carried out as ordered by the court.”
Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said that the execution provided “long-awaited justice for Alyssa Lynch and her brother Caleb, two innocent children whose lives were stolen in an act of unspeakable cruelty.”
Florida on the verge of tying last year’s execution record
In Florida, Jesse Guardado confessed and quickly pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing a 75-year-old woman inside her Walton County home in 2004 before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other valuables to support his drug habit. She had helped him get a job and housing.
A federal appeals court in 2024 said that Guardado, now 64, had received a “full and fair” hearing during the death penalty phase of his case.
Florida has carried out more than half the 32 total executions in the U.S. so far this year. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said that his goal is to bring justice to families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out.
Alabama man convicted of killings when he was 19
Michael Taylor, 54, faces execution in Alabama, 35 years after fatally beating an older couple with a metal bar during a robbery in their Gadsden home. Police arrested the 19-year-old Taylor with the victims’ Cadillac, an hour away in Birmingham. The execution would be the state’s third this year.
Death penalty opponents had urged Republican Gov. Kay Ivey to reduce Taylor’s sentence to life in prison, noting his age and immaturity at the time of the killings. She declined.
“If the state kills Michael, it is not the 19-year-old who made the worst mistake of his life who it kills. But the mature, well-respected, God-fearing man sitting in that cell today,” said Esther Brown of Project Hope to Abolish the Death Penalty.
The state plans to execute Taylor by lethal injection after a judge declared a nitrogen gas method unconstitutional. His attorneys objected to the last-minute switch to lethal injection since he selected nitrogen gas as his method several years ago, but a judge ruled against Taylor.
____
Fischer reported from Fort Lauderdale, Florida and Chandler from Montgomery, Alabama. Associated Press reporter Ed White contributed from Detroit.

title: Madawaska Wins Class D North as County Soccer Regional Finals Conclude
text:
Madawaska Heads to States as Northern Maine Soccer Championships Wrap Up
The Northern Maine regional soccer championships are complete, and five Aroostook County teams are heading to Saturday's state championship games.
Madawaska's boys added their name to that list Wednesday afternoon, defeating Fort Fairfield 2-0 in the Class D North championship at Presque Isle High School.
It was the third consecutive year the Owls and Tigers met for the regional title, and this time Madawaska took control early with two first-half goals.
Meanwhile, Presque Isle's girls saw their Class B championship hopes end against John Bapst, while Fort Fairfield's girls battled Penobscot Valley in a close Class D final before the Lady Howlers pulled away in the second half.
Here's how Wednesday's three championship games played out.
Girls Soccer
Class B North: John Bapst Ends Presque Isle's Championship Run
(1) John Bapst 3, (3) Presque Isle 0
Presque Isle's girls came into Wednesday's Class B North championship looking to knock off top-seeded John Bapst and earn a trip to the state finals.
But the Crusaders brought the Lady Wildcats' tournament run to an end with a 3-0 victory at Hampden Academy.
Presque Isle had put together an impressive postseason to reach the championship game.
The third-seeded Lady Wildcats defeated Skowhegan 3-1 in the quarterfinals before rolling past seventh-seeded Cony 4-0 in Saturday's semifinals.
Hailey Plant, Carrlyn Buck, Bridgid Schupbach and Willow Bugbee each scored in that semifinal victory, showing the offensive balance that helped Presque Isle reach the regional final.
Wednesday brought a tougher challenge against a John Bapst team that entered the game undefeated.
The Crusaders came away with the shutout and the Class B North championship, advancing to Saturday's state final.
For Presque Isle, the loss brings an end to a strong fall season that included a run to the Northern Maine championship game.
Class D North: Penobscot Valley Wins Fifth Straight Regional Championship
(1) Penobscot Valley 2, (2) Fort Fairfield 0
For the first 40 minutes Wednesday evening, there wasn't much separating Fort Fairfield and Penobscot Valley.
The top two seeds in Class D North battled through a scoreless first half at Presque Isle High School, with both teams making it difficult for the other to generate scoring opportunities.
But the Lady Howlers found the breakthrough in the 49th minute.
Charlotte Brochu scored to give Penobscot Valley a 1-0 lead, putting Fort Fairfield in a position where the Tigers needed to find an equalizer.
The game remained close until the 73rd minute, when McKenna Ireland added an insurance goal to make it 2-0.
Goalkeeper Brooklyn Raymond recorded another shutout for Penobscot Valley, securing the victory and the program's fifth consecutive Class D North regional championship.
Fort Fairfield entered Wednesday after consecutive tournament shutouts, defeating Washburn 4-0 in the quarterfinals and Central Aroostook 1-0 in the semifinals.
The Tigers had earned their place in the regional final with strong defensive performances of their own.
Although Wednesday's result didn't go their way, reaching the Class D North championship capped another successful postseason for Fort Fairfield.
For Penobscot Valley, the victory means another opportunity to compete for a state championship after five straight regional titles.
Boys Soccer
Class D North: Madawaska Scores Twice in First Half to Claim Regional Championship
(1) Madawaska 2, (3) Fort Fairfield 0
For the third consecutive season, Madawaska and Fort Fairfield met with the Class D North boys championship on the line.
And Wednesday afternoon, the top-seeded Owls made sure they would be the ones heading to states.
Madawaska scored twice in the opening 25 minutes and held Fort Fairfield scoreless the rest of the way, earning a 2-0 victory at Presque Isle High School.
Aiden Gagnon opened the scoring in the 13th minute, giving the Owls an early 1-0 advantage.
Just 12 minutes later, Josh Querze added another goal in the 25th minute to double Madawaska's lead.
Those two first-half goals would be all the Owls needed.
Goalkeeper Aleck Gendreau recorded the shutout, helping Madawaska secure the regional championship and a place in Saturday's Class D state final.
It was another strong postseason performance for the Owls, who reached Wednesday's championship after shutting out Hodgdon 2-0 in the semifinals.
Fort Fairfield had also earned its way into the final with a strong tournament run, including a 3-1 semifinal victory over second-seeded Central Aroostook.
But Madawaska's early scoring and defensive effort proved to be the difference Wednesday.
The Owls will now travel to Messalonskee High School on Saturday to face Class D South champion Monmouth.
The top-seeded Mustangs advanced with an 8-0 victory over Narraguagus in the Southern Maine regional championship.
That sets up a state championship matchup between two regional champions, with Madawaska looking to finish its season with one more victory.

title: Trump’s lawyers to appear before appeals court as he fights hush money conviction
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump’s lawyers will try to persuade a New York appeals court Thursday to throw out his hush money conviction, two years after it made history.
The conviction, on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to obscure a $130,000 payment to adult film performer Stormy Daniels, continues to nettle Trump enough that he denounced it on social media as recently as September. The president denies any wrongdoing, and he has turned to state and federal courts in hopes of unwinding the verdict.
He is not expected to attend Thursday’s court session.
The appeal turns on complex legal disputes, but political overtones aren’t hard to find. The very first paragraph of one of the Trump team’s court filings contends the case was the flimsy product of “immense political pressure” on a Democratic prosecutor to go after Trump — rhetoric that echoes the Republican president’s own oft-repeated claims in the court of public opinion.
In court papers, Trump’s attorneys have assailed prosecutors’ legal theory as “a house of cards” built on a shaky combination of alleged state and federal offenses, with “clearly insufficient” evidence and problematic jury instructions.
The appeal also concerns whether jurors should have been allowed to hear testimony about supposed White House conversations, workflow and even Trump social media posts during his first term. His lawyers cite presidential immunity for official acts, and they argue his official conduct included responding to the Daniels drama once it became public in 2018.
“When a president addresses the nation to defend himself from allegations of personal misconduct (as all presidents do), or discusses such communications with his aides, he is carrying out his constitutional duties and is protected by immunity,” lawyer Robert Giuffra Jr. wrote in a filing this October.
Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s office counters that the legal theory and jury instructions were legitimate and that the White House-related evidence was fair game. Some was public record, some was a general description of office practices, and the conversations were “unofficial conduct,” prosecutors say.
“A president’s discussions about a purely private matter, even with a White House advisor, do not constitute ‘official acts for which the president is immune,’” Bragg’s appeals chief, Steven Wu, wrote in a filing in July. Besides, he said, there was “a mountain” of other evidence against Trump.
The May 2024 verdict made Trump the first former — and now current — U.S. president with a criminal conviction. While historic, it didn’t impede his return to the White House or subject him to any punishment.
The trial involved $130,000 that Daniels got from Trump’s then-fixer and lawyer, Michael Cohen, weeks before the 2016 election. The money bought, for a time, her silence about an alleged sexual encounter with the married Trump a decade earlier. He says that nothing sexual happened between them.
Trump’s company reimbursed Cohen in 2017, logging those payments as legal expenses.
Saying the transactions all were meant to keep unflattering information about Trump away from the electorate, prosecutors argue that he “orchestrated a conspiracy” that violated federal campaign finance laws, among others.
Trump’s lawyers argue there’s only “weak” evidence that he even knew about Cohen’s dealings at the time. His trial attorneys also said that payments to Cohen were indeed legal expenses, and that any hush money expended on Trump’s behalf wasn’t hidden campaign spending, just an effort to avoid embarrassing his family.
The distinction matters because, under New York law, falsifying business records isn’t a felony unless it’s done with an intent to commit or conceal a separate crime.
While pursuing his state appeal, Trump also has been trying to shift the case to federal court and have it dismissed on immunity grounds. A federal judge said no — for the third time — in August. Trump’s attorneys are appealing that decision, and arguments on that appeal are set for Nov. 16.

title: Toy Hall of Fame: Pokémon cards, Bingo, Care Bears and the classic playground slide added
text:
Toy Hall of Fame inductees: Pokémon cards, Bingo, Care Bears and the classic playground slide added
Bingo, Care Bears, the Pokémon Trading Card Game and the humble playground slide have all made it into the National Toy Hall of Fame, taking their place alongside classics like Mr. Potato Head and G.I. Joe.
Related video above: Pokémon 30th anniversary: When it stopped being just a game
The winners emerged Thursday from a field of 12 finalists that included Bop It!, mahjong, Monster High dolls, Polly Pocket, Tickle Me Elmo, Yahtzee and the board games Sorry! and Mouse Trap.
Experts at The Strong National Museum of Play, home to the National Toy Hall of Fame, note that bingo, which "descends from an Italian lottery played around 1530," is now played virtually worldwide.
"While bingo is now often associated with an older audience, it has become increasingly popular with young adults. Recently, public bingo games have gone beyond fundraising and have become popular in bars and nightclubs," curator Mirek Stolee said in a statement.
The effort to get the Care Bears into the Hall was helped by earning nearly 1 million followers on social media, while Pokémon trading cards were buoyed by anime enthusiasts and manga readers.
The Hall said the slide helps children develop motor skills and encourages exploration. "People of all ages remember fondly the simple, satisfying, and energizing experience of racing down a slide," said Jeremy Saucier, vice president for collections.
While anyone can nominate a toy, the ones that make it into the Hall must be considered icons, have engaged multiple generations, fostered creativity, or profoundly changed play or toy design.
The four 2026 winners will join the 90 toys already enshrined in the National Toy Hall of Fame, a list that includes Cabbage Patch Kids, Dungeons & Dragons, Hot Wheels and Frisbee.

title: Wife shares husband's final moments before his death in Florida flooding
text:
Wife shares husband's final moments before his death in Florida flooding
Flooding in Brevard County, Fla., claimed the lives of 34-year-old Joshua Bennett and 78-year-old Archie Richards during Monday's storm.
A Silver Alert was issued on Monday for Richards after he was reported missing. The Brevard County Sheriff's Office said Richards was found dead inside his vehicle on Richards Lane and Hall Road on Tuesday.  
Palm Bay police said Joshua Bennett died when rising river water trapped his car on San Filippo Drive, submerging it with him inside.
Palm Bay Mayor Rob Medina announced the deaths Tuesday.
Quick trip ended in tragedy
For Joshua Bennett's family, Monday morning started like any other, but a quick trip to get coffee ended in tragedy.
His wife, Stacy Petit Bennett, said he called her on FaceTime, terrified, after floodwaters surrounded his truck on San Filippo Drive.
"He called me on FaceTime, and he was just crying like, 'I don't know what to do, I don't know what to do.' And he said he's in the middle of a river, and his car is, like, submerged with water all around," she said.
She said she urged him to break a window and get out, but then the call dropped. Stacy Petit Bennett called 911 and spent hours trying to get help for her husband.
Joshua Bennett was 34 years old, a husband, a father of four, and the center of his family's world.
"Joshua was an amazing husband and dad. He has a son and three daughters. He was super obsessed with them. He loved to do activities with them," Stacy Petit Bennett said.
She said they met in college while she was studying bio pre-med.
"We got married in 2020, and we ended up having kids. Twins. I had twin girls. They were born super early. They were preemies," Stacy Petit Bennett said. "They were born at 25 weeks, one-pounders. And they spent about three months in McHugh. And that was one of the main reasons I ended up becoming a stay-at-home mom."
She recalled their Sunday family traditions, including trips to indoor playgrounds, gymnastics and horseback riding. Stacy said Joshua Bennett also loved baking with his daughters and taking them out on his personal watercraft.
Now, she said, their children are left asking when their father is coming home.
"I was a stay-at-home mom, and we have three kids with special needs, so now we're essentially starting from scratch. He's not here. I don't have my support system. They don't have their father," Stacy Petit Bennett said.
She said her family is also trying to bring Joshua Bennett home to New Hampshire.
As they grapple with an unimaginable loss, she wants people to remember that his life — and every life — matters.
"Every life is important, and everyone deserves a chance to be rescued. To be saved. He was just 34 years old. His kids are young," Stacy Petit Bennett said.
The family has organized a GoFundMe to help support Joshua Bennett's wife and kids as they navigate the heartbreaking loss and flood damage. Anyone interested in donating can do so here.
