title: Expecting a new grandchild? Here’s why you may want to see your doctor before their birth
text:
Grandparents urged to get measles, flu, and other shots before meeting a newborn in the U.S.
When a baby is on the way, doctors often recommend that the mother get certain vaccinations to protect her newborn – and it turns out that other family members who may visit the infant, especially grandparents, are urged to be up to date on certain shots, too.
Related video above: CDC director urges Mass. families to rely on local health data as viruses circulate
With the United States in the midst of respiratory virus season and its worst measles outbreak in decades, immunized family members can play an important role in protecting newborns who are too young to receive many of their own vaccines. Babies remain especially vulnerable during their first weeks of life, relying largely on antibodies passed from their mother and the immunity of those around them.
“For that six months, zero to six months, they are really vulnerable and at risk, and we have to protect them,” said Dr. Dhaval Desai, a dual board-certified internal medicine and pediatrics physician at The Atlanta Internists.
Anyone who is around a newborn should be up to date on all routine vaccines, especially the whooping cough vaccine, known as tetanus, diphtheria and pertussis, or Tdap; and the seasonal flu vaccine, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Many doctors recommend some additional vaccinations too – and they emphasize that these vaccines are important for grandparents of children at any age. Mothers are given a lot of advice about vaccinations during pregnancy and in their baby’s first year, but grandparents may not have those same kind of check-ins with their doctors.
“This is a great time to make sure all vaccines are up to date,” Dr. Lori Solomon, associate professor and chair of family and community medicine at New York Medical College, said in an email.
Before meeting a new grandchild, ask your healthcare provider whether you’re up to date on these vaccines:
“Being up to date on all their vaccines is beneficial to grandparents for multiple reasons: First, it helps grandparents to keep themselves healthy and so that they don’t miss out on this special time with their new grandchild. Second, being vaccinated helps protect their new grandchild, especially in those early months when babies’ immune systems are still developing and they rely on all of us around them to be vaccinated to help keep infectious diseases away,” Dr. Michael Warren, chief medical and health officer at the maternal and infant health nonprofit March of Dimes, said in an email.
“New grandparents, or grandparents-to-be, should talk with their healthcare professional to find out whether they are up to date on all their vaccines or if they might need additional vaccines,” he said. “Ideally, grandparents should be up to date on all their vaccines before the baby arrives. And we know that babies don’t always arrive according to schedule, so getting a head start and getting vaccinated before the baby is due is a smart strategy.”
Vaccines for grandparents and other caretakers
Tdap
The Tdap vaccine can help prevent tetanus, diphtheria and pertussis.
“Pertussis is whooping cough,” Desai said. “It is a debilitating cough disease. We see babies stop breathing. It is a very frightening thing. Most recover from it, but it is something we want to prevent. So Tdap would be one of my non-negotiables for a new grandparent.”
For babies and young children especially, whooping cough is much more than just a bad cough; it can be incredibly dangerous. It triggers violent, uncontrollable coughing fits that make it hard to even catch a breath. Beyond that, severe infection can lead to complications like pneumonia, convulsions, permanent brain damage or death.
The Tdap vaccine is given as a single dose, and a booster is recommended for adults every 10 years.
Seasonal flu
Despite remaining low at the national level, seasonal flu activity is increasing in many parts of the country, and the CDC warns that early-season activity is higher than usual for this time of year.
Many people may think of the flu as just having cold-like symptoms, but for babies and toddlers, it can be especially dangerous. Because their immune systems are still developing, influenza can hit them hard and fast and can quickly spiral into serious complications including pneumonia, extreme dehydration, brain inflammation or death.
In general, everyone 6 months and older is urged to get an annual flu shot.
Protection provided by the vaccine lasts about six months in older adults, “so the recommendation is to get it in September or early October for protection during the typical winter flu season,” Texas-based pediatrician Dr. Ari Brown, a spokesperson for the American Academy of Pediatrics and author of the book “Baby 411,” said in an email.
“You can plan ahead depending on when the grandbaby is born and when you will be visiting with them.”
RSV
RSV is another common respiratory virus that can cause serious illness for babies and young children. Because their airways are so small, this virus can easily clog them with thick mucus, making it difficult to breathe. RSV was the leading cause of hospitalization among infants in the US before the introduction of RSV immunizations.
For older adults, a single dose of RSV vaccine is typically recommended.
“Talk to your doctor about the RSV vaccine, as it is given at age 50 to people with certain conditions like asthma, heart disease and insulin-dependent diabetes,” Solomon said. “For healthy adults the RSV vaccine is given at 75 or older.”
COVID-19
A single dose of the updated COVID-19 vaccine is recommended for all adults.
COVID-19 vaccination continues to be associated with a reduced risk of hospitalization, including among people at high risk of severe disease, such as older adults and infants. And getting vaccinated can help reduce the risk of spreading the virus to vulnerable family members like newborns.
A COVID-19 shot this season “protects you and lowers the chance” you’ll bring the virus home to loved ones, Dr. Celine Gounder, an infectious disease specialist at NYU Langone Health and editor-at-large for public health at KFF Health News, said in an email.
“The scariest thing a parent can get is a positive COVID test in a baby because you can’t do anything except supportive care,” Desai said. Infants are not old enough for treatment such as with the prescription medication Paxlovid.
“If I am a new grandparent and going to be watching a two-month-old once the parents go back to work, I want to be maximally protected against the routine viruses that are out there and protect my grandchild who cannot get the shot,” he said. “So, for a new grandparent, I think it’s very reasonable to get the COVID booster at this point.”
Measles, mumps, rubella
Unusually high numbers of measles cases have been reported in the United States this year, raising the risk of infections emerging in newborns.
Nationwide, more than 4,500 confirmed cases of measles have been reported to the CDC, and an ongoing outbreak in Pennsylvania has quickly become the largest and deadliest in the country in more than 30 years. Infants are among those who died this year.
But two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella or MMR, vaccine provide about 97% protection against measles.
“If you’re unsure about your measles immunity, there’s no harm in getting another shot of MMR,” Gounder said.
Measles immunity sometimes can be checked with a blood test or by reviewing your vaccine records. But “we don’t usually recommend checking antibody levels,” she said.
If you were born before 1957, “the CDC counts you as immune because most people caught measles as children back then,” Gounder said. “Born in 1957 or later, with no record of a dose: Get at least one dose.”
If you have only one documented dose in your medical history, “get a second if your local health department advises it,” she said. For example, adults who’d gotten one dose were recommended to get a second during a measles outbreak in Texas last year. “If you have one dose and help care for the baby in an outbreak area, I recommend a second.”
Measles is one of the most contagious diseases in the world. Viral particles can spread through the air and remain infectious for up to two hours, even after an infected person leaves the area. And infants and young children are at higher risk of complications and severe disease.
“Here’s the motto I’m telling patients: if you don’t know if you’ve had measles if you’re older, or if you don’t know you’ve had the shot, there is no harm in getting one MMR booster,” Desai said. “That’s safe. It gives you the immunity, and it’s very appropriate.”
When to get vaccinated
It’s important to be fully vaccinated before visiting a newborn at the hospital or at home. “Ideally, it’s best to vaccinate at least 30 days before the due date,” Solomon said.
Most of the vaccines recommended for grandparents can be given at the same time, Gounder said.
“You can get most of them on the same day, in different arms. The only hard rule is for live injected vaccines: if MMR and varicella vaccines aren’t given the same day, they must be at least 28 days apart,” Gounder said, adding that it’s important to remember that you may need more than one dose for some vaccines.
Most of the vaccines take about two weeks to mount an immune response.
Getting vaccinated “four to six weeks before the baby is born is a safe window. For most vaccines, within two weeks you start getting the antibodies,” Desai said.
“Four to six weeks will give plenty of time, especially if you’re getting multiple shots, maybe you can space them out. The Tdap and the flu you can space out a little bit, so it gives you enough time,” he said. “I would say for those that have expectant daughters or daughters-in-law, then that third trimester of pregnancy is when you really want to proactively plan.”
‘Kiss the toes, not the nose’
Along with vaccination, there are other steps grandparents can take to help keep a newborn safe: “Stay away when you’re sick, wash your hands before you hold the baby, and don’t kiss the baby’s face,” especially during respiratory virus season, Gounder said.
Desai added that he often tells grandparents: “Kiss the toes, not the nose.”
There are some other vaccines that grandparents may want to consider, too, for the sake of their own health.
- The shingles vaccine is recommended for adults 50 and older. Vaccination is more than 90% effective at preventing shingles and certain complications in older adults with healthy immune systems. It is given as two doses. “The second shingles dose comes two to six months after the first,” Gounder said.
- The pneumococcal vaccine is also recommended for adults 50 and older. In adults, it’s typically given as a single shot, but in some cases, additional vaccination may be recommended. The vaccine helps protect against pneumococcal infections, such as pneumonia and meningitis.
“If you want to be readily available for your grandchild, not get sick and not put them at risk, then follow the age-appropriate adult vaccine guidelines,” Desai said.

title: Who speaks for you? Choosing a medical power of attorney
text:
(Aging Untold) — Staying in control as you age can mean choosing someone you trust to make health care decisions if you can’t. The key is picking a person who knows your wishes and will keep them front and center.
The Aging Untold experts are talking about what a medical power of attorney covers, how to set one up and why you should have the document with you.
What a medical power of attorney can decide
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the person you name holds a wide range of decision-making power.
“They can decide whether you’re going to have surgery,” Cradduck said. “They can decide whether or not you’re going to go into a skilled facility in a rehab after a surgery. They can decide if you’re going to go into an assisted living. They can decide if you’re going to be at home, who your caregivers are going to be.”
The person you choose needs to be someone who can set their emotions aside, she said.
“You need to make sure that this person knows you, knows your wishes, will honor your wishes, and that they’re not going to be torn by emotion if it comes down to life and death decisions,” Cradduck said. “You need to know that this person can advocate for your wishes, not for their heart’s desire.”
A medical power of attorney is a document that goes by several names, including health care surrogate, health care power of attorney and health care proxy, and those names all refer to the same thing, aging expert Amy O’Rourke said.
Why being married is not enough
Married couples should not assume a spouse can make decisions for the other, O’Rourke cautioned.
“Don’t just think because you have a family relationship that you’re going to have the power to make these decisions,” she said.
O’Rourke said a spouse who goes to the hospital without a medical power of attorney could be turned away, depending on state rules and laws.
Keep the paperwork where it can be found
Another thing Cradduck said to keep in mind is that having the physical document matters.
A hospital does not have to honor a person who says they have power of attorney without the paper, she said.
In a car accident, “That doctor can be the one making the decisions and he doesn’t know what your wishes are,” Cradduck said.
Copies of the document should be easy to grab, people involved should have duplicates and know how to produce them.
“This needs to be something that a paramedic can find. Might be on your fridge,” aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said. “It is not something to have locked away in a safe deposit box. It needs to be with you.”
Choose someone with integrity and backbone
Cradduck compared the choice of medical power of attorney to picking a designated driver.
“This is literally picking out your designated driver before you go to the party,” she said.
Ambrose said the person you choose needs to be able to stand up to others.
“Even long lost relatives will show up during a medical crisis and try to say what they think their brother would want,” Ambrose said.
You can help that person by communicating your wishes to others, she said. You could also record a video of what you’ve asked them to do.
A video might not stand up in court, but it could persuade a sister or son, Ambrose said.
Ambrose also raised the idea of naming a backup person in case the first person isn’t available.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said a medical power of attorney does not take away your rights.
“It is not taking away your rights as long as you have capacity,” she said.
Where to get the paperwork
O’Rourke pointed to FiveWishes.org as a resource.
“Medical power of attorney is not that hard to get,” O’Rourke said. “There’s a lot available online, but FiveWishes.org is a wonderful site because it’s very expansive in the topics that they talk about.”
Ambrose said local charitable organizations may also offer essential documents. For more help, she said, an estate planning attorney can help put all essential documents in place.
Check your state’s rules, including when you travel
O’Rourke said a medical power of attorney does not need to be notarized in every state, but some states require it.
“Just go back and check your state rules and regulations to make sure that you’re following the protocol that your state set out,” she said.
Cradduck said people who are traveling should make sure that they have their bases covered. Do not assume a state that doesn’t require a notary has the same rules as the state you’re visiting.
Resource
Key takeaways
- Name a specific medical power of attorney. Standard powers of attorney don’t cover medical choices.
- Don’t count on your spouse being automatic. Spouses don’t automatically get to decide.
- Pick someone who knows your wishes. Choose a person who will honor them and not be torn by emotion in life-and-death decisions.
- Pick someone who can handle pressure. Don’t just choose your closest relative. Choose someone who can handle intense medical pressure and will fight for your wishes.
- Check your state’s rules and name a backup. Notary requirements vary by state, including where you travel. A backup person can step in if the first isn’t available.

title: What’s next for a Democratic Congress: Oversight. Maybe impeachment.
text:
What’s next for a Democratic Congress: Oversight. Maybe impeachment.
In the 1972 movie “The Candidate,” the politician played by actor Robert Redford wins his Senate election and then pulls his campaign aide aside, asking, “What do we do now?” Famously, the movie ends and he never gets an answer.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
That’s unlikely to be the case for the incoming Democratic majorities in the House and Senate after the party’s tectonic victories Nov. 3. Where the new majorities can find common ground on legislation with President Donald Trump remains to be seen. But under the constitutional order, the new Democratic congressional majority doesn’t need Trump’s permission to conduct oversight of the executive branch.
“Oversight can be a powerful tool, because Congress has subpoena power and the ability to use public hearings to put a spotlight on malfeasance or misconduct in the executive branch,” said Matthew Green, a Catholic University of America political scientist. “Even if the White House tries to stonewall Congress, the House and Senate can force White House allies to testify, such as heads of major corporations or law firms.”
What is congressional oversight?
According to Congress’ own Congressional Oversight Manual, lawmakers have the authority to ensure the executive branch complies with laws; improve government efficiency and effectiveness; and “investigate alleged instances of poor administration, arbitrary and capricious behavior, abuse, waste, dishonesty and fraud.”
This power has limits — especially during a period of divided government, like the one that will begin in January 2027. Congress would have little power to push the Justice Department to prosecute alleged malfeasance, and executive branch officials can stonewall lawmakers’ inquiries.
“Trump has a demonstrated track record of completely refusing to cooperate with any oversight requests,” said Frank O. Bowman III, a University of Missouri emeritus law professor and author of the forthcoming book, “Great and Dangerous Offenses: The Case for (and Against) Impeaching Trump a Third Time.” “He has resisted hundreds of ordinary oversight inquiries. This makes it less effective for discovering facts.”
Under Trump, the Office of Legal Counsel, a Justice Department division that issues influential opinions on constitutional matters, has issued one that argues for an expansive view of executive privilege, the legal doctrine that protects White House deliberations from being subpoenaed. The opinion said executive privilege can cover outside parties the president consults with, said Stanley Brand, a longtime Washington, D.C., attorney who serves as distinguished fellow at Penn State Dickinson Law.
Protracted battles over subpoena compliance are “very likely,” Brand said. “Committees will have to use informal means as well as subpoenas to elicit information from lower-level bureaucrats and willing outside sources to gain traction with their inquiries.”
Despite these shortcomings, using its oversight authority allows Congress to publicly flex its accountability muscles.
“The House can do a lot by securing testimony and documents from those not subject to Trump’s control, including former officials, officials who — like multiple witnesses in the first Trump impeachment — choose to defy Trump’s efforts to prevent them from testifying,” Bowman said. “It could also include people and companies outside the administration and the Trump family orbit.”
Some of the most important issues for voters, including tariffs, war powers and corruption, are “fertile ground for investigation,” said James Robenalt, a lawyer and historian of the Watergate scandal.
Oversight pressure could also prod lawmakers towards progress enacting legislation, said Steven Smith, an Arizona State University political scientist.
“On many issues, legislators can develop legislative approaches informed by oversight activities,” Smith said.
Democrats will need to decide on impeachment
Trump has already survived two impeachments, because of a combination of Republican senators’ loyalty and the requirement that two-thirds of the chamber vote for removal from office.
Republicans have warned that Democrats will follow their staunchest supporters’ desires by quickly impeaching Trump. But with a history of failed impeachments galvanizing the president’s supporters, some Democrats have expressed caution about impeaching Trump again.
“We’re not afraid to impeach him,” Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is in line to chair the House Judiciary Committee, told CNN the day after the election. “It’s a tool in the constitutional toolkit, but we understand it’s not a panacea.”
Raskin chalked up the talk of a new impeachment to Republican wishful thinking. “They would love us to impeach them,” he said. “That would solve a huge political problem for them.”
Scholars agreed that Democrats will need to balance the legal justification for an impeachment with the political consequences of launching one.
Bowman said he would not recommend prioritizing impeachment, because of the “vanishingly improbable” chance of a Senate conviction.
Experts said another avenue could be more fruitful for the new Democratic majority: impeaching Cabinet members.
There is precedent for this. Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached in 1876, and Homeland Security Secretary Alexander Mayorkas was impeached in 2024. Neither was convicted.
While the bar for a conviction would be high, an ouster might not be impossible for such Cabinet members as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth or Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Green said. An outgoing Republican House member, Tom Massie of Kentucky, has already begun the process of impeaching Hegseth.
Hearings “could build broader public support for impeachment and, ideally from the Democrats’ perspective, might pressure those Cabinet officials to resign before the Senate is forced to have a trial.”
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

title: Bicyclist Injured in Damariscotta Hit-and-Run
text:
A 65-year-old female bicyclist was seriously injured when a motor vehicle struck her at the intersection of Main Street and Biscay Road in Damariscotta on the morning of Wednesday, Nov. 4.
According to a Facebook post from Damariscotta Police Department, a 911 call was made to the Lincoln County Communications Center at approximately 5:26 a.m. advising that a woman on a bicycle had been struck by a vehicle and the vehicle had left the scene.
When emergency responders arrived on scene, the vehicle and the operator were not present, according to the department’s post. The woman was transported by Central Lincoln County Ambulance Service to MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital for treatment.

title: UMaine offers buyouts to roughly 20% of faculty amid budget deficit
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The University of Maine is offering voluntary early retirement packages to 158, or roughly 20%, of its faculty members as it attempts to close a $19 million budget gap.
Faculty are eligible if they are at least 55 years old and have 10 years of service to the school. The offer applies to faculty at both the flagship campus in Orono and the university’s regional campus in Machias. Those who accept it will receive a one-time payment equivalent to the value of their annual salary.
The school announced in September that it would lay off faculty and staff to make up for its budget deficit, which has been driven by declining enrollment, rising operating costs and stagnant state funding.
In a letter Thursday, President Joan Ferrini-Mundy and the university’s provost and president of human resources said they won’t know how many faculty will take the offer until the Jan. 2 deadline for accepting the buyout. At that point, the administrators will be able to determine how much of the budget gap they have closed. Eligible faculty were notified on Tuesday.
As of last October, the university had 810 faculty members, plus 32 at the Machias campus, according to system employee data.
The university previously committed to cutting the academic affairs budget by $10 million, and announced an additional $6 million in cuts last month, including staff layoffs and the elimination of vacant positions from athletics, student life and the president’s office.
Thursday’s announcement provides the first look at which faculty members might leave the university as it attempts to cut spending.
“Participation is entirely voluntary and a deeply personal decision, and no faculty member will be treated differently because of the choice they make,” the letter reads.
The University of Maine System, of which UMaine is the flagship school, has committed to fund up to $6 million of the one-time payout costs, although a portion of that will also support early retirement incentives at the University of Maine at Farmington.
Last week, a coalition of unions for faculty, staff and graduate workers at the university hosted an emergency town hall to question the budget cuts and warn about the impact they would have on the student experience.
Faculty Senate President Brian McGill noted that UMaine had already lost many faculty members through previous retirement incentives.
“What are the students going to have left when that’s done?” McGill said.

title: California USPS employee faces federal charges for obstructing delivery of campaign mail
text:
California USPS employee faces federal charges for obstructing delivery of campaign mail
Federal charges have been filed against a California United States Postal Service employee accused of delaying and obstructing the delivery of political campaign mail, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of California.
Antoine Rashad Polite, 35, was employed as a letter carrier for the USPS in Sacramento County and was responsible for the delivery of mail along a specific route, the U.S. Attorney's Office said.
According to court documents, Polite improperly withheld and delayed the delivery of hundreds of pieces of political mail intended for residents on his route between Sept. 23 and Oct. 27. This included campaign materials relating to candidates and ballot propositions appearing on the Nov. 3 midterm election ballot.
When postal management discovered approximately 493 pieces of political mail placed in an area designated for undeliverable bulk business mail, an investigation began, officials said. Those pieces of mail were supposed to go to deliverable addresses on Polite's route.
An additional 527 pieces of political mail were found in "undeliverable mail" containers inside Polite's postal vehicle, the U.S. Attorney's Office said. Many of the pieces of mail were reportedly labeled as vacant or undeliverable and had the addresses marked through despite postal officials determining the addresses were valid and deliverable.
The U.S. Attorney's Office said postal officials recovered and delivered the vast majority of the mail to the intended recipients.
Polite is facing a maximum penalty of six months in prison for obstruction of mail and one year in prison for the delay or destruction of mail.

title: Texas' new attorney general composed music for nearly 70 'Dragon Ball Z' episodes
text:
Texas' newly elected attorney general composed music for nearly 70 'Dragon Ball Z' episodes
Before Texas state Sen. Nathan Johnson won the race for Texas attorney general and became the first Democrat to hold the office in more than two decades, he composed music for “Dragon Ball Z” episodes and movies.
Johnson said in a June interview that he had written musical scores for numerous episodes of the show.
Johnson, a Dallas Democrat, serves as a Texas state senator. On Tuesday, he beat Republican state Sen. Mayes Middleton in the race for state attorney general.
What did he do before becoming a Texas senator?
In the 2000s, before entering politics, Johnson worked as a composer for “Dragon Ball Z,” writing musical scores for the anime series and movies, he said in an interview with Texas state Sen. Taylor Rehmet that was posted to Facebook in June.
“If you grew up watching Dragon Ball Z, you might know me better than you think,” Johnson wrote in the post. “I composed the musical scores for 67 episodes and five movies, and had a great time doing it.”
Johnson’s IMDb profile shows that he worked on “Dragon Ball Z: Fusion Reborn” (1995), “Dragon Ball Z: Wrath of the Dragon” (1995) and “Dragon Ball Z: Broly – Second Coming” (1994). He also worked as a voice actor in 2012 and 2013 for “Berserk: The Golden Age Arc I” and “Berserk: The Golden Age Arc III.”
Johnson practiced business law and bankruptcy law before running for the state Senate seat he has now held for three terms, according to Entertainment Weekly.

title: 17-year-old accused of killing pregnant mother, unborn baby in Spirit Halloween shooting
text:
(Gray News) - A 17-year-old is accused of killing a pregnant mother and injuring six others inside a Spirit Halloween store in California, prosecutors announced.
The Solano County District Attorney’s Office charged the 17-year-old with two counts of murder, three counts of attempted murder, three counts of assault with a semiautomatic firearm and several weapons enhancements, a press release said.
Prosecutors are requesting that the teen be tried as an adult.
The Oct. 30 shooting killed 31-year-old Constance Hages, a mother of four, and her unborn child.
Six other victims were injured during the attack.
Police reported that as of Monday, four individuals remained hospitalized, including a 19-year-old man listed in critical condition.
Three others, ages 16, 23 and 32, are in stable condition, while two additional victims, ages 19 and 43, were treated and released.
“This heartbreaking loss has left behind four children, grieving parents, and a family trying to face a pain that words can barely hold,” Hages’ family wrote on a GoFundMe page organized for funeral expenses and support for her children.

title: Citibank office shooter targeted company over a $2,500 debt collection, Florida sheriff says
text:
TAMPA, Fla. (AP) — A gunman who killed a woman before being fatally shot by a security guard at Citibank’s sprawling office complex in Tampa, Florida, targeted the campus because he was angry over a $2,500 debt collection, a sheriff said Thursday.
About three hours before Wednesday’s shooting, 35-year-old Jacob Pearson called an attorney affiliated with Citibank and threatened violence if a court hearing over the debt wasn’t canceled, Hillsborough County Sheriff Chad Chronister told a news conference.
Pearson drove from his home in Orlando to Tampa, about 90 miles (144 kilometers) away, crashed his car through a fence at Citibank’s campus and plowed into a courtyard where employees were eating lunch, Chronister said.
The sheriff said Pearson got out of his car with a rifle and shot the first employee he saw. An executive who is part of Citibank’s armed security time shot the gunman five times before he could hurt anyone else. Pearson was pronounced dead at a hospital.

title: Volunteers step up to honor fallen veterans
text:
WRITTEN BY JEN LYNDS
One of the most formative high school field trips Kathryn Fitzpatrick took during her senior year was to the local cemetery. It was a short undertaking, but one she plans to repeat in the future.
For U.S. Air Force MSgt. Larry Harrison, it is a journey he has taken countless times before and one he never plans to cease.
The rural towns of Aroostook are dotted with small, historic cemeteries that contain the graves of veterans. Each year, volunteers from veterans’ organizations, civic groups, scouting organizations, schools, and community service clubs place flags and wreaths in preparation for Memorial Day, Veterans Day, and National Wreaths Across America Day. Despite the generational gap, both Fitzpatrick and Harrison aimed to commemorate those who sacrificed.
This act of reverence was familiar to Harrison, who retired after a 20-year career in the United States Air Force. He spent his last 16 years at the former Loring Air Force Base. Harrison led the Honor Guard, which participated in military funerals, parades, and other ceremonies across northern Maine and New Brunswick.
“We performed more than 100 funerals,” he said. “I knew that when I retired from the military, I would keep honoring veterans the way that I had in the military. I wanted to keep doing that whenever I could.”
Harrison has been a member of the American Legion for 36 years and a scoutmaster for Washburn Boy Scout Troop 177 for 49 years. He has also been a member of the Washburn Rotary Club for 47 years.
“The American Legion post in Washburn used to place flags on veterans’ graves in Washburn, Perham, and Wade, and I was a part of that,” he said. “To me, patriotism is part of who I am. You can never forget the sacrifices of those who came before you. It is so important to get down and place that flag.”
The Rotary Club now maintains the graves of the 40 veterans.
To Harrison, cleaning gravesites and planting the flags in remembrance of a veteran is always an emotional experience.
“Most affecting to me are the veterans who died young. Those who really did not get a chance to live,” he said. “Each year, it hits you differently.”
One grave also affects him personally.
“There is one gentleman that I knew from the military, and he was involved in scouting, too,” he noted. “Each year I place his flag, I put my hand on his headstone, and I make sure to leave a flag there and tell him that I miss him. I thank him for everything that he did.”
Back in Houlton, Fitzpatrick recalled meeting her peers in the Jobs for Maine Graduates (JMG) class on a cold mid-December day at Evergreen Cemetery. Jessica Swimm is the JMG specialist and Wreaths Across America coordinator for Houlton High School. Wreaths Across America’s mission is to remember the fallen, honor those who serve, and teach the next generation the value of freedom. The class of 2026 raised money to lay 906 wreaths at veterans’ headstones. The cemetery has 1,000 veterans buried there.
Fitzpatrick said that she had never participated in honoring veterans and found it “really impacting.”
“I have veterans in my family, so it was a chance to honor their service and sacrifice,” she said. “I made sure to get the flag just right before I put the wreath on. I put down more than 80 wreaths. It was a challenging day, because we received more than a foot of snow right before, but it was worth it.”

title: MaineDOT commissions new hybrid ferry named in honor of Ellsworth’s Captain Almer Dinsmore
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine (WABI) - The Maine Department of Transportation officially commissioned the newest addition to the Maine State Ferry Service on Thursday, commissioning the state’s first diesel-electric hybrid ferry, the M/V Captain Almer Dinsmore.
Capable of carrying 250 passengers and 23 vehicles, the ship has been assigned to the Rockland–Vinalhaven route. Maine DOT officials estimate the hybrid propulsion system will cut fuel consumption by roughly 25%.reliability
“We have a lot of very old boats in the ferry service, and often they’re taken offline for repairs, and that can cause a lot of disruption,” said U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, “Ferries are really the lifeline for people who live on all of the islands. This is our first hybrid, and so it’s exciting to be able to use dual fuels, especially with the increasing cost of diesel, and trying to keep an eye on the cost of the ferry service.”
Maine DOT Commissioner Dale Doughty emphasized that modernization is critical for communities that depend on the water for daily survival.
“Most goods and services, building materials, craftsmen pass back and forth, but individuals, you know, kids coming to school, kids playing sports, all of the things that we all take for granted in our communities are related to the ferry service,” Doughty said. “It needs to work every day. It needs to provide people all that lifeline that we all take for granted when we go out at the end of the driveway and we turn right or left.”
The vessel honors Ellsworth native Captain Almer Dinsmore, a 1968 Maine Maritime Academy graduate who served 26 years with the Maine State Ferry Service. Dinsmore, who attended Thursday’s ceremony, said having the pioneering vessel bear his name is deeply humbling.
“It’s pretty overwhelming to know that that plaque is going to be there long after I’m gone,” Dinsmore said. “I’m glad my name is on this particular vessel with this new technology, because when I was going to sea, I was always embracing new technology. And, you know, this is what it’s about today is converting over to electric propulsion.”

title: Kingfield Artwalk afoot, November 6
3 singer-songwriters and a 20-year Maine tradition at Bath arts center
text:
It all started with an invitation. More than 20 years ago, Maine singer-songwriter Lynn Deeves was organizing showcases in Maine featuring artists she’d discovered through Indie Girl, an organization supporting independent women singer-songwriters. A few years in, she discovered two musicians, Trina Hamlin and Colleen Sexton, and fell in love with their music.
Deeves invited both of them to Maine to perform and, in her words, “I never invited anybody else after that.” Twenty years later, the three are still meeting up yearly to make music together in Maine.
What began as a musical connection turned into a friendship that has carried them through marriage and divorce, births and deaths. Hamlin and Sexton even sang at Deeves’ mother’s funeral. Over time, they’ve cultivated a soul-level musical and personal connection, and their annual week together is a highlight of the year for all three.
At their core, Deeves, Hamlin, and Sexton are folk musicians and accomplished singer-songwriters, but they all cross genres, bringing rock, blues, roots, soul, and gospel flavors into the mix. When they play together, it’s full of rich, three-part harmonies and a breadth of instruments. They each have a distinctive voice and songwriting approach, and the combination makes for a powerful and layered sound.
Lynn Deeves got her start fronting bands as a rock singer on the New England and Canadian club circuit in the ’80s and ’90s. Over time, her songwriting has gone in a folk-rock direction, with soulful vocals and a playful, humorous stage presence. She plays guitar, flute, harmonica and percussion, and has released four solo albums, plus collaborations with other Maine musicians. For Deeves, music is the conduit through which she can express herself and share the gift of music with others.
Trina Hamlin has toured throughout the U.S. and Europe, performed at the Newport Folk Festival and has shared the stage with artists such as Taj Mahal, John Hiatt, and Rickie Lee Jones. She is a multi-instrumentalist who plays piano, guitar and harmonica. Her blues and rock-inspired rhythms and powerful vocals are a driving force in the trio.
Colleen Sexton combines thoughtful lyrics with a vocal sound that can be both intimate and gritty, and a keen sense of rhythm and skillful guitar work. Her live album, “Colleen Sexton LIVE,” captures her vocal range and ability to connect with the audience.
The talent runs deep when these three get together: big lead vocals, three-part harmonies, rhythmic guitar, piano, harmonica and the occasional flute solo. Over the years, they’ve learned each other’s songs and always find new ways to play them. Twenty years of collaboration have created a musical connection that allows them to experiment freely with harmonies and instrumental arrangements. Deeves says the three have a “mutual admiration society”— there’s no competition or jockeying for the spotlight. They enjoy one another’s music and the creative freedom of playing together.
There’s also plenty of laughter. Their performances include stories, banter, a few covers, and the kind of spontaneous moments that come from creative trust and years of friendship. The trio has written only one song together, titled “Joyful Noise,” which is an apt description for the musical synergy they create. Come experience this Maine tradition in person, and let the music fill your cup.
Lynn Deeves, Trina Hamlin, and Colleen Sexton perform at 7:30 p.m. on Saturday, Nov. 14, in the Annex theater at the Chocolate Church in Bath.
Catherine Gleason is the marketing and communications director at the Chocolate Church Arts Center.

title: The 2028 election season begins as both parties navigate midterm fallout
text:
The 2028 election season begins as both parties navigate midterm fallout
The final midterm votes are still being counted, but make no mistake: The next election season has already begun.
Presidential prospects in both parties jockeyed for position on Wednesday, even as the political world was digesting the impact of the Democratic wave that crashed over American politics the night before. Democrats celebrated their party's stunning success — and began promoting themselves — while dejected Republicans scrambled to distance themselves from President Donald Trump's wreckage.
The Republican with the most at stake was likely Vice President JD Vance, who entered Tuesday night as the GOP's leading presidential prospect and woke up on Wednesday far more vulnerable — like any Republican who is close to Trump.
"The reason we lost is the war," Vance said in a morning postmortem post on X. "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest."
He added, "And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."
Vance has struggled to square his history of opposing foreign intervention with his defense of Trump's war. He has said publicly that the conflict was necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon, but his private skepticism has been widely reported.
Trump did not dispute Vance's assessment, even as he defended the war. But he also made no effort to help Vance's potential prospects, telling reporters, "Maybe he won't run." Vance had said he would make a decision after the election.
Voters still processing an extraordinary midterm campaign may not welcome an immediate pivot to 2028. But for would-be candidates, there is real urgency to move toward a White House bid in what is expected to be a wide-open contest in both parties.
Possible 2028 contenders have been making moves
The first presidential primary votes will be cast in little more than a year. And some prospects, including Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, have already had preliminary conversations with potential presidential campaign staff.
Former vice president and 2024 Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris told The Associated Press on Wednesday that she was elated to see Democrats' commanding performance — particularly across the South — and wants to play a role, regardless of whether she decides to run again.
"I believe I have a responsibility to contribute to the direction of the party, in particular around lifting up voices and issues that I have an experience with," she said. "Whether I'm in office or not, that's the role I feel compelled to play."
Rahm Emanuel, who has spent much of the past year laying the groundwork for a potential presidential campaign, demurred when asked about his future plans.
"Don't worry about the next election," he said in an interview. "There's a time and a season. And right now is the governing time."
The Democrats, in particular, have a deep bench of high-profile leaders who strengthened their political brands on Tuesday.
Blue-state governors like Maryland's Wes Moore and Illinois' JB Pritzker both scored decisive reelection wins and offered sweepy victory speeches. California's outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom had worked to boost Democratic candidates all over, especially in the South. He also had a personal role in Democrats winning the House majority, having led Proposition 50, California's response to the Texas Republican mid-decade gerrymander.
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro arguably had the most impressive performance with a commanding win in one of the nation's most important swing states, while also helping his party win control of the state legislature and flipping four congressional seats.
Shapiro faced immediate questions about his presidential ambitions during a round of interviews Wednesday morning on national television.
"The numbers were so big, I was wondering if you want to take this opportunity … to say, 'You know what, I'm in for 2028.' Or do you want to talk about something else?" CBS anchor Gayle King asked.
"I want to answer all your other questions, Gayle," Shapiro laughed, before addressing his party's future. "People want fundamental change, real reform. More importantly, they want their leaders to get stuff done, they want real results."
And as the Democratic governors speak up, a fresh wave of Democrats will take the Senate majority, perhaps elevating the likes of Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff or even Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed from Michigan.
Progressives seized on El-Sayed's victory in the Midwest as they quietly discussed who might take the progressive mantle from Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who at age 85 has ruled out another presidential bid. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez remains the dominant name in that conversation, but at 37, it's unclear if she'll take that step.
"This changes the 2028 presidential race," Adam Green, co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, said of El-Sayed's win. "A bold anti-establishment economic fighter can win battleground states. Period."
GOP's deep midterm losses may give some Republican hopefuls an opening
On the Republican side, the blowout could provide an opening to others in the party who had been wary about crossing Trump by beginning the process of moving on from his time at the helm.
Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich said the quiet part out loud in assessing Vance's political strength.
"If the administration had won a big victory, Vice President JD Vance would have had an enormous argument to be the inevitable nominee," Gingrich wrote on X. "Now ... a good bit of the luster has come off the bloom."
Gingrich listed a half dozen other Republicans who could compete with Vance: "The scale of the Republican defeat is so great that it makes the race for the GOP presidential nomination wide open."
Former Trump rival Ron DeSantis, the outgoing Republican governor of Florida, was unsparing Wednesday in describing the scope of GOP losses, calling it "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country." He held up his state, which elected Republicans to the governor's office and U.S. Senate, as an exception and an example of "how you can deliver big results."
Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, who invested significant time and resources trying to help Republicans who ended up losing, had already been openly weighing another White House run.
Trump's fiercest critics were also vindicated. They include New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie, who has been mulling his own repeat bid.
Emboldened by the midterm results, however, the Democratic field is eager to move forward.
New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker, a former presidential candidate who begins the 2028 cycle with more than $20 million in his federal campaign account, offered an inspirational victory speech that left little doubt about his intentions.
"We have ended an election, but this has got to be the start of a movement," Booker said. "America, tonight is the start of our comeback, baby."
___
Associated Press writers Bill Barrow, Steven Sloan and Linley Sanders contributed to this report.

title: These homeowners claim company sold them homes with ‘defective pipes’
text:
DALLAS, Ga. (InvestigateTV) - For more than a dozen homeowners outside Atlanta their dream home came with a costly surprise.
The complaint filed Dec. 22, 2025, with the American Arbitration Association, named 16 households in the Stonewood Creek subdivision in Dallas, Georgia. All the homes were built by D.R. Horton and contain cross-linked polyethylene (PEX) pipes manufactured by Uponor Inc. The homeowners said the pipes began leaking approximately four years after they moved in.
Matthew Ardis purchased his home in the subdivision in 2019. He said the pipes have leaked so many times his home looks like Swiss cheese inside. He said he’s repaired dozens of leaks.
“I stopped counting somewhere in the teens for a little while because they were coming one after the other, day after day,” Ardis said.
Ardis said D.R. Horton is responsible for the damage.
“I’m realistic that as a homeowner, there’s going to be repairs, but nothing to this extent,” he said. “They have the responsibility to provide me with a livable home.”
Other homeowners in the subdivision described similar experiences.
Rosemary Pastula said the situation has left her in a constant state of anxiety.
“We’re just waiting,” she said. “It’s like a time bomb. I’m a nervous wreck all the time, wondering when it’s going to hit the fan.”
Yazmin Roman said the leaks have altered daily routines.
“You don’t want to go out,” she said. “You don’t do your normal routines because you’re so worried that when you come home, you’re going to deal with a disaster.”
The homeowners said the cost to repair the leaks have been significant. Roman said she has spent approximately $5,000 out of pocket, with total estimates exceeding $50,000. Ardis said he has spent close to $30,000 out of pocket, with total damages exceeding $100,000.
Complaint: Builder repaired some homes but not claimants’
The arbitration complaint alleged D.R. Horton constructed approximately 95 single-family homes in the Stonewood Creek subdivision. It stated the company contracted Uponor as the pipe supplier. The claimants purchased their homes between 2018 and 2023.
According to the complaint, D.R. Horton and Uponor repaired or replaced the alleged “defective pipes” in other homes in the subdivision but have refused to do the same for the 16 households in the pending arbitration complaint. The complaint also alleges D.R. Horton has declined to disclose which entity is performing the repairs or to notify all subdivision homeowners their pipes may be defective.
Chuck Douglas, who represents one of the homeowners in the arbitration claim, said D.R. Horton is responsible for the damages.
“They made a promise to these homeowners in the form of a warranty, and they’re now not living up to that promise,” Douglas said.
Atlanta News First Investigates called and emailed D.R. Horton multiple times. We did not receive an official response to these claims.
Pipe manufacturer denies systemic defect
Uponor declined interview requests but provided a written statement that reads in part: “Independent experts have categorically stated there is not a systematic issue with our PEX pipe. We recognize the disruption plumbing issues can cause and have been actively engaged in working toward fair and appropriate resolutions.”
The arbitration complaint alleged the pipe failures stem from micro-cracks and holes that cause the pipes to expel water and damage the homes.
Each homeowner received a 10-year limited warranty from D.R. Horton upon purchase of their home, according to the complaint. Uponor also issued a 25-year express warranty on the pipes. The complaint said all pipe failures occurred within the respective warranty periods.
Here is Uponor’s full statement:
“Our PEX piping has demonstrated a low in-field failure rate across billions of feet installed worldwide and is manufactured under rigorous quality controls to meet or exceed recognized industry standards. Independent experts have categorically stated there is not a systematic issue with our PEX pipe.
“We take all concerns seriously. When issues are reported, we review them carefully and, in many cases, engage independent experts to evaluate the specific installation and operating conditions. Like all plumbing materials, PEX piping is designed to perform within applicable code requirements and recommended operating parameters. Findings, and therefore resolutions, can vary depending on the circumstances of each situation.
“We recognize the disruption plumbing issues can cause and have been actively engaged in working toward fair and appropriate resolutions.”
Court records show that home and business owners in at least 10 states have filed multiple federal lawsuits against the pipe manufacturer.

title: US contractor admits passing US top-secret information to Ethiopia
text:
US contractor admits passing US top-secret information to Ethiopia in its war against rebels
A former U.S. government contractor has admitted passing classified intelligence to Ethiopia that officials used in military operations, the U.S. Justice Department said Tuesday.
Abraham Teklu Lemma, 54, supplied secrets to senior Ethiopian officials for more than two years, urging them to deploy drones against fighters battling the government, according to the U.S. attorney’s office in Washington.
Video above: What to know about the DOJ's record deployment of election monitors
Lemma, of Silver Spring, Maryland, pleaded guilty Tuesday to conspiring to transmit national defense information to a foreign government. He worked as an information technology contractor at the State Department, Justice Department and National Reconnaissance Office, prosecutors said.
According to prosecutors, the information reached Ethiopia’s military and intelligence branches between 2021 and August 2023, when he was arrested.
Prosecutors described a December 2021 message in which Lemma pressed an Ethiopian contact to act against their government opponents.
“We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia,” he wrote, according to the Washington prosecutor’s office.
The Ethiopian government has not released any public statements on the case.
An FBI counterintelligence official, Roman Rozhavsky, said Lemma admitted that Ethiopian officials used the intelligence he supplied in military operations. The Justice Department statement did not publicly reveal the specific operations or say whether anyone was killed as a result of the intelligence breach.
An FBI affidavit filed in 2023 alleged that Lemma sent top-secret satellite imagery and classified reports through an encrypted messaging application to Ethiopian government operatives.
Video below: Trump administration warns Wisconsin election officials about record-keeping penalties
The disclosures began during Ethiopia’s 2020–2022 war between federal forces and Tigrayan fighters. Researchers at Belgium’s Ghent University estimated that 500,000 civilians died through violence, famine and the collapse of health services.
The Pretoria peace agreement ended that war, but fighting resumed in September. Government-allied fighters entered Mekelle, Tigray’s capital, on Oct. 4, after the Tigray People’s Liberation Front withdrew.
The U.S. statements did not name any of the armed groups that the Ethiopian government targeted with Lemma’s intelligence.
His plea agreement with U.S. federal prosecutors provides for a prison term of between 10 years and 21 years and 10 months, subject to the court accepting. Lemma is due to be sentenced on April 14, 2027, the Justice Department said.

title: Harpswell voters send Golek back to House, continue support for Democrats
text:
Harpswell voters continued the town’s recent trend, backing Democratic candidates by lopsided margins across the ballot on Tuesday.
State Rep. Cheryl Golek, a second-term Democrat who lives on Harpswell Neck, received 2,229 votes to 1,313 for political newcomer Braeden Webber, a Republican who lives on Great Island. Golek’s House District 99 also includes part of Brunswick. With results from the neighboring town, Golek swept to victory with 64.1% of the vote.
State Sen. Matthea “Mattie” Daughtry, D-Brunswick, gained Harpswell’s support on her way to a fourth consecutive term. Daughtry, who currently serves as president of the Senate, received 2,139 Harpswell votes to 1,375 for challenger Bernard “Ben” Porter, a Republican who lives on Orr’s Island.
Daughtry won the race by 47 percentage points. In addition to Harpswell, Senate District 23 also includes the towns of Brunswick, Chebeague Island, Freeport, Pownal and part of Yarmouth.
Harpswell — which has not backed a Republican for president since 1992 — also gave an edge to Democrats in races for Congress, governor, district attorney and county commissioner.
Local voters backed Troy Jackson for U.S. Senate with 2,059 votes to 1,478 for the Republican incumbent, Susan Collins. The five-term senator conceded the race to Jackson, a former president of the Maine Senate, early Wednesday.
Harpswell contributed to Democrat Hannah Pingree’s comfortable win in the race for the Blaine House. The Bangor Daily News and Decision Desk HQ called the race at 10:30 p.m.
Hannah Pingree, a former House speaker and director of the Governor’s Office of Policy Innovation and the Future, picked up 2,132 votes in Harpswell to 1,144 for Republican Bobby Charles and 274 for independent Rick Bennett. Hannah Pingree will replace Gov. Janet Mills, a fellow Democrat who could not run for reelection after two straight four-year terms in office.
U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, Hannah Pingree’s mother, racked up the most Harpswell votes of any candidate in a contested race as she cruised to a 10th consecutive two-year term as representative of Maine’s 1st Congressional District. Harpswell cast 2,260 votes for Chellie Pingree to 1,266 for her Republican challenger, Ronald Russell.
District Attorney Jackie Sartoris, a Brunswick Democrat, garnered 2,041 votes in Harpswell to 1,152 for independent Stephanie Anderson, who held the office as a Republican from 1990-2018.
Sartoris won reelection by roughly 37,000 votes — 99,178 to 61,527 — according to the Portland Press Herald.
In the race for District 3 county commissioner, Freeport Democrat Amy Leshure bested Cumberland independent Robert Vail by more than 1,000 votes, 2,098 to 1,052. She received 72.8% of the vote overall in the contest to replace Stephen Gorden, a Yarmouth Democrat.
In county races with just one candidate, Harpswell voters cast 2,772 votes for Cumberland County Sheriff Kevin Joyce, a Standish Democrat, and 2,697 for Judge of Probate Paul Aranson, a Scarborough Democrat.
A total of 3,589 ballots were cast in Harpswell, according to unofficial results from the town clerk’s office.
J.W. Oliver is the editor of the Harpswell Anchor. A former editor and reporter at The Lincoln County News, he was the Maine Press Association’s Journalist of the Year for 2017-18.

title: Rounds of rain may affect only parts of Maine
text:
Rounds of rain expected through the weekend
Shifting to a cooler, more active weather pattern
Rounds of rain expected through the weekend
Shifting to a cooler, more active weather pattern
A wet stretch of weather is expected through the weekend. Steady rain develops along a stalled front offshore on Friday, with showers moving onto land late morning. A few sprinkles are possible beforehand, along with patchy fog.
Showers impact southern Maine and parts of central Maine Friday afternoon and evening, coming in waves. Showers reach farther north late Friday evening and overnight.
The heaviest rain will focus along the midcoast and especially around the Penobscot Bay islands and points east, where totals could approach 2 inches. Amounts will drop off considerably farther inland and to the west. Around 1 to 1.5 inches of rain is likely for much of southern and central Maine, while less than half an inch is likely in the mountains.
A brief lull in the rain is possible Saturday morning in western Maine before another round of widespread showers develops Saturday afternoon and night, continuing into Sunday morning. Most of the showers should taper off by Sunday afternoon.
Colder air returns Sunday night into next week, with highs mainly in the 40s in the mountains and 50s elsewhere. A few rain or snow showers are possible, especially in the mountains, where some light snow could develop at higher elevations.

title: Portugal great Cristiano Ronaldo announces retirement from international soccer
text:
LISBON, Portugal (AP) — Cristiano Ronaldo announced on Thursday he won’t play for Portugal anymore, ending a career that spanned six World Cups and included a European title and the men’s all-time international scoring record.
The announcement marked the end of a lauded career that began more than two decades ago before Euro 2004 and finished with him walking out on the national team after falling out with coach Jorge Jesus.
“To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the No. 7 shirt of our national team,” the 41-year-old Ronaldo said in a long video message on social media. “I never felt it belonged to me alone but for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world.
“Today the time has come to pass it on to the future. It was not an easy decision because some decisions are not made with the mind alone. They are also made with the heart. A journey that began in August 2003 and changed my life forever has come to an end.”
Portugal plans tribute to ‘greatest of all time’
While long-time peer Lionel Messi finished his career with Argentina after a much anticipated farewell match last month, Ronaldo’s final appearance with Portugal has ended up being on Sept. 24 in a 1-0 win over Wales in the Nations League.
Jesus kept him on the bench for the following match and said he didn’t plan to start him in the next one, so Ronaldo decided to leave the team’s training camp. Jesus later said Ronaldo would be welcome back and the decision to return was up to him.
The Portuguese soccer federation released a statement expressing “deep gratitude and immense admiration” for Ronaldo’s service to the country.
“Cristiano Ronaldo has raised Portugal’s profile and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps; for many of us, he is the greatest player of all time!” the federation said.
It said it intends to organize a tribute to Ronaldo “in which the fans and the country can one more time applaud and celebrate a player who has given us so much.”
Like Messi, Ronaldo will keep playing at club level, and is expected to finish his club career at the end of this season with Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia.
He is in pursuit of his 1,000th career goal and sits on 985. Of those, a record 146 goals came in 234 appearances with Portugal.

title: 19-year-old wins county clerk election for nation's 4th-largest county
text:
Arizona 19-year-old wins county clerk election for nation's 4th-largest county
Sebastian Matta, a 19-year-old Arizona State University student, has been elected as the clerk of the Superior Court for Maricopa County, the fourth-largest county in the United States.
Republican Jeff Dial, a former state senator, called Matta to concede the race. Matta, who graduated high school last year, will now lead the clerk’s office.
"I mean, I vehemently enjoy campaigning. I vehemently enjoy everything that I've done up to this point, and I'm sure I'm vehemently going to enjoy the clerk's office," Matta said. "I'm a normal kid who's running for office."
Matta said he'll build a foundation before tackling his agenda.
"I don't plan on instituting some of my campaign changes for a couple of months, even a year in. The first long while of my tenure will be getting to be friendly with the staff, ensuring them that their jobs are safe. I mean, I understand that it's very scary to have a 19-year-old be your boss, but I'm not just any 19-year-old," he said.
Matta studies philosophy of law, politics, and morality at Arizona State University. His hobbies include fencing, theater, and debate.

title: Gorham resident sues town over zoning change that could allow quarry expansion
text:
A Gorham resident is suing the town over a zoning change that allows Shaw Brothers Construction to pursue expanding the Brickyard Quarry toward Queen Street.
The lawsuit, filed by John Wise in Cumberland County Superior Court this week, alleges that the Gorham Town Council’s 4-3 decision in September to change the zoning of 14 acres adjacent to the quarry from “urban residential expansion” to “industrial” is illegal. According to the lawsuit, the decision contradicts the town’s comprehensive plan and future land use plan, allowing industrial activity where the town did not intend it.
Shaw Brothers Construction has been trying to expand the quarry for over three years, but has met resistance from neighbors who say the dust, noise, asphalt smell and blasting damage their quality of life, their homes and potentially their health. Residents have voiced concerns that quarry expansion will worsen those impacts.
According to the lawsuit, there are approximately 2,251 residential homes within 2 miles of the quarry.
The town’s comprehensive plan, a guide for growth and development last updated in 2016, designates the 14 acres beside the quarry as a “Village Expansion” area and stipulates it should be used for housing. The lawsuit alleges that allowing mining on that land is out of harmony with town goals.
Gorham officials declined to comment on the case and Shaw Brothers representatives did not respond to a request for comment. They joined the lawsuit as an interested party.
Shaw Brothers’ application to the Gorham Planning Board to expand the roughly 40-acre quarry by 6 acres underwent a public hearing Monday. The company says it wants to expand the quarry to lengthen its lifespan from 50 years to 60 years. When it runs out of rock to mine, the company will continue crushing at the site.
Dan Shaw, co-owner of Shaw Brothers Construction, has said that he and his employees address dust- and blast-related complaints for neighbors promptly and that residents are concerned for no reason, and that expansion will not worsen conditions. The company runs six quarries and 13 gravel pits in Maine, and Shaw said he has not heard of similar issues from neighbors of the other quarries.
After hearing several objections from residents Monday, the board delayed its decision because the company’s application was incomplete, missing information such as an updated noise study and review of air quality impacts. Shaw Brothers will also need a permit from the Maine Department of Environmental Protection to move forward.
The lawsuit and pending application come as the Gorham Town Council in September approved using $35,000 of tax increment financing to hire a consultant to review the strength of the town’s quarry ordinances and recommend changes to address residents’ concerns. Staff will meet next week to finalize the scope of work and begin that project, Town Manager Ephrem Paraschak said.
Many residents have said the planning board should not approve Shaw Brothers’ application until the consultant is able to complete the review. Any ordinance changes would not apply to the existing Brickyard Quarry, and would not apply to the expansion if it is approved before ordinance changes go into effect.
“I am concerned that this proposal is moving forward toward approval while certain questions remain unanswered and studies unsubmitted,” Emily Hamblen, whose family’s land abuts the quarry property, said on Monday.
Planning board member David Walsh requested data about the content of the silica dust the quarry emits and its potential health impacts, and board member William Benson said he wanted to know more about how often the DEP and the town inspect the facility. David Madore, DEP deputy commissioner and communications director, said in July that the most recent DEP air inspection of the facility was in June 2023.
Walsh also expressed surprise when Pete Bennett, division manager at Maine Drilling and Blasting, said that there are no regulations on the weather conditions that his company can blast in and asked for more information on what kind of restrictions have been put in place elsewhere.
Lee Pratt, general manager of Shaw Brothers Construction, said that he coordinates ahead of time with the blasting company if conditions look cloudy and could cause unusually high noise and pressure, but that they proceed with blasts regardless when those conditions cannot be predicted.
An aerial photo taken by a resident with a drone showing the quarry after a blast on Oct. 27 is attached to the lawsuit. Bennett said most of the visible material that rises after a blast is gas that dissipates, rather than particles that can be carried by the wind to residents’ homes.
“Gorham’s a beautiful place, and it’s taking this quarry process, and it wants to bring it closer to where people are,” said Andre James Hungerford, the attorney representing Wise. “No one has studied the effects of the particulates of the fugitive dust.”

title: Cyberattack on blood bank freezers thwarted, follows supermarket fridge hacks
text:
PARIS (AP) — A cyberattack on several blood banks tried to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but was thwarted before it could do any damage to blood products or samples, French authorities said.
The incident comes after supermarkets in a number of European countries reported this week that their fridges and freezers warmed up after they were remotely taken over, resulting in tons of spoiled food at a total cost of millions of dollars (euros).
The French Blood Establishment, or EFS, said “temperature and defrosting thresholds were raised to extremely high levels” on Monday at three of its cold-storage sites for plasma, in a statement released late Tuesday. Monitoring systems quickly detected the problem, allowing staff to take action in time so that “no blood products or samples were compromised,” it said.
French weekly newspaper Le Canard Enchaîné, which first reported the cyberattack, said that the attack had attempted to reset temperatures that normally are at minus 30 Celsius (minus 22 Fahrenheit) to as high as 110 C (230 F).
The cyberattack hit a supplier of refrigeration equipment at three EFS sites. The products stored were bags of plasma intended for transfusions and plasma used to manufacture medicines, and were either transferred or secured, the EFS statement said.
“No health consequences have been identified, and no blood products were lost,” the blood bank said.
The EFS said blood collection and distribution operations remain uninterrupted, ensuring continued services for patients at hospitals and other healthcare.
The company supplying the refrigeration equipment, Coolworld, said in a statement it “is aware” of the cybersecurity incident.
“The vulnerability currently being reported in the media relates to a component from a third-party supplier and was outside Coolworld’s direct control,” the statement said. The company said only a limited number of units were affected and it was taking “appropriate measures.”
France’s national cybersecurity agency and the Health Ministry are investigating the incident.
This week’s cyberattacks on refrigeration systems mirrored an episode in mid-October that targeted fridges and freezers at hundreds of supermarkets and independent stores across France, Belgium and the Netherlands.
One of the chains hit in that earlier incident, Dutch supermarket chain Ahold Delhaize, said Wednesday that it expected the cyberattack to reduce its sales in the fourth quarter by as much as 250 million euros ($281 million), and crimp its operating income for the period by up to 100 million euros.
“While most of the disruption was contained within two weeks, work continues to fully restore our normal operations,” CEO Franz Muller said. “As we all recognize, cyber threats are an increasingly harsh reality of doing business today,” he said in a statement released with Delhaize’s quarterly earnings.
The company had earlier blamed “malicious actions by others” and proactively took some of its systems offline, including websites and apps for its various brands in Europe as well as in the United States.

AP journalist Kelvin Chan in London contributed to the story

(CNN) - More than 3.5 million ladders have been recalled due to a safety risk and fall hazard.
The brand name is Little Giant.
They were sold at Lowe’s and Costco stores nationwide, as well as online at those sites, Amazon and other sites.
Several ladder models are involved in the recall.
They all have rapid locks that are black and orange and are located on each ladder leg. The ladders can suddenly retract if the locks are not fully engaged, posing a fall hazard.
Little Giant has received 19 reports of injuries.
