title: MVHS Nurse Named Maine School Nurse of the Year
text:
Sherri Vail, the nurse for Medomak Valley High School, was recognized as the Maine School Nurse of the Year by the Maine Association of School Nurses on Monday, Nov. 2.
“It’s so rewarding to be recognized for your work because, in education and healthcare, sometimes you have sparse thankfulness,” Vail said. “To be recognized in this way was just so – I felt so honored.”
The award recognizes an outstanding Maine school nurse for their contributions to the school and community they serve, according to the Maine Association of School Nurses website. The association has selected a School Nurse of the Year since 1994.
Vail was recognized during an assembly at the high school, which she graduated from in 1984 and where has worked for 11 years, on Monday, Nov. 2.
“She brings care and compassion every day, and we’re proud to see that she’s being recognized,” Principal Dan Joseph said.
Vail received several standing ovations from staff and students throughout the assembly.
“School nursing requires so much more than medical knowledge,” RSU 40 Assistant Superintendent Karen Overlock said. “It means caring for a student who is physically unwell while also recognizing when students need reassurance, a listening ear, or someone they can trust. Ms. Vail is that person for so many of our students.”
Vail has been a practicing nurse for 37 years. She began her career in the obstetrics unit of the U.S. Air Force as a lieutenant for four years, then as a labor and delivery nurse at Miles Memorial Hospital, now MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital, in Damariscotta for almost 20 years. Vail then worked as a surgical quality specialist at Pen Bay Hospital in Rockport for another four years before joining Medomak as a school nurse in 2015.
For her first four years on the job, Vail was the nurse for both MVHS and Medomak Middle School.
“I love being a steady presence for kids,” she said. “Some kids will just poke their head in and say good morning. Some kids will come for little needs, and some kids will come with serious, very serious, huge needs … I was a cheerleader here, so I suppose still am a cheerleader.”
In addition to student physical health, Vail is passionate about student mental health. She is a co-leader of the Sources of Strength, a student mental health focus group at Medomak Valley, and member of the Multi-Tiered Systems of Support staff team, which helps combat truancy.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, Vail pursued a master’s degree in human relations from Husson University to further learn how to support student mental health. She referred to herself a “lifelong learner.”
“I wanted to learn the skills that I could better help my kids,” Vail said.
The school nurse also helped spearhead the opening of a MaineHealth School-Based Health Center at the high school in 2019. The center, which operates in part of Vail’s office, is staffed by a nurse practitioner twice a week and a licensed clinical social work three days a week to support students and staff.
“Parents would have to leave work and come and pick up the kid and take them to the doctor, and this way they can just be seen,” Vail said.
Additionally, Vail became the RSU 40 wellness ambassador last year, a position she hopes to do more with this year, and coordinated a medical emergency response team of staff when she first joined the school in 2016.
She also coordinated Peers with Diabetes group for diabetic students in 2023 between and MVHS and MMS, which she hopes to revive it in the future.
Vail was nominated for the award by former Medomak Valley Principal Linda Pease, who retired from the district in the spring. Vail was made aware of her win in May, she said, but was not officially presented the award until a Maine Association of School Nurses town hall event on Oct. 17.
Six letters were written to the association in support of Vail, including from one of her students.
“I felt like I already won after I read (the student’s) letter,” she said.
Vail will also be nationally recognized with state School Nurse of the Year awardees across the country at the National Association of School Nurses annual conference in June 2027.

title: Arrest made in Damariscotta hit-and-run that seriously injured bicyclist
text:
Maine man arrested following Damariscotta hit-and-run that seriously injured bicyclist
A Maine man faces multiple charges in connection with a hit-and-run crash in Damariscotta that left a bicyclist seriously injured.
John Barczak, 67, of Rockland, was arrested and charged with elevated aggravated assault, leaving the scene of an accident involving serious bodily injury and reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon.
The crash happened at about 5:25 a.m. Wednesday at the intersection of Biscay Road and Main Street.
Damariscotta Police Chief Erik Josephson said a 65-year-old woman who was riding a bicycle sustained serious injuries in the crash. The woman was transported by ambulance to Miles Memorial Hospital, but she was later transferred to Maine Medical Center in Portland due to the severity of her injuries.
Josephson said the vehicle involved in the crash had left the scene before first responders arrived.
After examining physical evidence, surveillance footage and vehicle-related information, Damariscotta Police Officer William Smith identified the suspect vehicle, a red Toyota Tacoma pickup truck, which was later found at a local business.
Josephson said that Smith identified Barczak as the driver of the truck through further investigation.
Barczak was interviewed as part of the investigation, and at about 4 p.m. Wednesday, he was taken into custody without incident and brought to the Two Bridges Regional Jail in Wiscasset.
Josephson said the investigation remains active and ongoing. The police chief also acknowledged the assistance the Damariscotta Police Department received from the Lincoln County Sheriff's Office, Lincoln County District Attorney's Office, Damariscotta Fire Department and Central Lincoln County Ambulance.

title: OUT Maine opens new OUT Maine Action Fund
text:
ROCKLAND — On Oct. 30, 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization OUT Maine announced the opening of a new 501(c)(4) nonprofit organization to expand their work for LGBTQIA2S+ rights and civic engagement across the state: OUT Maine Action Fund.
OUT Maine Action Fund fights for queer and trans youth in Maine’s biggest cities as well as the smallest rural towns. From lobbying in Augusta to advocating at school boards, and empowering the next generation of leaders, the organization aims to protect the rights of LGBTQIA2S+ youth and adults at the local and state level. Their official mission reads: “OUT Maine Action Fund is dedicated to building a Maine where all LGBTQ+ youth are safe, celebrated, and empowered through leadership development, legislative advocacy, and public education. We develop emerging leaders, champion affirming policies, and build inclusive communities where every young person has the opportunity to thrive.”
Where OUT Maine focuses on providing youth programming with a variety of themes and subject areas guided by social and emotional learning outcomes, OUT Maine Action Fund will focus more heavily on legislative policy work.
“Starting the OUT Maine Action Fund was the logical next step for our growing organization, so that we could expand our policy work beyond the limits of a 501(c)(3) nonprofit,” Sue Campbell, executive director of both OUT Maine and OUT Maine Action Fund, said. “Our team is looking forward to continuing and amplifying advocacy efforts at the legislative level for queer and trans youth.”
OUT Maine’s Policy Director, Ash Northey, will be taking the lead on much of the work under OUT Maine Action Fund. “This is huge for us,” she says. “And the support we’ve gotten over the last few years is proof that communities in Maine are willing to stand up and fight for LGBTQ+ rights. Now we’ll have a better platform to do so alongside them.”
OUT Maine Action Fund’s new website was launched, as well as social media profiles.
To support the OUT Maine Action Fund, folks can place donations through the new website. The organization is also accepting applications for volunteers, especially those willing to provide future testimony, attend school board meetings, contact legislators, and more. Learn more about ways to get involved at outmaineactionfund.org.

title: These homeowners claim company sold them homes with ‘defective pipes’
text:
DALLAS, Ga. (InvestigateTV) - For more than a dozen homeowners outside Atlanta their dream home came with a costly surprise.
They’re blaming one of the nation’s biggest home builders for selling them houses with defective plumbing. Homeowners say the pipes began leaking about four years after they moved in.
The complaint filed Dec. 22, 2025, with the American Arbitration Association, named 16 households in the Stonewood Creek subdivision in Dallas, Georgia. All the homes were built by D.R. Horton and contain cross-linked polyethylene (PEX) pipes manufactured by Uponor Inc. The homeowners said the pipes began leaking approximately four years after they moved in.
Matthew Ardis purchased his home in the subdivision in 2019. He said the pipes have leaked so many times his home looks like Swiss cheese inside. He said he’s repaired dozens of leaks.
“I stopped counting somewhere in the teens for a little while because they were coming one after the other, day after day,” Ardis said.
Ardis said D.R. Horton is responsible for the damage.
“I’m realistic that as a homeowner, there’s going to be repairs, but nothing to this extent,” he said. “They have the responsibility to provide me with a livable home.”
Other homeowners in the subdivision described similar experiences.
Rosemary Pastula said the situation has left her in a constant state of anxiety.
“We’re just waiting,” she said. “It’s like a time bomb. I’m a nervous wreck all the time, wondering when it’s going to hit the fan.”
Yazmin Roman said the leaks have altered daily routines.
“You don’t want to go out,” she said. “You don’t do your normal routines because you’re so worried that when you come home, you’re going to deal with a disaster.”
The homeowners said the cost to repair the leaks have been significant. Roman said she has spent approximately $5,000 out of pocket, with total estimates exceeding $50,000. Ardis said he has spent close to $30,000 out of pocket, with total damages exceeding $100,000.
Complaint: Builder repaired some homes but not claimants’
The arbitration complaint alleged D.R. Horton constructed approximately 95 single-family homes in the Stonewood Creek subdivision. It stated the company contracted Uponor as the pipe supplier. The claimants purchased their homes between 2018 and 2023.
According to the complaint, D.R. Horton and Uponor repaired or replaced the alleged “defective pipes” in other homes in the subdivision but have refused to do the same for the 16 households in the pending arbitration complaint. The complaint also alleges D.R. Horton has declined to disclose which entity is performing the repairs or to notify all subdivision homeowners their pipes may be defective.
Chuck Douglas, who represents one of the homeowners in the arbitration claim, said D.R. Horton is responsible for the damages.
“They made a promise to these homeowners in the form of a warranty, and they’re now not living up to that promise,” Douglas said.
Atlanta News First Investigates called and emailed D.R. Horton multiple times. We did not receive an official response to these claims.
Pipe manufacturer denies systemic defect
Uponor declined interview requests but provided a written statement that reads in part: “Independent experts have categorically stated there is not a systematic issue with our PEX pipe. We recognize the disruption plumbing issues can cause and have been actively engaged in working toward fair and appropriate resolutions.”
The arbitration complaint alleged the pipe failures stem from micro-cracks and holes that cause the pipes to expel water and damage the homes.
Each homeowner received a 10-year limited warranty from D.R. Horton upon purchase of their home, according to the complaint. Uponor also issued a 25-year express warranty on the pipes. The complaint said all pipe failures occurred within the respective warranty periods.
Here is Uponor’s full statement:
“Our PEX piping has demonstrated a low in-field failure rate across billions of feet installed worldwide and is manufactured under rigorous quality controls to meet or exceed recognized industry standards. Independent experts have categorically stated there is not a systematic issue with our PEX pipe.
“We take all concerns seriously. When issues are reported, we review them carefully and, in many cases, engage independent experts to evaluate the specific installation and operating conditions. Like all plumbing materials, PEX piping is designed to perform within applicable code requirements and recommended operating parameters. Findings, and therefore resolutions, can vary depending on the circumstances of each situation.
“We recognize the disruption plumbing issues can cause and have been actively engaged in working toward fair and appropriate resolutions.”
Court records show that home and business owners in at least 10 states have filed multiple federal lawsuits against the pipe manufacturer.
The lawsuits consistently allege Uponor’s PEX pipes are prematurely deteriorating, causing them to crack. Uponor said the lawsuits we reviewed have resulted in dismissals.

title: Police: 3 people injured in shooting at Iowa post office; suspect detained
text:
Woman charged in Iowa post office shooting
Woman charged in Iowa post office shooting
A 39-year-old woman has been charged after police say she opened fire on coworkers at the main post office in Iowa on Thursday morning, injuring two people.
Jennifer Christine Pledger, of West Des Moines, faces two counts of attempted murder, two counts of willful injury causing serious injury and one count of intimidation with a dangerous weapon, according to police. She has been booked into the Polk County Jail and is being held without bond.
Evidence, including witness and victim statements, indicates Pledger opened fire into a group of fellow employees on the second floor of the post office, police said. She is accused of shooting one woman, causing her to fall, then standing over her and firing again. Police said she also fired toward other employees as they fled.
The shooting was reported around 9:10 a.m. Thursday at 1165 Second Ave., a U.S. Postal Service processing and distribution facility. Des Moines police Sgt. Paul Parizek said officers arrived within three minutes as part of a “massive response.” Police later said the first officer arrived at 9:13 a.m. and officers learned the shooter had left the building.
Officers detained Pledger without incident at 9:21 a.m. near the Des Moines River, east of the post office. A 9mm handgun was recovered where she was detained. Police said Pledger has not commented on a motive.
Two women, ages 45 and 53, were shot. A 55-year-old man was injured in a fall while fleeing the shooting. All three are employees at the facility and are expected to survive. The two women took themselves to MercyOne Medical Center in Des Moines, and a police patrol officer took the man there.
The Des Moines Police Department’s Crimes Against Persons Section is leading the investigation. The U.S. Postal Inspection Service is partnering with police, and the FBI and ATF are assisting.
Postal Inspection Service officials said they were “actively investigating” the shooting but declined to provide further details.
“The U.S. Postal Inspection Service, along with local, state, and federal law enforcement partners, is actively investigating a shooting at a USPS facility in Des Moines, Iowa. A suspect is in custody. We are also aware of injuries to multiple victims. At this time, there is no ongoing risk to the public and no further details can be provided while this is an ongoing investigation.”
The post office is less than a mile north of Casey’s Center, where hundreds of schoolchildren were attending an Iowa Wild game for “Education Day.” Officials there said they were in constant communication with authorities and, because of the quick police response, events continued as usual.
After police notified them about the shooting around 9:20 a.m., Des Moines Public Schools placed nearby Carver Elementary School, the DMPS Welcome Center and the Central Nutrition Center in “secure status,” meaning no one could enter or leave the buildings. The status was lifted about 30 minutes later.
State Rep. Rob Johnson, whose district includes the area, said he learned about the incident through the news and came to the scene to speak with police and gather information. He expressed worry for the residents who use the post office, the employees who work there, and the law enforcement officers investigating the case.
“Just hug your loved ones a little bit tighter today,” he said. “Anytime moments like this happen, it sends a ripple effect throughout the community. No matter if you knew the person or you knew someone that worked here. This is still our community.”
Community leaders also noted concerns about the mental health of the shooter, suggesting it may be an area to examine as the investigation continues.
Des Moines Mayor Connie Boesen said she was “thankful for the incredibly rapid and effective response from our Des Moines Police Department and partnering agencies who helped bring a swift and decisive end to a dangerous situation.”
“Our concern now is for the well-being of those injured and all others impacted by this senseless act of violence in our city.”
Police said Second Avenue is open to traffic. Additional information about the ongoing investigation will be shared as it becomes available.

title: Lady Gaga, Shakira, Jack White and Boy George lead the 2027 Songwriters Hall of Fame nominees
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Lady Gaga, Shakira, Pink, Boy George, Jack White, Sia, Vince Gill, Ne-Yo, Blondie’s Debbie Harry and Chris Stein and many more are among the impressive list of nominees for the 2027 Songwriters Hall of Fame class, an especially eclectic mix of pop, hip-hop, Latin, funk and rock innovators.
Also on the ballot are America’s Gerry Beckley and Dewey Bunnell, Grandmaster Melle Mel, ZZ Top’s Frank Beard, Billy Gibbons and Dusty Hill as well as War’s Thomas Sylvester Allen, Harold Ray Brown, Morris “B.B.” Dickerson, Jerry Goldstein, LeRoy L. Jordan, Lee Oskar Levitin, Charles William Miller and Howard E. Scott.
And that’s just scratching the surface.
A long list of talented songwriters
The Hall annually inducts performers and non-performing songwriters alike. The latter category’s nominees this year include Boy Meets Girl — the dream duo of George Merrill and Shannon Rubicam — responsible for Whitney Houston’s biggest hits like “I Wanna Dance with Somebody (Who Loves Me)” and “How Will I Know.”
Then there’s Bob Feldman, Jerry Goldstein and Richard Gottehrer, the trio behind the 1960s American songwriting and record production company FGG Productions. Also known as simply Feldman, Goldstein & Gottehrer, they are responsible for The Angels’ “My Boyfriend’s Back” and The Strangeloves’ “I Want Candy.” (Fun fact: FGG were The Strangeloves; they just pretended to be a band of brothers from Australia.)
Also recognized are Maurice Starr (New Edition’s “Candy Girl,” New Kids on the Block’s “Step By Step”) and Stock Aitken Waterman — aka, Mike Stock, Matt Aitken and Pete Waterman — known for Rick Astley’s “Never Gonna Give You Up” and Kylie Minogue’s “I Should Be So Lucky.”
The same goes for Dan Wilson (Semisonic’s “Closing Time,” Adele’s “Someone Like You”) and Toni Wine (Phil Collins’ “A Groovy Kind of Love,” Tony Orlando’s “Candida”).
For the R&B pop fans, Kandi Burruss is nominated (known for TLC’s “No Scrubs,” Destiny’s Child’s “Bills, Bills, Bills,” NSYNC’s “It Makes Me Ill”), as are Mikkel S. Eriksen and Tor Erik Hermansen, the Norwegian duo known as Stargate behind Beyoncé’s “Irreplaceable” and Rihanna’s “Diamonds.”
Excitingly, will.i.am is also nominated (Black Eyed Peas’ “Where Is the Love,” and “I Gotta Feeling” as well as Usher’s “OMG” and John Legend’s “Ordinary People”). It might be strange to see a name like his, or Burruss’, or Wilson’s in the non-performing songwriter category, since they are all performers as well, but that is because they are being recognized for their work with a variety of artists beyond their own catalogs.
And for country fans, all eyes are on Tom Douglas (Miranda Lambert’s “The House That Built Me,” Tim McGraw’s “Grown Men Don’t Cry”).
2027 Songwriters Hall of Fame voting starts
Eligible voting members have until midnight Eastern Standard Time on Dec. 14 to turn in ballots with their choices of up to three nominees from the songwriter category and up to three from the performing-songwriter category.
This year, a few songwriters are getting another shot at entry. That’s true for Starr, Douglas, Gill, Boy George and members of Blondie and America.
Pink was nominated in 2026 but didn’t make the final cut. It’s the same case for Swedish pop producer of the legendary Cheiron Studios, Andreas Carlsson, known for such hits as Backstreet Boys’ “I Want It That Way,” NSYNC’s “Bye Bye Bye,” and Katy Perry’s “Waking Up In Vegas” and disco songwriter Pete Bellotte (known for his work with Donna Summer on “Hot Stuff,” “I Feel Love” and “Love To Love You Baby”).
Bob McDill, known for country classics like Don Williams’ “Amanda” and Dan Seals’ “Everything That Glitters (Is Not Gold),” is also a returning nominee, having been on the ballot six times in 15 years.
New inductees will join a historic institution
The Songwriters Hall of Fame was established in 1969 to honor those creating popular music. A songwriter with a notable catalog of songs qualifies for induction 20 years after the first commercial release of a song.
Some already in the hall include Elton John and Bernie Taupin, Brian Wilson, James Taylor, Bruce Springsteen, Tom Petty, Carole King, Paul Simon, Billy Joel, Lionel Richie, Bill Withers, Neil Diamond, Phil Collins, R.E.M., Steely Dan, Dean Pitchford, Hillary Lindsey and Timbaland.
The 2026 class included Taylor Swift, Kiss’s Gene Simmons and Paul Stanley, Christopher “Tricky” Stewart, Alanis Morissette and Kenny Loggins as well as nonperformers like the duo Terry Britten and Graham Lyle (Tina Turner’s “What’s Love Got To Do With It”) and Walter Afanasieff, who helped Mariah Carey with her smash “All I Want for Christmas Is You.”
The 2027 inductees will be announced in early 2027.

title: Oxford County sheriff’s race likely headed to recount with 17-vote margin
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
The Oxford County’s sheriff race is likely headed for a recount after only a handful of votes appeared to separate the top two contenders.
Democrat Timothy Holland was just 17 votes ahead of the embattled Republican Sheriff Christopher Wainwright as of midday Thursday, according to incomplete results tallied by the Bangor Daily News. The candidates said that by their own counts, Wainwright is ahead by about 12 votes.
“Every vote counts, and every person matters,” Holland wrote Thursday morning, adding that he would seek a recount.
Neither candidate has heard anything official.
“I have a great deal of respect for Tim Holland, and regardless of the outcome, I am confident that the people of Oxford County will be well served,” Wainwright said Thursday.
Wainwright’s conduct has been the subject of multiple BDN investigations during his tenure. In 2022, he pressured a deputy to dismiss a traffic ticket for an acquaintance. When the deputy reported that pressure, Wainwright berated him on a recorded phone call.
Since 2023, BDN found that Wainwright sent uncertified officers into schools, traded guns and gun parts with little paperwork. A county investigation concluded that likely violated state law. In February 2024, the all-Republican county commission asked Gov. Janet Mills to remove him.
She declined, saying that his conduct was unprofessional but didn’t rise to a standard that would require his removal. She added that voters should ultimately decide his fate.
Wainwright joined the sheriff’s office at 19, and spent decades there. He gained prominence as a whistleblower who helped remove then-Sheriff Wayne Gallant, who was accused of sexually harassing several people.
A robust majority voted against Wainwright, who had just over a third of votes counted by Thursday. Both of his challengers foresaw the possibility of handing Wainwright a plurality victory.
Justin Brown, an independent who received about 30% of the vote, had cooperated with a county investigation into Wainwright’s trade of guns and gun parts that found he had likely broken the law. He filed a complaint with the Maine Human Rights Commission in August, alongside two colleagues.
Holland ran a more positive campaign, he and Wainwright said.
“It’s awesome that people come out and voted the way they did,” Holland said. “After the recount, it’ll be whichever way it goes. We’re satisfied with that.”
Daniel O’Connor is a Report for America corps member who covers rural government as part of the partnership between the Bangor Daily News and The Maine Monitor, with additional support from BDN and Monitor readers.

title: Increasing Clouds This Morning... Scattered Showers & Mild This Afternoon
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Skies will continue to cloud over early this afternoon as a cold front approaches from the west. Scattered showers will move west to east across the state this afternoon. The shower activity is expected to be light with most areas only picking up a couple hundredths of an inch of rain at best. Mild air ahead of the front will allow temperatures to top off in the 60s to near 70°. The cold front will move into the state tonight then stall out near the coast Friday morning. We may see a few showers as the front moves through tonight... especially closer to the coast.
Our Friday will feature mostly cloudy skies on average with the best chance for some sunshine being over northern locales. The aforementioned cold front will be stalled out near the coastline. Low pressure riding northward along the front will bring increasing rain chances to areas closer to... and along... the coast during the afternoon and evening. Areas north of Bangor will see a dry day. Temperatures will remain mild with highs in the 60s Friday afternoon. Rain will spread further inland Friday night as low pressure continues to ride northward along the front. It looks like the rain will be confined to areas along and to the south and east of I-95 with the heaviest rain falling near the coastline. At this point... little to no rain is expected for areas north and west of the interstate. Rain will continue Saturday morning... tapering off from west to east as the low moves to our east. We may see a few scattered showers sticking around Saturday afternoon otherwise expect mostly cloudy skies and drier conditions for the second half of our Saturday. Temperatures will be cooler Saturday with highs in the 50s. Rainfall totals by early Saturday afternoon will range from around .5″-1.5″ Downeast and along the coast with locally higher amounts closer to 2″ possible along the coast. Amounts will quickly taper off to less than .5″ as you head further inland. Little to no rain expected north and west of I-95.
Upper-level energy coming out of the Great Lakes Region Friday night will cause a new area of low pressure to develop near the Mid-Atlantic Region Saturday morning. This new low is forecast to move northward through the Gulf of Maine later Saturday through Saturday night and Sunday morning. The exact track is still a bit uncertain with some of the data bringing the low closer to the coast and some tracking it further offshore. A track closer to the coast would mean a more widespread rainfall whereas a track further offshore would focus the rain over areas south and east of the interstate again. Stay tuned for updates as we get a bit closer. Drier and cooler weather is expected Monday. Upper-level energy moving through could bring a few rain and snow showers to northern locales otherwise expect a mix of sun and clouds with highs in the 40s.
Rest of Today: Turning cloudy with scattered showers possible. Highs between 62°-68°... coolest along the coast. South/southwest wind 5-15 MPH.
Tonight: Partly to mostly cloudy. A few scattered showers possible... mainly closer to the coast. Lows in the 50s. Southwest wind 5-10 MPH.
Friday: Partly to mostly cloudy with rain possible during the afternoon and evening... especially closer to the coast. Highs in the 60s. Light and variable wind.
Saturday: Mostly cloudy with rain likely during the morning... especially along and to the south and east of I-95 then scattered showers possible during the afternoon. Cooler with highs in the 50s.
Sunday: Mostly cloudy with rain likely... mainly during the morning. Highs in the upper 40s to low 50s.
Monday: Mix of sun and clouds. A few rain and snow showers possible across the north. Highs in the 40s.

title: Growing wildfire on Maine border believed to be human-caused
text:
Growing wildfire on Maine border believed to be human-caused
The U.S. Forest Service believes the Wild River Fire that has burned almost 900 acres along the Maine-New Hampshire border was caused by humans; new closure order now in effect.
Growing wildfire on Maine border believed to be human-caused
The U.S. Forest Service believes the Wild River Fire that has burned almost 900 acres along the Maine-New Hampshire border was caused by humans; new closure order now in effect.
The White Mountain National Forest has closed trails and roads near the Wild River Fire along the Maine-New Hampshire border, where the fire has burned 856 acres as of Thursday morning.
According to the U.S. Forest Service, the fire is still only 11% contained. Dry conditions and persistent drought are contributing to the fire's growth.
The fire is burning in Coos County, about 7 miles southeast of Gorham and about 1 mile west of the Maine-New Hampshire border. Smoke may be visible in the surrounding communities and could be having an impact on air quality.
The new closure order prohibits people from entering the affected area to preserve access for firefighters and other emergency personnel.
It includes all of Shelburne Trail and Wild River Road, along with sections of High Water Trail and other trails. The Forest Service has posted the closure order and map on its Wild River Fire information page.
More firefighting crews are planning to head to the area on Thursday, in addition to the 90 personnel, helicopters and drones already deployed.
“I am proud of the firefighters who responded quickly and continue to work tirelessly to contain the Wild River Fire,” said Josh Sjostrom, District Ranger for the White Mountain National Forest’s Androscoggin Ranger District in a news release. “We will continue to work with our neighbors, and local and state partners to contain this fire.”
The cause of the fire is under investigation, but officials believe it was caused by humans. Officials at the U.S. Forest Service are reminding people to practice campfire safety and never leave a campfire unattended and to make sure the fire is completely out.
Community members are now being invited to attend a public meeting Thursday night from 6-7 p.m. at the Shelburne, New Hampshire Town Hall to receive the latest information about the Wild River Fire.

title: ‘A beautifully American story’: Abdul El-Sayed’s historic Senate victory resonates with Muslim Americans
text:
DEARBORN, Mich. (AP) — Campaigning relentlessly across Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed didn’t highlight the possibility that he could become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. But with victory in hand, he savored his triumph over the vitriol aimed at him and his fellow Muslim Americans.
“They tried to demonize people because of how they pray,” he told The Associated Press on Wednesday. “And Michigan — the whole Michigan — clapped back. People don’t want that. They’re sick of it.”
He showed his pride in his victory speech, declaring: “My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed.”
Twenty-five years after the Sept. 11 attacks and their aftermath yanked anti-Muslim sentiment into the forefront of American life, those emotions are shared by many Muslim Americans in Michigan and across the country.
They saw a surge of anti-Muslim rhetoric after Zohran Mamdani’s election as New York City mayor a year ago, and they saw the attacks intensify as El-Sayed became the new prime target. President Donald Trump called him a “jihadist” who was “on the side of the terrorists.” Dozens of Trump’s fellow Republicans in Congress formed a Sharia-Free America Caucus, depicting Islam’s religious code as a threat to the U.S. Constitution.
But now, after El-Sayed’s defeat of GOP rival Mike Rogers was confirmed early Wednesday, there is a pervasive sense that a broader victory is at hand.
The outcome “represents a historic turning point for American Muslim political engagement and a historic defeat for the politics of hate,” said Nihad Awad, national executive director of the Council on American-Islamic Relations.
“Anti-Muslim extremists, Israel lobby groups and even the president of the United States used every smear in the book to paint Dr. El-Sayed as a Muslim boogeyman,” he said. “None of it was true, and none of it worked. Anti-Muslim hate was on the ballot, and it failed.”
In Dearborn, talk of ‘a beautifully American story’
Excitement over El-Sayed’s victory was palpable in Dearborn, a city near Detroit with a sizable Arab American population. The mayor, Abdullah Hammoud, said residents showed up at the ballot box in huge numbers.
“What a beautifully American story,” Hammoud said. “One of our brightest and best earned the support of the majority of Michiganders who participated in yesterday’s election. And regardless of the direction in which he prays, they’re sending him to the U.S. Senate.”
Hammoud, who has known El-Sayed for more than a decade, said although his win was important for many Arab Americans, people voted for him because of his platform, not his identity. He cited support in Dearborn for independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders’ 2016 presidential campaign. Sanders, who is Jewish and caucuses with Democrats, ran on a progressive platform.
U.S. SENATE BALANCE OF POWER
In El-Sayed, residents of Dearborn “finally saw themselves and a candidate who appealed to them, but it had to do with far more than just his ethnicity or his religion,” Hammoud said. “It was honestly because of the policies and building a coalition with this community in an honest way.”
When Zaynah Jadallah, 26, canvassed for El-Sayed in Dearborn, she said most people told her they already planned on voting for him before inviting her in for water or food. She credited the name recognition to El-Sayed’s grassroots campaigning and his pride in his Egyptian heritage.
“He’s always been proud of his identity. He never shied away from it or from saying his name,” Jadallah said.
Yasmin El-Sayed, no relation to the senator-elect, took her two daughters to the Detroit watch party from New York. She teared up after the victory speech.
“Having grown up in a post-9/11 world, being Muslim, being Arab myself, never in a million years did I think we would see what we saw today,” she said.
In a time of suspicion of government, a message of representation
El-Sayed depicted his election as a victory for all those “who don’t see themselves reflected in our government or who’ve been told that they don’t belong for some reason or another — not just how they pray but who they love, how they identify, the color of their skin, where they grew up.″
“I didn’t run to be the first Muslim senator. I ran to be the next senator of the state of Michigan who happens to be Muslim,” he said. ″But I also know that democracy is constantly about the conversation about who we are, who we want to be.”
“Michigan proved just how big we are. Rejected a hateful, spiteful campaign that had nothing to say about the issues and only wanted to point to my name and my face,” he added. ″I want all of those folks out there who have been told that America’s not big enough for them to reflect on that. America really is big enough for all of us.”
Mohamed Gula, CEO of the Muslim American advocacy group Emgage Action, said he was elated by El-Sayed’s triumph after a year of “extremely Islamophobic and disgusting rhetoric being used as a campaign strategy.”
“For Abdul to come out last night and use his full name meant the world to someone who grew up in post-9/11 America, where the Muslim American community was seen through a national security lens,” Gula said.
“Our children, years from now, will be able to run for office,” he said, ”to be seen as who they are.”
A debate over the place of Sharia law — and its very definition
Among the most frequent targets of anti-Muslim rhetoric was Sharia, the religious code that provides Muslims with guidance on how to lead righteous lives. At the Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas, some of the loudest cheers came after GOP Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas declared: “Sharia law has no place in America.”
Muslim American civic leaders and scholars — in Texas and other states — responded forcefully to the anti-Sharia rhetoric that dates back more than 15 years.
They passionately defended Sharia — the way it’s practiced in the United States — as positive guidance that shares elements with the codes of other faiths, such as the Ten Commandments and the collective body of Jewish law derived from the Torah. They rebutted the claims of GOP critics that Sharia is a coercive code that threatens the Constitution and the judicial system.
Gula noted that Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott and Attorney General Ken Paxton were among the leaders of the anti-Sharia campaign. Abbott lost his bid for reelection in Tuesday’s voting, and Paxton was trounced by Democrat James Talarico in the race for a U.S. Senate seat.
“I saw this as not just Muslims standing against Islamophobia as never before,” Gula said. “I saw Americans saying hate will not be used as a campaign issue ... we are not going to accept hate.”
Asma Uddin, a professor at Michigan State University’s College of Law, has argued that many American politicians are depicting ordinary Muslim religious practices — such as prayer, choice of apparel, family counseling and mosque attendance — as evidence of political danger.
“What I find especially exciting is that El-Sayed won in a political climate where being visibly Muslim can still be a liability,” she said. His victory “gives us real reason for optimism. It suggests that anti-Muslim attacks don’t necessarily carry the political weight that those deploying them assume they do.”

title: After GOP midterm debacle, Trump is left to weigh his next move in Iran war
text:
WASHINGTON — As he takes stock of his Republican Party’s midterm drubbing, President Donald Trump now faces the difficult question of what to do about his unpopular 8-month-old war against Iran.
For weeks, Trump has threatened to return to a full-scale bombardment of Iran once the U.S. elections were in the rearview mirror if Tehran did not come to a settlement under terms acceptable to him.
In his first comments Wednesday after Democrats’ resounding election victory — a wave powered in part by the American electorate’s dissatisfaction with the war — Trump largely agreed with Vice President JD Vance, who publicly ruminated on the war being a catastrophe for Republicans.
“It’s largely true because it drove gasoline up a little bit,” Trump said. Still, he doubled down on his decision to launch the conflict despite its big political cost. “At the same time, if I had to do it again, I’d do it again,” he said.
The strikes, and counterstrikes, have caused tens of billions of dollars of damage in the region. And the conflict has reached into the pocketbook of families around the globe with elevated gas prices and rising costs in just about every sector.
Now, as Trump ponders his next move, the stakes couldn’t be higher for Iran, the Middle East and the global economy writ large.
Trump may be less restrained, but the conflict is now more complicated
While oil is flowing again from the Strait of Hormuz with the help of U.S. Navy escorts for international tankers, the conflict has spread to the Red Sea with Iran-backed Houthi rebels and a Saudi Arabia -led coalition fighting it out.
The situation in the Red Sea remains particularly volatile. The Houthis are attacking Yemeni civilians and Saudi infrastructure, and are looking to bolster ties with militant groups across the Horn of Africa.
The attacks by the Yemen-based Houthis on areas controlled by the internationally recognized Yemeni government have also worsened a growing humanitarian crisis.
The threat that the region faces from Iran and its proxy groups, noted a senior Yemeni government official, “did not change overnight” with the U.S. elections, urging Washington to avoid hasty decisions. The official was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the basis of anonymity.
“There’s reason to suspect that Trump may feel less restrained given that the political damage is done,” said Brian Haggerty, a former senior analyst at the Central Intelligence Agency who focused on Middle East security issues. “At the same time, the strategic calculus or the strategic logic of what you hope to achieve through an escalation of strikes against Iran is no different today than it was a week ago or a month ago.”
Trump has at least a few options, analysts say
Haggerty, who now works with Defense Priorities, a Washington think tank, said Trump could choose to maintain something close to the current posture, with the U.S. military carrying out what it calls “defensive strikes” while continuing its naval blockade to restrict the flow of Iranian oil to the global market.
Another option is striking Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to its nuclear program that is buried deep underground in central Iran, said David Schenker, who served as assistant secretary of state for Near Eastern affairs in Trump’s first term. Trump has repeatedly suggested he was considering targeting the site.
Schenker said Trump could then walk away and contend he had done sufficient damage to Iran’s nuclear program — and perhaps try to pursue a “fig leaf agreement” that restores freedom of navigation to the Strait of Hormuz, offers Iran some degree of sanctions relief, and punts additional nuclear talks to the future.
Yet another option would be to follow up on threats Trump made earlier in the war to launch massive attacks on Iranian infrastructure. “The Iranians may believe the president is wounded and constrained by Congress, but the opposite can also be true,” Schenker said.
But such escalation would likely exacerbate the oil and energy price problem that many voters cited as a reason for supporting Democrats on Tuesday, Schenker said.
The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil tumbled below $95 on Wednesday after the election, touching its lowest level in two months, a signal that markets do not expect major strikes.
Regional officials are on high alert for what Trump does next
Middle East officials had been hanging on Trump’s every word in the weeks leading up to the U.S. elections, looking for clues on how the Republican leader was weighing his next steps.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pressed for renewed strikes on Iran during a call over the weekend with Trump, who would not commit to taking military action, according to a person who was briefed on it.
Three Middle Eastern government officials said Wednesday that Trump and his administration had seemed to be signaling to Iran that its leverage would only diminish after the U.S. elections were over.
Administration officials had privately suggested in diplomatic channels that Trump might be more willing to restart strikes after Nov. 3 because he’d have little left to lose politically, according to the officials, who were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
After Tuesday’s electoral shellacking, there was lingering concern that Trump might be more emboldened to carry out full-scale or new limited strikes against Iran, the officials said.
A fourth official said the results of the election gave mediators a measure of optimism about finding a pathway to resolving the conflict.
Meanwhile, Vance appeared to more forcefully pin the electoral debacle on the Iran war than his boss Trump, who initially blamed the GOP’s candidates for the big loss.
“The reason we lost,” Vance said of the midterm elections in a lengthy social media post, “is the war.”
Vance, a potential 2028 presidential contender, had been among the most skeptical inside the White House on the wisdom of launching the war but got on board with Trump’s decision once he made it.
Voter data shows Iran had an impact but was not the top issue
Several Democratic candidates who scored upsets Tuesday noted voter discontent with the Iran war in their victory speeches.
“Wherever I went, I heard the same thing,” said Sen.-elect Josh Turek of Iowa. “They would say, Josh, I’m struggling just to keep food on the table, keep a roof above my head, pay my electric bill. And with this war in Iran, I’m struggling just to keep gas in my tank.”
About 6 in 10 voters said the U.S. made the “wrong decision” in taking military action against Iran, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 voters in the United States.
Most of those voters dissatisfied with the Iran war backed the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race, but the survey suggested the Iran war was not the top issue for most voters.
Only about one-third of voters said the war in Iran was “crucial” to shaping how they voted for Congress. That was well below the roughly half who said that about the cost of living or government corruption.
Nearly all voters who backed the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race said going to war with Iran was the “wrong decision,” while roughly 8 in 10 voters who backed the Republican candidate said it was the “right decision.”
Meanwhile, about 6 in 10 voters nationally said they were “very concerned” about the cost of gasoline and diesel, the poll showed — and about two-thirds of that group voted for the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race.
But Trump, for his part, said even in hindsight he’d approach Iran exactly as he has.
“I can tell you that as far as that war is concerned I would have done nothing different,” the president said.
Story by Aamer Madhani, Linley Sanders, Samy Magdy and Matthew Lee.

title: Dunlap concedes, Maine's 2nd Congressional district race still goes to ranked choice
text:
Dunlap concedes, 2nd Congressional district race still goes to ranked choice
Two hours after the Maine Secretary of State's Office announced the race between Matt Dunlap and Paul LePage would go to ranked choice, Dunlap conceded. The race still has to go to tabulation.
Dunlap concedes, 2nd Congressional district race still goes to ranked choice
Two hours after the Maine Secretary of State's Office announced the race between Matt Dunlap and Paul LePage would go to ranked choice, Dunlap conceded. The race still has to go to tabulation.
Democrat Matt Dunlap has conceded to Paul LePage in the race for Maine's 2nd Congressional district.
The concession came just about two hours after the Secretary of State's Office announced the race was going to a ranked choice tabulation.
Under the state's current ranked choice voting law, a tabulation is automatically triggered if a candidate does not reach 50% plus one vote regardless of concession.
"Someone could leave the first choice blank and pick a second choice as a protest. It is unlikely, but it can happen," Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said. "It is permissible under the law. And so that's why we can't automatically eliminate those blanks under the current ranked choice voting statute. "
According to the Secretary of State's Office, LePage received 49.894% and Dunlap received 48.307%; 0.036% were write-ins and 1.763% of ballots were left blank.
Therefore, LePage was just short of the 50% needed because blank ballots are included in the total votes and therefore factored into percentages of votes.
Bellows said this has happened in the past in this district multiple times, including just two years ago.
"Jared Golden was leading on election night. There were some, there were a significant number of blanks over 9,000 blanks in that race, plus just over 500 write-in votes in that race," she said.
The blanks did not change the outcome of that race.
LePage will likely join Sen. Angus King, Senator-Elect Troy Jackson and Congresswoman Chellie Pingree as part of Maine's Congressional delegation.
"I congratulate him. Look forward to working with him. Obviously, I was a supporter of Matt Dunlap, and I think [he] ran a great campaign, worked very hard, but the voters have decided it was a tight race. And Paul LePage has a lot of experience in government. It's going to be a very, very challenging time in Washington, and I look forward to meeting with him soon," Pingree said.
Ranked choice tabulation begins on Monday at 10 a.m.

title: Trump administration held talks with Iran on deporting Iranians during the war, court documents show
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Court documents reveal President Donald Trump’s administration held secret talks with Iran about deporting Iranians during the ongoing war.
The court documents unsealed Thursday show the Republican administration as recently as mid-October said it had plans to deport the Iranians through an unnamed third country, although it was unclear when it intended to do so. The judge in the case ordered the government to give the court 24-hour notice of any finalized plans to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country and five days’ written notice before any such deportation is carried out.
The documents show that the administration maintained contacts with Iranian officials during the war over the removals, specifically for submitting travel documents and figuring out “possible avenues for removal.”
“We are at war with a country where the President of the United States has said, as recently as two or three days ago, if not yesterday, that it is essentially lawless ... A country that is an enemy of the United States, according to the current president. A country that, according to our president, murdered tens of thousands of protestors,” Judge Ana Reyes said according to the Oct. 15 transcript.
“And what you’re telling me is that the United States of America is going to send individuals back to that region, facing what you and I and everyone who would ever look at this would know would be, at a minimum, a serious threat of certain death.”
“Yes, your honor,” Justice Department attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel said. “The government is executing lawful orders of removal.”
The Department of Homeland Security had no immediate comment.
The development emerged from an ongoing lawsuit that alleges the Trump administration’s immigration agencies have been sharing confidential information about Iranian asylum seekers with the Iranian government, violating national immigration regulations and endangering countless Iranians, court filings argue.
The new court documents show the coordination continued during the war.
The lawsuit depicts a coordinated campaign between the U.S. and Iranian governments to identify Iranians in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody and pressure them to return to Iran — a marked departure from decades of diplomatic hostility between the two governments and an ongoing war. DHS has denied that it is sharing asylum application records with the Iranian government.
Hundreds of emails exchanged between U.S. immigration officials exposed how the two countries worked together to arrange for more than 100 Iranians to be flown back to Iran on three immigration flights in September and December 2025 and January 2026.
Deportations of Iranians back to their home country are historically rare, owing to the lack of diplomatic relations between the U.S. and Iran and the possible persecution they could face if they were sent to Iran.
But under the Trump administration, ICE has aggressively pushed to deport people even from countries that have typically been reluctant to take people back or with whom the U.S. has had icy or no diplomatic relations.
Sometimes that has meant sending people back to their home country but it has also meant deporting people to other countries that they have no connection with.
The Trump administration has deported people, including Iranians, to countries other than their own in an attempt to circumvent diplomatic hurdles with governments that won’t take their people back. During Trump’s second term, countries including El Salvador, Costa Rica and Panama have accepted noncitizens from the U.S.
In June, an Iranian woman was among the two dozen migrants the U.S. deported to the Central African Republic.
Activists abroad have expressed concern about deportees returning to Iran, whose theocracy has been cracking down on intellectuals and where the government vociferously cracks down on any dissent.

title: Recount expected as Wainwright leads by 12 votes in Oxford County sheriff’s race
text:
By a razor-thin margin, Timothy Holland has beaten incumbent Christopher Wainwright in the race for Oxford County sheriff.
With nearly 30,000 votes cast, the final tally gave Democrat Holland, 69, a 68-vote victory over the Republican Wainwright, 55, who was seeking his third term. Justin Brown, 47, an unenrolled candidate from Hartford, finished third.
“We ran everything up front, clean and very open to everyone and we prevailed,” Holland said by phone Thursday night.
Reached Thursday evening, Wainwright said he is committed to a smooth transition and will do what he can help the sheriff’s office. “I have called to congratulate him and wish him the best,” he said. He is not pursuing a recount.
Speaking after the election as the results came in, Wainwright said, “I have a great deal of respect for Tim Holland, and regardless of the outcome, I am confident the people of Oxford County will be well served. Our shared commitment has always been to the citizens of this county, and that remains my focus.”
The three candidates have 107 years of law enforcement experience combined: Wainwright, 36; Holland, who is a Paris police patrolman, school resource officer and former Oxford County Sheriff’s Office supervisor, 45-plus; and Brown, an Oxford County deputy, 26.
All three candidates cited finances, public trust, and accountability as their top issues during their campaigns.
They all stressed the need for careful budget management, reducing unnecessary costs, and using taxpayer’ resources efficiently. They also acknowledge the need to address department staffing, improve recruitment and retention of deputies and corrections officers, and rebuild internal morale and teamwork.
Wainwright beat Brown to retain his sheriff position in 2022.
Brown is one of three Oxford County deputies to file complaints against Wainwright for alleged retaliation after he reported what he said was unlawful or improper conduct by Wainwright and he cooperated with a county-ordered investigation that led county commissioners to petition Gov. Janet Mills for Wainwright’s removal in February 2024.
Referring to the complaints, which are currently before the Maine Human Rights Commission, Wainwright said in October he is “confident that the facts will speak for themselves through the process.”
Regarding the petition to Mills, she appointed retired Maine Supreme Court Justice Donald Alexander to investigate. Alexander recommended against removal, finding that the actions did not violate state laws or a code of ethics to the level required.
In other contested races Tuesday in Oxford County, former Sheriff Lloyd “Skip” Herrick, a Republican from Paris, won the District 3 seat on the county board of commissioners over challenger Janet Jamison, a Democrat from South Paris.
In the Oxford County treasurer’s race, Christopher Davis, a Republican from Oxford, beat Savannah Sessions of Lovell, who is unenrolled.

title: Putin special envoy speaks at White House event on Oleshky ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Russian President Vladimir Putin’s envoy appeared with first lady Melania Trump at the White House on Thursday as she brought together Russian and Ukrainian officials to mark the localized ceasefire she brokered between their nations.
Speaking at the invitation of the first lady, Kirill Dmitriev thanked Trump for her “distinguished humanitarian role” in securing the ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. President Donald Trump did not appear.
Dmitriev added that Putin personally gave instructions as part of the operation and sent his thanks to Melania Trump. The event included officials from Russia and Ukraine to honor the ceasefire, which was signed Oct. 23.
The head of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s party and Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Davyd Arakhamiia, also spoke at the event.
Trump said that she hoped the suspension of hostilities in the ravaged, Russian-occupied Ukrainian village of Oleshky can lead to something more enduring than the six day ceasefire.
“What matters is not the modesty of this beginning but the determination to turn into something extraordinary,” she said.
The White House announced Oct. 23 that the first lady had brokered a ceasefire in the ravaged, Russian-occupied Ukrainian village of Oleshky so that humanitarian aid can be delivered and civilians can be evacuated from a place she said was “on the brink of disaster.”
The announcement came after Ukrainian, Russian and U.S. negotiators had reached an agreement to deliver relief to Oleshky in the war-divided region of Kherson in southern Ukraine.
The local ceasefire was in effect from Oct. 27 to Nov. 1 and amounted to the most significant truce since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine 4½ years ago.
An estimated 2,000 people remained in Oleshky when the temporary truce took hold on Oct. 27, lasting for six days before ending on Nov. 1. They were offered the choice of evacuating to territory controlled by Ukraine or Russia, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.
During the pause in hostilities, residents of Oleshky crossed into Ukrainian-held territory in a major evacuation operation. Evacuees wrapped in blue and yellow Ukrainian flags stepped off buses at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border and reunited with family members.
Ukrainian authorities have not said how many residents were evacuated from Oleshky and have restricted details of their route to protect those who remained and safeguard future humanitarian missions. Melania Trump said on social media that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.

title: 'The day has come': Cristiano Ronaldo announces retirement from international soccer
text:
'The day has come': Cristiano Ronaldo announces retirement from international soccer
Cristiano Ronaldo has announced his retirement from international soccer after a record-breaking career with Portugal.
The 41-year-old broke the news on Thursday in a long Instagram video where he read a letter to his supporters.
“The day has come for me to hand back the number 7 shirt of our national team,” he said, referring to his iconic shirt number.
“I never thought it belonged to me alone. But for 23 years, I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it.”
Related video: Lionel Messi plays his last match for Argentina's national team
Ronaldo played a record 234 times for his country, scoring a record 146 international goals.
The highlight of his international career came in 2016 when he lifted the European Championship trophy for his country. He also helped Portugal to victory in the UEFA Nations League in 2019 and 2025.
Despite all his success, though, his relationship with the national team has slowly soured over the last few years –in large part because of his declining performances on the field.
Despite age clearly catching up with him, Ronaldo continued starting despite his impact waning and fans began to grow frustrated.
After this summer’s World Cup in North America, the striker then clashed with new head coach Jorge Jesus and stormed out of a national team training camp last month.
Ronaldo’s announcement comes shortly after rival Lionel Messi also retired from playing international soccer with Argentina.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

title: Residents vote to keep Ashland Police Department
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Ashland’s police department isn’t going anywhere, residents decided Thursday.
Voters chose 154-73 to keep the department open in a special town meeting that drew about 225 people.
The meeting followed a Wednesday hearing that lasted more than two hours, during which residents largely supported the police department but also favored lower taxes.
The decision means the eight-member force that serves the town of about 1,200 people will remain a full-time police department, and officials will seek other ways to save money.
“I’m glad that the voice of the people was heard, and we know what direction they want us to go,” Ashland Town Council Chair Sherri Calhoun said after the meeting.
Thursday’s meeting started 23 minutes late due to the large crowd registering.
Moderator Jordan Beaulier suggested and residents approved a secret ballot rather than a verbal vote because of the crowd’s size.
The warrant read: “To see if the town will vote to continue operating a municipal police department effective January 1, 2027.” A yes vote would mean keeping the force and a no vote would disband it, Beaulier said.
Voting lasted about 20 minutes. Many applauded when Beaulieu read the tally.
The possibility of cutting police services arose during an Oct. 19 Town Council meeting, when the group discussed residents’ property tax concerns. The group slated a public hearing, which was held Wednesday and also drew a sizable crowd.
For the council, it isn’t a question of whether the town needs police, but whether residents feel they can pay for it amid other important items such as ambulance service and road maintenance, Calhoun told the crowd at the hearing.
“The council recognizes the important role that the Ashland Police Department plays in our community,” she said. “At the same time, we have a responsibility to examine the cost of providing services.”
Residents shared concerns Wednesday about the town’s declining population and their tax bills. Some said they had moved to Ashland for its small-town feel, reduced crime and the fact that it has a police department.
The department’s closure would have transferred policing services to the combined coverage of the Maine State Police and Aroostook County Sheriff’s Office, who have also taken up duties for the other three nearby departments that have closed.
In the last six years, five small Maine towns have dissolved police forces, largely because of recruiting difficulties. Millinocket closed in 2020, followed by Van Buren in 2021, Limestone in 2023, Washburn in 2024 and Mexico last year.
Deputies and state troopers have divided The County into six zones. Each organization takes on three zones for a month and then they switch.
Response times for both agencies average about 30 minutes, Sheriff Peter Johnson and State Police Lt. Brian Harris said at Wednesday’s hearing.  
Ashland’s operation includes Montpetit, two full-time and five reserve officers.
As people offered him handshakes and hugs after the vote, Montpetit said he felt “really good.”
“It was humbling seeing this many people show up for this, and it was humbling seeing the positive effect that we’ve had on this community,” he said. “And I look forward to another year.”

title: LePage claims win in uncalled Maine 2nd District race
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - While the race for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District has not been officially called by the Associated Press, one candidate has declared victory.
Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage made the announcement Wednesday afternoon, saying he was confident he had beaten Democrat Matt Dunlap.
“Public numbers have us up about 4,000, and the team has been calling all the towns that haven’t come in yet, and there’s no path to victory for my opponent,” LePage said. “We’re very, very pleased for the outcome. Looking forward to going to Washington and doing what I said I was going to do is work for the Maine people.”
LePage was joined by family, campaign workers, supporters and public officials in celebrating the declared victory.
“This is something that I was looking forward to, and I know a lot of my constituents were looking forward to,” said Rep. Jim Thorne, who represents Carmel and Hermon. “He has an open dialogue with the President of the United States, which bodes well for Maine and some of the things that we want to accomplish.”
In the wake of a cross-country blue wave, this was the only seat in the nation to be flipped by a Republican.
When it comes to working in a now Democratic-majority Congress, LePage said: “If it helps Maine, I’m all in. If it hurts Maine, I’m all out. And I will work with anybody to help make this country a better country.”
Thorne cited LePage’s history as governor and the large conservative base in the 2nd Congressional District as reasons the race was an outlier nationally.
Sofia Pride, 19, who is part of the University of Maine College Republicans club, also pointed to volunteer field work.
“Quite a few of our members volunteered for them and people were really into doing the door knocking and connecting with voters and everything and they just obviously did such a great job and it’s really exciting for them.”
While LePage declared an early victory, Dunlap said the contest remains too close to call.
“Maine has the most reliable elections staff in the world, and I want to thank them as they diligently finish the count,” Dunlap said in a statement. “This race is very close and there are plenty of ballots left to count. Thank you to every volunteer who worked their heart out on this campaign and thank you to every voter. We’ll have more to say as we learn more.”
As of 5 p.m. Wednesday with an estimate 91.7% of votes in, LePage holds 50.3% of the vote with Dunlap at 49.7%.
