title: California governor says he'll commute all 548 death sentences in state
text:
California governor says he'll commute all 548 death sentences in state to life without parole
California Gov. Gavin Newsom said Thursday that he’ll change more than 500 death sentences in the state to life in prison without the possibility of parole, though the state Supreme Court will have the final say in hundreds of those cases.
“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” Newsom said in a public letter.
Newsom’s decision comes as he prepares to leave office after eight years and considers a run for president. The Democrat, who’s long been opposed to the death penalty, placed a moratorium on executions in California in 2019.
Related video above: Newsom says he will commute all death sentences in California to life without possibility of parole
His latest move came after he realized “the limits of what government can justly accomplish,” he said.
Newsom moved to grant clemency to 548 people currently sentenced to death in California, of whom 529 are men and 19 are women, according to numbers provided by his office.
The state constitution requires the California Supreme Court’s approval to grant clemency to anyone convicted of a felony more than once, which means the court would have to approve 382 of those commutations, or roughly 70%, according to Newsom's office.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Newsom’s action represents the largest mass clemency in American history. If they are all approved, it would reduce the U.S. death row population by nearly 30%, the center said.
California voters upheld the death penalty
Americans have long been divided over the death penalty. Nearly half of U.S. states have banned capital punishment outright, but executions are still carried out routinely around the country. On Thursday alone, Florida, Alabama and Indiana carried out lethal injections.
Californians voted to uphold the death penalty in 2012 and 2016 ballot measures. No one has been executed in the state since 2006 and California has the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.
Among the most notorious convicted killers on California’s death row are Richard Allen Davis, who kidnapped and murdered 12-year-old Polly Klaas in 1993, and Randy Kraft, the so-called “Scorecard Killer” who kept a list of his 16 victims in the 1970s and ’80s. Other prominent killers, including Scott Peterson and the Manson family members, received death sentences that were later commuted to life in prison.
Jess Nichol, Klaas' sister, said she previously believed Davis deserved the death penalty, but her views evolved.
“The system tells survivors that execution matters to our healing,” Nichol said in a statement. “It doesn’t. It’s a distraction from what we actually need.”
The American Civil Liberties Union, which has said the implementation of the death penalty reflects racial bias, applauded the announcement.
“These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long,” Executive Director Anthony Romero said in a statement.
The ACLU is involved in an ongoing legal challenge to California’s death penalty statute, alleging it is racially discriminatory and unconstitutional.
Victims' groups and prosecutors decry the decision
Patricia Wenskunas, founder of the California advocacy nonprofit Crime Survivors, which opposed the abolition of the death penalty, criticized Newsom's decision.
“My heart hurts for every one of the victims and every one of their family members,” she said, calling the decision “offensive” and “outrageous.”
Steve Herr, whose son Sam Herr was murdered along with his friend Julie Kibuishi by Daniel Wozniak in 2010, said he was “absolutely disgusted” by the governor's decision. He said the death of his son's killer would have meant closure.
“When somebody commits such a heinous crime, they do not deserve to live,” Herr said. “To hear what Newsom just did … he’s just an outright coward.”
The California District Attorneys Association condemned the decision. Last month, the group sent a letter to Newsom expressing “grave concerns” about him considering the move and warning that such a sweeping action would inflict additional pain on victims’ relatives.
“With the stroke of a pen, Governor Newsom has disregarded the decisions of hundreds of jurors and judges, and the anguish of families who lost loved ones to the worst crimes imaginable,” CDAA President Jeannine M. Pacioni said in a statement. “The victims were never given a commutation. Their families were never given a choice. They deserve far better than this.”
San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow called the move a “sickening abuse of power.”
Dow referenced Rachel Newhouse and Aundria Crawford, two women who were kidnapped, raped and murdered by Rex Allan Krebs in 1999, and Kesha Gurke, a 19-month-old girl tortured and murdered by Michael Whisenhunt in 1995.
“San Luis Obispo County juries sentenced both men to death. A unanimous California Supreme Court affirmed both judgments. Their families have waited decades for the State of California to keep its word. Today, the Governor broke it,” Dow said.
Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer also condemned the decision, calling it “mercy for the wolves and while inflicting the ultimate act of cruelty on the sheep.”
Other governors have taken similar actions
Newsom has said in the past that it is wrong for the government to kill its citizens and that capital punishment in practice has discriminated against mentally ill people and people of color.
Other governors have granted broad clemency to all death row prisoners in their states, including Gov. Kate Brown in Oregon in 2022 and Gov. Jared Polis in Colorado in 2020. Both are Democrats. In 1986, then-New Mexico Gov. Toney Anaya, a Democrat, commuted the death sentences of all five inmates then on death row.
In 2024, President Joe Biden also granted clemency to 37 out of 40 federal prisoners sentenced to death.
Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who will take over from Newsom in January, has said he will extend the state’s moratorium on the death penalty.

title: 3 people have been injured in a shooting at an Iowa post office
text:
DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — A suspect was in custody in Des Moines, Iowa, Thursday after two people were shot at the city’s main post office and a third was injured trying to escape, authorities said. None of the injuries were believed to be life-threatening, police said.
“They’re all at the hospital, they are being cared for right now,” Sgt. Paul Parizek said of the victims.
Parizek said officers responded within three minutes. The shooting happened on the second floor of the post office and reports started coming in of shots fired around 9:10 a.m. local time.
The main post office is just north of downtown Des Moines and across the street from one of the city’s main hospitals. The building is a four-story regional sorting facility with a walk-in service counter accessible to the public.
The Associated Press has several phone calls out seeking more information.
Gov. Kim Reynolds said she’s in contact with the Department of Public Safety regarding the shooting.
“The suspected shooter is in custody and the investigation is ongoing,” she posted online. “We are monitoring the situation and our prayers are with everyone involved. Grateful for the immediate response by law enforcement.”
Des Moines Public Schools said that after being notified by police at 9:20 a.m. of the shooting at the post office, the district’s nearby elementary school, welcome center and nutrition center went into a secure status, meaning no one was allowed in or out of the buildings. The district said the secure status was lifted after police notified them at 10 a.m. that a suspect was in custody.

title: After taking control of Congress, Democrats vow major probes into Trump’s ‘tentacles of corruption’
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Corruption topped the list of concerns for voters who ousted Republicans and handed Democrats control of Congress in the midterm elections. Now, the newly empowered Democratic Party is putting the issue front and center as its leaders chart their course for investigations and policymaking.
Senior Democrats in both chambers of Congress have vowed to marshal the subpoena powers and larger investigative staffs that come with their soon-to-be majorities to probe what they say is the self-enrichment that President Donald Trump and people in his orbit have done at the public’s expense. The Republican president and his White House have long denied any wrongdoing.
House Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda to look at how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office — and Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who’s in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Trump for a third time.
Months ago, Jeffries tasked the ranking Democrats on the Oversight and Judiciary committees, Rep. Robert Garcia of California and Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, with leading the effort, as Democrats work to link the costs of public corruption to the affordability concerns hitting Americans’ pocketbooks.
“Lawyer up,” Garcia posted on X as election results favoring Democrats began coming in on Tuesday night.
The Senate is expected to conduct similar investigations.
“Americans want us to clean up corruption in government,” said Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., who is poised to return as Senate majority leader next year. “No American should have to make tradeoffs at the supermarket while Trump is making inside trades on the stock market.”
Investigation targets could include ICE raids, Epstein and DOGE
Garcia, the top Democrat on the Oversight and Government Reform Committee, has outlined five priorities, including Trump family business dealings, the administration’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations. Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the ranking Democrat on the Natural Resources Committee, said he wants to dig into Trump’s White House ballroom and other construction projects, as well as the Trump family’s role in mineral deals.
With the House majority comes an infusion of congressional committee staff and resources, and the effort is expected to be sprawling, involving House committees with authority to conduct oversight on Cabinet officials and the agencies they lead.
In the Senate, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., who is expected to become the chairman of the Homeland Security Committee’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, said his panel will want to look into Trump’s real estate projects around the nation’s capital and his crypto dealings with special envoy Steve Witkoff. Witkoff is a longtime ally who partnered with Trump on the president’s family cryptocurrency venture, World Liberty Financial.
“The tentacles of corruption reach deep in this administration, and they have added costs to everyday Americans,” Blumenthal said in an interview with The Associated Press on Wednesday. The senator added that he also wants hearings on ICE raids, the actions of the Department of Government Efficiency and Medicare plans he says are too restrictive and have cost some patients care.
Meanwhile, Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, who is in line to become Senate Finance Committee chairman, ticked off several investigative targets that he describes as part of an “accountability” agenda, including banks that he contends ignored red flags about the financial dealings of Epstein and pharmaceutical companies that have profited from their ties to the Trump administration.
“When I am chair, they will be forced to answer to the Senate Finance Committee for their role in hurting the American people and enabling Trump’s corruption,” Wyden said in a statement Wednesday.
The issue of corruption resonated for voters, The AP Voter Poll shows
Many U.S. voters in Tuesday’s elections expressed deep concerns about government corruption and the state of democracy, according to The AP Voter Poll, which surveyed more than 100,000 voters nationwide.
While roughly 4 in 10 voters said the economy was the top issue facing the country, about 3 in 10 said that “the state of democracy” was the top issue. About half of U.S. voters said government corruption was “crucial” to their vote for Congress, and most of those voters supported the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race, while about one-third said they voted for the Republican.
About 8 in 10 voters who said “the state of democracy” was the top issue facing the country supported the Democrat, while about 2 in 10 supported the Republican.
Older voters, those age 65 or older, were more likely than voters under 65 to say “the state of democracy” was the most important issue facing the country. About 4 in 10 older voters pointed to this as the nation’s top problem, compared with about 3 in 10 who said the economy. That view was reversed with younger voters, who were more likely to call the economy the top issue.
That explains why anti-corruption played such a central role in Democratic campaigns this cycle, with candidates accusing their Republican opponents of looking out for themselves or their donors rather than a broader constituency. They embraced stock trading bans and bans on former members of Congress becoming lobbyists and promised to be part of an effort to root out corruption.
Democrats’ challenge: Focusing on corruption without ignoring cost-of-living issues
In his public comments since his party lost the elections, Trump has taken a conciliatory tone toward Democrats, conceding that they “did a good job” in their campaigns as he’s tried to skirt personal blame for the GOP’s midterm thrashing. That could change as investigations ramp up.
“As the president has said, he’s willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said Wednesday. “If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people.”
Schumer insisted that congressional Democrats will be able to balance legislating on key issues, such as affordability, while launching investigations to target “rampant corruption.”
In a letter to Democratic lawmakers announcing his candidacy for House speaker, Jeffries said the “days of the House functioning like a wholly owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over.”
“The massive corruption the country has experienced from the Trump Cartel explains why very little is getting done to help everyday Americans,” Jeffries wrote as he promised to target price gouging and push for a stock trading ban for lawmakers. “That changes immediately.”
The challenge for Democrats will be to continue to tie corruption to the affordability issues that topped the list of concerns for voters.
The Congressional Integrity Project, an advocacy group initially created to combat Republican investigations into President Joe Biden’s Democratic administration, is now shifting its focus to help Democratic lawmakers make that connection. In a memo, the group urged congressional Democrats to trace the Trump administration’s actions to people in and outside government, as well as corporations, who may be profiting from those moves.
“Corruption is not just corruption,” said the group’s senior adviser, Jack Miller. “It is costing taxpayers and costing Americans in their everyday lives.”
Some Democratic lawmakers are already stressing that congressional investigations have to be directly tied to affordability issues, while urging restraint.
Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt., said that Democrats need to earn voters’ trust, and while investigations are an important part of the Democratic agenda, “we can’t turn this into just a vengeance tour.”
“We have to be careful, cautious and judicious about that,” Welch said.
___
Associated Press writer Lisa Mascaro and polling writer Linley Sanders contributed to this report.

title: Woman assaulted by home intruder defends her fiance, accused of planning the attack
text:
BUCKEYE, AZ (AZFamily/Gray News) — A woman who was attacked in Arizona last month defended her partner in court on Wednesday against accusations that he planned the attack online.
Police said the woman’s fiancé, 23-year-old Zarian Dyer, plotted the Oct. 16 attack with Adrian Ayala, 20, over Reddit.
She told a judge that it’s not true, despite police saying they have messages and other evidence tying Dyer to the plot.
“My partner was forced to deal with false accusations fabricated by the defendant during his frantic attempt to make excuses,” she told the court, referring to claims by Ayala that her partner sent him.
Court documents say Dyer told Ayala when to come, where to park and how to get inside. A prosecutor alleged Dyer wanted Ayala to FaceTime him during the attack. Police said the woman did not consent.
During the hearing, the victim broke down in tears, explaining what happened during the attack.
“My security sensor alerted me that my front door was opening,” she said. “Assuming it was my partner returning from bringing in groceries, my daughter and I walked to the door to assist him. Instead, I found a stranger at my door.”
She said Ayala asked to use her restroom. After she refused, she said he barged into her home and attacked her.
Ayala is also accused of kicking the woman’s 17-month-old daughter.
Ayala, who was arrested Oct. 17, is out of custody. A judge entered not guilty pleas on his behalf on five counts and kept his release conditions in place, including no contact with the victims.
The woman also described losing income and facing eviction since the arrests.
Dyer is still in custody with a bond set at $500,000.

title: 'I usually have a wrench in my hands': Pipefitter's pipes will be new voice of Logan Airport
text:
'I usually have a wrench in my hands': Pipefitter's pipes will be new voice of Logan Airport
A pipefitter from Arlington, Massachusetts, was announced Thursday as the winner of Boston Logan International Airport's "Voice of Logan" contest.
Christopher Donisi will provide the voice for the official overhead announcements, as travelers visit, return home from or pass through the airport.
"It feels amazing; I am so thrilled to be able to represent my city. It is unreal," Donisi said while appearing on "Good Morning America."
Donisi said his mother encouraged him to audition for the contest, which had more than 6,000 applicants.
"You have to follow your dreams, but you also have to follow your mother's dreams," Donisi said.
After his appearance on national television, Donisi spoke to reporters at Logan and said that despite his new role, he is keeping his day job.
"This is my 10th time in front of a microphone, and it's all been today. I usually have a wrench in my hands," he said.
Massport CEO Richard Davey said the agency couldn't be happier with the choice and said Donisi will start recording holiday announcements next week.
Donisi, a married father with two children, said he's expecting to have "a good, long career" at Logan.
The contest was all about finding someone with an authentic Boston accent who can make a Bostonian feel at home.
Donisi's voice will bring an end to the nearly 25 years of service by Joe LoGiudice, whose voice has been heard by millions of travelers.
LoGiudice is not retiring from Massport. Instead, he will continue focusing on his other duties at the airport, where he has worked since graduating from Bridgewater State University in 1993.

title: Trump administration held talks with Iran on deporting Iranians during the war, court documents show
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Court documents reveal President Donald Trump’s administration held secret talks with Iran about deporting Iranians during the ongoing war.
The court documents unsealed Thursday show the Republican administration as recently as mid-October said it had plans to deport the Iranians through an unnamed third country, although it was unclear when it intended to do so. The judge in the case ordered the government to give the court 24-hour notice of any finalized plans to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country and five days’ written notice before any such deportation is carried out.
The documents show that the administration maintained contacts with Iranian officials during the war over the removals, specifically for submitting travel documents and figuring out “possible avenues for removal.”
“We are at war with a country where the President of the United States has said, as recently as two or three days ago, if not yesterday, that it is essentially lawless ... A country that is an enemy of the United States, according to the current president. A country that, according to our president, murdered tens of thousands of protestors,” Judge Ana Reyes said according to the Oct. 15 transcript.
“And what you’re telling me is that the United States of America is going to send individuals back to that region, facing what you and I and everyone who would ever look at this would know would be, at a minimum, a serious threat of certain death.”
“Yes, your honor,” Justice Department attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel said. “The government is executing lawful orders of removal.”
The Department of Homeland Security had no immediate comment.
The development emerged from an ongoing lawsuit that alleges the Trump administration’s immigration agencies have been sharing confidential information about Iranian asylum seekers with the Iranian government, violating national immigration regulations and endangering countless Iranians, court filings argue.
The new court documents show the coordination continued during the war.
The lawsuit depicts a coordinated campaign between the U.S. and Iranian governments to identify Iranians in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody and pressure them to return to Iran — a marked departure from decades of diplomatic hostility between the two governments and an ongoing war. DHS has denied that it is sharing asylum application records with the Iranian government.
Hundreds of emails exchanged between U.S. immigration officials exposed how the two countries worked together to arrange for more than 100 Iranians to be flown back to Iran on three immigration flights in September and December 2025 and January 2026.
Deportations of Iranians back to their home country are historically rare, owing to the lack of diplomatic relations between the U.S. and Iran and the possible persecution they could face if they were sent to Iran.
But under the Trump administration, ICE has aggressively pushed to deport people even from countries that have typically been reluctant to take people back or with whom the U.S. has had icy or no diplomatic relations.
Sometimes that has meant sending people back to their home country but it has also meant deporting people to other countries that they have no connection with.
The Trump administration has deported people, including Iranians, to countries other than their own in an attempt to circumvent diplomatic hurdles with governments that won’t take their people back. During Trump’s second term, countries including El Salvador, Costa Rica and Panama have accepted noncitizens from the U.S.
In June, an Iranian woman was among the two dozen migrants the U.S. deported to the Central African Republic.
Activists abroad have expressed concern about deportees returning to Iran, whose theocracy has been cracking down on intellectuals and where the government vociferously cracks down on any dissent.

title: A Universal Monster Roller Coaster Is Coming to Epic Universe
text:
An Indoor Monster Roller Coaster is Coming to Universal’s Epic Universe
Just one year after its splashy opening, Universal’s Epic Universe theme park is already expanding.
The company announced today that its Dark Universe land — inspired by Universal’s classic movie monsters like Frankenstein and Dracula — is getting a third major attraction, this one “an all-new indoor coaster” that will be located next to the area’s superb dark ride, Monsters Unchained: The Frankenstein Experiment.
According to Universal, “the upcoming attraction will immerse guests in an all-new story inspired by the iconic Universal Monsters franchise. Construction is already underway, with an opening planned in the years ahead.”
They didn’t quite specify which of the Universal Monsters the ride will feature or emphasize. Monsters Unchained features a potpourri of monsters including the Creature from the Black Lagoon, Dracula, and Frankenstein. The Dark Universe area of Epic Universe already includes an outdoor spinning roller coaster called Curse of the Werewolf, based on [checks notes] the Phantom of the Opera. (Okay fine, werewolves.)
READ MORE: Every Ride at Epic Universe, Ranked
Epic Universe, Universal’s third major theme park in Orlando, first opened in the spring of 2025. It contains four different areas themed to different pop culture brands. Besides the Dark Universe, it also features an How to Train Your Dragon area, a Super Nintendo World, and a Harry Potter land that looks like 1920s Paris with wizards.
Each land is connected to a central hub, Celestial Park, which also features the park’s most intense (but outdoor) roller coaster, Stardust Racers. The park’s other coasters include the Donkey Kong-themed Mine Cart Madness, and a launching (but still family-friendly) thrill ride called Hiccup’s Wing Gliders in the Isle of Berk land inspired by How to Train Your Dragon.
The Dark Universe area of the park looks like a creepy European village known as Darkmoor. In addition to its rides, it also includes walk-around characters like Frankenstein and Igor, a store where you can get elaborate monster makeup, a heavily themed restaurant called Das Stakehouse (with food items like a panna cotta that looks like a brain and a red velvet cake covered in “maggots”) and a bar called The Burning Blade Tavern topped by a windmill that catches fire every 15 minutes in tribute to the classic Universal monster movies.

title: Dolly Parton's manager moves to drop complaint accusing late singer's nephew of threatening estate
text:
Dolly Parton ’s longtime manager moved Thursday to drop a complaint that accused the late singer’s nephew who acted as her head of security with threatening her estate and its employees.
The manager, Danny Nozell, who runs She’s Alive, an entity founded to manage and protect Parton’s estate, had secured a temporary restraining order against Bryan Seaver and his security company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services, in September. Nozell was seeking to turn the order into a permanent injunction against Seaver.
A very brief filing in a Tennessee court Thursday gives no reason why the complaint is being withdrawn.
It says only that a proposed order was being drafted for the judge’s approval to dismiss the case without prejudice, meaning it can be refiled again. A court filing from a day earlier said the two sides had reached an agreement, but that gave no details either.
The first public hearing on the matter, pushed several times over the course of a month, was slated for Tuesday.
The Associated Press sent emails seeking comment from lawyers for She’s Alive, Seaver and his company.
The case exposed a serious rift in Parton’s inner circle that spilled into public view in the weeks after her Aug. 25 death.
She’s Alive terminated Seaver and SAPS in early September, and the following week petitioned for the restraining order against him, arguing that his “terrorizing conduct made their continued retention untenable.”
The petition said that starting shortly before Parton’s death and continuing after, Seaver made threats and aimed them directly at She’s Alive’s “personnel, counsel, and business partners. In writing, he vowed to ‘destroy the entire brand.’”
It says he “called himself ‘literally an international arms dealer and mercenary,’” and said everyone “needs to be worried about what I might do.”
In granting the temporary order, Chancellor I’Ashea L. Myles cited Seaver’s “claimed access to weapons, experience with violence, and intention to retaliate.”
Seaver said in court filings that he considered Nozell a close friend and ally before Nozell took out the restraining order.
In an affidavit, Seaver said text messages Nozell cited as evidence of his threats were a “private conversation between two friends who were both frustrated, grieving and discussing strategy.”
“I have never threatened physical harm to Mr. Nozell, to any SAL employee, contractor, attorney, advisor, or business partner, or to anyone else associated with SAL,” Seaver said. “I have no intention of doing so.”

title: Trump threatens veto power as Democrats prepare to lead Congress
text:
Trump threatens veto power as Democrats prepare to lead Congress
President Donald Trump has indicated he will use his veto power to block Democratic legislation as the party prepares to take control of the House and Senate following historic midterm election wins
Trump threatens veto power as Democrats prepare to lead Congress
President Donald Trump has indicated he will use his veto power to block Democratic legislation as the party prepares to take control of the House and Senate following historic midterm election wins
This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com.
As Democrats swept the midterm elections, taking control of the U.S. House and Senate, Republican President Donald Trump vowed to use one of his most significant remaining tools to block them: the presidential veto.
After several races were called for Democrats on election night, Trump posted a picture on Truth Social of a red baseball hat emblazoned with the word "Veto."
He told some news outlets that his administration will "work with the Democrats" and that he "doesn’t want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything."
But on Fox News, he said Democrats’ power was limited: "They’re in control, but they’re really not in control because they can send over, you know, 50 different great bills that they’re all excited about, and I send them back with a nice stamp veto."
In his second term, Trump has benefited from his party holding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Republican control of the White House and Congress allowed him to pass his signature tax and spending law in 2025 and remain essentially unchecked in his war with Iran and mass deportation agenda.
That’s all going to change, leaving open questions about how liberally the president may use his veto power and to what extent Congress will face legislative gridlock or forced compromise. Trump could also rely on executive actions to push his own policies, though those have limits.
What is the presidential veto and how do overrides work?
The U.S. Constitution says that the president can veto any bill passed by Congress before it becomes law.
Congress can override the veto, but only by a two-thirds supermajority in both chambers. Democrats handily won control of Congress in the midterms, taking 233 House seats and 54 Senate seats as of midday Nov. 4. Their margins are still well below the 290 in the House and 67 in the Senate needed to successfully override the veto.
One party holding a two-thirds majority in both chambers has happened before, but it is exceedingly rare.
Charles Cameron, a politics and public affairs professor at Princeton University and author of "Veto Bargaining: Presidents and the Politics of Negative Power," said the president’s veto is going to be back "in a big way" after the new Congress is sworn in early January 2027.
But Democrats know that, which will likely lead to "blame game vetoes," he said, where Democrats cue up certain bills to force Trump to veto them.
"The bills will be popular items whose veto will cast the President in the worst possible light," Cameron said in an email to PolitiFact. "An example may be bills to defund the Iran war. Others may be bills to restore the huge cuts to health insurance subsidies under the ACA (Obamacare) that are going to be kicking in soon."
Although the veto doesn’t allow the president to change legislation, Congress may also preemptively shape bills with the threat of Trump’s veto in mind.
The threat of a potential veto can be powerful in its own right, leading Congress to preemptively shape bills with it in mind.
"In many ways, the veto threat is more important because it comes sequentially before an actual veto and therefore can prompt important bargaining and negotiation between the president and Congress that can shape the bills that land on the president’s desk," said Robert Spitzer, a State University of New York-Cortland political scientist and author of "The Presidential Veto" and "President and Congress."
Trump could also use something called the pocket veto, which is when the president doesn’t sign a bill within 10 days of it being sent to the Oval Office. This happened with a bipartisan housing bill that Trump refused to sign earlier this year.
If Congress stays in session, the bill passes anyway. The bill would die if Congress adjourns, but with Democrats controlling both chambers, an adjournment to kill their own bill is unlikely.
Trump will likely resort to executive actions in certain situations when legislation hits a stalemate, experts said, but those can only go so far — they can be challenged in court, checked by Congress or revoked by the next president.
"Trump’s prolific use of unilateral presidential actions like executive orders up until now (far more than his predecessors) also demonstrate the limits of that strategy," Spitzer said. "Major policy change still runs through Congress. The question then is whether Trump will make a new effort to deal constructively with Congress. My belief is that the answer will be mostly no."
This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com.
It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

title: Mother honors stillborn son by bringing comfort to grieving families
text:
MARSHALL, Mich. (InvestigateTV) — Sabrina and Brenden Miller walked through the doors of Oak Lawn Hospital with 17 bags full of comfort items, a delivery they make each year on their son’s birthday.
Nurses in the birth center received the bags, which will eventually go to mothers of stillborn children.
“I always hope that they just like sit in the room and get dusty and take up space, but knowing that that’s not what’s going to happen, and that someone’s going to find comfort in them, it’s bittersweet,” Sabrina Miller said.
They’re called Beau’s Bags, named after the Millers’ son Beau Anthony, who was stillborn five years ago.
“My two best friends brought care packages to the hospital for us, which is where Beau’s Bags came from,” Sabrina Miller said.
The Millers assemble the bags at a children’s table in their home. Each bag contains socks, lotion, a notebook, a water bottle and other self-care items.
“Writing letters to Beau helped a lot,” she said.
Jill Hays, a nurse at Oak Lawn Birth Center, said the bags provide something tangible for grieving mothers.
“By having something that’s prepared by a mother that’s gone through the same process or journey, they will have something to hold onto,” Hays said.
Miller said she blamed herself after Beau’s death.
“I blamed myself and my own body, and like if my body couldn’t take care of him, then I’m not taking care of my body, so I always try to do a fun water bottle and a reminder to drink your water, like it’s not your fault, take care of yourself,” she said.
Brenden Miller, Beau’s father, said the bags help keep their son’s memory alive.
“You find yourself not thinking about him and then you feel bad for not thinking about him, so every chance that we can get to spread his name out there a little bit more, it’s like he’s still here,” he said.
The Millers have four other children. Beau remains part of their family count.
“He’s still in our count of kids, and we still celebrate him every year,” Sabrina Miller said.
Each year on or around Beau’s birthday, May 4th, family and friends release balloons with birthday wishes. The annual hospital visit with Beau’s Bags has become an early May tradition as well.
“He is 5 today,” Sabrina Miller said on this year’s delivery day. “I love walking in and they all know me and make me feel at home.”
Miller said she hopes Beau’s Bags help other mothers feel comfortable talking about their babies.
“The bags and these things are in memory of him, I think has helped other moms feel more comfortable in talking about their babies, and I hope that keeps going for years and years,” she said.

title: Russell Brand has been convicted of rape and sexual assault
text:
LONDON (AP) — Russell Brand was convicted Thursday of rape and sexual assault charges on allegations dating back more than 20 years.
Judge Joel Bennathan said Brand would receive a prison term when he is sentenced Monday. He was taken into custody.
A prosecutor said the British actor-comedian was a ruthless, calculating, manipulative “sexual predator.”
Brand, 51, denied the charges and testified that he was obsessed with sex as a young man and once led a promiscuous life but had never forced anyone to do something against their will.
Brand was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault involving four women. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault.
The jury of eight men and four women in Southwark Crown Court deliberated more than eight hours over two days.
Known for risqué stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek” and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.
In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.
Brand said the criminal case had a devastating impact on his life and family.
“My entire life has been consumed by these events, these allegations, these accusations,” he said.
Brand’s lawyers argued that the alleged victims were undermined by the fact that they only went to police years after the alleged assaults, and following the broadcast of a 2023 documentary that contained anonymous allegations against Brand.
Brand testified that friends and colleagues had abandoned him.
His wife, Laura, who accompanied him to court, testified as a character witness in his defense, but no one with relevant evidence was willing to give evidence on his behalf, Brand said.

title: New Hampshire dads who protested transgender athletes by wearing pink wristbands score court victory
text:
CONCORD, N.H. (AP) — Two fathers who oppose allowing transgender athletes to play high school sports will be allowed to wear pink wristbands marked “XX” to games, a federal judge said Thursday in an order ending more than two years of litigation.
Kyle Fellers and Anthony Foote sued the Bow school district after they were banned from school grounds for wearing the wristbands to a 2024 soccer game that included a transgender girl on the opposing team.
In a dismissal order Thursday, U.S. District Court Judge Steven McAuliffe said the men have a First Amendment right to silently wear the wristbands and that school officials violated it. Under a settlement agreement, the district’s risk pool will pay $225,000 to the Institute for Free Speech, which represented the men in court, and $50,000 to the men’s attorney. The plaintiffs will each get $17.91, an amount that symbolizes the year states ratified the First Amendment.
Fellers said he missed half of his daughter’s soccer games during her senior year because he stood up for what he believes in. The wristbands were marked “XX” to represent female chromosomes.
“It took more than two years, but the court has recognized that what happened to us was wrong,” he said in a statement.
School officials argued the district had a duty to protect students from harassment from adults on school grounds. They said Foote had called himself a “real leader” who was prepared to take action, and that another parent overheard others talk about heckling the transgender athlete. Both men testified at a hearing that they didn’t intend to harass or otherwise target the player.
The court had previously blocked the men from wearing the wristbands while the case proceeded, but a federal appeals court later ruled in their favor, finding that school officials “cannot favor one side of a debate involving parental speech on an issue of prominent public concern.”
“Parents don’t surrender their First Amendment rights when they walk into a high school soccer game,” said Endel Kolde, attorney for the Institute for Free Speech.
An attorney for the school district did not respond to an email seeking comment.

title: Family of missing Turner teen pleads for her safe return
text:
Family of missing teen from Turner, Maine, pleads for her safe return
The family of a 14-year-old girl from Maine is making a plea for her safe return, as she has been missing for more than 48 hours.
Skylar Rowe was last seen at about 1 p.m. Tuesday at her grandmother's home on County Road in Turner.
"Skylar, come home. You know we love you and we miss you," said Valerie Rowe, Skylar's grandmother.
Valerie Rowe thinks Skylar might have snuck out of the house while she was babysitting other children in the family.
"I still have a feeling she went through the window, not out (the front door), because I would have seen her," Valerie Rowe said.
Skylar lives with her aunt, Tiffani Rowe, who said she has legal guardianship of her niece.
"Skylar reached out on a private number to her father, William Rowe, and said, 'I'm safe,' and hung up the phone," Tiffani Rowe said.
Tiffani Rowe said that phone call was made on Wednesday.
The Androscoggin County Sheriff's Office said that due to Skylar's age and the circumstances surrounding her disappearance, there are serious concerns for her safety and well-being.
It is believed that Skylar may be with her mother, Kasey Rowe, and her mother's boyfriend, Michael Rias.
Armand Rowe, Skylar's grandfather, has shared multiple videos on social media in the hopes that it will lead to his granddaughter's safe return.
"Skylar, you need to come home," Armand Rowe said. "Your Mimi has got leukemia. You know that. She can't take this. So, Skylar, get home."
Skylar's family said she could be in the Lewiston-Auburn area, Portland or may even be headed to Tennessee, where Kasey Rowe and Rias once lived.
"I'm just worried about her because I have two young girls of my own, and if they were 14 running the roads — it's a scary world we live in today," Tiffani Rowe said.
Authorities are asking anyone who has any information regarding Skylar's whereabouts to immediately call 911 or the Androscoggin County Sheriff's Office at 207-753-2599.

title: Elon Musk spent at least $445 million to boost Republicans in the midterms
text:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — Elon Musk spent at least $445 million in a gambit to help Republicans keep control of Congress, an amount roughly equivalent to someone on a $100,000 annual salary saving every penny for 4,400 years.
To the world’s first trillionaire, it’s a pittance, but the billions of dollars’ worth of business his companies do with the federal government is not. And on Tuesday night, a Republican Party that had embraced Musk lost again and again, ceding control of Congress to a Democratic Party leery of the world’s richest person and keen to put his companies and his work at the Department of Government Efficiency under a microscope.
Nobody may have suffered bigger losses Tuesday than President Donald Trump. But few others had more on the line than Musk, who gambled big and came up holding the midterm’s worst return on investment. Democrats in Congress were already queuing to get their shot at Musk, with possible subpoenas and investigations.
As the bloodiest election for Republicans in recent history wore on, Musk joked on X, the social media site he owns. “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time,” he wrote with a shrug emoji.
Musk now faces new threats to his bottom line in places including Texas, where he has based himself and several of his companies. Musk spent at least $5 million to try to reelect Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who lost. Democrats also secured control of the Texas House and the U.S. Senate, partly by beating Texas Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, who effectively benefited from $158 million of Musk’s spending but lost his Senate race against Democrat James Talarico.
It was the first statewide win for Democrats in Texas in more than 30 years, and the candidates won in part by hammering Musk, the tax breaks and grants his companies receive, and his relationships with elected Republicans.
“This era of open corruption is going to come to an end,” said Rep. Gene Wu, chairman of the state legislature’s newly empowered Democratic Caucus.
Musk did not respond to messages seeking comment.
Musk’s reputation did not help with many Texas voters
Slightly more than half of Texas voters said they had an unfavorable opinion of Musk, according to The AP Voter Poll of more than 5,000 voters in the state. While Musk is overwhelmingly viewed positively by MAGA Republicans, those numbers dip for non-MAGA GOP voters and plummet for independent and Democratic voters.
Those were the voters who Talarico and Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who beat Abbott in the governor’s race, were targeting. The two often framed politics not through partisanship but as billionaires versus everyday Texans, and Musk’s emergence as a major Republican benefactor played into that message.
“Paxton is funded by one dude. Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator,” Talarico told a crowd in his final rally of the election, just after Hinojosa gave a similar excoriation on the same Austin stage.
“We know that Elon Musk got a $1.7 billion property tax break here in Texas, property taxes that the rest of us have to pay full price on,” Hinojosa said.
Even as Musk’s money helped blanket Texas in negative ads largely against Talarico, the Democrats’ message was aimed at the heart of an electorate whose median household income of $85,000 a year is under a pressure test as the prices of gas, groceries, rents and mortgages keep climbing.
Outgoing Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, said there was a point where the sheer amount of Musk’s donations became unhelpful to the GOP’s effort.
“You’re reaching the upper bound of the benefit of any of these dollars,” he said in an interview. “People are so turned off by all of the ads, and all you’re doing is running the same ad every single time.”
Investor jitters after election drop Musk’s net worth by $45 billion
Musk’s two publicly traded companies, Tesla and SpaceX, both saw prices for their shares drop considerably on Wednesday even as the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite index climbed.
Tesla shares declined Wednesday afternoon and wiped out about $40 billion from the electric carmaker’s market capitalization, standing at $1.54 trillion. SpaceX also lost about $40 billion from its market value, now at $1.83 trillion.
Musk lost about $45 billion of his net worth on Wednesday, which stood at $865.6 billion, according to Forbes, though it could rebound.
Investors are signaling some jitters about the impact of the election on Musk’s businesses. Worries that he may face congressional investigations “contributed to the early plunge for his benchmark firms,” said Joe Mazzola, head trading and derivatives strategist at Charles Schwab.
Musk’s genius is also his danger, said Michael Morris, a professor of leadership at Columbia Business School.
“I can understand that the same strategic mind that makes him so good at some of the business ventures and the hedging, it makes him think that he can also take control of politics, but it’s a different animal,” he said.
“He obviously has way more money than he will ever need, and his companies are doing well,” Morris continued. “I do think it’s kind of a game to him.”
Musk now faces a leery Congress
Democrats have not forgotten Musk’s time in Washington last year heading DOGE, which blitzed through agencies culling federal workers, and a recent fiasco in which SpaceX internet service in Ukraine, Starlink, was throttled amid the war with Russia.
“Elon Musk waved a chain saw on stage and laughed while he fired public servants and gutted the services Americans rely on,” wrote Rep. James Walkinshaw, a Virginia Democrat, in an X post just before the election. “He must answer for it under oath.”
Back home in Texas, with an incoming Democratic governor, Musk’s dealings with the state, including tax breaks, could face similar scrutiny.
In August, Musk’s companies received a $30 million grant through a state program to build a semiconductor plant that is estimated to create 3,000 jobs, one of several cash infusions he’s received through state programs. And he’s successfully pushed the state legislature to pass laws favorable to his businesses.
Musk has also railed against what he’s called the “woke mind virus,” which appears to be a partisan motivation for him, and shot off a slew of posts on X leading up to the election against Talarico, almost entirely for past stances the Democrat has taken on transgender rights and other progressive causes. That was Paxton’s central attack against Talarico, too, though it fell far short.
“You know you couldn’t pull the wool over their eyes anymore with these culture wars, and they are frustrated with the costs,” said Rep. Christina Morales, a state Democrat from Houston now in the majority in the state’s House.
“We’re not saying you don’t belong here,” she said, but “Texans can’t be bought.”

title: Do Mainers really save energy with daylight saving time?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Now that you’ve set your clock back, look at your thermostat. If its clock is an hour off, every program fires at the wrong time. If it holds the same temperature at 3 a.m. as at noon, it’s doing what many American thermostats do: holding one number whether anyone is home or awake. A basic programmable thermostat that doesn’t adjust for daylight saving time needs you to adjust it. And you need to make sure the temperature isn’t staying the same when those in the household are sleeping, or at noon when people are at work, or at dinner, when everyone is home and in the room.
This week’s step on the energy pathway is one of the simplest: Set your thermostat back when you’re asleep or away, and raise it during the hours you actually use each space in your home. It costs nothing, needs no contractor, and works whether you rent or own.
SET BACK AND SAVE
Daylight saving time comes from the era of incandescent bulbs: Shift the clock so people are awake during more daylight, and they’ll use less energy to see by. Congress adopted it in 1918 to conserve fuel for World War I and extended it into November in 2007.
The evidence for savings is thin. The U.S. Department of Energy found the 2007 extension saved just 0.03% of the nation’s yearly electricity. In Indiana, which adopted daylight saving time statewide in 2006, economists Matthew Kotchen and Laura Grant studied more than 7 million household electric bills and found residential electricity use rose about 1%, and 2-4% in the fall. Daylight saving time cuts lighting but shifts routines toward colder mornings, when people turn up the heat.
WHERE YOUR HOME’S ENERGY ACTUALLY GOES
According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, heating and cooling account for 52% of home energy use, with space heating alone at about 42%. Lighting is now about 6% of household electricity, and shrinking as LEDs take over. Your thermostat controls the biggest slice of energy directly.
A THERMOSTAT IS ONLY AS SMART AS ITS SCHEDULE
DOE estimates you can save up to 10% a year on heating and cooling by turning your thermostat back 7-10 F for eight hours a day. The catch: more than two-thirds of EIA survey households with a programmable thermostat never programmed it. Even smart thermostats run on a schedule. If it was set for last winter’s routine, it’s heating your house for times that may not apply this year.
BUILD YOUR WINTER SCHEDULE
• Sketch your week. Note when your household wakes, leaves, returns, and goes to bed, on weekdays and weekends.
• Pick your numbers. DOE suggests about 68 F while you’re awake and home, set back by 7-10 F while you sleep or the house is empty. Start smaller and add a degree weekly if needed.
• Time the warmup. Start the “wake” period 30-60 minutes before you get up.
• Think room by room. Give each heating zone its own schedule. With ducted systems, leave doors and vents open.
USE WHATEVER IS ON YOUR WALL
• Smart thermostat: Review the schedule with fresh eyes, and confirm that the “away” setting actually lowers the temperature.
• Programmable thermostat: Set the correct time and day. Make sure it isn’t stuck on “hold,” and replace old batteries.
• Manual thermostat: Turn the dial down at bedtime, tied to a nightly habit like locking the door. Note: Many utilities offer rebates on Energy Star-certified smart thermostats.
• Heat pump: Keep setbacks modest. Recovering from a cold house can trigger costly backup resistance heat. Steam and radiant floor systems also do best with small setbacks.
A SIDE STEP FOR OUTDOOR LIGHTS
Any outdoor light on a schedule set months ago is probably running at the wrong hours. Put lights on a photocell or astronomical timer, and trim their hours to when they help someone. Every dark hour saves electricity and helps nocturnal wildlife.
YOUR 1 STEP THIS WEEK
Fix your thermostat’s clock, then program a heating-season schedule: about 68 F when people are home and awake, set back by 7-10 F overnight and when the house is empty. In cooling season, flip the logic: about 78 F when home, 7-10 F higher when away. Write the schedule down, and set a reminder to revisit it at the next clock change to adjust the schedule for the new season.
Sustainable Practice empowers you to protect our planet in practical ways. Share this article with the person in your household who always fixes the microwave clock. Next time, have them adjust the thermostat, too.
Fred Horch and Peggy Siegle are principals of Sustainable Practice. You can pick up their new 2026 edition of “Your Earth Share: Seven Pathways to Sustainable Living” or any of their other publications at SustainablePractice.Life. Join their community of sustainable practitioners at that address for both benefits and books.

title: After years of trying, Ellsworth businessman picked for public office at 78
text:
After two decades of unsuccessfully running for state and local seats, a prominent but controversial Ellsworth businessman has been elected to a public office.
John Linnehan, 78, won one of two open seats in the five-way race for Ellsworth School Board Tuesday evening. Incumbent Kelly McKenney was elected to her fourth term in the first contested School Board election in five years.
His victory marks the first time the conservative area businessman has won an election after more than two decades of launching failed, religiously-centered campaigns for public office.
“Sometimes if there wasn’t a candidate that I thought was a good candidate, I would step up and get involved if I believed in the particular issues that were involved,” Linnehan said Wednesday. “I try to do what I believe personally is the right thing, and sometimes you have to get involved to put a spotlight on issues to make sure people are educated to know what’s happening.”
Many of those issues have centered around fiscal responsibility and Christian values, he said.
“I’ve never really run with the intent to win an election,” Linnehan said. “I just want to focus on what the issues are and try to make the public aware of how to correct them.”
He has never knocked on doors during a campaign, including this year’s School Board race, because he was more focused on bringing attention to financial accountability over winning votes.
Linnehan, who built his career as a lucrative car dealer and real estate manager, has run in every Ellsworth City Council race over the past five years — except for this election cycle, so as not to divert votes from two fiscally conservative candidates already running, he told the Bangor Daily News. One of those candidates, newcomer Robert Grant Sr., was elected Tuesday.
Last year, Linnehan, a lifelong Ellsworth resident who married high school sweetheart, Heather, lost his council bid by just two votes.
Linnehan, who describes himself as an original intent constitutionalist, has also competed for several Maine House and Senate seats in past years.
Most recently, he lost in 2022 to Democrat J. Mark Worth for House District 13, which includes Ellsworth, Waltham and Fletcher’s Landing. That seat is currently held by Republican Russell White, who held a narrow lead on Democrat Micheal Cunningham II in Tuesday night’s election.
Linnehan launched unsuccessful bids for the state Senate in 2004 and 2020.
The longtime political candidate has come under past public fire for various controversies around business and private School Board matters.
He was kicked off the School Board of a now-defunct Trenton Christian school, for which he was a major financial supporter. He then tried to bar school officials from accessing the Route 3 building, where he served as property manager. The School Board later sued Linnehan and others.
“If I feel an issue is not being represented biblically, spiritually or in a constitutional manner, I’m always prone to take up the defense or offense, whatever it takes to get that corrected,” Linnehan said.

title: Trump's lawyers to appear before appeals court as he fights hush money conviction
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump’s lawyers will try to persuade a New York appeals court Thursday to throw out his hush money conviction, two years after it made history.
The conviction, on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to obscure a $130,000 payment to adult film performer Stormy Daniels, continues to nettle Trump enough that he denounced it on social media as recently as September. The president denies any wrongdoing, and he has turned to state and federal courts in hopes of unwinding the verdict.
He is not expected to attend Thursday’s court session.
The appeal turns on complex legal disputes, but political overtones aren’t hard to find. The very first paragraph of one of the Trump team’s court filings contends the case was the flimsy product of “immense political pressure” on a Democratic prosecutor to go after Trump — rhetoric that echoes the Republican president’s own oft-repeated claims in the court of public opinion.
In court papers, Trump’s attorneys have assailed prosecutors’ legal theory as “a house of cards” built on a shaky combination of alleged state and federal offenses, with “clearly insufficient” evidence and problematic jury instructions.
The appeal also concerns whether jurors should have been allowed to hear testimony about supposed White House conversations, workflow and even Trump social media posts during his first term. His lawyers cite presidential immunity for official acts, and they argue his official conduct included responding to the Daniels drama once it became public in 2018.
“When a president addresses the nation to defend himself from allegations of personal misconduct (as all presidents do), or discusses such communications with his aides, he is carrying out his constitutional duties and is protected by immunity,” lawyer Robert Giuffra Jr. wrote in a filing this October.
Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s office counters that the legal theory and jury instructions were legitimate and that the White House-related evidence was fair game. Some was public record, some was a general description of office practices, and the conversations were “unofficial conduct,” prosecutors say.
“A president’s discussions about a purely private matter, even with a White House advisor, do not constitute ‘official acts for which the president is immune,’” Bragg’s appeals chief, Steven Wu, wrote in a filing in July. Besides, he said, there was “a mountain” of other evidence against Trump.
The May 2024 verdict made Trump the first former — and now current — U.S. president with a criminal conviction. While historic, it didn’t impede his return to the White House or subject him to any punishment.
The trial involved $130,000 that Daniels got from Trump’s then-fixer and lawyer, Michael Cohen, weeks before the 2016 election. The money bought, for a time, her silence about an alleged sexual encounter with the married Trump a decade earlier. He says that nothing sexual happened between them.
Trump’s company reimbursed Cohen in 2017, logging those payments as legal expenses.
Saying the transactions all were meant to keep unflattering information about Trump away from the electorate, prosecutors argue that he “orchestrated a conspiracy” that violated federal campaign finance laws, among others.
Trump’s lawyers argue there’s only “weak” evidence that he even knew about Cohen’s dealings at the time. His trial attorneys also said that payments to Cohen were indeed legal expenses, and that any hush money expended on Trump’s behalf wasn’t hidden campaign spending, just an effort to avoid embarrassing his family.
The distinction matters because, under New York law, falsifying business records isn’t a felony unless it’s done with an intent to commit or conceal a separate crime.
While pursuing his state appeal, Trump also has been trying to shift the case to federal court and have it dismissed on immunity grounds. A federal judge said no — for the third time — in August. Trump’s attorneys are appealing that decision, and arguments on that appeal are set for Nov. 16.

title: Flooding prompts state of emergency in Georgia as crews conduct more than 30 rescues
text:
MCCAYSVILLE, Ga. (WANF/Gray News) — Flash flooding prompted a state of emergency in McCaysville, Georgia, and flash flood warnings in several other cities in north Georgia on Thursday.
Storms dropped heavy rain across a mountainous area that drains into the Toccoa River between McCaysville, Georgia, and Copperhill, Tennessee, causing life-threatening flooding on both sides.
As much as 8 to 10 inches fell overnight between the north Georgia towns of Blue Ridge and Ellijay, and runoff from uncontrolled streams swelled the rivers below, according to the Tennessee Valley Authority.
The Toccoa River reached a record high Thursday morning of 18 feet, according to a river gauge in Copperhill.
More than 40 water rescues were undertaken by emergency personnel manning boats, according to McCaysville police Chief Michael Earley.
“I’ve never seen flooding like this in my life,” Earley said. “I have one of my police cars that’s floating down the river right now. Don’t know where it’s at, but it’s somewhere down there.”
Earley said the water in some areas downtown is 6 to 7 feet high.
“Anybody who’s willing to help, we’re asking for help,” he said.
Chatsworth, Ellijay and Blue Ridge, Georgia, received flash flood warnings until 7 a.m. The National Weather Service put McCaysville under a flash flood emergency until 9 a.m.
The Fannin County Emergency Management Agency advised residents to stay off the roads due to dangerous floodwaters.
“We still have numerous residents who need to be evacuated, including some in areas that emergency crews are currently unable to access or reach due to flooding and dangerous conditions,” the agency said.
Robert Poole, spokesperson for the Fannin County Emergency Management Agency on the Georgia side, estimated that about 20 people had been rescued, with no reported injuries or deaths. The water had begun receding by late Thursday morning, he said.
The downtown areas of McCaysville and Copperhill are a tourist destination for scenic railroad rides on the Blue Ridge Railway and Copperhill Special.

title: Town of Penobscot to vote on allowing on-site alcohol sales
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PENOBSCOT, Maine (WABI) - Penobscot voters will decide Nov. 20 whether to change a local law that makes the town partially dry.
Under the current law, alcohol must be sold in sealed containers.
Jamie Macnair, owner of Northern Bay Market wants to open a pub that serves alcohol for on-site consumption.
MacNair said the town held a vote in 2019 to allow the sale of alcohol in closed containers.
MacNair said her plan is for a small pub that follows the same hours as the store, which closes at 7 p.m.
“I live upstairs,” Macnair said. “I envision being home and in bed by 9 p.m. that sounds like heaven to me.”
She said the market is a mom and pop shop and that she has to look for other forms of income to stay in business.
“We want to stay that way, but to do that, we need to grow,” Macnair said. “We need to think of other ways to bring in income or I won’t be able to stay here.”
MacNair said the goal of the pub is to create a space in Penobscot where people can gather after work to strengthen the community.
“You know, there’s no place to have a book club or have a trivia night, other than it being at the church. And so, it would be really great to have a space where you can come, enjoy pizza, lobster, and a beer if you choose, or coffee, tea, a soda. You know, we’re not encouraging drinking. We’re just giving people a place to do that if they so choose. But mostly it’s about bringing the community together,” MacNair said.
Macnair said if anyone is concerned about allowing for a pub to be built, that she is willing to have a conversation with them.
“I think it’s been more of understanding what we’re looking to do, there’s no fear of Dollar General coming to Penobscot, Maine, this change in this vote wouldn’t make that happen anyway,” Macnair said. “I think if you can just dial the conversation back and think about who I am and what we’re doing here at the market and moving forward.”
The town will hold a public hearing on allowing on-site alcohol sales Nov. 10. The town vote is Nov. 20.

title: Postal employee shot 2 coworkers at an Iowa post office before being captured, police say
text:
DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — A female postal worker shot two female co-workers at the main post office in Iowa’s capital city Thursday before being captured nearby and faces attempted murder charges, authorities said.
Jennifer Christine Pledger, 39, of West Des Moines stood above one woman who she had shot and fired again, police said, and continued firing as she fled the building.
A male employee was injured in a fall while trying to escape. None of the injuries were believed to be life-threatening, according to police.
“They’re all at the hospital. They are being cared for right now,” Des Moines police Sgt. Paul Parizek said of the victims, who included two women, 45 and 53, and a 55-year-old man. All were in stable condition.
Pledger is being charged with two counts of attempted murder, two counts of willful injury causing serious injury and intimidation. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach possible relatives were unsuccessful and information was not immediately available on an attorney who could speak on her behalf.
The shooting happened on the facility’s second floor, in an area not accessible to the public. Witnesses reported hearing 10 to 12 shots, he said.
Parizek said officers responded within three minutes and quickly captured Pledger, who was detained along a nearby bike path without resistance. A 9 mm handgun was recovered where she was detained.
Police began receiving calls about the shooting around 9:10 a.m., and the suspect was detained at 9:21 a.m., Parizek said.
The post office is just north of downtown Des Moines and across the street from one of the city’s main hospitals.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Postal Inspection Service said in an email that it was investigating the shooting along with local, state and federal law enforcement.
Gov. Kim Reynolds said she was in contact with the Department of Public Safety regarding the shooting.
“We are monitoring the situation and our prayers are with everyone involved,” she posted online. “Grateful for the immediate response by law enforcement.”
Des Moines Public Schools said the district’s nearby elementary school, welcome center and nutrition center temporarily barred anyone from entering or leaving the facilities due to the shooting. Those restrictions were lifted after police told them the suspect was in custody.
Past shootings at postal facilities have prompted the Postal Service to study employee safety.
In 1986, a disgruntled postal worker went on a deadly rampage at a post office in Edmond, Oklahoma, shooting 14 fellow workers before killing himself. In 1991, a fired postal worker killed four former co-workers at his former post office in Royal Oak, Michigan, before killing himself. After those and other shootings, postal officials commissioned a study released in 2000 to examine workplace violence around the time that the term “going postal” was becoming conversational.
The report issued several recommendations to flag violent tendencies while concluding that “going postal” was a myth and that postal employees are less violent than the national workforce.
Other attacks have occurred since the report, including a 2006 shooting in Goleta, California, where a former postal worker stormed into a sorting facility and fatally shot six workers before killing himself.
___
Associated Press writers R.J. Rico in Atlanta and Jamie Stengle in Dallas contributed to this report.

title: US charges son of Ecuador's former president, 4 others with cocaine trafficking
text:
Federal prosecutors have charged a son of Ecuador’s former president, a former member of Ecuador’s legislature and three other Ecuadorians with trafficking tons of cocaine to the United States and Europe in part by hiding it in containers carrying tuna, the U.S. attorney’s office in New York City announced Thursday.
The five defendants played a “critical role” in turning Ecuador into a key transit point for the vast majority of cocaine sent to the U.S. and Europe, U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said.
“The charges announced today represent a coordinated effort to dismantle political corruption and narcotics trafficking that had wreaked havoc in Ecuador and plagued the country with increasing violence in recent years,” McDonald said in a statement.
Jacobo Abdala Bucaram-Pulley, the ex-president’s son, and Jaime Estrada Medranda, who previously served in Ecuador’s National Assembly, were arrested this month, the former in Ecuador and the latter while traveling in Panama, prosecutors said in a news release.
Court records did not list attorneys for them or the other three defendants: Jaime Estrada Bonilla; Geovanny Fernandez Menendez; and William Jose Briones Lopez.
Ecuador has struggled to contain drug violence as rival cartels partner with local gangs in a battle to control coastal ports and other routes used to smuggle cocaine. The country is wedged between Colombia and Peru, the world’s top cocaine-producing countries.
The Trump administration has reached agreements with Ecuador and other Latin American countries to carry out joint military operations against criminal groups even as it has maintained the right to unilaterally bomb vessels suspected of drug trafficking.
Prosecutors say Medranda, 41, and Bonilla, Medranda’s 71-year-old father and a former mayor in Ecuador, used their seafood company to help drug traffickers smuggle large quantities of cocaine out of Ecuador using containers packed with legitimate goods, such as tuna.
Bucaram-Pulley, 48, was one of those traffickers and also served as an intermediary for shipments from other drug traffickers, according to a grand jury indictment. Bucaram-Pulley’s father is Abdalá Bucaram, who was elected president of the small South American nation in 1996 and ousted by Congress less than six months later for “mental incapacity.” He was accused of corruption and nepotism during his brief time in office.
Menendez, 53, and Lopez, 47, allegedly served as representatives for Medranda and his father.
All five are charged with conspiring to import cocaine, possessing machine guns and conspiring to possess machine guns.

title: Former Patriots coach Bill Belichick a finalist for Hall of Fame
text:
Bill Belichick again is among five coaching candidates for the Pro Football Hall of Fame.
Tom Coughlin, Mike Holmgren, Dan Reeves and Mike Shanahan join Belichick in the Coach category for possible election into the Hall’s Class of 2027.
The list was announced Thursday by the Pro Football Hall of Fame.
Members of the Hall’s coaching subcommittee made their selections from an original field of 14 nominees. The subcommittee will select one candidate to be considered when the Hall’s selection committee determines a new class of enshrinees in early 2027.
All five reached this stage last year when Belichick advanced in the process but the six-time Super Bowl champion head coach was not elected in his first year of eligibility. Belichick’s snub was criticized intensely around the NFL.
“If he’s not a first-ballot Hall of Famer, there’s really no coach that should ever be a first-ballot Hall of Famer, which is completely ridiculous because people deserve it. He’s incredible,” Tom Brady said.
Belichick and Brady won six Super Bowls with the New England Patriots. Belichick also won two as a defensive assistant coach with the New York Giants.
Belichick’s career included a sign-stealing scandal dubbed “Spygate” in the 2007 season. He was fined $500,000 after the team was caught filming defensive signals from the New York Jets during a game.
Belichick’s final season in New England was 2023. He’s in his second season coaching in college at North Carolina.
Coughlin won two Super Bowls with the Giants, beating Belichick, Brady and the Patriots both times. He was 182-157 in 20 seasons with the Giants and Jacksonville Jaguars. Coughlin also won a title with Giants as an assistant coach.
Holmgren led the Green Bay Packers to one Super Bowl title and was 174-122, including postseason, in 17 seasons with the Packers and Seattle Seahawks. He also won two Super Bowls as an assistant with the San Francisco 49ers.
Reeves was 201-174-2 in 23 seasons with the Denver Broncos, Giants and Atlanta Falcons. He led the Broncos to the Super Bowl three times and the Falcons once, going 0-4. Reeves won a title as an assistant with the Dallas Cowboys.
Shanahan won back-to-back Super Bowls with Denver and was 178-144 in 20 seasons with the Broncos and Washington Redskins. He also won a title with the 49ers as an assistant coach.
On Wednesday, the Hall of Fame announced the five contributors who have advanced in the process: Ralph Hay, Robert Kraft, Virginia McCaskey, Doug Williams and John Wooten.
The final list of 15 candidates will include one contributor, one coach and 13 modern-era players. The group will be reduced to 10 and then seven candidates.
A 25-person selection committee will be able to vote for six people, with 80% of support needed. The Hall said that would lead to a range of three to seven Hall of Famers each year, with by far the most likely number to get the necessary support being either five or six people.
The Pro Football Hall of Fame’s Class of 2027 will be announced at “NFL Honors” in Los Angeles in February and enshrined next August in Canton.
KRAFT WILL miss the induction of Rob Gronkowski into the franchise’s hall of fame on Saturday as well as New England’s home game with the Green Bay Packers on Sunday as he recovers from back surgery.
Kraft, 85, told ESPN on Thursday that doctors have instructed him to remain off his feet. That will prevent him from being in attendance for this weekend’s celebration of the former tight end, who was voted into the team’s hall by fans in April. Kraft also won’t be able to travel with the team for their game in Munich, Germany, on Nov. 15.
Gronkowski’s addition to the team’s hall follows Julian Edelman in 2025, Tom Brady in 2024 and current coach Mike Vrabel in 2023.
Gronkowski played for nine seasons (2010-18) with the Patriots after entering the NFL as a second-round draft pick out of Arizona in 2010. He was a part of nine AFC East division championship teams, eight conference final teams, five AFC championship teams and three Super Bowl wins with the Patriots.

title: 🤫 Discover Maine's Best-Kept Secret: This Tiny Town Deserves WAY More Love!
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This Tiny Maine Town Is One of the Most Underrated in America
Quiet, quaint, and totally worth the trip! America’s underrated town you need to put on your radar.
Love Exploring is a website that covers everything from budget travel to luxury, destination features, city guides, travel deals, photo galleries, and more.
When it comes to undiscovered gems, Maine has plenty of them! Sure, OOB, Portland and Bar Harbor get most of the attention, but when Love Exploring put together a list of the most underrated towns in the United States, their pick for the 207, was an inspired one.
Stonington, Maine is trip well worth making for a fun, quiet getaway. First things first...to get there, you have to cross a pretty infamous bridge.
The Deer Isle Bridge, is a brightly colored suspension bridge connecting mainland Maine, with Deer Isle. It has swooping cables for support, which is part of what makes it so unique.
The first thing you notice is that it looks like a giant on-ramp when you enter. Then, it is basically like driving up, and then down a scary hill. Also, for a bridge of that size, it is very narrow.
Read More: When Will Bangor-Brewer's Chamberlain Bridge Return To Two Lanes?
The voyage over the bridge is all worth it, because when you finally hit Stonington, you will find a creative spot, packed with artists' studios and galleries, and there's an iconic opera house for live music and theater.
Foodies will be satisfied, because fresh Maine lobster is priority one there, plus you can eat it while looking over the bay.
It’s a small town, with just over a thousand residents, but a place so small, it has a ton of personality. The harbor is buzzing with lobster boats hauling in the day’s catch, seagulls squawking for scraps, and salty air that is impossible not to enjoy.
Take a stroll on the narrow streets and you'll walk past charming 19th-century homes, tiny shops, and small cafés where you get the ultimate cozy vibe, kinda like you are in a Hallmark Christmas movie.
Stonington is also a nature lover’s dream. Rugged cliffs, pine-scented forests, and a cluster of tiny islands just offshore make it perfect for kayaking, hiking, or just gazing out at the water.
I have been there several times, and always enjoy visiting Stonecutters Restaurant. Its casual, fun and perfect for seafood lovers, and for those who enjoy an adult beverage or two. Comes with a great view too!
