title: Portland will reopen Payson Park road that’s been closed for safety test
text:
The city of Portland will reopen a heavily traveled road through Payson Park this month after testing the closure’s impact on traffic safety.
This week, crews installed a series of speed humps along the portion of Catafalque Drive that intersects with Baxter Boulevard. That stretch has been closed to vehicle traffic since June, and the city plans to reopen it on Nov. 16.
The project, which also included installing bike lanes through the park, is tied to the city’s larger Vision Zero pedestrian safety initiative and was based on a speed study that showed vehicles consistently drive too fast through the park.
City staff said this week that the speed humps, along with other elements like narrowing the roads, have already worked to slow down cars, and that there are no plans for another road closure.
The park is one of the city’s most-used, featuring several ball fields, tennis/pickleball courts, a basketball court and a disc golf course. It’s also a popular destination for winter recreation. Its location between the highly traveled arterials of Washington and Ocean avenues also makes it an attractive cut-through for motorists looking to avoid peak-hour traffic.
City staff said residents and community groups like Friends of Payson Park pushed for the traffic-calming measures after long observing motorists speeding on Catafalque Drive and the park’s other main thoroughfare, Arboretum Road, both of which have posted speed limits of 15 mph.
A study conducted in March found that 97% of drivers were speeding on Arboretum Road — where vehicles enter from Ocean Avenue — with an average speed of 24 mph.
Ethan Hipple, director of parks, recreation and facilities, said that since the installation of bike lanes and speed humps, the average vehicle speed on Arboretum Road has been reduced by 6 mph. Catafalque Drive saw a 4 mph reduction, and the average speed is now 13 mph.
The work was funded through proceeds from the Back Cove Music Festival.
The Payson Park changes weren’t entirely popular. In early October, a city of Portland social media post attempted to explain the project after someone scrawled “why” on one of the “Road Closed” signs.
Predictably, reaction in the post’s comments was mixed. Several commenters said the city’s traffic-calming measures are making congestion worse, while many others encouraged the city to continue its efforts.
“Please keep it closed,” one person wrote. “My family uses the park every day and Catafalque has always been treated as an extension of the (Interstate 295) on/off ramp.”
Residents have consistently asked staff to install as many speed tables as possible to slow vehicles, said city spokesperson Jessica Grondin.
On Election Day, a crew installed six more speed humps in the park: two on Catafalque Drive, two on Inlet Road and two more on Arboretum Road. Three speed tables with crossings were previously installed in June.
Hipple said the city’s analysis will be presented to officials at an upcoming sustainability and transportation committee meeting.
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Nov. 6 to add an interview with Ethan Hipple.

title: Waldoboro Library Joins Statewide Borrowing Program
text:
The Waldoboro Public Library is now a member of the Maine Reciprocal Borrowing Program, allowing anyone with a valid library card from a participating library to check out materials in person in Waldoboro.
Patrons must be in good standing to use their card at the other libraries, meaning the card is current and has no fees or fines.
The library is also part of the Maine Library Passport Challenge. Participants visit at least one library in each of Maine’s 16 counties and collect a stamp or signature at each stop to add to their Maine Library Passport.

title: Multiple flights in Europe diverted because of bomb threats after earlier hoaxes
text:
Multiple flights in Europe diverted because of bomb threats after earlier hoaxes
Multiple flights in Europe made emergency landings on Thursday after being diverted because of bomb threats, authorities said. The incidents followed hoax bomb threats earlier this week that prompted searches, diversions and in one case a military escort.
At least eight flights from Copenhagen, Dublin, Helsinki, Madrid, Milan and Warsaw were confirmed to have been targeted with bomb threats, most diverted to other airports for emergency landings while others landed safely at their destinations. So far inspections have not turned up hazardous or suspicious materials.
Czech police said they deployed at Prague’s Vaclav Havel Airport to prepare for the landing of four planes after receiving a threat of explosive devices on board. Police said that "all necessary security measures have been activated.”
Related video: Disruptive passenger duct-taped to first-class seat on plane
Earlier, a flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a military air base in western France because of a bomb threat, the French prime minister’s office said. The flight landed safely at the base in Evreux in Normandy, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s office said. All 151 passengers and six crew members were safe and military bomb disposal teams were examining the plane, the office said.
It added that it was following the situation in real time. No other information was immediately released.
A LOT Polish Airlines flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed at its destination, where inspections found no hazardous or suspicious items, the airline said. A Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest landed safely in Bucharest following a bomb threat, airport spokesman Teo Postelnicu said.
Finnair said that Flight 1761 from Helsinki to Rome was targeted by a bomb threat, but nothing out of the ordinary was found after it landed in the Italian capital, Finnish broadcaster Yle reported.
Three Ryanair flights bound for Sofia, Bulgaria, had to make emergency landings because of bomb threats on board. Two of the flights, one from Copenhagen, Denmark, and the other from Madrid, landed safely at Sofia’s Vasil Levski Airport, airport officials told reporters. The third Sofia-bound flight, from London’s Stansted Airport to Sofia, had been diverted and landed safely at the airport in Plovdiv, Bulgaria’s second-largest city, Plovdiv Airport CEO Krassimir Peshev said.
Several flights across Europe received hoax bomb threats this week that prompted searches, diversions and, in one case, an escort by the Italian air force until landing, officials said.
The flights included Polish airline LOT, Scandinavian Airlines, Wizz Air and Ryanair. The hoax threats came a day after a plane headed for Bulgaria was diverted to Hungary after receiving a similar bomb threat while in the air. No one was injured.
Such threats aren't a new phenomenon but come at a time of increased geopolitical tensions and signs of “disruption,” like attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems, drone incursions in Europe and mysterious triggers to alert apps — even as authorities have warned that hybrid threats abound.

title: Damariscotta Passes RSU 48 Charter Amendment in Second Chance Vote
text:
Damariscotta residents approved the charter amendment accurately reflecting the formation of RSU 48 at the polls on Tuesday, Nov. 3, in a 1,106-158 vote.
The approval comes after voters first considered the amendment as part of the June 2025 annual town meeting. It was approved 277-24, but the question required a minimum of around 390 votes to equal 30% of the last gubernatorial election.
The article comes two years after voters approved the reorganization plan that turned the Great Salt Bay Consolidated School District into RSU 48.

title: Dunlap concedes Maine's 2nd Congressional District race to LePage
text:
Matt Dunlap concedes Maine's 2nd Congressional District race to Paul LePage
The concession happened less than two hours after the Secretary of State's Office announced the election would proceed to a ranked-choice voting tabulation.
Matt Dunlap concedes Maine's 2nd Congressional District race to Paul LePage
The concession happened less than two hours after the Secretary of State's Office announced the election would proceed to a ranked-choice voting tabulation.
State Auditor Matt Dunlap (D) conceded the race for Maine's 2nd Congressional District seat in the U.S. House to former Gov. Paul LePage (R), less than two hours after the Maine Secretary of State's Office announced that the election would proceed to a ranked-choice voting tabulation.
The Secretary of State's Office said at 11 a.m. Thursday that there were 341,248 total ballots cast in the race, with 170,263 votes for LePage (49.894%), 164,845 votes for Dunlap (48.307%), 123 votes for declared write-in candidates (0.036%) and 6,107 blank votes (1.763%). The lone declared write-in candidate in this race is Gregory Ward, an independent.
In ranked-choice voting races, like the race for CD2, a candidate must receive more than 50% of first-choice votes as counted on Election Day in order to win the race outright. If no candidate receives more than 50% of the total ballots cast, the Secretary of State's Office makes the determination to proceed with a ranked-choice voting tabulation.
At 12:20 p.m., Dunlap's campaign released a statement in which the Democratic candidate said his team does not currently believe that ranked-choice voting will change the results of the race.
"This isn’t the result we were hoping for, and I’m disappointed that we came up short. Congratulations to Paul LePage, I wish him the best," Dunlap said in a statement. "I want to thank every volunteer who knocked doors, made calls, and made their voices heard. Your support inspired me, and I’m honored to have worked side by side with you over the past year."
"A huge congratulations to Congressman-elect Paul LePage on his election victory! Maine was well served during the LePage administration, and we are grateful he is returning to public service," Maine Republican Party chairman Jim Deyermond said in a statement. "Gov. LePage brought common sense back to the Blaine House, and now he is bringing it to Washington, D.C., on behalf of Congressional District 2. Paul LePage always puts people before politics, without fail. In Congress, he will fight to lower costs, keep our streets safe, and defend our freedoms. Thank you to every Mainer who voted for LePage and showed up at the polls. This victory would not have been possible without the outstanding LePage for Congress campaign team. We are deeply grateful for their hard work and dedication."
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said that even though Dunlap has conceded the race, the ranked-choice tabulation must still be completed in order to have a certified election under the state law.
These developments come one day after LePage declared victory in the U.S. House race.
Brent Littlefield, LePage's senior advisor, said he spoke with Bellows and that the campaign is aware initial indications show a small number of blank votes and write-ins may trigger the ranked-choice tabulation process based on election officials' interpretation of the law.
"It is very clear from our campaign team's work (on Wednesday) talking one-on-one with local town clerks, and the publicly available numbers, that Paul LePage is the Congressman-Elect," Littlefield said in a statement. "Paul’s vote margin is extremely large. Decision Desk HQ alone reports Paul LePage has over 4,400 more votes than Mr. Dunlap. That is in line with our campaign’s estimate of a 4,500 vote lead as Paul declared victory. Paul LePage looks forward to working for all of the people in Maine’s 2nd District. He will work with anyone, regardless of party, to put Maine first.”
Dunlap and LePage have been vying to replace outgoing Congressman Jared Golden, a Blue Dog Democrat who announced nearly a year ago that he would not be running for reelection.
"Four times, the people of Maine's 2nd District chose me to represent them in Congress. I know what an incredible honor it is to earn their trust. For their faith, I will always be thankful," Golden said in a statement shared on social media. "I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances. So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami. I stand ready to work with him to ensure the smooth transition that Mainers deserve."
More info about CD2
Maine's 2nd Congressional District is the largest congressional district by area east of the Mississippi River. CD2 includes all of Androscoggin, Aroostook, Franklin, Hancock, Oxford, Penobscot, Piscataquis, Somerset, Waldo and Washington counties, as well as the Kennebec County communities of Augusta, Belgrade, Chelsea, Farmingdale, Fayette, Gardiner, Hallowell, Manchester, Monmouth, Mount Vernon, Oakland, Randolph, Readfield, Rome, Sidney, Vienna, Wayne and Winthrop.
How ranked-choice voting works
Bellows said that the first step in the process will be to verify the vote totals from every municipality to ensure accuracy.
"Once the election night totals are verified, assuming neither candidate received a majority of the votes, which is what we are observing now, we will proceed to the ranked choice voting tabulation," Bellows said in a statement.
When the ranked-choice process begins, the votes are tabulated in rounds, with the lowest-ranked candidate eliminated in each round until there are only two candidates remaining. The candidate determined to have received the majority of the votes — more than 50% — in the final round is declared the winner.
The tabulation is scheduled to begin at 10 a.m. on Monday, Nov. 9, at the Maine Department of Public Safety Headquarters, which is located at 45 Commerce Drive in Augusta. The process is open to the public and will be livestreamed on the Secretary of State's YouTube page.
More info about the candidates
LePage has nearly 30 years of political experience, as he was first elected to the Waterville City Council in 1997 and served two terms before being elected mayor of Waterville in 2003. He served as mayor for seven years and stepped down in January 2011, when he was sworn in as governor after winning the 2010 gubernatorial election.
He was reelected governor in 2014 and left office in January 2019, as anyone who holds the Maine governor's office cannot serve more than two consecutive terms. LePage ran for a third nonconsecutive term as governor in 2022, but he was unable to defeat incumbent Gov. Janet Mills.
Dunlap is in his second stint as state auditor. He first held the position from January 2021 to October 2021 and had to resign from office because he failed exams to become a certified public accountant, which is a requirement. A person who is not a CPA can be elected as Maine's state auditor, but they must become one within nine months of assuming office. Dunlap later became a CPA and the Maine Legislature once again selected him to serve as state auditor in November 2022.
Before his time as state auditor, Dunlap served as Maine's secretary of state for two separate terms (2005-11, 2013-21). He also served in the Maine House of Representatives from December 1996 to January 2005.

title: Bangor looking to upset Oxford Hills in football playoffs for 2nd-straight season
text:
Last season, the Bangor High School football team upset Oxford Hills/Buckfield in the Class A North semifinals, 35-6, one week after the Vikings had thumped the Rams 34-7 in the regular season finale.
The 4-4 and fourth-seeded Rams will look to replicate that on Friday night at 7 p.m. when they visit South Paris to take on 7-1 top seed Oxford Hills/Buckfield after losing to the Vikings 28-0 last week in Bangor.
The high school football playoffs are in full swing with all six classes involved.
In the other Class A North semifinal on Friday night, second seed Portland (7-2) will entertain No. 3 Windham (6-3) for a 6 p.m. kickoff. Defending regional titlist Portland beat Windham 39-13 during the regular season.
In Class B North, fourth seed Fryeburg Academy, 5-4 and a 48-6 winner over Messalonskee of Oakland in a quarterfinal matchup, will travel to play top seed Lawrence of Fairfield, 8-0, at 7 p.m. on Friday with third seed Skowhegan, 6-3, venturing to Augusta to face second seed Cony High, 7-1, beginning at 6 p.m.
Skowhegan blanked Brunswick 35-0 in the quarterfinals.
Lawrence and Cony earned first-round byes.
Lawrence beat Fryeburg Academy 27-14 in their regular season matchup and Cony edged Skowhegan 42-35.
There are four Friday night quarterfinal games in statewide Class C with all listing a 7 p.m. kickoff.
Eighth seed Gardiner (3-6) will trek to Turner to face top seed Leavitt (9-0), second seed and defending state champ Greely of Cumberland Center (7-1) will entertain No. 7 Oceanside/North Haven (5-4), third seed Hermon (7-2) will take on No. 6 Nokomis of Newport (4-5) and No. 4 Foxcroft Academy of Dover-Foxcroft (7-2) will await fifth seed Wells (6-3).
Leavitt bested Gardiner in the regular season, 48-7, while Hermon beat Nokomis 28-6 and Greely bested Oceanside/North Haven 35-8.
Foxcroft Academy and Wells did not play during the regular season.
In Class D North, third seed John Bapst/Bangor Christian, 5-4, will visit Pittsfield to face No. 2 Maine Central Institute (6-2) on Friday night at 7 p.m. in one semifinal and, on Saturday at 1 p.m., top seed Winslow (7-1) will host fifth seed Madison (3-6) in the other.
John Bapst/Bangor beat Oak Hill of Sabattus 43-33 in the quarterfinals and Madison upset Mattanawcook Academy of Lincoln, 6-0.
John Bapst and MCI did not play during the regular season but Winslow beat Madison 50-18.
Regional champions will be crowned in Eight-Player football.
In Eight-Player Large Schools title games, 6-3 Mount Desert Island, winner of four straight and the second seed, will travel to Old Town (8-1) for a 1 p.m. North championship tilt on Saturday with the winner taking on the Yarmouth (9-0) and Spruce Mountain of Jay (7-2) victor in the state title game the following weekend.
MDI advanced to the final with a 22-14 win over rival Ellsworth/Sumner and Old Town beat the Houlton/Hodgdon cooperative team 60-2. Old Town beat MDI during the regular season 50-12.
Yarmouth bested Gray-New Gloucester 52-6 in the semifinals and Spruce Mountain beat Cape Elizabeth, 44-16.
In Eight-Player Small Schools, 4-4 Orono will visit defending state champ Stearns/Schenck (9-0) for a 7 p.m. Friday North title game with the Southern final on Saturday at 6 p.m. between 9-0 Old Orchard Beach and 6-2 Boothbay Region.
Orono beat Washington Academy of East Machias 64-22 in the semifinals and has won four of its last five games while Stearns/Schenck eliminated Bucksport 54-0.
Stearns/Schenck beat Orono 40-20 during the regular season.
Boothbay Region upended Telstar of Bethel 44-17 in the South semis with Old Orchard Beach ousting Maranacook of Readfield, 42-0.
Old Orchard Beach earned a 50-26 regular season victory over Boothbay Region.

title: 2028 White House talk begins after historic Midterm Election Day
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Politicians are already looking ahead to the 2028 presidential race after Democrats swept key races across the nation on Nov. 3.
Among the victory speeches and concession messages were signs of groundwork for 2028 and possible presidential runs by candidates on both sides of the aisle.
For example, Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., who has been rumored as a possible Democratic candidate, made headlines for the speech he gave after winning a second term in the Senate.
“Tonight in Georgia we’ve proven not just that unity is possible, but that we can overcome division without sacrificing clarity of purpose,” Ossoff said.
“In every corner of Georgia, this campaign urged the necessity of banning corporate and secret money from politics, of American leadership for peace and human rights around the world, and of guaranteeing healthcare for every single American,” Ossoff said.
Other names mentioned for 2028 include Govs. Wes Moore of Maryland, JB Pritzker of Illinois and Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania.
But it’s not just Democrats already looking toward the future; Vice President JD Vance posted on social media about the midterm election results with a marked shift in tone.
“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance said in the post, which was soon shared by Donald Trump, Jr.
Meanwhile, Rep. Greg Steube, a Florida Republican, blamed GOP leadership for the Election Night losses, another example of a lawmaker looking to adapt to the quickly shifting political climate.

title: Vikings sit Murray with hamstring strain, will start Wentz at QB against the Bills on Monday night
text:
EAGAN, Minn. (AP) — Minnesota Vikings quarterback Kyler Murray will miss at least the next game because of a hamstring strain, coach Kevin O’Connell announced on Thursday.
Carson Wentz will start instead against Buffalo on Monday, with Max Brosmer serving as the backup. Murray’s status will be evaluated week to week, O’Connell said, with the hope he can be ready to play by Nov. 15 when the Vikings (6-1) visit Green Bay. Murray is not under consideration for injured reserve, O’Connell said, which would require a minimum four-game absence.
“We do feel like we’d be putting him at risk by possibly turning this into a more significant injury than it already is,” O’Connell said.
Murray was forced out of the season opener after 11 snaps because of a concussion that also kept him out of the following game. Wentz threw three touchdown passes in the rally to beat Green Bay and started the rainy victory at Chicago, going 23 for 39 for 276 yards with six sacks and no turnovers while Murray was out.
Wentz, the second overall pick in the 2016 draft, went 2-3 as the starter last year while J.J. McCarthy was sidelined. O’Connell sidestepped a question about whether Wentz could keep the job with a strong performance even after Murray is cleared.
“There’s a ton of confidence in Carson,” O’Connell said. “He’s already helped us.”
Murray was hurt on a read-option run in the fourth quarter at Detroit last week when he turned the corner past star defensive end Aidan Hutchinson for a 9-yard gain. Murray remained in the game as the Vikings took their first loss, but an MRI exam on Monday confirmed the strain after he had reported soreness.
O’Connell, who declined to specify the severity of the injury, stressed the importance of a cautious approach with an injury that can linger if it’s not fully healed. Wide receiver Justin Jefferson wound up missing seven games with a hamstring strain in 2023. With Murray struggling to find a rhythm throwing the ball, the Vikings will be wary to send him out if he can’t run at full speed.
“Just knowing that Kyler needs his mobility, it’s a big huge part of what makes him an effective player,” O’Connell said.
Since Kirk Cousins tore his Achilles tendon at Green Bay on Oct. 29, 2023, O’Connell and the Vikings over a span of 52 games will have switched starting quarterbacks for injury or performance 17 different times, including 14 in-season changes and five in-game.

title: Honoring Gold Star families and those who served
text:
WRITTEN BY KATIE SMITH
This fall, Maine’s first Woody Williams Gold Star Family Memorial Monument was unveiled in the Balsam Valley Tip Lands, located in Columbia Falls. Owned by Morrill Worcester, the co-founder of Wreaths Across America (WAA), this land is where balsam trees are grown and harvested to produce millions of remembrance wreaths for veterans’ graves across the nation.
The Woody Williams Foundation, named in honor of Medal of Honor Recipient Hershel “Woody” Williams, works to establish permanent Gold Star Families Memorial Monuments in communities throughout the United States. Gold Star Families are those related to a U.S. military service member who died while serving.
Worcester and WAA executive director Karen Worcester both spoke at the event about the deep honor they felt to house Maine’s first-ever Woody Williams Gold Star Families Memorial Monument. Gold Star mothers and committee members Dolly Sullivan and Lorna Harris made an honorary wreath placement during the event.
“We were incredibly honored to have two Maine Gold Star Families participate as acting members of the planning committee: Dolly and Jim Sullivan, proud Gold Star parents of Capt. Christopher J. Sullivan, KIA Baghdad, Iraq, Jan. 18, 2005, and Lorna Harris, proud Gold Star mother of SPC Dustin J. Harris, KIA Bayji, Iraq, April 6, 2006. We were grateful to hear their stories and carry on their legacy,” said Amber Caron, WAA staff member and volunteer chairperson of the Woody Williams Gold Star Families Memorial Monument Planning Committee.
“We wanted to create a permanent place in Maine, WAA’s home, where their sacrifice, and the lives and service of their loved ones would always be remembered,” Caron said. “The Woody Williams Foundation’s Gold Star Families Memorial Monument offers a meaningful way to make that commitment tangible and lasting.”
The hope is that the monument becomes a place for reflection and learning, explained Caron.
“We at WAA believe that it is our responsibility not only to remember those who have served and sacrificed but also to teach future generations why this service matters,” Caron said. “We hope that young people visit, ask questions, and learn stories of our nation’s heroes and Gold Star Families. This monument is not simply a structure, but a place where legacy lasts and our American Heroes are remembered.”
People of all ages are encouraged to visit, ask questions, and really get to know the stories of service members and their families who have sacrificed so much.

title: Aging Untold: How to choose a medical power of attorney
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we break down medical power of attorney, helping you choose a trusted healthcare proxy and ensure your wishes are honored.
Then, we examine the causes of chronic dry mouth and share simple ways to protect your oral health.
And, we explore the powerful physical and mental health benefits of the outdoors, showing how even a short daily dose of nature can ease anxiety and boost overall well-being.
If you cannot make health care decisions for yourself, who would do it for you?
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the person you name as your medical power of attorney holds a wide range of decision-making power.
“They can decide whether or not you’re going to go into a skilled facility in a rehab after a surgery. They can decide if you’re going to go into an assisted living. They can decide if you’re going to be at home, who your caregivers are going to be,” Cradduck said.
She said you need to know that this person can “advocate for your wishes, not for their heart’s desire.”
Dry mouth affects 40% of adults 80 and older and 30% of adults 65 and older, according to the American Dental Association. It can show up along with soreness, bad breath and trouble with dentures.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said there are several causes for dry mouth and finding that reason is the first step.
There are several possible causes, including dehydration, damage to nerves, cancer, underlying autoimmune disorders and medications, Rogers said.
Dry mouth can be an early sign in a person who is otherwise healthy, she added.
Dr. Nathaniel Mann, a Prisma Health emergency doctor, spent two years traveling the world, practicing medicine in remote environments.
Across his years in medicine, he has found that being outside is one of the most powerful treatments.
Mann, who also practices wilderness medicine, said he thinks people should be prescribed time outside the way they are prescribed medicine.
“I absolutely think we should,” he said.
Centuries worth of iron frame the city of New Orleans’ architecture, from balconies to fences and gates.
Darryl Reeves is one of the few blacksmiths who, like his grandfather before him, carry on the tradition.
“That’s what gives me joy,” Reeves said. “How many people get to beat on metal, especially if you’re frustrated with something and get it out? How many people do that?”

title: Is a 90-day blackout coming? What the U.S. military’s new readiness initiative actually means
text:
JACKSON, Tenn. (WBBJ/Gray News) — Viral doomsday posts on social media are gaining traction, claiming the nation will soon face a 90-day blackout.
The rumor that the U.S. released a doomsday plan for a 90-day blackout began circulating after U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth unveiled a long-term strategic plan on Sept. 30.
Experts said, however, that people have been misinterpreting the FORTRESS America initiative in the strategic plan, which is essentially a plan to be prepared for modern-day attacks.
The initiative is not an announcement of an active blackout, power cut or impending attack. Rather, it is a prepared plan to ensure the U.S. military will have the ability to “fight and win under any circumstances,” including a cyberattack.
“We know that more nations are engaging in cyber attacks,” Sean Evans, chair and professor of political science at Union University, said. “We’re concerned about sabotage, so the whole idea is that if something happens that our military will be prepared. They’ll have a 90-day supply of energy. They’ll have back up ammunition.”
The FORTRESS America initiative is organized around five pillars: energy independence, supply-chain and defense-industrial base resilience, a strategic defense reserve, installation hardening and cyber resilience, and resilience in space and spectrum.
Under this initiative, every military department and defense agency will have the ability to operate independently for at least 90 days. This includes access to water, electricity, fuel and communications.

title: Reporter forced out of Republican candidate’s election party during profane-laced speech on live television
text:
AMSTERDAM, New York (WWNY/Gray News) - Republican congressional candidate Anthony Constantino ordered a 7 News reporter and cameraman to leave his election-night party while he was thanking supporters and criticizing the news media.
Speech carried on 11 p.m. news
Constantino was leading Democratic opponent Blake Gendebien in the race for the 21st Congressional District Tuesday night.
7 News aired 15 to 16 minutes of Constantino’s live speech to lead the 11 p.m. news in which he thanked President Donald Trump “for having my back.”
Constantino also thanked former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani and political strategist and advisor Roger Stone.
However, the Republican candidate also criticized “the evil news media.”
Constantino and other people who came to the stage used inappropriate language before 7 News left live coverage to report on other election results in the region.
Reporter ordered to leave
Constantino continued to speak before randomly singling out 7 News reporter Garrett Domblewski.
He called Domblewski and 7 News anchor Jeff Cole a**holes. He also called a reporter from a different organization a “f**king a**hole.”
Constantino then ordered Domblewski to leave and led the crowd in a chant, “Kick him out. Kick him out.”
Five or six security guards escorted Domblewski out of the building.
While Domblewski was led outside, Constantino and the crowd chanted, “F**k the evil media.”
Reporter unsure of reason
Domblewski was unsure what prompted Constantino to order him to leave.
He said he conducted a cordial interview with Constantino earlier in the evening, a portion of which aired in the 10 p.m. newscast.
Live report from parking lot
After Domblewski was escorted outside, he reported live from the parking lot.
Campaign invited media
Constantino’s campaign invited 7 News and other news media to his election-night party in Amsterdam, about a 3-hour drive from Watertown.
Constantino’s team was aware that the news crew was coming to the event and, in an email, said, “Looking forward to seeing you all.”
Constantino was leading Democratic opponent Blake Gendebien in the race for the 21st Congressional District Tuesday night.

title: ‘A beautifully American story’: Abdul El-Sayed’s historic Senate victory resonates with Muslim Americans
text:
DEARBORN, Mich. (AP) — Campaigning relentlessly across Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed didn’t highlight the possibility that he could become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. But with victory in hand, he savored his triumph over the vitriol aimed at him and his fellow Muslim Americans.
“They tried to demonize people because of how they pray,” he told The Associated Press on Wednesday. “And Michigan — the whole Michigan — clapped back. People don’t want that. They’re sick of it.”
He showed his pride in his victory speech, declaring: “My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed.”
Twenty-five years after the Sept. 11 attacks and their aftermath yanked anti-Muslim sentiment into the forefront of American life, those emotions are shared by many Muslim Americans in Michigan and across the country.
They saw a surge of anti-Muslim rhetoric after Zohran Mamdani’s election as New York City mayor a year ago, and they saw the attacks intensify as El-Sayed became the new prime target. President Donald Trump called him a “jihadist” who was “on the side of the terrorists.” Dozens of Trump’s fellow Republicans in Congress formed a Sharia-Free America Caucus, depicting Islam’s religious code as a threat to the U.S. Constitution.
But now, after El-Sayed’s defeat of GOP rival Mike Rogers was confirmed early Wednesday, there is a pervasive sense that a broader victory is at hand.
The outcome “represents a historic turning point for American Muslim political engagement and a historic defeat for the politics of hate,” said Nihad Awad, national executive director of the Council on American-Islamic Relations.
“Anti-Muslim extremists, Israel lobby groups and even the president of the United States used every smear in the book to paint Dr. El-Sayed as a Muslim boogeyman,” he said. “None of it was true, and none of it worked. Anti-Muslim hate was on the ballot, and it failed.”
In Dearborn, talk of ‘a beautifully American story’
Excitement over El-Sayed’s victory was palpable in Dearborn, a city near Detroit with a sizable Arab American population. The mayor, Abdullah Hammoud, said residents showed up at the ballot box in huge numbers.
“What a beautifully American story,” Hammoud said. “One of our brightest and best earned the support of the majority of Michiganders who participated in yesterday’s election. And regardless of the direction in which he prays, they’re sending him to the U.S. Senate.”
Hammoud, who has known El-Sayed for more than a decade, said although his win was important for many Arab Americans, people voted for him because of his platform, not his identity. He cited support in Dearborn for independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders’ 2016 presidential campaign. Sanders, who is Jewish and caucuses with Democrats, ran on a progressive platform.
U.S. SENATE BALANCE OF POWER
In El-Sayed, residents of Dearborn “finally saw themselves and a candidate who appealed to them, but it had to do with far more than just his ethnicity or his religion,” Hammoud said. “It was honestly because of the policies and building a coalition with this community in an honest way.”
When Zaynah Jadallah, 26, canvassed for El-Sayed in Dearborn, she said most people told her they already planned on voting for him before inviting her in for water or food. She credited the name recognition to El-Sayed’s grassroots campaigning and his pride in his Egyptian heritage.
“He’s always been proud of his identity. He never shied away from it or from saying his name,” Jadallah said.
Yasmin El-Sayed, no relation to the senator-elect, took her two daughters to the Detroit watch party from New York. She teared up after the victory speech.
“Having grown up in a post-9/11 world, being Muslim, being Arab myself, never in a million years did I think we would see what we saw today,” she said.
In a time of suspicion of government, a message of representation
El-Sayed depicted his election as a victory for all those “who don’t see themselves reflected in our government or who’ve been told that they don’t belong for some reason or another — not just how they pray but who they love, how they identify, the color of their skin, where they grew up.″
“I didn’t run to be the first Muslim senator. I ran to be the next senator of the state of Michigan who happens to be Muslim,” he said. ″But I also know that democracy is constantly about the conversation about who we are, who we want to be.”
“Michigan proved just how big we are. Rejected a hateful, spiteful campaign that had nothing to say about the issues and only wanted to point to my name and my face,” he added. ″I want all of those folks out there who have been told that America’s not big enough for them to reflect on that. America really is big enough for all of us.”
Mohamed Gula, CEO of the Muslim American advocacy group Emgage Action, said he was elated by El-Sayed’s triumph after a year of “extremely Islamophobic and disgusting rhetoric being used as a campaign strategy.”
“For Abdul to come out last night and use his full name meant the world to someone who grew up in post-9/11 America, where the Muslim American community was seen through a national security lens,” Gula said.
“Our children, years from now, will be able to run for office,” he said, ”to be seen as who they are.”
A debate over the place of Sharia law — and its very definition
Among the most frequent targets of anti-Muslim rhetoric was Sharia, the religious code that provides Muslims with guidance on how to lead righteous lives. At the Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas, some of the loudest cheers came after GOP Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas declared: “Sharia law has no place in America.”
Muslim American civic leaders and scholars — in Texas and other states — responded forcefully to the anti-Sharia rhetoric that dates back more than 15 years.
They passionately defended Sharia — the way it’s practiced in the United States — as positive guidance that shares elements with the codes of other faiths, such as the Ten Commandments and the collective body of Jewish law derived from the Torah. They rebutted the claims of GOP critics that Sharia is a coercive code that threatens the Constitution and the judicial system.
Gula noted that Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott and Attorney General Ken Paxton were among the leaders of the anti-Sharia campaign. Abbott lost his bid for reelection in Tuesday’s voting, and Paxton was trounced by Democrat James Talarico in the race for a U.S. Senate seat.
“I saw this as not just Muslims standing against Islamophobia as never before,” Gula said. “I saw Americans saying hate will not be used as a campaign issue ... we are not going to accept hate.”
Asma Uddin, a professor at Michigan State University’s College of Law, has argued that many American politicians are depicting ordinary Muslim religious practices — such as prayer, choice of apparel, family counseling and mosque attendance — as evidence of political danger.
“What I find especially exciting is that El-Sayed won in a political climate where being visibly Muslim can still be a liability,” she said. His victory “gives us real reason for optimism. It suggests that anti-Muslim attacks don’t necessarily carry the political weight that those deploying them assume they do.”

text:
This Tiny Maine Town Is One of the Most Underrated in America
Quiet, quaint, and totally worth the trip! America’s underrated town you need to put on your radar.
Love Exploring is a website that covers everything from budget travel to luxury, destination features, city guides, travel deals, photo galleries, and more.
When it comes to undiscovered gems, Maine has plenty of them! Sure, OOB, Portland and Bar Harbor get most of the attention, but when Love Exploring put together a list of the most underrated towns in the United States, their pick for the 207, was an inspired one.
Stonington, Maine is trip well worth making for a fun, quiet getaway. First things first...to get there, you have to cross a pretty infamous bridge.
The Deer Isle Bridge, is a brightly colored suspension bridge connecting mainland Maine, with Deer Isle. It has swooping cables for support, which is part of what makes it so unique.
The first thing you notice is that it looks like a giant on-ramp when you enter. Then, it is basically like driving up, and then down a scary hill. Also, for a bridge of that size, it is very narrow.
Read More: When Will Bangor-Brewer's Chamberlain Bridge Return To Two Lanes?
The voyage over the bridge is all worth it, because when you finally hit Stonington, you will find a creative spot, packed with artists' studios and galleries, and there's an iconic opera house for live music and theater.
Foodies will be satisfied, because fresh Maine lobster is priority one there, plus you can eat it while looking over the bay.
It’s a small town, with just over a thousand residents, but a place so small, it has a ton of personality. The harbor is buzzing with lobster boats hauling in the day’s catch, seagulls squawking for scraps, and salty air that is impossible not to enjoy.
Take a stroll on the narrow streets and you'll walk past charming 19th-century homes, tiny shops, and small cafés where you get the ultimate cozy vibe, kinda like you are in a Hallmark Christmas movie.
Stonington is also a nature lover’s dream. Rugged cliffs, pine-scented forests, and a cluster of tiny islands just offshore make it perfect for kayaking, hiking, or just gazing out at the water.
I have been there several times, and always enjoy visiting Stonecutters Restaurant. Its casual, fun and perfect for seafood lovers, and for those who enjoy an adult beverage or two. Comes with a great view too!

title: What causes dry mouth, and what can you do about it?
text:
(Aging Untold) — Dry mouth can show up alongside soreness, bad breath and trouble with dentures.
It affects 40% of adults 80 and up and 30% of adults 65 and up, according to the American Dental Association.
What causes dry mouth?
Dry mouth happens when the salivary glands do not produce enough fluid, and there are several causes for it, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said. Finding that reason is the first step.
“Basically your salivary glands are just not producing enough fluid. And so you want to know why. You know, always find your why,” Rogers said.
Rogers listed several possible causes:
- Dehydration
“If you’re dehydrated you’re not producing fluid,” Rogers said.
- Damage to nerves
- Cancer
- Underlying autoimmune disorders
Rogers said a cause such as an autoimmune disorder might be a clue that “something else is going on.”
- Medications
Rogers also said dry mouth can be an early sign in a person who is otherwise healthy.
“That might be their clue that you have something going on in your body. And this is your early sign,” Rogers said.
Why saliva matters
“Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said saliva does more than keep the mouth wet.
“People don’t realize just how important saliva is,” she said. “Think about driving a car without any engine oil. It’s not going to last long.”
Without enough saliva, Cradduck said talking, eating and chewing are difficult.
“It is the mouthwash for your body. It really is,” she said.
Rogers added that saliva cleanses and protects the enamel.
Dentures do not make saliva less important, she said. Dry mouth can affect how dentures fit and how a person chews, and it can lead to discomfort, pain and more sores.
Ways to manage dry mouth
Cradduck said she has dealt with dry mouth for a long time because of an autoimmune condition and shared what she does.
“I keep gum in all the time. There is gum in my mouth right now. I sleep with gum in, candy, little hard drops, things like that that cause your mouth to salivate,” Cradduck said.
Cradduck also brought up mouthwash.
“A lot of mouthwash has alcohol, and alcohol is drying, so that’s counterintuitive,” she said.
“A lot of the things that will dry your mouth, you need to stop doing and avoid doing,” Cradduck said, and named drinking and smoking.
Cradduck also mentioned sticky drops that can be placed on the gums.
“It helps, for some people,” she said.
Cradduck described a person who had salivary glands removed because of cancer and uses stickers that go around the gums.
Rogers said treatments either stimulate a gland that is underproducing or provide moisture when the gland cannot produce.
Talk with your dentist
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said a regular conversation with a dentist can help.
“I think that idea of having a conversation with your dentist every year or twice a year, however often you go: How’s my mouth doing? How’s the dryness?” O’Rourke said.
She said possible signs of trouble with dry mouth include coughing a lot, having recurring infections and avoiding certain foods.
“Stay on top of it by reaching out to the professionals,” O’Rourke said.
Key takeaways
- Dry mouth means the salivary glands are not producing enough fluid. Dehydration, nerve damage, cancer, autoimmune disorders and medications can all play a role, according to Dr. Rhea Rogers.
- Dry mouth can be an early sign. Rogers said it can point to something going on in the body, even in a person who is healthy and not taking medications.
- Dentures are affected too. Dry mouth can change how dentures feel and how a person chews, and it can lead to pain and sores, Rogers said.
- Ask your dentist. Bring up dryness at regular visits, and mention coughing, recurring infections or avoiding certain foods, Amy O’Rourke said.

title: Senate Democrats will not let Trump put a 'right-winger' on the Supreme Court, Schumer vows
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer is vowing that Democrats will not allow President Donald Trump to put “a right-winger” on the Supreme Court once they take power, raising the possibility that his party could block a presidential nominee if there is a vacancy in the next two years.
In an interview with The Associated Press on Thursday, Schumer would not say if he would hold a Supreme Court vacancy open until after the next presidential election, as former Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell did in 2016. But he said that Democrats are “not going to allow any crappy nominees” to be confirmed to the Supreme Court — or to the lower courts or Trump’s Cabinet, either.
“The bottom line is we’re not going to allow a right-winger on the court,” Schumer said.
Schumer’s pledge came two days after Democrats won a decisive Senate majority in the midterm elections — a feat few predicted a year ago, when Schumer was facing intense criticism from progressives within his party and Senate Republicans were betting that a favorable map and backing from Trump would help them keep power.
While there is still frustration with Schumer in some corners of the party, the New Yorker is expected to easily be reelected as leader by his caucus after leading them to wins in Republican-leaning states across the country. Democrats could have as many as 56 seats in the Senate if they win Mississippi and Alaska, which still have not been called — “a durable majority,” Schumer predicts, that has been 20 years in the making as he has been directly or indirectly in charge of his party’s Senate campaign operation.
With so many seats, Schumer is betting that “it’s not just a flip of the Senate once.” And the party will have the power not only to reject any of Trump’s nominees, forcing him to seek more moderate choices, but also to halt the Iran war and alter policies that they have been unable to counter in the minority.
Navigating divided government, Schumer says focus will be on costs
Schumer says the party’s agenda will center around lowering prices, along with five issues that they have focused on in the minority — healthcare, housing, Trump’s tariffs, childcare and lowering energy bills. Democrats also want to investigate Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids across the country and scrutinize the Trump administration, which he says is the “most corrupted administration by far in American history.”
But Schumer would not get into specifics, or how he plans to get around Trump — who posted a picture of a red hat with the word “veto” in large letters on election night.
Beyond Trump, Schumer will also have to navigate his own caucus, including progressives who have criticized him and incoming freshman who won red states and would not commit to supporting him for leader during their campaigns. And to pass any legislation, he will still have to win Republican support as well.
He predicts that Republicans will suffer more losses “and keep following Trump over the cliff” if they don’t work with Democrats in a bipartisan way.
But that will not be easy. Schumer would not say if he would try and eliminate the filibuster, which he tried and failed to do when he was majority leader during President Joe Biden’s term, to allow Democrats to pass legislation with a simple majority instead of 60 votes.
“The focus has got to be on getting things done,” he says. “That’s all I am saying.”
Asked if he would support a third Trump impeachment after Trump was impeached and acquitted twice during his first term, Schumer responds that he would support an impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, an effort that House lawmakers have already launched.
And Trump? “That’s up to the House,” Schumer said.
Election wins two decades in the making
Schumer first led his party’s campaign arm in the 2006 cycle and has had a hand in every election since then, with mixed results.
He attributes this year’s wins to his own candidate recruitment and a focus on local issues in Republican states — the effect of Trump’s tariffs on farms in Iowa, where Democrat Josh Turek won, Trump’s war with Canada in Maine, where Democrat Troy Jackson beat Republican Sen. Susan Collins, and data centers in Ohio, where former Sen. Sherrod Brown won after losing his seat two years ago to Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno.
Still, the party’s focus on lowering costs was “a message that resonated everywhere,” he says. “That’s a big difference than in the past.”
The Democrats who won were not all his recruits — in Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed represents the progressive wing of the party and beat Schumer’s original choice for the seat, Haley Stevens, in the primary. But Schumer poured $67 million into that race to help El-Sayed and the two “talk regularly,” he said.
Schumer’s future is unclear
Even with his winning record this year, it is still unclear how long he will stay in power — and how long the party will support him as some call for a new generation of leadership. He is up for reelection in 2028, and he won’t say if he’ll run again for a sixth term.
“I’m focused on 2027,” said Schumer, who became the party’s Senate leader in 2015.
Senators in his caucus are sticking by him, but many are also agitating for change as they enter a new era of power.
Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a potential contender for the 2028 presidential nomination who has not committed to supporting Schumer, said in an interview with the AP on Wednesday that Democrats need to have an “open and honest discussion” about the next leader.
Vermont Sen. Peter Welch said in a separate interview that Schumer “has to adjust and open things up and take into account the criticism of our efforts.”
Still, Welch said, there’s no indication of a leadership challenge. “Schumer did an incredible job on this campaign,” he said.
___
Associated Press writers Joey Cappelletti and Lisa Mascaro contributed to this report.

title: FBI agent struck pedestrian with government car then lied about NYC hit-and-run, prosecutors say
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — An FBI agent drove his government car the wrong way down a busy Brooklyn thoroughfare, blew through a red light and then struck a pedestrian before speeding away, federal prosecutors said Thursday.
Andrew Reyes later lied to investigators about the Feb. 3 hit-and-run that left the victim seriously injured, according to an indictment unsealed in U.S. District Court.
Reyes, a 30-year-old Brooklyn resident, was arrested Thursday morning and his arraignment was scheduled for later in the day. He faces charges including willfully depriving an individual of his constitutional rights while acting under color of law and making false statements.
Reyes’ attorney, Federal Public Defender Nora Hirozawa, said he would be pleading not guilty. She declined further comment.
Reyes had the car’s emergency lights activated as he sped against traffic on Ocean Parkway, a six-lane boulevard, when he hit the man and knocked him to the pavement, according to court documents. Then Reyes got out of the car, dragged the unconscious victim out of the street and placed his bag next to him on a bench before fleeing the scene, the documents said.
Prosecutors said when investigators asked Reyes if he’d ever hit a person and not reported it, Reyes falsely stated that he had not.
“The defendant’s alleged conduct demonstrated a shocking disregard for human life and his sworn oath to uphold the law,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella said in a statement Thursday. “The charges announced today send the clear message that no one is above the law and those who abuse their position of trust and deprive citizens of their constitutional rights will be prosecuted.”
The victim was not identified and his condition wasn’t known.
Court papers list Reyes as a former FBI Special Agent. The bureau didn’t immediately respond to inquiries about his employment history and status.

title: Maine's 2nd District Race Heads To Ranked-choice Tabulation Despite Dunlap's Concession
text:
Dunlap Concedes: Maine’s 2nd Congressional District Moves to Ranked-Choice
Matthew Dunlap has conceded the 2nd Congressional race to Paul LePage, but Maine's Secretary of State says officials will hold ranked-choice tabulations on Monday.
Maine Will Use Ranked Choice Tabulations to Decide the 2nd Congressional District Winner
Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows says ranked-choice tabulation is necessary because neither candidate achieved a majority of first-choice votes cast on Election Day.
Voters cast 341,248 ballots in the 2nd Congressional District race.
170,263 people voted for Paul LePage, while 164,845 voted for Matthew Dunlap.
123 votes went to write-in candidates, and 6,017 were blank, with no candidate chosen.
Since no candidate received more than 50% of the total ballots cast, the ranked choice tabulation is necessary.
Maine's 2nd District Ranked Choice Tabulations to Begin on Monday, Despite Concession
WABI-TV reports Matthew Dunlap conceded the race on Monday and congratulated LePage on his victory.
Despite the concession, Secretary of State Bellows says the ranked choice process is still required by law.
Those tabulations are scheduled to begin on Monday, November 9, 2026, at 10 a.m. at the Maine Department of Public Safety Headquarters building in Augusta.
The public can view the tabulations on the Secretary of State's YouTube page.
Ranked choice tabulations happen in rounds, with the lowest-ranked candidate eliminated from each round until only two candidates remain.
The candidate who receives the majority (more than 50%) of the votes in the final round will be declared the winner.
Maine's 2nd Congressional District Includes 10 Counties
Maine 2nd Congressional District includes 10 counties:
- Androscoggin
- Aroostook
- Franklin
- Hancock
- Oxford
- Penobscot
- Piscataquis
- Somerset
- Waldo
- Washington
At over 27,000 square miles, it is the largest district east of the Mississippi River.
We'll update this story as more details become available.

title: Leon Black sues US Rep. Robert Garcia for defamation over Epstein comments
text:
Billionaire Leon Black sues US Rep. Robert Garcia for defamation over Epstein comments
Billionaire Leon Black on Wednesday filed a federal defamation lawsuit against California Rep. Robert Garcia for public comments the Democratic congressman made tying him to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.
The court filing comes less than two months after the House approved a resolution holding Black in contempt of Congress for defying the Oversight Committee's subpoenas in its investigation into Epstein.
In June, Black appeared for a voluntary interview at the committee during which he denied any knowledge of Epstein's sex trafficking network.
Weeks later, Garcia said during a TV interview that "Leon Black is at the center of Jeffrey Epstein's crimes" and that Black "was one of the last people to actually interact" with Epstein before he committed suicide in prison.
In addition, Garcia said that he had "talked to survivors that have credibly named Leon Black as someone that was involved in direct abuse of women and was directly involved" with Epstein.
Those statements were false and were made maliciously, Black asserts through his lawyers. The defamation lawsuit filed in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York seeks a jury trial and $7.25 million in compensatory and punitive damages.
"Congressman Garcia's knowing lies have caused real and significant ongoing harm to Mr. Black. His physical safety has been threatened, he has received a barrage of hateful calls, emails, and social media posts, and his business and philanthropic endeavors have suffered," the filing states.
Garcia's office didn't immediately respond to requests for comment on the lawsuit.
In September, Garcia called the contempt resolution against Black "an important step toward justice and accountability."
Black had refused to respond to subpoenas asking him to appear and to turn over any potential nondisclosure agreements involving the investigation into Epstein.
Black's lawyers have repeatedly denounced the Oversight Committee's pursuit of the former head of a private equity firm as an abuse of congressional power. They have maintained he had no knowledge of any of Epstein's criminal conduct.
Black was among several prominent figures, including Bill Clinton and Bill Gates, who had been asked to appear as part of the Oversight Committee's long-running probe of Epstein. Survivors of Epstein's alleged sexual abuse have told personal stories of being young women in a trafficking enterprise organized by Epstein and his colleague Ghislaine Maxwell.
Black co-founded the private equity firm Apollo Global Management and stepped down in 2021 during the fallout over his ties to Epstein.
Lawmakers have alleged that Black paid Epstein $180 million during their yearslong relationship.
A 2021 review commissioned by Apollo found that Black paid Epstein $158 million from 2012 to 2017, after Epstein pleaded guilty in 2008 to soliciting prostitution from a minor. The review said the payments were for "bona fide tax, estate planning and other related services."

title: A brutal sell-off for AI stocks sends Wall Street reeling, and the S&P 500 tumbles 4.4%
text:
A brutal sell-off for AI stocks sends Wall Street reeling, and the S&P 500 tumbles 4.4%
A brutal sell-off swept through Wall Street Thursday, led by stocks tied to the buildout of AI data centers. The wipeout more than erased the U.S. stock market's gain from the day before, which was its best in three months.
The S&P 500 fell 4.4% for its worst day since President Donald Trump shook markets worldwide in April 2025 with his "Liberation Day" tariffs. The Dow Jones Industrial Average sank 1,833 points, or 3.4%, while the Nasdaq composite tumbled 5.5%.
The Nasdaq, which is full of AI-related and other tech stocks, sank 11.9% below its all-time high set last month. Stock geeks call a loss of more than 10% a "correction."
Stock markets around the world felt pressure from continued drops for companies that had benefited from the boom in the artificial-intelligence technology industry, and South Korea's Kospi index tumbled 5.3%. Such stocks have been swinging for months on worries that the construction of further AI data centers may slow because of how expensive it's become to borrow money. Critics also said AI stock prices had shot too high and were in a bubble.
Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections added another challenge. The nationwide victories for Democrats raised the possibility that governments could force pauses in construction of more data centers. Voters across political parties say they're wary about AI and don't like the increases to power bills caused by data centers.
Any slowdown in construction of AI data centers would mean fewer purchases of AI chips, not to mention electricity and other products and services that are getting vacuumed up in the AI frenzy, which is driving much of the U.S. economy's growth.
Nvidia, the chip company that quickly became the face of the AI boom, fell 9.3% and was by far the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. It's now down 2.6% for the year so far following annual gains of roughly 39%, 171% and 239% in the last three years.
Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 17.3%. CoreWeave, a company that rents access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, fell 9.8%. GE Vernova, which has been helping to power data centers, sank 7.5%.
Compounding the pain for investors, AI chip stocks are some of Wall Street's most influential because they've become some of the largest. A 1% move for Nvidia, for example, has more effect on the S&P 500 than a 1% move for nearly any other U.S. stock.
Thursday's losses were broad after gains for the majority of stocks on Wall Street during the morning quickly evaporated.
Among the handful of winners was AppLovin, which jumped 31% after the marketing platform reported both revenue and profit that topped analysts' expectations. The company's board also approved a program to send up to $3.2 billion to investors by buying back its own stock, bringing the program's total potential value to $3.6 billion.
Tapestry rallied 7.1% after the company behind the Coach and Kate Spade brands likewise delivered a stronger profit than expected. It also raised its forecasts for revenue and earnings this fiscal year.
Stock prices tend to follow where corporate profits and interest rates go over the long term, depending on them much more than on who controls what in Washington.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 334.89 points to 7,353.73. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,833.06 to 51,523.06, and the Nasdaq composite sank 1,421.52 to 24,315.00.
In other financial markets, the initial knee-jerk reaction to the U.S. midterm election results faded a bit. The price of a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 3.9% to $98.29 and recovered a chunk of its nearly 9% drop from the day before. Uncertainty still reigns about what will happen in the war with Iran and when the global energy industry can return to normal.
In the bond market, Treasury yields continued to tumble. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.84% from 4.90% late Wednesday. It had been at 4.95% on election night and above 5.30% last month. That could be a signal that investors are herding into U.S. Treasury bonds in search of something that's safer to own as stock prices tumble.
The drop in yields came despite some encouraging reports on the U.S. economy. Fewer U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week. A separate report, meanwhile, suggested overall productivity for U.S. workers improved by more during the summer than economists expected. That could help the economy grow without adding pressure to the nation's high inflation.
In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. Besides South Korea, Japan's Nikkei 225 also felt the sting of drops for tech and AI-related stocks and sank 1.8%.
London's FTSE 100 dipped 0.4% after the Bank of England increased its main interest rate for the first time in three years to help limit high inflation.
The bank said its next moves on interest rates will largely hinge on what happens with the Iran war, which sent oil prices and inflation higher worldwide.
"We've seen encouraging news in the past 48 hours," Bank Gov. Andrew Bailey said at a press briefing. "The best thing that can happen is to resolve the conflict in the Middle East; there's no question about it."
___
AP Business Writer Elaine Kurtenbach contributed to this report.

title: Mother honors stillborn son by bringing comfort to grieving families
text:
MARSHALL, Mich. (InvestigateTV) — Sabrina and Brenden Miller walked through the doors of Oak Lawn Hospital with 17 bags full of comfort items, a delivery they make each year on their son’s birthday.
Nurses in the birth center received the bags, which will eventually go to mothers of stillborn children.
“I always hope that they just like sit in the room and get dusty and take up space, but knowing that that’s not what’s going to happen, and that someone’s going to find comfort in them, it’s bittersweet,” Sabrina Miller said.
They’re called Beau’s Bags, named after the Millers’ son Beau Anthony, who was stillborn five years ago.
“My two best friends brought care packages to the hospital for us, which is where Beau’s Bags came from,” Sabrina Miller said.
The Millers assemble the bags at a children’s table in their home. Each bag contains socks, lotion, a notebook, a water bottle and other self-care items.
“Writing letters to Beau helped a lot,” she said.
Jill Hays, a nurse at Oak Lawn Birth Center, said the bags provide something tangible for grieving mothers.
“By having something that’s prepared by a mother that’s gone through the same process or journey, they will have something to hold onto,” Hays said.
Miller said she blamed herself after Beau’s death.
“I blamed myself and my own body, and like if my body couldn’t take care of him, then I’m not taking care of my body, so I always try to do a fun water bottle and a reminder to drink your water, like it’s not your fault, take care of yourself,” she said.
Brenden Miller, Beau’s father, said the bags help keep their son’s memory alive.
“You find yourself not thinking about him and then you feel bad for not thinking about him, so every chance that we can get to spread his name out there a little bit more, it’s like he’s still here,” he said.
The Millers have four other children. Beau remains part of their family count.
“He’s still in our count of kids, and we still celebrate him every year,” Sabrina Miller said.
Each year on or around Beau’s birthday, May 4th, family and friends release balloons with birthday wishes. The annual hospital visit with Beau’s Bags has become an early May tradition as well.
“He is 5 today,” Sabrina Miller said on this year’s delivery day. “I love walking in and they all know me and make me feel at home.”
Miller said she hopes Beau’s Bags help other mothers feel comfortable talking about their babies.
“The bags and these things are in memory of him, I think has helped other moms feel more comfortable in talking about their babies, and I hope that keeps going for years and years,” she said.

title: FBI agent struck Brooklyn pedestrian, dragged him to a bench and lied about it, prosecutors say
text:
FBI agent struck Brooklyn pedestrian, dragged him to a bench and lied about it, prosecutors say
An FBI agent dragged a pedestrian across a snowy sidewalk, left him on a bench and sped away in his government-issued car after hitting and severely injuring him while driving the wrong way down a busy New York City street, federal prosecutors said Thursday.
Andrew Reyes, 30, blew through a red light and struck the man as he was crossing the street on Feb. 3 in Brooklyn, prosecutors said. He later lied to investigators about it, denying that he'd ever hit a person with his FBI vehicle and not reported it.
Through his lawyer, Reyes pleaded not guilty to charges of willfully depriving an individual of his constitutional rights while acting under color of law and making false statements. He was released on a $100,000 bond co-signed by his parents, whom he lives with.
If convicted, Reyes faces up to 10 years in prison.
Judge declines prosecutors' request for a mental health evaluation
Prosecutors had sought to have Reyes ordered to undergo a mental health evaluation, citing the alleged cover-up attempt and an alarming comment he made about a gun during a law enforcement interview, but a judge said one wasn't warranted.
Reyes, who is no longer with the FBI, teared up as his parents spoke to the judge at his arraignment. His lawyer, Nora Hirozawa, handed him tissues and placed a hand on his back to comfort him. He is due back in court on Dec. 2. The man he's accused of hitting wasn't in court for the arraignment. He has not been publicly identified.
Reyes had his car’s emergency lights activated when he hit the pedestrian as he sped against traffic on six-lane Ocean Parkway south of Prospect Park, prosecutors said. He then got out of the car, dragged the unconscious man out of the street and placed the man and his bag on a bench before fleeing the scene, prosecutors said.
Interviewed on May 1 by the Justice Department Inspector General’s office, Reyes denied involvement in any hit-and-run, prosecutors said. Toward the end of questioning, Reyes asked what an investigator would do if he grabbed the investigator's gun, Assistant U.S. Attorney Gilbert Rein told Magistrate Judge Clay Kaminsky.
“Just out of the blue?” Kaminsky asked.
“Yes, unprompted,” Rein said.
Hirozawa said she hadn’t reviewed a recording of the interview but characterized Reyes' gun remark as an “offhand” comment, albeit a “very odd” one. Kaminsky agreed that the comment was odd but declined to add a mental health evaluation to bail conditions that require Reyes to surrender his passport and limit travel to New York and New Jersey.
Circumstances led to case being tried in federal court
Reyes was arrested Thursday morning, prosecutors said. He was brought into court from a holding area in an untucked button-down shirt and Under Armour jogging pants.
While local prosecutors typically handle alleged hit-and-runs, Reyes’ role as an FBI agent, use of a government vehicle and alleged lying to Justice Department investigators led to the case being tried in federal court rather than state court.
Reyes, clutching his release paperwork, declined to comment as he left court with his lawyer and parents.
Hirozawa said in court that Reyes worked for the agency for more than nine years. His indictment said he became a special agent in 2023. Since leaving the agency, he has been working at a home remodeling business, Hirozawa said.
In response to questions about Reyes, the FBI said it was made aware of his alleged criminal conduct in April and promptly terminated his employment.
“This employee demonstrated an utter disregard for human life and the rule of law and did not uphold the values of this organization and all for which we stand,” the FBI's New York field office said in a statement. “We moved quickly to ensure their immediate dismissal and continue to fully cooperate with this investigation."
U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella said Reyes' alleged conduct “demonstrated a shocking disregard for human life and his sworn oath to uphold the law.”
The charges against him “send the clear message that no one is above the law and those who abuse their position of trust and deprive citizens of their constitutional rights will be prosecuted,” Nocella said in a statement.

title: New Maine ferry honors longtime captain, marks first hybrid vessel for state
text:
New Maine ferry honors longtime captain, marks first hybrid vessel for state
The 154-foot vessel, the M/V Captain Almer Dinsmore, can carry up to 250 passengers and 23 vehicles and will serve the Rockland-to-Vinalhaven route
New Maine ferry honors longtime captain, marks first hybrid vessel for state
The 154-foot vessel, the M/V Captain Almer Dinsmore, can carry up to 250 passengers and 23 vehicles and will serve the Rockland-to-Vinalhaven route
The Maine State Ferry Service introduced its first hybrid diesel-electric ferry Thursday, naming the vessel after a longtime captain who spent decades serving the state's island communities.
The 154-foot vessel, the M/V Captain Almer Dinsmore, can carry up to 250 passengers and 23 vehicles. It will serve the Rockland-to-Vinalhaven route.
The ferry is named for Captain Almer Dinsmore, who spent 45 years at sea and joined the Maine State Ferry Service in 1978. He served on routes connecting several island communities before retiring in 2013.
During a commissioning ceremony Thursday in Rockland, officials unveiled a plaque bearing Dinsmore's name and likeness aboard the new vessel.
Dinsmore said the recognition was overwhelming, especially considering his upbringing in Steuben.
“Just little old me growing up in Steuben, Maine, I never would've thought of nothing like this,” Dinsmore said. “It's awesome.”
The new ferry uses a hybrid propulsion system that combines diesel engines with electric motors. The technology is designed to improve fuel efficiency and reduce emissions.
U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, who lives on North Haven and relies on the ferry system to travel to and from the mainland, said the hybrid technology could help reduce operating costs for the service.
“Being able to bring down the fuel costs for these ferries by making them hybrid is critically important, especially in a time of tight budgets,” Pingree said.
The new vessel is expected to begin carrying passengers immediately on the Rockland-to-Vinalhaven route.

title: Amazon adds Uber Eats to list of services for Amazon Prime members
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Amazon adds Uber Eats to list of services for Amazon Prime members
Amazon is adding a new restaurant delivery perk for its Prime members, escalating the food delivery wars.
Video above: How to save money on takeout and delivery every time
The Seattle-based online behemoth said Thursday that it has agreed to add Uber Eats to its list of services for Amazon Prime members in the U.S. The service, which will be effective immediately, will allow members to order from hundreds of thousands of restaurants from Uber Eats directly from Amazon.com and within the retailer's shopping app with no delivery fees for orders over $25, the companies said in a joint release.
At launch, Prime members can get started with $20 off the first two Uber Eats orders of $25 or more, eligible for the first 14 days, according to the release.
The tie-up with Uber Eats marks Amazon's second partnership with a restaurant delivery partner. In 2024, Amazon added Grubhub for Amazon Prime members and has been adding more perks for these members who pay $14.99 monthly, or $139 annually, for an annual subscription for free shipping. The offer with Grubhub for these customers will wind down when the Uber Eats partnership kicks in, Amazon said.
Andrew Macdonald, president and chief operating officer of Uber, noted in the release that together with Amazon, it “built an experience for Prime members designed to make restaurant delivery feel as natural, convenient, and affordable as ordering anything else on Uber Eats.”
The announcement comes as DoorDash announced last month that it was offering $17 billion to buy Instacart in a deal that could consolidate the grocery delivery business in the U.S. and abroad.
The companies said the tie-up would combine DoorDash’s global reach and expertise in logistics with Instacart’s purpose-built technology and long relationships with grocers. It could also help the companies better compete with rivals moving into restaurant delivery.
Also on Thursday, ride sharing company Lyft unveiled a rideshare and delivery membership program with DoorDash. For $9.99 per month, or $96 annually, members can get credits toward future rides or delivery orders.
Walmart is also pushing into restaurant delivery. In its first deal with a restaurant delivery partner, Walmart partnered with Subway, its largest in-store restaurant tenant, this past summer. It has since expanded to select locations at Dunkin’ and Papa Johns. The company said it now has 2,400 restaurant locations on its restaurant delivery platform.
Since launching delivery with Subway, 65% of those orders have included other items from Walmart, according to Greg Cathey, Walmart’s senior vice president of e-commerce transformation.

title: Showers moving through, gloomy stretch begins
text:
Showers moving through, gloomy stretch begins
Showers moving through, gloomy stretch begins
A brief round of rain moves through Maine midday on Thursday, with only a few hundredths to a couple of tenths of an inch expected by sundown. After a mainly dry evening, an isolated shower will be possible overnight, along with patchy fog.
Despite the gloom, temperatures are running well above average for early November, with highs in the 60s and low 70s and only falling into the 50s in most spots overnight.
Another unseasonably warm day is expected on Friday before temperatures return to normal this weekend (highs in the 40s and 50s). A cold front arrives and stalls near the coast, and several waves of low pressure move along the front, bringing rounds of showers and some much-needed rain.
Friday will be a nicer day inland than at the coast, with highs mainly in the 60s. Patchy fog is possible in the morning before showers approach the coastline. Partly sunny to mostly cloudy skies are expected inland, with a lower chance for showers there late in the day.
Along and near the coast, showers are possible Friday afternoon and likely by the evening. Spotty showers continue Friday night and may push farther inland.
Saturday is trending drier but will still be a gloomy, unsettled day. Scattered showers are possible across the area, mainly in the morning, with another round expected overnight.
Sunday is trending wetter, with scattered showers expected through much of the day as an area of low pressure develops in the Gulf of Maine. Sunday's showers are expected to be widespread, and some wet snow may mix in in the mountains.

title: Teen missing for over a year found at home of man who sexually assaulted her, removed braces with pliers, police say
text:
HUNTINGTON, Ore. (AP) — A 17-year-old girl from Utah who went missing in May 2025 was found at the home of an Oregon man who’s been charged with transporting her across state lines with the intent to engage in criminal sexual activity.
Authorities acting on a tip rescued the girl Sunday at a home in Huntington, Oregon, and arrested Adam Hunter Harmel, 39, in a traffic stop about 30 miles away.
The missing girl told another child she met online that she had run away and was being held against her will at a man’s house in Oregon.
On Sunday, a parent of the other child contacted the missing Utah girl by video — and the FBI listened in.
During the call, the missing girl said that she met Harmel on social media and that he had driven her from Utah to Oregon, an FBI agent said in court records.
She also said Harmel threw her phone in a river; told her she couldn’t leave his home; made her sleep against a wall to prevent her from escaping from the bed they shared; often hit her; sexually assaulted her; and forced her to remove her braces with pliers so she couldn’t be identified, according to the FBI.
No lawyer for Harmel was listed in court records.
The federal public defender’s office in Utah declined to comment when The Associated Press asked if it represented Harmel. The AP also reached out through social media to someone believed to be related to Harmel.
