title: House fire in Brooklyn kills 6 people and injures 7, more than 200 firefighters respond
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Six people died in a fire that barreled through a two-story home in New York early Thursday and seven others were injured, including three firefighters, the city’s fire department said.
Heavy fire was reported in the row frame building at 1:40 a.m. in Brooklyn. More than 200 first responders reported to the fire in the borough’s Sunset Park neighborhood. It was brought under control in about 3 hours.
Four people died at the scene, the fire department said in a statement. Two people with critical injuries were taken to a hospital, where they were later pronounced dead. Four people suffered non-life-threatening injuries.
Three firefighters suffered minor injuries as well, the department said.
No names or ages of the victims have been released.
Fire marshals were investigating. A lithium-ion battery was found at the scene, but it was unknown if it was related to the cause of the fire, the department said.

title: 'Catastrophic flood event' prompts rescues, evacuations in parts of Tennessee, Georgia
text:
'Catastrophic flood event' prompts rescues, evacuations in parts of Tennessee, Georgia
Homes are flooded and water rescues and evacuations are in progress as flash flood emergencies — the highest level of flood warning — impact North Georgia and southern Tennessee.
The flash flood emergencies are in effect for McCaysville, Georgia, and Copperhill, Tennessee, on the Georgia-Tennessee border.
Record flooding is ongoing there along a river known as the Ocoee River in Tennessee and the Toccoa River in Georgia once it flows across the border.
Related video: Flooding in the Southwest, Colorado town
The river crested just above the previous record flood set in 1990 just after 6 a.m. ET in McCaysville and Copperhill, above the level that causes a "catastrophic flood event" in the two towns, according to the National Weather Service.
A state of emergency has been issued in McCaysville, and the city is closed until further notice, according to the city's police chief Michael Earley.
"We're actively trying to water rescue people, and we've still got several people trapped in homes that we're trying to get to," Earley told CNN affiliate Atlanta News First. "The water keeps rising, so just bear with us as much as you can and please say a prayer for them and their families."
There were still "numerous residents" that needed evacuations in Fannin County, where McCaysville is located, the county's emergency management said early Thursday morning.
Evacuations were ordered for residents in McCaysville on West Tennessee Avenue and East Tennessee Avenue, where a Georgia DOT camera showed streets and buildings swamped by the flooded river.
"DO NOT DELAY YOUR EVACUATION. LEAVE THE AREA NOW," Earley said in a social media post.
A separate flash flood emergency was also issued overnight for other parts of Fannin County and Gilmer County in Georgia.
Emergency management in both counties reported "widespread flooding, with multiple homes flooded and some completely surrounded by water" and water rescues.
Widespread rainfall totals of 3 to 6 inches from slow-moving overnight storms were reported across parts of North Georgia, with over 8 inches in isolated spots.
Up to 6 inches of rain fell in just six hours at multiple rain gauges in the area. This equates to at least a 1-in-200-year rainfall — a rate that has only a 0.5% chance of happening in a given year, under normal circumstances.
Such extreme rainfall is becoming more common as planet-warming pollution pushes temperatures higher as warmer air can hold more moisture.
The rain has come to an end across northern Georgia and southern Tennessee. No additional downpours are expected through the weekend, but dangerous river flooding will remain a threat throughout the day.

title: Bangor, Maine Teen On Electric Motorcycle Arrested After Chase Through City Streets
South Bristol Fire Chief Proposes Replacement for 25-Year-Old Truck
text:
The South Bristol Select Board gave Fire Chief Allen Spinney permission to look into either replacing or refurbishing the department’s oldest truck during its Thursday, Oct. 29 meeting.
The 25-year-old fire engine is the department’s most-used vehicle, which responds to motor-vehicle crashes, storm incidents, and medical calls, lacks space, and has started to have its own “old truck issues,” Spinney said.
The 2001 manual Ford chassis occasionally drops the engine’s speed, decreases from its operating level without warning, and doesn’t have enough room to store emergency medical service gear, according to Spinney.

title: More than one in three Americans think debt for the latest phone is worth it
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — More than one in three Americans think it is worth putting a new phone on a credit card and taking on debt to get the latest model, according to a new WalletHub survey.
The same survey found almost nine out of 10 people say new phones are overpriced. Nearly half say they would feel inferior using a budget cell phone plan.
John Kiernan, managing editor of WalletHub, said the conflicting results show the phone is still seen as a status symbol.
“A lot of it has to do with keeping up with appearances and presenting a certain image to others,” Kiernan said. “For example, 32% of people say someone who always has the latest iPhone is quote unquote rich, and a lot of us want to give off that impression whether or not it’s true.”
Kiernan also said that because phones can do so much, having the latest model is sometimes more about keeping up with technology for work.
For people trying to save, Kiernan’s first suggestion is to shop around.
“Look into what kind of option you have from phone carriers and phone plans,” Kiernan said. “A lot of times if you switch from one carrier to another you can get a new phone and maybe a bunch of other devices as well.”
Kiernan also said buyers can choose the model behind the latest phone. It will not be the newest, but it could be more affordable. He said researching bundled services may also lead to a good deal on a new phone.

title: Trump signs proclamation he says will prevent future changes to the Oval Office and Cabinet Room
text:
Trump makes the Oval Office a national monument. But future presidents can still redecorate
President Donald Trump on Thursday signed a proclamation that he says will preserve the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as a national monument, his first official action after his party was swept aside in midterm elections on Tuesday.
But the action does not prevent future presidents from restyling the iconic office that Trump has filled to the brim with gold flourishes, nor does it prevent a successor from rolling back the proclamation itself. Trump himself has reversed national monument designations made by his predecessors.
Trump, however, described the Oval Office order in expansive terms. "It will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape," Trump said. "We like the Oval Office, and it's a symbol, like the White House itself."
It was the third day this week that the president, a real estate mogul, delivered remarks fixated on his pet projects in Washington. On Wednesday, a day after Republicans suffered defeats in key races across the country, Trump gathered reporters to sign the final beam being raised during construction of his opulent ballroom project. On Monday, he went to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to talk about his renovation of the landmark.
The proclamation, released after Trump's remarks, says that nothing in it will "restrict the President's authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument's historic structure or architectural character."
It orders the Interior secretary to manage the Oval Office and requires "documentation, review, and consideration of alternatives before any action that would substantially alter or demolish the monument." Trump separately said any major changes would need review from Congress, though such a requirement is not in the document's text.
"If they want to say, 'Let's not have oval anymore, let's make it square,' what happens is they have to go back to Congress and hopefully the Congress, the people in Congress, will be smart enough not to let that happen," said Trump — who notably demolished the East Wing of the White House to make room for his ballroom.
A red baseball cap with "VETO" on the front was sitting on the Resolute Desk as Trump signed the document, a not-so-subtle nod to the shifting of powers in Congress.
His effort to preserve changes at the White House comes as Democrats gear up for new scrutiny of Trump. Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal, the top Democrat on the Homeland Security Committee's Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, sent a flurry of letters Thursday to known donors to Trump's ballroom, demanding that they provide information or face "alternative measures to obtain compliance."
Since returning to the White House, Trump has overseen numerous design changes to various rooms, including the Oval Office, where he has filled the wall space with portraits, a copy of the Declaration of Independence and numerous golden accents.
As he talked about his interior decorating decisions, Trump highlighted new chandeliers that he says were installed in the Cabinet Room to address "very bad lighting." His other additions to the Oval Office include numerous gold wall appliqués and gold-framed portraits.
Trump did not elaborate on precisely what he was hoping to prevent but suggested that the Oval Office might face some threat in the future. Trump himself has faced several lawsuits alleging that his Washington beautification projects were done without the necessary approval.
"If anybody ever decides to come and start knocking down walls, you call me wherever I may be," Trump said, "and I'll come back here and I'll make sure it never happens."

title: Ballot measures include early Christmas present for Kennebunkport
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Beyond Tuesday’s high-profile midterm elections, voters in Maine said yes to two Kennebunkport measures related to funding for the York County town’s annual Christmas Prelude celebration but bah, humbug, to South Portland’s $88 million public safety bond.
Here’s a short recap of local ballot measures.
In Augusta, voters authorized a $53.4 million bond issue to renovate and expand Farrington Elementary School. Voters also approved a $7.4 million bond issue to fund capital improvements including the purchase of equipment at the Augusta Civic Center and a mechanical study into the renovation, repair and improvement of the building.
In South Portland, voters rejected an $88 million proposal to replace the city’s main fire and police stations. The proposal failed by a vote of 8,568 against and 5,002 in favor. The city had planned to build a new Central Fire Station on Broadway at Anthoine and a new police station in Cash Corner. The new buildings were intended to provide safer, more modern facilities, improve emergency service and help attract qualified police and fire personnel to the city.
Kennebunkport voters approved two ballot measures allowing the town to help fund municipal services during its annual Christmas Prelude celebration. One measure calls for amending a town ordinance to allow the funding of municipal services at certain community events, while the other authorizes the use of $17,500 from the town’s undesignated funds to help cover services during this year’s event, a major contributor to the local economy.
Measures to restrict development of data centers passed by wide margins in Peru, Wells, North Berwick and Wiscasset.

title: Fort Kent and Maranacook girls soccer teams face off for Class C state final rematch
text:
The Fort Kent High School girls soccer team will get another crack at Maranacook High of Readfield in Saturday’s state Class C soccer game in Lewiston beginning at 1:30 p.m.
Maranacook beat the Warriors 5-0 in last year’s final.
Fort Kent punched its ticket to another state game appearance by shutting out its three C North playoff opponents, including the 3-0 triumph over Orono in Tuesday’s final.
Senior striker Reese Doucette had a pair of goals, and freshman Hayden Plourde had the other, all in the first half.
“We played pretty well,” said fourth-year head coach Mindy Forino. “There are definitely some things we could finetune a little more but, overall, it was a good game.”
The Warriors had beaten Orono 4-2 and 3-2 during the regular season, and Forino felt if her team played up to its potential, it would triumph for a third time.
“The girls put it all together,” said Forino.
Forino had stressed to them that they needed to come out strong and they did.
“I told them they had to come out fired up from the first whistle and not give up until the end of the game. I was so proud of them because they really, truly did that.”
Forino said she has a “wonderful team,” and unlike other teams she has coached, it doesn’t rely on just one or two players.
She said everyone contributes.
“All 11 of our starters are talented and then we have bench players we can rely on,” said Forino, who has guided the Warriors to a 14-1-2 record with the only loss coming to Class B North finalist Presque Isle. “The talent is a little deeper than usual.”
She said the other thing that sets this team apart from her other teams is the “team chemistry.”
“They truly click as a whole. They love each other and show up and play for each other and the community,” Forino said. “We haven’t had anything that has divided the team.”
She has a dynamic one-two scoring punch up front in senior Doucette, who has scored close to 100 goals for her career, and sophomore Tilly Daigle. They have combined with Plourde, who comes off the bench, to score the vast majority of the team’s 62 goals.
Sophomores Lilly Bouchard and Laney Caron and senior Kiley Marquis supply the Warriors with a formidable attacking midfield and they are well-supported by defensive midfielders Karley Robichaud, a sophomore, and Avery Werntgen, a senior.
The solid back line features senior Niah Durost, junior Avery Marquis and senior Kamryn Martin.
Sophomore Trinity Daigle is the goalkeeper.
Forino said Saturday’s game with Maranacook will be interesting.
“I’m excited. I think we can definitely compete,” Forino said. “It’s just a matter of figuring out between now and then the things we need to work on, working on them in practice and analyzing Marancook.”
She said last year’s final was a “tough game.”
“I’m hoping the morale is a little bit different this year,” Forino said. “You know how it is, on any given day, every team is beatable.”

title: Wiscasset Halloween Event Expands to Include More of Town
text:
Trick-or-treaters ventured from Federal Street to the Wiscasset waterfront during the annual Nightmare on Federal Street on Halloween, Saturday, Oct. 31.
The event, run by the Wiscasset Parks and Recreation Department, Wiscasset Area Chamber of Commerce, and the volunteer group named The Pirates of Wiscasset, includes a block party on Federal Street, a parade of costumed participants, and displays.
This year, the Pirates of Wiscasset, formerly known as the Pirates of Federal Street, put on its display at the Customs House on Water Street. Volunteers dressed as pirates and stood beside treasure chests, on constructed ship sets, and by a replica of stocks.
Tracey Whitney said the change came after the Octagon House on Federal Street transferred ownership, and volunteers had been receiving feedback from homeowners off of Federal Street that they wanted trick-or-treaters as well.
Pirate volunteers guided trick-or-treaters across Route 1 at the crossing near the post office
Customs House owner Chris Soucier, who offered his property when he heard about the change in ownership at the Octagon House, said he “couldn’t be happier” to host the pirates.
“I think that people look like they’re having a real good time,” Soucier said. “I see young and old and I see a lot of smiles.”
Sky Wentworth welcomed trick-or-treaters at the Customs House. He said he has volunteered with The Pirates of Wiscasset for three years.
“Wiscasset is a big old seaport and pirates just seems to be a logical theme to have in the neighborhood,” Wentworth said. “Here we are and at the Customs House, it seems like the ideal spot for our setup.”
Wentworth said the event was “doing very well” before dark, and he had seen a “decent crowd.”
Federal Street was blocked off by the Wiscasset Police Department for the block party. Jan Flowers, who passed out pizza to visitors, said number of volunteers has increased to include people from across town as well.
“It’s the whole community, and it’s a lot of fun,” Flowers said.
This year, the gas station and convenience store Wiscasset Quik Stop provided nine or 10 pizzas and volunteers purchased 30 more, Flowers said. Before the night was up, volunteers passed out 400 pieces of pizza.
At the Wiscasset waterfront, employees of waterfront kayak outfitter Sheepscot Boating handed out cups of apple cider.
Wiscasset Parks and Recreation Director Duane Goud said he has heard positive feedback about the change.
“It’s a big group effort and it’s become more of a bigger group,” Goud said. “It’s grown into a nice event.”
For more information, go to wiscassetme.myrec.com, email [email protected], or call 882-8230.

title: A brutal sell-off for AI stocks sends Wall Street reeling; S&P 500 sees worst day since 2025 ‘Liberation Day’ tariffs
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A brutal sell-off swept through Wall Street Thursday, led by stocks tied to the buildout of AI data centers. The wipeout more than erased the U.S. stock market’s gain from the day before, which was its best in three months.
The S&P 500 fell 4.4% for its worst day since President Donald Trump shook markets worldwide in April 2025 with his “Liberation Day” tariffs. The Dow Jones Industrial Average sank 1,833 points, or 3.4%, while the Nasdaq composite tumbled 5.5%.
The Nasdaq, which is full of AI-related and other tech stocks, sank 11.9% below its all-time high set last month. Stock geeks call a loss of more than 10% a “correction.”
Stock markets around the world felt pressure from continued drops for companies that had benefited from the boom in the artificial-intelligence technology industry, and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbled 5.3%. Such stocks have been swinging for months on worries that the construction of further AI data centers may slow because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money. Critics also said AI stock prices had shot too high and were in a bubble.
Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections added another challenge. The nationwide victories for Democrats raised the possibility that governments could force pauses in construction of more data centers. Voters across political parties say they’re wary about AI and don’t like the increases to power bills caused by data centers.
Any slowdown in construction of AI data centers would mean fewer purchases of AI chips, not to mention electricity and other products and services that are getting vacuumed up in the AI frenzy, which is driving much of the U.S. economy’s growth.
Nvidia, the chip company that quickly became the face of the AI boom, fell 9.3% and was by far the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. It’s now down 2.6% for the year so far following annual gains of roughly 39%, 171% and 239% in the last three years.
Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 17.3%. CoreWeave, a company that rents access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, fell 9.8%. GE Vernova, which has been helping to power data centers, sank 7.5%.
Compounding the pain for investors, AI chip stocks are some of Wall Street’s most influential because they’ve become some of the largest. A 1% move for Nvidia, for example, has more effect on the S&P 500 than a 1% move for nearly any other U.S. stock.
Thursday’s losses were broad after gains for the majority of stocks on Wall Street during the morning quickly evaporated.
Among the handful of winners was AppLovin, which jumped 31% after the marketing platform reported both revenue and profit that topped analysts’ expectations. The company’s board also approved a program to send up to $3.2 billion to investors by buying back its own stock, bringing the program’s total potential value to $3.6 billion.
Tapestry rallied 7.1% after the company behind the Coach and Kate Spade brands likewise delivered a stronger profit than expected. It also raised its forecasts for revenue and earnings this fiscal year.
Stock prices tend to follow where corporate profits and interest rates go over the long term, depending on them much more than on who controls what in Washington.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 334.89 points to 7,353.73. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,833.06 to 51,523.06, and the Nasdaq composite sank 1,421.52 to 24,315.00.
In other financial markets, the initial knee-jerk reaction to the U.S. midterm election results faded a bit. The price of a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 3.9% to $98.29 and recovered a chunk of its nearly 9% drop from the day before. Uncertainty still reigns about what will happen in the war with Iran and when the global energy industry can return to normal.
In the bond market, Treasury yields continued to tumble. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.84% from 4.90% late Wednesday. It had been at 4.95% on election night and above 5.30% last month. That could be a signal that investors are herding into U.S. Treasury bonds in search of something that’s safer to own as stock prices tumble.
The drop in yields came despite some encouraging reports on the U.S. economy. Fewer U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week. A separate report, meanwhile, suggested overall productivity for U.S. workers improved by more during the summer than economists expected. That could help the economy grow without adding pressure to the nation’s high inflation.
In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. Besides South Korea, Japan’s Nikkei 225 also felt the sting of drops for tech and AI-related stocks and sank 1.8%.
London’s FTSE 100 dipped 0.4% after the Bank of England increased its main interest rate for the first time in three years to help limit high inflation.
The bank said its next moves on interest rates will largely hinge on what happens with the Iran war, which sent oil prices and inflation higher worldwide.
“We’ve seen encouraging news in the past 48 hours,” Bank Gov. Andrew Bailey said at a press briefing. “The best thing that can happen is to resolve the conflict in the Middle East; there’s no question about it.”

title: Dodge announces its return to the NASCAR Cup Series
text:
Dodge announces its return to the NASCAR Cup Series beginning at the Daytona 500
Dodge is returning to the NASCAR Cup Series in 2027, a year earlier than initially expected.
The Stellantis-owned Dodge brand announced its return at the Specialty Equipment Market Association Show in Las Vegas on Monday.
Video above: Tyler Reddick chats about his historic NASCAR season
Dodge will once again give the Cup Series four manufacturers, joining Chevrolet, Ford and Toyota in fielding entries to compete in a 36-race schedule that begins in mid-February and crowns a champion in early November.
Kaulig Racing will use the Dodge Charger to field a two-car team, likely beginning with the exhibition Clash at Daytona International Speedway on Feb. 13. A more telling debut will come in the Daytona 500 eight days later.
AJ Allmendinger and Ty Dillon are expected to fill those Kaulig seats, although a formal driver announcement is planned for NASCAR's championship weekend in Homestead, Florida.
“Everyone said it was impossible to get back in one year. We said, ‘Watch this,’” said Tim Kuniskis, head of American Brands at Stellantis North America. “Sure, we could spend three years planning, testing and perfecting … or we could do all three in real time, on the track. It’s going to be exponentially harder this way. But slow has never been part of Dodge DNA."
Dodge raced in NASCAR through the 2012 season and left the same month it celebrated the Cup title with Brad Keselowski and Penske Racing. It was Dodge’s first Cup championship since Richard Petty’s sixth of seven titles in 1975.
“Dodge’s return to the NASCAR Cup Series is a significant milestone for the sport,” NASCAR CEO Steve O’Donnell said in a statement. “This commitment speaks to Dodge’s belief in our sport and gives fans another reason to be excited about what’s ahead.
“The partnership between NASCAR, Kuniskis and the entire team at Stellantis has been nothing short of phenomenal. They have a deep passion for NASCAR and its ability to showcase the world’s top brands, and we can’t wait to see Dodge on the racetrack for the Daytona 500 and beyond.”
Dodge re-entered the NASCAR Truck Series with its Ram brand in 2026, with eyes on expanding to the premier Cup Series in 2028. Kuniskis vowed to be disruptive while doing it “unlike anyone else.”
Kuniskis said Ram planned to tap into NASCAR’s estimated fan base of 20 million “and turn it into 80 or 100 million.” Kaulig had five trucks race this season, all of which are outside the top 10 in the series standings heading to Homestead.
Normally, it would have taken Dodge years to get ready for the Cup Series. But Dodge reportedly bypassed part of the timeline required to develop a new engine by partnering with Earnhardt Childress Racing to build Dodge-spec powerplants alongside its regular Chevrolet operations.
The Athletic reported that Chevrolet, Ford and Toyota allowed that unique partnership in part because they believed a fourth manufacturer in NASCAR would be good for the overall health of the racing series.
John Probst, president of NASCAR Event Management, said the sanctioning body continues to search for additional manufacturers and noted that an appealing entry point could coincide with a new engine platform planned between 2030 and 2032.
“The North American car market is probably one of a handful in the world that there’s money to be made on car sales," Probst said. “And I think that when you’re trying to sell cars and trucks and using motorsports as a platform to talk to your fans and your customers, there’s no better place to be than in NASCAR.”

title: More than 3 million ladders sold at Costco and Lowe’s recalled following several reported injuries
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(CNN) - More than 3.5 million ladders have been recalled due to a safety risk and fall hazard.
The brand name is Little Giant.
They were sold at Lowe’s and Costco stores nationwide, as well as online at those sites, Amazon and other sites.
Several ladder models are involved in the recall.
They all have rapid locks that are black and orange and are located on each ladder leg. The ladders can suddenly retract if the locks are not fully engaged, posing a fall hazard.
Little Giant has received 19 reports of injuries.
Customers who own one are advised to stop using it now and review the recall information on the company’s website.
The company will either send a repair kit, offer a replacement ladder or a refund.

title: Scarborough Town Council unanimously approves ban on data centers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Scarborough Town Council unanimously approves ban on data centers
The council voted to lift a 180-day moratorium on data centers after approving zoning changes prohibiting them in all districts
Scarborough Town Council unanimously approves ban on data centers
The council voted to lift a 180-day moratorium on data centers after approving zoning changes prohibiting them in all districts
The Scarborough Town Council voted unanimously Wednesday night to ban data centers across town.
The council also unanimously voted to lift a temporary moratorium on data center development following its approval of the ordinance.
They approved changes to the town's zoning ordinance that prohibits data centers in all zoning districts.
The vote comes five months after the town enacted a 180-day emergency moratorium on data centers over concerns about electricity consumption, noise, water usage and impacts on surrounding properties.
According to town documents, Scarborough's Sustainability Committee determined that the potential drawbacks of data centers outweigh their benefits.
The committee cited concerns about increased electricity costs, strain on the electrical grid, water consumption, air pollution and limited long-term employment opportunities.
The council also voted to repeal the temporary moratorium, which town officials said would no longer be necessary following the zoning changes.
The new ordinance establishes a definition for data centers but excludes smaller server rooms and similar spaces used by businesses, schools and other institutions.

title: KVCAP opens 37 affordable apartments in Waterville
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WATERVILLE, Maine (WABI) -KVCAP celebrated the opening of 37 new affordable apartments in Waterville on Thursday with a ribbon cutting at a site that holds decades of memories for the city.
The event marked the end of a multi-year redevelopment project in the city’s South End.
David Pelton, president and CEO of KVCAP, said the apartments can take some responsibility off residents.
“If they have an affordable, nice place to live that isn’t going to have things breaking down in it because it’s new...If we can play some role in taking that off their plate, then it allows people to focus on something else like, you know, their job or taking care of their kids or taking care of an elderly parent,” Pelton said.
Apartment details
The complex includes a range of unit types, including accessible units.
Justin Amoroso, construction superintendent for E.W. Littlefield, described the apartments.
“There’s one, two and three bedroom apartments. There’s ADA units for handicapped. It’s for basically any families. There’s nice kitchens, walk-in showers,” Amoroso said.
Former South End Arena site
The apartments stand on the former site of Art Gagne’s South End Arena, a skating rink and arcade.
The grandchildren of Art Gagne said the site remains part of the family’s memories.
“I can remember 40 years plus of history in this place. So, it’s really sentimental and we did a lot of things,” grandchild Shane Gagne said.
The new complex includes a first-floor community room named Art’s Place.
“It was just really nice and that they named the room after Pepe is just very special. Very special,” grandchild Tara Bradstreet said.
How to apply
The apartments are intended for low- to moderate-income households. Applicants must meet income guidelines.
For more information on applying, contact the Waterville Housing Authority or visit its website.

title: Democrats set to take power as midterm voter data shows shift among young men
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - With Democrats set to take power on Capitol Hill, data on who voted in the midterm elections shows changes in the electorate.
President Donald Trump’s failure to deliver on key campaign promises from 2024 is a main reason a wide range of voters participated this midterm cycle, with some crossing party lines to send a message to lawmakers. Trump says he is still favored.
“I mean our speeches were really, the speeches made at the 30 rallies. And those speeches were, that was tremendous love. It was it was pretty amazing,” Trump told reporters Wednesday.
Two years ago, young people turned out to vote for Trump, especially young men (ages 18-29).
Data from Tufts University shows that has changed. Fifty-six percent of young men supported Trump two years ago. Tuesday, 58% favored a Democratic House candidate.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Republicans must choose how to proceed.
“Americans hate the direction our country is going in right now,” he said. “So now, Republicans are going to have to choose whether to keep listening to the nonsense that’s coming out of 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue or start acting in the interests of the American people. If they continue to embrace Trump, they’re going to be following him right over the cliff, as this election has shown, and it’ll get even worse for them.”
The Associated Press Voter Poll found concerns about inflation, tariffs, the war in Iran and other unfulfilled campaign promises by Trump were driving choices at polling places.
Education levels remain a strong indicator of whether Americans vote Democratic or Republican, the data shows.

title: Harmeet Dhillon exits after radical overhaul of Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Harmeet Dhillon, a conservative attorney who oversaw a radical reshaping of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, celebrated the mass departures of career lawyers and spearheaded sweeping investigations into elite universities, said Thursday that she had resigned from her post.
Dhillon had been a powerful and divisive figure inside President Donald Trump’s Justice Department since her confirmation last year as assistant attorney general, where she dramatically changed the direction of a division created during the country’s Civil Rights Movement to protect the rights of minorities.
“We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women and girls’ sports, and so much more,” Dhillon said in a social media post announcing her departure, using the acronym for diversity, equity and inclusion. She called serving in the position “the honor of a lifetime.”
Though the resignation was announced on the heels of midterm elections in which Democrats swept the House and Senate in a startling rebuke of Trump, Dhillon said in an interview with Fox News Digital that she had made the decision to depart weeks earlier but was asked by the White House to remain in her post until after the elections. She said she wanted to return to the private sector and had not been asked to resign.
“My decision, my choice,” she said.
As leader of the division, Dhillon drew fierce criticism from former Justice Department attorneys who accused her of abandoning its traditional civil rights enforcement mission in favor of conservative causes. More than three quarters of the unit’s workforce at the beginning of Trump’s second term have left — a move Dhillon has called the “biggest single personnel self-purge in DOJ history.”
She accused the past administration of pursuing a misguided liberal agenda and welcomed the departures of attorneys not aligned with the Trump administration’s priorities, saying in an interview last year with conservative pundit Glenn Beck that “the job here is to enforce the federal civil rights laws — not woke ideology.”
During her tenure, the Civil Rights Division scrapped police reform settlements and investigations and launched probes into universities the Trump administration saw as improperly prioritizing diversity and inclusion, discriminating against white applicants in the admissions process and failing to crack down on antisemitic conduct on campus.
Her pressure campaign against schools led to numerous settlements, and in one case, the resignation of the president of the University of Virginia. She also led an effort to pressure states to turn over detailed voter records despite repeated court losses.
Attorney General Todd Blanche wrote in a social media post announcing Dhillon’s departure that she had led the division with “conviction” and “defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor.”
“The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors,” Blanche wrote.
But Stacey Young, a former Civil Rights Division attorney who now leads a network of Justice Department alumni, called her “the most destructive, lawless and hateful” head of the division in department history.
“Americans’ civil rights don’t enforce themselves. For almost 70 years, the Civil Rights Division brought to fruition the civil rights laws that Americans demanded,” Young said in an emailed statement Thursday. ”Dhillon decimated it.”
Dhillon, who was born in India and immigrated with her Sikh family to the United States as a child, was a prominent figure in conservative legal and political circles well before being tapped to her Justice Department position.
As a California lawyer, she was involved in numerous high-profile causes and legal fights, including challenging that state’s stay-at-home order during the coronavirus pandemic and filing a lawsuit that accused the state of failing to verify citizenship for voter registration.
She launched a bid to become chair of the Republican National Committee but lost in January 2023 to Ronna McDaniel in a race that exposed fierce internal divisions in the party.
Dhillon and her law firm also represented Trump himself as a House committee investigating the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol issued a subpoena for his testimony. The panel ultimately abandoned that effort and wrapped up its work without forcing the issue, prompting Dhillon to boast on the social media platform X that the committee had “waved the white flag.”

title: JetBlue raises checked baggage fees again ahead of holiday travel, cites fuel and operating costs
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Ahead of holiday travel, JetBlue raises baggage fees for a second time as jet fuel prices stay elevated
JetBlue has raised its checked baggage fees for the second time this year, making it more expensive for travelers to check luggage just as the busy holiday travel season gets underway.
The new fees for tickets purchased on or after Nov. 3 mean most economy passengers flying within the United States, Canada, Latin America and the Caribbean will pay at least $50 each way for their first checked bag, up from $39 previously.
Related video above: Energy experts predict high gas prices will stick around
The price climbs to $55 during peak travel periods, including Thanksgiving and the winter holidays, if passengers pay at least 24 hours before departure. Those who wait until the final 24 hours will pay $60 during off-peak periods and $70 during peak periods.
“We’re adjusting checked bag fees to help offset rising fuel and operating costs," JetBlue said in an emailed statement. “This helps us keep our base fares competitive while giving customers the choice to pay for a checked bag only if they need one.”
At the start of the year, the first checked bag on most economy domestic JetBlue flights cost $35 during off-peak periods. But that was before the Iran war started in late February with U.S.-Israeli strikes and sent jet fuel prices swinging.
The fee for a second checked bag has also increased, starting at $70 each way during off-peak periods and $75 during peak travel. Passengers checking their bags at the airport can pay as much as $85 for a second bag.
JetBlue, which has its flagship terminal at New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport, previously raised its checked baggage fees in March. That increase helped set off a broader round of baggage fee hikes among major U.S. airlines, including Delta, United, American and Southwest.
The war with Iran remains unresolved, keeping traffic largely restricted through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical shipping route for global oil supplies. The disruption has kept jet fuel prices elevated.
JetBlue executives said last week during the airline's third-quarter earnings call that demand has remained resilient even as fares have risen in response to higher jet fuel prices. JetBlue said its average fuel price reached $3.91 per gallon in the summer, up 57% from a year earlier, and is expected to climb to $4.64 during the final three months of the year, up 85% from the same time last year.
Some travelers, including eligible co-branded credit card holders and members of JetBlue’s loyalty program, can still check bags for free, the airline said.

title: Will Democrats impeach Trump? Party leaders lay out priorities after winning control of Congress
text:
Will Democrats impeach Trump? Party leaders lay out priorities after winning control of Congress
Democrats say they're focused on affordability and accountability, with mixed views on impeachment.
Will Democrats impeach Trump? Party leaders lay out priorities after winning control of Congress
Democrats say they're focused on affordability and accountability, with mixed views on impeachment.
Democrats won big in the midterm elections, securing majorities in the House and the Senate. Now, party leaders are laying out what they plan to do with that power when the new Congress kicks off in January.
"Relief is on the way," Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer declared on Wednesday. "We are going to work hard to drive costs down with the president or without him, period."
The reality is that Democrats will face barriers as they pursue their priorities. President Donald Trump has the power to veto bills that he doesn't like, and 60 votes are needed to advance most legislation in the Senate, requiring at least some bipartisan support.
Many of the priorities Democrats laid out on Wednesday are likely to face resistance from Trump. They include restoring enhanced subsidies for Affordable Care Act enrollees, reversing Medicaid spending cuts, undoing tariffs, and ending the war with Iran.
Schumer suggested that Democrats could withhold defense funding as leverage.
"The Founding Fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people," Schumer said.
Democrats are also pledging to ramp up Congressional oversight into the president and his allies.
In a statement on Wednesday, Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia, who is poised to become chair of the House Oversight Committee, vowed to focus on "the Trump Crime Family, corporate corruption, DHS and ICE abuses, and the cover-up of the Epstein files."
 “Lawyer up," Garcia wrote in a social media post directed at the White House. 
Democrats have mixed views on whether to pursue another impeachment against Trump, who was acquitted by the Senate twice during his first term.
"Are we taking it off the table? No way are we taking it off the table, but are we obsessed with it the way Donald Trump is? No, not at all," Rep. Jamie Raskin, who is positioned to become the next chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee, told CNN on Wednesday.
Raskin said impeachment is "not a panacea" and should be weighed against other priorities, given Congress' limited time and resources.
"If they make the next two years about retribution and lawfare and partisan games, every American will suffer by that," Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson warned on Tuesday.
As Democrats enter a new chapter on Capitol Hill, the party will welcome newly-elected members from across the ideological spectrum, from centrists who flipped deep-red states to progressives who campaigned on major changes like "Medicare for All" and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement
Asked whether Democrats will be able to reconcile those differences to deliver on the range of promises that candidates made this election cycle, Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin said, "I know people want to make a big deal about the small differences in this party, but those are rather small and minor compared to the big issues that unite Democrats, and will actually help form an agenda that will pass in this newfound majority."

title: These Are the 10 Best Comic Book Movies of the Last 10 Years

title: Trump’s lawyers to appear before appeals court as he fights hush money conviction
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump’s lawyers will try to persuade a New York appeals court Thursday to throw out his hush money conviction, two years after it made history.
The conviction, on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to obscure a $130,000 payment to adult film performer Stormy Daniels, continues to nettle Trump enough that he denounced it on social media as recently as September. The president denies any wrongdoing, and he has turned to state and federal courts in hopes of unwinding the verdict.
He is not expected to attend Thursday’s court session.
The appeal turns on complex legal disputes, but political overtones aren’t hard to find. The very first paragraph of one of the Trump team’s court filings contends the case was the flimsy product of “immense political pressure” on a Democratic prosecutor to go after Trump — rhetoric that echoes the Republican president’s own oft-repeated claims in the court of public opinion.
In court papers, Trump’s attorneys have assailed prosecutors’ legal theory as “a house of cards” built on a shaky combination of alleged state and federal offenses, with “clearly insufficient” evidence and problematic jury instructions.
The appeal also concerns whether jurors should have been allowed to hear testimony about supposed White House conversations, workflow and even Trump social media posts during his first term. His lawyers cite presidential immunity for official acts, and they argue his official conduct included responding to the Daniels drama once it became public in 2018.
“When a president addresses the nation to defend himself from allegations of personal misconduct (as all presidents do), or discusses such communications with his aides, he is carrying out his constitutional duties and is protected by immunity,” lawyer Robert Giuffra Jr. wrote in a filing this October.
Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s office counters that the legal theory and jury instructions were legitimate and that the White House-related evidence was fair game. Some was public record, some was a general description of office practices, and the conversations were “unofficial conduct,” prosecutors say.
“A president’s discussions about a purely private matter, even with a White House advisor, do not constitute ‘official acts for which the president is immune,’” Bragg’s appeals chief, Steven Wu, wrote in a filing in July. Besides, he said, there was “a mountain” of other evidence against Trump.
The May 2024 verdict made Trump the first former — and now current — U.S. president with a criminal conviction. While historic, it didn’t impede his return to the White House or subject him to any punishment.
The trial involved $130,000 that Daniels got from Trump’s then-fixer and lawyer, Michael Cohen, weeks before the 2016 election. The money bought, for a time, her silence about an alleged sexual encounter with the married Trump a decade earlier. He says that nothing sexual happened between them.
Trump’s company reimbursed Cohen in 2017, logging those payments as legal expenses.
Saying the transactions all were meant to keep unflattering information about Trump away from the electorate, prosecutors argue that he “orchestrated a conspiracy” that violated federal campaign finance laws, among others.
Trump’s lawyers argue there’s only “weak” evidence that he even knew about Cohen’s dealings at the time. His trial attorneys also said that payments to Cohen were indeed legal expenses, and that any hush money expended on Trump’s behalf wasn’t hidden campaign spending, just an effort to avoid embarrassing his family.
The distinction matters because, under New York law, falsifying business records isn’t a felony unless it’s done with an intent to commit or conceal a separate crime.
While pursuing his state appeal, Trump also has been trying to shift the case to federal court and have it dismissed on immunity grounds. A federal judge said no — for the third time — in August. Trump’s attorneys are appealing that decision, and arguments on that appeal are set for Nov. 16.

title: Maine's 2nd District Race Heads To Ranked-choice Tabulation Despite Dunlap's Concession
text:
Dunlap Concedes: Maine’s 2nd Congressional District Moves to Ranked-Choice
Matthew Dunlap has conceded the 2nd Congressional race to Paul LePage, but Maine's Secretary of State says officials will hold ranked-choice tabulations on Monday.
Maine Will Use Ranked Choice Tabulations to Decide the 2nd Congressional District Winner
Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows says ranked-choice tabulation is necessary because neither candidate achieved a majority of first-choice votes cast on Election Day.
Voters cast 341,248 ballots in the 2nd Congressional District race.
170,263 people voted for Paul LePage, while 164,845 voted for Matthew Dunlap.
123 votes went to write-in candidates, and 6,017 were blank, with no candidate chosen.
Since no candidate received more than 50% of the total ballots cast, the ranked choice tabulation is necessary.
Maine's 2nd District Ranked Choice Tabulations to Begin on Monday, Despite Concession
WABI-TV reports Matthew Dunlap conceded the race on Monday and congratulated LePage on his victory.
Despite the concession, Secretary of State Bellows says the ranked choice process is still required by law.
Those tabulations are scheduled to begin on Monday, November 9, 2026, at 10 a.m. at the Maine Department of Public Safety Headquarters building in Augusta.
The public can view the tabulations on the Secretary of State's YouTube page.
Ranked choice tabulations happen in rounds, with the lowest-ranked candidate eliminated from each round until only two candidates remain.
The candidate who receives the majority (more than 50%) of the votes in the final round will be declared the winner.
Maine's 2nd Congressional District Includes 10 Counties
Maine 2nd Congressional District includes 10 counties:
- Androscoggin
- Aroostook
- Franklin
- Hancock
- Oxford
- Penobscot
- Piscataquis
- Somerset
- Waldo
- Washington
At over 27,000 square miles, it is the largest district east of the Mississippi River.

title: 2 more executions set in Florida and Alabama, hours after lethal injection in Indiana
text:
Florida and Alabama plan to execute two men Thursday for killing older adults during home robberies, just hours after Indiana put a prisoner to death in the first of three lethal injections scheduled for the same day in the U.S.
It would be Florida’s 19th execution this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, matching a record set by the state in 2025, and the second time this year that three people would be put to death on the same day.
The death penalty has faced renewed scrutiny since the September failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee, although courts have rejected efforts to halt other executions after she survived two doses of pentobarbital.
In Indiana, Jeffrey Weisheit, 50, was pronounced dead at 12:45 a.m. at the state prison in Michigan City, said Noelle Russell, spokesperson at the Department of Correction.
She said Weisheit’s final meal was barbecue ribs and he had no final words. He had acknowledged killing his girlfriend’s two children in a house fire in the Evansville area in 2010 but had hoped that Gov. Mike Braun would grant clemency and change his sentence to life in prison. Braun declined.
Most executions this year have been in Florida
Florida has carried out more than half the 32 executions in the U.S. so far this year. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said he wants to bring justice to families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out.
Jesse Guardado confessed and quickly pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing a 75-year-old woman inside her Walton County home in 2004 before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other valuables to buy drugs. She had helped him get a job and housing.
A federal appeals court in 2024 said that Guardado, now 64, had received a “full and fair” hearing during the death penalty phase of his case.
Death penalty foes cite Alabama man’s age
In 1991, Michael Taylor, then 19, fatally beat two people, ages 83 and 79, with a metal bar during a robbery in their Gadsden, Alabama, home. Police arrested him with the victims’ Cadillac an hour away in Birmingham.
Death penalty opponents had urged Republican Gov. Kay Ivey to reduce Taylor’s sentence to life in prison, noting his age and immaturity at the time of the killings. She declined.
“If the state kills Michael, it is not the 19-year-old who made the worst mistake of his life who it kills. But the mature, well-respected, God-fearing man sitting in that cell today,” said Esther Brown of Project Hope to Abolish the Death Penalty.
The state plans to execute Taylor, 54, by lethal injection after a judge declared a nitrogen gas method unconstitutional. His attorneys objected to the last-minute switch to lethal injection since he selected nitrogen gas as his method several years ago, but a judge ruled against Taylor.
Lawyers had asked for a life sentence for Weisheit
In Indiana, lawyers failed to persuade Braun, a Republican, to allow Weisheit to undergo brain scans in an effort to reinforce their argument that he has a history of head injuries and mental health problems that should foreclose execution.
Weisheit’s last objection centered on the state’s planned use of lethal drugs purchased from a pharmacy that is facing a disciplinary hearing next week at the Indiana Pharmacy Board. The Indiana Supreme Court declined to intervene Wednesday night, though two of the five justices wanted a 10-day stay for more information about the drugs’ expiration and storage.
The execution provided “long-awaited justice for Alyssa Lynch and her brother Caleb, two innocent children whose lives were stolen in an act of unspeakable cruelty,” Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said.
____
Fischer reported from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, and Chandler from Montgomery, Alabama. Associated Press reporter Ed White contributed from Detroit.

title: Google will let schools turn off AI, but they may lose Search
text:
Google will let schools turn off AI, but they may also lose Search
Google is rolling out new controls for schools to limit students' access to the company's artificial intelligence tools. But if schools opt out of AI altogether, they'll also lose access to Google Search.
Video above: Got a suspicious Amazon text? This AI tool checks if it’s real
The policy change could mark a major shift in how students and educators interact with one of the biggest providers of education technology in the world. Google's Chromebook laptops are used by tens of millions of students, sometimes starting in kindergarten.
The move comes as many communities have pushed for stricter limits on screen time and AI use in schools, amid growing fears that the technology could stunt students' learning and development or pose safety risks. A number of school districts, including New York City and Los Angeles public schools, banned generative AI tools for many or all students this school year.
Google on Tuesday said its products that use AI, like its Gemini assistant and Google Search, will be off by default for K-12 student accounts, until school administrators "explicitly turn them on." The change reverses an earlier move by Google in August to turn on Gemini by default in its Google Classrooms app.
But now, if schools want to turn off AI entirely, they'll also lose access to Google Search.
The company said the changes are in response to calls from educators and policymakers for more control over AI tools.
Video below: Dartmouth holds forum on AI after provost resigns
Chris Phillips, vice president of education at Google, told the New York Times that "search and AI are deeply integrated," and that schools that ban AI "will not have access to search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available."
Google has made AI central to Search in recent years — adding "AI overviews" summarizing answers at the top of many results pages and expanding the size of the search bar to accommodate longer queries.
Google's Tuesday blog post does not offer specifics on how these controls will work, or what students might see if they tried to access Google Search from a school that has banned AI. Phillips wrote in the post that the company will, "share more specifics with schools in the coming months ahead of the changes rolling out so they have time to prepare and enable a smooth transition."
Google did not respond to multiple requests for comment from CNN.
Video below: Use of artificial intelligence in campaign ads draws scrutiny
The policy change came as part of a larger announcement by Google about a slate of updates to its AI tools for learning, based on the idea that the technology should help students work through problems rather than simply giving them answers. Under this new "guided learning" principle, Google says that when its systems detect, for example, that a student is using Search for homework help, they'll be prompted to walk through the problem or topic step-by-step rather than receiving a single answer.
It's an approach also being taken by other AI companies, as they seek to convince educators and parents that their products are valuable learning tools, and that experience with AI in school is essential to success in the workforce later.
OpenAI in August announced "ChatGPT for Teens," which, in addition to safety controls, focuses heavily on learning, allowing parents and teens to turn on "Study Mode" to work through questions. Many tech companies have also provided funding to train teachers in AI.

title: House Democrats pick Ambureen Rana of Bangor as new assistant leader
text:
The bolstered Democratic majority of the Maine House of Representatives re-selected Ryan Fecteau of Biddeford to serve as speaker on Thursday.
The Democratic caucus also kept Rep. Matt Moonen of Portland as majority leader. With former Assistant Majority Leader Rep. Lori Gramlich termed out, Democrats selected Rep. Ambureen Rana of Bangor to assume the role.
The latter was the only contested position when Democrats met behind closed doors in Augusta to decide on their leadership team, though formal votes are held when the Legislature convenes to get sworn in on Dec. 2. Senate Democrats are expected to make their leadership decisions on Friday, as are House and Senate Republicans.
In a statement, Fecteau said he’s “honored by the continued trust my colleagues have placed in me to lead House Democrats in the 133rd Legislature.”
“Together, we will work steadfast to address the challenges we face – from healthcare to childcare to affordable housing to energy costs – so that every family in Maine can get ahead, not just get by,” he continued.
“As I have done throughout my career, I will continue to work across the aisle, building trust and making sure that we respect people’s time, work productively, and most importantly, deliver results for Maine people.”
First elected to the House in 2014, Fecteau became the first openly gay speaker and one of the youngest to hold the leadership position at age 28 when he assumed the role in 2020. His caucus selected him as speaker again in 2024, when he returned to the House after being term-limited in 2022.
The speaker presides over chamber sessions, appoints all committee members and committee chairs in conjunction with the Maine Senate president and oversees the flow of legislation, among other responsibilities.
Moonen, a leader in progressive politics in the state, is entering his seventh non-consecutive term in the House. He served as the House majority leader during the 129th Legislature and in the most recent 132nd Legislature, a role in which he represents the party on the chamber floor and helps direct legislative priorities and debate.
Finishing her second term in the House, Rana previously served on the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee, which sets the state budget. Before becoming a legislator, Rana worked with the Health Equity Alliance and as a community organizer with Maine Equal Justice.
With each of these leadership positions also comes a seat on the Legislative Council, which is responsible for the overall management of the legislative branch and has authority over whether to approve after deadline bills.
After Tuesday’s election, Democrats have at least 85 seats in the 151-member House, up from 76 last session, based on races called by The Associated Press so far.

title: Future voter arrives early: Woman goes into labor at polling place
text:
TOPEKA, Kan. (WIBW/Gray News) — Tessa Von Fange went into labor after a trip to the Shawnee County Elections Office in Kansas, where she went to vote.
Tessa Von Fange is a longtime voter. She said she has missed very few elections.
“I don’t think there are too many elections that I’ve missed,” Tessa Von Fange said. “So, especially as I’ve gotten older, I don’t miss them at all really.”
Labor begins during the trip
Tessa Von Fange thought her baby would be born after Election Day.
“I’m going to make it to that induction. I had already really thought I wasn’t going to have her before then,” Tessa Von Fange said.
Her husband, Chris Von Fange, said an election worker told him his wife was in labor.
“Shocked, I was overwhelmed,” Chris Von Fange said. “Just to hear from the election worker that your wife is in labor is like millions of questions.”
“I was 100% in denial until my water broke,” Tessa Von Fange added.
Baby’s name
The couple had already chosen the baby’s name before the trip.
“We had her name picked out already,” Tessa Von Fange said. “Her name is Morgan, but it did make me think, what would that be? If she were a boy, Chad. I thought that was funny.”
Message to voters
The Von Fanges said everyone should make time to vote.
“No matter what you have going on, there’s always a half-hour of your time that can be spent to go to a polling place to have your vote cast,” Chris Von Fange said.
Tessa Von Fange received a future voter sticker at the elections office.
“That was the only sticker I got, but I stuck it right on my belly and came to the hospital with it on,” she said.
Morgan was born at 1:16 a.m. on Nov. 3. She weighed 8 pounds, 1 ounce.

title: ‘JD, habibi.’ Arabs celebrate El-Sayed’s use of a term of affection to mock his foes
text:
BEIRUT (AP) — From Michigan to the Middle East, Arabs are celebrating Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate win and delighting in his introduction of Arabic terms like “habibi” and “inshallah” to the American political lexicon.
After being the target of Islamophobic rhetoric on the campaign trail, the rising political star who will be the first Muslim American U.S. senator has mocked his critics on the right while championing the Palestinian cause and leaning into his faith and Egyptian heritage.
“JD, habibi,” El-Sayed said in his victory speech, addressing U.S. Vice President JD Vance, who had warned that the candidate would lead rioters in burning down Detroit. “There is this delicious irony in the fact that you’re constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January.”
‘Habibi’ is a term of affection
“Habibi” literally translates to “my beloved” and is peppered through Arab pop songs. In everyday speech, it often means “buddy,” “pal,” or “bro.” El-Sayed’s supporters have sported shirts reading “Habibi for Abdul.”
El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, said his campaign had turned “inshallah” — “God willing” — into “hamdulillah,” which means “thank God.”
Arabs thrilled to the gentle ribbing of the vice president, with many posting music video clips featuring “habibi” to social media. It was a rare outpouring of joy in a region traumatized by past and present conflicts — which have also fueled negative stereotypes in the West.
One user on X posted a video of Egyptian diva Shireen Abd El-Wahab dancing to one of her most popular songs, joking that El-Sayed would make it the new national anthem.
Egyptians are renowned in the Arab world for their sense of humor and are known for cracking jokes in the face of life’s difficulties, a spirit that has been popularized in films and by famous comedic actors.
Riffing off El-Sayed’s victory speech, some shared a meme from an Egyptian film in which a man attends a funeral while high and is unable to stop laughing. “I came here to crack jokes,” read the caption, quoting a line from the film.
An Egyptian academic, Khalil al-Anani, praised El-Sayed on X, saying: “‘Habibi’ is the sweetest word.” He thanked the senator-elect for bringing joy to Egyptians.
Signs of change after decades of prejudice
Arab and Muslim Americans have faced prejudice for decades, with popular films depicting them as terrorists and politicians on the right fanning baseless fears about the imposition of sharia, or Islamic law.
During the campaign, U.S. President Donald Trump referred to El-Sayed as a “jihadist,” evoked the Sept. 11 attacks and deliberately misstated the candidate’s name.
On social media, users responded to such attacks by posting light-hearted videos, including of Lebanese diva Haifa Wehbe belly dancing and young veiled women breakdancing in the streets.
“Donald, look, I know you’ve struggled with my name,” El-Sayed said in his victory speech. “So after JD swears me in in January, you can just go on and call me ‘senator.’”

title: New Orleans blacksmith preserves centuries-old ironwork tradition
text:
NEW ORLEANS (Aging Untold) — In New Orleans, the city’s architecture is often framed in iron. Centuries of old balconies, fences and gates have survived fires and hurricanes.
At Andrew’s Welding and Blacksmith Shop, Darryl Reeves is one of the few who still carry on the tradition. His grandfather was a blacksmith as well.
Reeves remembers being shooed away as a boy from his grandfather’s shop, but the memory of the blacksmith stuck with him.
“We used to just pass through and just watch these guys beat on this metal with the sparks and all,” Reeves said. “I think that had a lot of influence with me enjoying to work with metal.”
Crafting iron by hand
Reeves said he loves taking a raw piece of metal and transforming it.
“That’s what gives me joy,” Reeves said. “How many people get to beat on metal, especially if you’re frustrated with something and get it out? How many people do that?”
From iron hinges to hand-forged designs like metal leaves, Reeves makes what he needs, including his ironworking tools.
Reeves has restored historic ironwork throughout New Orleans, including the fence in front of the Cabildo, using plans dating back to the 1790s.
“That’s learning from the past. That’s given a conversation with the person that actually fabricated it,” Reeves said.
Training the next generation
A younger generation is now learning from Reeves.
His apprentice, Karina Roca, moved to New Orleans from Boston.
“Well, I’ve always secretly wanted to be an iron worker,” Roca said. “And then I saw a PBS program on Darryl Reeves over 10 years ago at this point, and I was like, ‘Yep, I’m going to study under that guy.’”
Roca, who is working on a master’s degree in historic preservation at Tulane, has been working in the blacksmith shop for five years.
“It works in so many ways to kind of keep this aesthetic of New Orleans alive,” Roca said. “It’s very Spanish. It’s very West African. It’s very French. So it’s sort of this symbol, this beacon of a space where all of these cultures have come together for centuries now.”
For Reeves, blacksmithing is more than bending metal. It’s preserving history, culture and the spirit of New Orleans, one hand-forged piece at a time.

title: NASA space telescope plunges to Earth after two decades studying cosmic explosions
text:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — One of NASA’s premier space telescopes plunged to Earth on Wednesday, ending its 22-year investigation of the universe’s biggest explosions.
The Swift Observatory’s demise came less than three months after a long-shot rescue mission failed.
The U.S. Space Force confirmed Swift’s reentry near Indonesia after tracking its sinking orbit, the result of intense solar activity the past few years.
NASA hired a private company to whip together an orbit-boosting effort, but Katalyst Space’s three-armed robotic craft ran into trouble following its July launch and came crashing down in September.
It was not immediately known how much of the 1 ½-ton spacecraft burned up in the atmosphere. NASA anticipated some of the denser pieces surviving.
Swift rocketed into orbit in 2004 on what was expected to be a two-year study of gamma ray bursts and exploding stars. It observed thousands of them over a mission that lasted 11 times longer than planned, serving as a first responder for other telescopes that could probe deeper.
NASA is gauging industry’s interest in mounting a rescue mission for another observatory whose orbit is being chipped away by solar storms: the Hubble Space Telescope. Launched in 1990, Hubble is expected to come crashing down by the mid-2030s, according to recent analyses.
The space agency is looking for input from private companies on whether and how they might boost Hubble’s orbit, upgrade its systems or guide it to a controlled reentry — or all three. Any such mission would need to happen by 2032.
Unlike the rush job with Swift, the space agency has more time to explore options for saving Hubble, said Nicky Fox, NASA’s science mission chief.
“Hubble still has important science ahead of it,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a statement, “and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible.”

title: Democratic socialist Nithya Raman ousts embattled Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass
text:
Democratic socialist Nithya Raman ousts embattled Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass
Nithya Raman, a little-known Los Angeles City Council member backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, has defeated Mayor Karen Bass, an upset that will alter the trajectory of the nation’s second-largest city.
The India-born Raman's upstart campaign marked a generational shift at City Hall as voters followed the lead of New York, where democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani was elected last year. Raman, though, never attracted the same level of national attention and stressed her willingness to break with the progressive party at times during the campaign.
Her entry into the race marked a stunning change of heart after she had initially endorsed Bass, once her ally. She said the city had reached a “breaking point” and announced her own candidacy just hours before the filing deadline, setting in motion a meteoric rise that would lead her to the mayoralty.
In a video with the downtown skyline behind her, Raman paid tribute to Bass and thanked her volunteers. She promised to “build housing that people can afford, parks for our children to play in, a transit system that can get people where they need to go, a city that is safe for its working people and its families, and a city government that is actually capable of delivering on its promises.”
Bass said in a statement that she called Raman to congratulate her on her victory.
“While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken,” Bass said. “I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition. Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us.”
Bass becomes the first Los Angeles mayor in two decades to lose a bid for reelection. Her first term was undone by the deadly Palisades Fire, which ignited when she was out of the country and caught the fire department unprepared. The devastation left many voters with the unshakeable feeling that Bass should be held to account, and she never recovered.
As votes were being counted earlier this week, Raman delivered an election night speech Tuesday that marked a campaign coda, summing up voters’ frustration with a city that seemed to be adrift, and her vision for the future.
“For too long, our broken and unjust status quo has convinced Angelenos that this is the best that we can do,” she said. “LA stopped being a place where we could build things, where we could open things, where we could film things, where we could create things.”
She said she would restore “that ambitious Los Angeles, that joyful Los Angeles, that creative Los Angeles, that entrepreneurial Los Angeles."
Raman's rise came in a year that saw Democratic divisions across the country, with insurgent left-wing candidates challenging establishment rivals.
Raman is promising to oust the police chief, whom she views as too accommodating to federal immigration authorities. She also wants to improve basic services that have deteriorated for years and left neighborhoods with dirty, pothole-ridden streets, buckled sidewalks and broken streetlights.
Raman called Bass’ efforts to reduce homelessness ineffective. She's promising a new approach to the crisis that would expand medical teams for people who live in encampments and on the streets in an effort to build trust and eventually bring them indoors. Raman also wants to provide more housing to move people out of hotels rented by the city for those who are homeless.
She said her plans could reduce the number of people sleeping in tents and encampments by at least half by 2028, when the city will host the Olympic Games. However, the problem has long proved intractable, despite billions spent in the region.
Raman offered change
Raman, 45, was the face of change in a year when voters were restless over long-running problems that persisted under the 73-year-old Bass. A Berkeley IGS/LA Times poll conducted from Oct. 19 to 25 found that about 4 in 10 likely voters said reducing the number of homeless encampments should be a top priority for the next mayor to address, while about 3 in 10 said that about ensuring public safety or building more affordable housing.
She was able to overcome criticism from Bass that she was “not ready for primetime” and too inexperienced to run a city with 3.8 million people, and she capitalized on anxiety over the future.
“Our city is in crisis,” she said in one ad. The ad showed a lectern with no one behind it at the site of a massive warehouse fire from last summer, the homeless epicenter of Skid Row and shuttered malls and storefronts. “Where is our mayor?” Raman asked.
Bass argued that she made enough progress to merit a second four-year term, and she branded Raman’s views on policing and homelessness as “extreme.”
Top Democrats lined up with Bass
Raman's victory came despite limited backing from the Democratic establishment. Bass had support from Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, along with nearly every member of the City Council. Bass served in the state Legislature and Congress before becoming mayor in 2022 and was under consideration to be former President Joe Biden’s running mate in 2020.
In an important signal to the business community, billionaire developer Rick Caruso said he was voting for Bass, but stopped short of formally endorsing the candidate he lost to in the 2022 mayoral race.
Raman, an urban planner, picked up notable support from advocacy and political groups, including Our Revolution, which was founded by Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, and the Sierra Club. But she was thin on endorsements from prominent local politicians.
She landed a widely publicized private meeting with former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, who was not involved in the race, that hinted at her efforts to broaden her circle. Expanding her network of allies could be crucial as she begins governing a city that's home to a struggling entertainment industry, a major port, world-class universities and research institutions and serves as a major tourist destination.
