title: Alaskans wait for more votes in US Senate, governor’s races. Both could go to ranked tabulations
text:
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — Alaskans settled in Wednesday to await more results from key races on the general election ballot, including a bitterly fought U.S. Senate campaign and an open seat for governor.
A ballot measure seeking to repeal Alaska’s unique system of open primaries and ranked vote general elections also was too early to call.
If no candidate wins more than 50% of first-choice votes, rankings will come into play. Alaska accepts ballots from overseas voters for up to 15 days after the election, making Nov. 18 the date targeted by state elections officials to tabulate under the ranked vote system.
The major candidates in the Senate race are two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola.
In the governor’s race, former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is trying to become the first Democrat elected to the office in a generation. He faces three other Republicans, including business owner Bernadette Wilson, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump.
Litigation and allegations of partisan tricks rocked the Senate race
The contest dominated headlines ahead of Tuesday’s election and attracted the attention of the U.S. Department of Justice.
With less than two weeks before Election Day, the agency sued at President Donald Trump’s direction seeking to block certification of the race if Sullivan loses. The lawsuit cited potential confusion with another Sullivan on the ballot, retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan.
A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit, but the department has appealed.
Suspicions long held by the senator and his supporters that the lesser-known Sullivan was running to sow confusion gained new life last week, when The New York Times reported that top political aides to Peltola appeared to be involved in recruiting him.
The report was based on interviews with a former Peltola campaign manager, who was fired shortly before the August primary. It also cited text messages and campaign finance documents indicating that an operative trying to recruit candidates was paid by a group backing Peltola.
Federal authorities have confirmed the existence of a criminal investigation in the matter.
Peltola denied any involvement. Dan J. Sullivan, who has denied running at the behest of Democrats, has not responded to messages seeking comment in the last week.
The senator elevated the issue in his closing argument to voters and questioned Peltola’s denials.
On Wednesday his campaign expressed confidence in Sullivan’s chances, “despite the biggest election cheating scandal in the history of Alaska” and “despite a bloodbath for Republicans everywhere else in the country.”
Sullivan and Peltola say the vote count will take time
Both campaigns urged patience as the ballot count continues.
Peltola addressed supporters Tuesday night after news broke that Democrats had won enough seats to gain control of the Senate. She was joyful — even taking a selfie with the crowd — but said it will take time for the state to count ballots.
Alaska allows up to 10 days to receive absentee ballots sent from within the U.S., a timeline that can be critical for ballots from rural Alaska communities that are often accessible only by air or water and rely on air service for mail delivery.
“It’s going to take a long time to make sure we’re counting every vote from every far-flung hinterland community, from every tiny outpost, from all of our service members serving overseas, our young people going to colleges,” Peltola said.
Democrat seeks to reclaim governor’s office
Kreiss-Tomkins expressed excitement about the early vote results when speaking to supporters on election night, saying, “What a night this is for the future of our state.”
He cast himself as a consensus builder in the race to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy and said he would work across party lines to address the state’s challenges.
State Republican leaders urged their voters to rank the three GOP candidates in the race to maximize the party’s chances of success.
But Trump, speaking at a rally in support of Republican candidates including Sullivan and Wilson last month in Wasilla, called ranked voting a “scam.” And he railed on social media against the other two Republican gubernatorial candidates, former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson and former state Attorney General Treg Taylor.
Wilson said in a statement Wednesday that she was “cautiously optimistic for the days ahead.”
Alaska’s last Democratic governor was Tony Knowles, who had back-to-back terms from 1994 to 2002. The state had an independent governor from 2014 to 2018.
Ballot measure seeks to repeal unique elections process
Alaskans were asked to decide for the second time in two years on a ballot measure seeking to repeal the open primary and ranked vote general election system.
Voters approved the system in 2020, and it took effect for elections in 2022. Voters narrowly rejected a repeal effort two years ago.

title: Met Gala exhibit will examine everyday items of clothing, replacing scuttled Galliano show
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — And now, Take 2: The new Met Gala exhibit will celebrate everyday garments and materials like jeans and puffer jackets, paper and plastic — and how fashion designers transform them.
The new theme announced Thursday sounds about as far as can be imagined from the glittering, elaborate designs of John Galliano, the British designer originally slated to be the subject of the Met’s fashion exhibit next spring — before that idea was scuttled amid an outcry over past antisemitic statements.
The replacement show at the Met’s Costume Institute, “extraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday,” will be launched by the 2027 Met Gala, held traditionally on the first Monday in May. Using items in the museum’s collection, as well as loans and acquisitions, the exhibit aims to explore “how designers rework familiar garments, everyday objects, and commonplace materials through craft, construction, material experimentation, and conceptual wit,” the museum says.
When the original exhibit was canceled, there was ‘no Plan B’
It is being assembled, as always, by the institute’s head curator, Andrew Bolton. The idea had to come together quickly once the museum, along with Galliano himself, decided to cancel the scandal-plagued retrospective under pressure from donors, city officials and the Jewish community.
In an interview this week, Bolton described the challenge of coming up with a new idea from scratch after the cancellation of the Galliano show. The institute had already been collecting Galliano designs for the original show, which had been announced with fanfare in late July. The museum had promised to confront the British designer’s “derogatory conduct that fundamentally altered his career and public reception” — a reference to past antisemitic and racist statements. A month later, the show was scrapped entirely.
“I had no Plan B, to be honest,” Bolton said. “There wasn’t another exhibition already researched and ready to go.” He said the new idea had occurred to him while he was working on last year’s show, “Costume Art,” but had remained merely “a twinkle in my eye.”
That previous show, he said, “sort of led me to think more about how we experience clothing in everyday life, obviously through wearing it but (also) through memory and movement.”
“Everyday clothes carry extraordinary amounts of meaning,” Bolton said. “We have a favorite T-shirt, we have a favorite pair of jeans, and we wear them until they literally fall apart. And those meanings develop through wearing.”
The show looks at how designers make these garments into something different and unique. “I like the idea that designers turn these familiar things into these incredible sources of wonder,” he said.
The Met Gala’s hosts and dress code will be announced at a later date
The spring exhibit is launched each year by the starry Met Gala, a fundraiser for the museum’s Costume Institute, where guests tour the show during cocktail hour. The most visible and photographed event on the fashion calendar is a much-coveted invite, drawing a mix of luminaries from the worlds of entertainment, business, sports and politics.
The exhibit’s theme influences the evening’s dress code, which will be announced at a later date — as will the newest slate of celebrity hosts for the May 3 gala.
One of the foremost critics of the Galliano exhibit was a past attendee, New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin, who said she’d met many times with museum leaders to voice opposition. The gala would have, in 2027, fallen on Holocaust Remembrance Day. The daughter of a Holocaust survivor, Menin said in August that the cancellation was “the correct decision, as the harm and pain this was causing was simply unacceptable.”
Galliano, long recognized as one of the fashion world’s biggest talents, spent years as creative director of Christian Dior. He was fired when a series of racist and antisemitic comments from 2010 and 2011 went viral, leading to his conviction in an antisemitism trial in France. Galliano spent several years involved in public and private efforts to make amends. He made a comeback in 2014 when he was hired by Paris fashion house Maison Margiela, where he remained for a decade.
“I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry for it,” Galliano said in a statement when his exhibit was canceled.
The gala is overseen by Anna Wintour, Vogue’s global editorial director, one of the most influential figures in fashion and a longtime supporter of Galliano.
“John’s decision that the exhibition devoted to his work should not take place at this time is very courageous and a measure of the man he is,” Wintour said in an August statement. “I believe this is the right decision, and both he and the Museum have my full support.”

title: General Motors issues recalls for more than 80,000 vehicles
text:
General Motors issues recalls for more than 80,000 vehicles
General Motors has issued two recalls, covering more than 80,000 vehicles.
The first affects more than 67,000 Cadillac and Blazer vehicles. A software defect in the brake system control module may cause a loss of braking during “certain driving conditions,” the recall report says.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration report said that as of Oct. 29, GM was aware of 20 minor accidents associated with the Cadillac and Blazer vehicles. Two resulted in alleged minor injuries.
GM described the driving conditions that could trigger the issue as follows: “When the brakes are lightly applied at low speeds during a sharp turn and the vehicle encounters a bump or depression – such as at the end of a driveway – a momentary release and reapplication of the brakes may cause the software’s slip calculation to misinterpret wheel movement. In some instances, this may result in a temporary loss of braking.”
The second recall is for more than 12,000 Chevrolet Express and GMC Savana vehicles. That recall concerns a loose steering gear assembly nut. The company hasn’t heard of any crashes or injuries related to this recall, the report says, and it estimates that 1% of the vehicles recalled could have a loose nut.
Makes and models affected by the braking system recall, though not every vehicle is affected:
- Cadillac Celestiqs from 2025-26
- Cadillac Lyriqs from 2023-27
- Cadillac Vistiqs from 2026-27
- Chevrolet Blazer EVs from 2024-27
For vehicles that are capable of receiving software changes using wireless over-the-air (OTA) technology, owners who have accepted the relevant terms and conditions will be able to accept the software changes to resolve the issue via OTA without having to bring their vehicle to a dealership, the report said. However, all owners can have the updates performed at a GM dealer.
Makes and models that may be affected by the loose nut:
- Chevrolet Expresses from 2025-26
- GMC Savanas from 2025-26
Dealers will check the steering gear serial number and replace the steering gear assembly if it's affected by the recall.
Owners can reach out to GM’s customer service for more information on the recalls and next steps.

title: Russell Brand has been convicted of rape and sexual assault
text:
LONDON (AP) — Russell Brand was convicted Thursday of rape and sexual assault charges on allegations dating back more than 20 years.
Judge Joel Bennathan said Brand would receive a prison term when he is sentenced Monday. He was taken into custody.
A prosecutor said the British actor-comedian was a ruthless, calculating, manipulative “sexual predator.”
Brand, 51, denied the charges and testified that he was obsessed with sex as a young man and once led a promiscuous life but had never forced anyone to do something against their will.
Brand was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault involving four women. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault.
The jury of eight men and four women in Southwark Crown Court deliberated more than eight hours over two days.
Known for risqué stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek” and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.
In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.
Brand said the criminal case had a devastating impact on his life and family.
“My entire life has been consumed by these events, these allegations, these accusations,” he said.
Brand’s lawyers argued that the alleged victims were undermined by the fact that they only went to police years after the alleged assaults, and following the broadcast of a 2023 documentary that contained anonymous allegations against Brand.
Brand testified that friends and colleagues had abandoned him.
His wife, Laura, who accompanied him to court, testified as a character witness in his defense, but no one with relevant evidence was willing to give evidence on his behalf, Brand said.

title: Trump administration sues Penn State over in-state tuition for students in the US illegally
text:
The Department of Justice filed a complaint Thursday against Penn State challenging its policy of offering in-state tuition rates to some immigrants in the country illegally, part of a sweeping crackdown by President Donald Trump’s administration.
Two dozen states once offered the tuition breaks, which often had bipartisan support. But as the Trump administration began suing last year, the policies ended in places including Kentucky, Illinois, Nebraska, Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas and Florida. More recent challenges have focused on individual schools, including a lawsuit filed last month against the University of Delaware.
A Penn State spokesperson said the university was aware of the complaint and reviewing it.
The suit against Penn State, which has 86,000 students, comes as the nation looks for clues about how education and immigration policy might shift after a bruising midterm election rout for Republicans.
The federal government argues federal law prevents states from providing preferential benefits to immigrants in the U.S. illegally, regardless of whether or not they meet residency requirements.
“The Department of Justice today continues its efforts to ensure that no state law or university policy gives preferential treatment to illegal aliens over our Nation’s own citizens,” Stanley Woodward, a top Justice Department official, said in a news release.
However, supporters of the tuition breaks argue they don’t violate federal law if they provide the same rates to U.S. citizens in the same circumstances — meaning they are residents of the state and graduates of one of its high schools. Many of the students were brought to the U.S. by their parents when they were children, and supporters of the laws say they are as much a part of their communities as U.S. citizens.

title: Wall Street, AI stocks tumble as voter backlash threatens data center expansion
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Wall Street, AI stocks tumble as voter backlash threatens data center expansion
Wall Street's AI selloff follows election victories for candidates promising to restrict data centers. As investors question the economic stakes, the Trump administration is exploring building facilities on federal land to address growing opposition.
Wall Street, AI stocks tumble as voter backlash threatens data center expansion
Wall Street's AI selloff follows election victories for candidates promising to restrict data centers. As investors question the economic stakes, the Trump administration is exploring building facilities on federal land to address growing opposition.
Wall Street saw a sharp selloff Thursday, with all three major stock indexes falling as investors questioned whether the artificial intelligence boom that has helped power the U.S. economy is running out of steam.
The losses in the stock market come just two days after voters across the country delivered a setback to the data centers needed to sustain that boom.
"Opposition to data centers is perhaps one of the most surprising stories of 2026," said economic analyst Mark Hamrick.
Hamrick said investors had largely assumed there would be few obstacles to the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure. But Tuesday's election results have raised new questions.
"The stock market had been basically moving forward on the expectation that there was very little to restrict the data center build-out and the expansion of artificial intelligence," Hamrick said.
In three states with significant data center development: Ohio, Georgia and Texas, voters in those states elected governors who campaigned to temporarily halt new construction.
The opposition extends well beyond those states.
According to Ballotpedia, voters from rural Florida to urban California sided with greater restrictions on data center development in 46 out of 47 ballot measures decided this year.
But that pushback could come with an economic cost.
"The data center and artificial intelligence build-out has been a key factor in the growth of GDP in our country," Hamrick said.
Economists at J.P. Morgan estimate AI-related investment has accounted for nearly a quarter of America's economic growth over the past year.
President Donald Trump has warned that communities rejecting data centers risk becoming "backwards and poor."
In a statement to Hearst Television, White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said Trump is "committed to maintaining American leadership in SI (Super Intelligence), which will continue to fuel revenue growth, innovation, and productivity across our economy."
The White House argues data centers create jobs and generate substantial tax revenue for local governments. It pointed to Virginia, where data centers have generated more than $2.6 billion in state and local tax revenue, and Loudoun County, where they contributed $875 million in taxes in 2024.
But critics have raised concerns about environmental impacts, how many permanent jobs data centers actually create, and rising electricity costs.
"People are upset with inflation and this has been a contributor to the rise in electricity costs," Hamrick said.
The administration said data centers should cover their own electricity costs rather than passing those expenses on to American families. The White House said its voluntary Ratepayer Protection Pledge now includes hundreds of participating organizations, although those commitments do not guarantee electricity bills will remain unchanged.
A different place to build
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum told Hearst Television that the administration is exploring an alternative: building more data centers on "vast amounts of federal land."
"We're looking at every opportunity to help site those because again, it's a question of national security," Burgum said. "We must have them, but they certainly don't have to be in people's backyards."
Burgum pointed to remote locations such as North Dakota and Alaska, where colder weather could reduce cooling costs and relatively inexpensive electricity could make operations more affordable.
Congress could become the next battleground
Democratic lawmakers have already introduced proposals ranging from a nationwide moratorium on new data center construction to legislation requiring technology companies to shoulder more of their electricity costs.
Those proposals could receive renewed consideration under the incoming Democratic majorities.
But even if Congress passes new restrictions, Trump would still have to sign them into law, or lawmakers would need enough votes to override his veto.
That sets up a potential confrontation between an administration determined to accelerate America's AI expansion and voters increasingly concerned about what that expansion means for their communities.

title: Bangor man killed in Pearl Harbor attack returns home nearly 85 years later
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Almost 85 years after he was killed in the attack on Pearl Harbor, a man from Bangor has finally come home.
Bangor Police say they were part of an escort Wednesday night that brought Private First Class Willard C. Orr back to Bangor.
They say State Police lead the escort from the New Hampshire line to the Brookings and Smith Funeral Home.
Orr was formally identified and accounted for in November 2025, according to the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency.
Orr was 21 years old when he was killed on December 7, 1941.
He reportedly died when Japanese forces expanded their attack to Hickam Field where Orr worked as one of the head cooks.
He is the only resident of the city who died at Pearl Harbor.
Orr is memorialized on a pedestrian bridge in Downtown Bangor.
He is the recipient of both a presidential citation and a Purple Heart.

title: Gather to Grow Food Pantry has new hours
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LEWISTON, ME – Beginning Thursday, October 29th, the Gather to Grow Food Pantry (formerly the St. Mary’s Food Pantry) will have new hours. The food pantry will now be open every Thursday from 11 am to 6 pm and will no longer be open Tuesdays and Fridays. Gather to Grow will combine two food pantry days into one but will be open approximately the same number of hours per week.
Gather to Grow remains committed to serving the 600+ households they support each week with fresh produce, meat, and culturally important food through their choice-centered “food pantry store” and their weekly delivery program for housebound residents.
The team at Gather to Grow understands the impact that this change will have on community members, particularly during this incredibly difficult moment in time. Nearly 23,000 Mainers have lost SNAP benefits, including 7,000 eligible children, and Maine’s school-meals-for-all policy could also be affected. Costs for basic needs continue to rise, creating hardship for more families every day. They know that food pantries like theirs are increasingly needed to help provide food stability in people’s lives.
This change, however, will allow the organization to more sustainably provide the care and resources needed to keep serving as a trusted, welcoming, and safe food pantry for all, over the long term. The change will also allow Gather to Grow to continue to strengthen other areas of work that support food stability, including their community garden program where residents can grow food for themselves and their families in one of Gather to Grow’s 10 urban gardens.
The Gather to Grow team will continue to listen to community members as this change unfolds and are ready to support those who may be disproportionately impacted. For more information, please visit www.gathertogrowmaine.org or contact 207 513 3848 or info@gathertogrowmaine.org
Note on the annual Thanksgiving Food Giveaway: Despite the change to regular hours, Gather to Grow’s Thanksgiving Food Giveaway will still occur on the Tuesday before Thanksgiving, Tuesday November 24th.

title: Maine women’s basketball’s Maddie Fitzpatrick is ready to break out
text:
ORONO — There’s no brace on Maddie Fitzpatrick’s rebuilt right knee. There’s no outward sign of the injury that erased her freshman season with the University of Maine women’s basketball team before it began.
There was no hesitation in Fitzpatrick’s game on Thursday night. The 2024 Miss Maine Basketball winner at Cheverus, Fitzpatrick was a key player in Maine’s season-opening 70-68 win over Siena in the Pit.
Two years removed from the torn ACL, Fitzpatrick is finally ready to show that she’s a player who can help keep the Black Bears in contention for the America East championship. It’s a one-game sample, but it’s an impressive one.
Fitzpatrick led Maine with 17 rebounds, 15 at the defensive end. Her 14 points were second to Gardiner’s Lizzy Gruber (18). Her 36 minutes, 13 seconds of playing time was second only to Lala Woods (38:32). Her three assists were tied with three teammates for the team lead.
As if trying to emphasize the point that her knee is fine, Fitzpatrick dove into Siena’s bench in the final minute of a tie game, chasing down a loose ball. The ball ended up in the hands of Saints guard Francesca Schiro near midcourt, but Maine got the stop and took the lead on Olivia Alvarez’s layup with two seconds remaining.
“I thought it was going to be good, then I saw it go into the Siena girl’s hands, and I was like, maybe I shouldn’t have done that,” Fitzpatrick said. “But you know what? It worked out in the end.”
Fitzpatrick had barely been on campus when the knee injury occurred in the summer before her freshman season. That first collegiate season was lost to rehab. When Fitzpatrick played last season, she was learning the college game on the fly. She played in 27 games, starting one at Penn in early December. She averaged 1.5 points and 1.4 rebounds.
Maine coach Amy Vachon understands the pressures Fitzpatrick faces as well as anybody. Herself a former Miss Maine Basketball, Vachon knows all the fans who watched Fitzpatrick dominate games for Cheverus expected her to step right in with the Black Bears and do the same thing.
“It just doesn’t work that way,” Vachon said.
Last season, Fitzpatrick struggled playing defense, Vachon said. The coach doesn’t expect that to be a problem this season. Fitzpatrick is quicker and stronger, and knows what to expect on the court now.
“This summer when she came back, you could tell how hard she’d worked,” Vachon said. “She came back, and it was like she’s a different kid defensively.”
Fitzpatrick acknowledged the adjustment to college ball was made more challenging because she was recovering from her injury. She credited Maine’s training staff and coaches, as well as leaders from last season’s team, like Sarah Talon and Adrianna Smith, for making a tough process easier.
“I wouldn’t trade it for the world,” Fitzpatrick said.
Fitzpatrick’s role on the Black Bears is to score and rebound. Vachon doesn’t expect 17 boards every game, but attack the glass like she did Thursday, and the rebounds will come. Of course, Fitzpatrick can improve. She missed her first five 3-point attempts before draining one early in the third quarter to push Maine’s lead to 39-27. That said, none of the misses were bad shots, and Vachon wants Fitzpatrick to keep taking them. They both know the shots will fall.
“She has a beautiful shot and she’s a scorer,” Vachon said.
The win was a good way for the Black Bears to open the season. At times they looked dominant, opening a double-digit lead in the third quarter that was still 10 points in the fourth. Maine showed resilience in the face of adversity when Siena made a run to take the lead.
The ups and downs of those 40 minutes are a good way to build a team, Fitzpatrick said.
“Siena had a good comeback there, and we have to learn how to keep our composure and keep pushing,” she said.
Fitzpatrick had to adjust to the speed and tempo of college basketball all while learning to trust a rebuilt knee. When it comes to composure, she has it down cold.

title: Flooding prompts state of emergency in Georgia as crews conduct more than 40 rescues
text:
MCCAYSVILLE, Ga. (WANF/Gray News) — Flash flooding prompted a state of emergency in McCaysville, Georgia, and flash flood warnings in several other cities in north Georgia on Thursday.
Storms dropped heavy rain across a mountainous area that drains into the Toccoa River between McCaysville, Georgia, and Copperhill, Tennessee, causing life-threatening flooding on both sides.
As much as 8 to 10 inches fell overnight between the north Georgia towns of Blue Ridge and Ellijay, and runoff from uncontrolled streams swelled the rivers below, according to the Tennessee Valley Authority.
The Toccoa River reached a record high Thursday morning of 18 feet, according to a river gauge in Copperhill.
More than 40 water rescues were undertaken by emergency personnel manning boats, according to McCaysville police Chief Michael Earley.
“I’ve never seen flooding like this in my life,” Earley said. “I have one of my police cars that’s floating down the river right now. Don’t know where it’s at, but it’s somewhere down there.”
Earley said the water in some areas downtown is 6 to 7 feet high.
“Anybody who’s willing to help, we’re asking for help,” he said.
Chatsworth, Ellijay and Blue Ridge, Georgia, received flash flood warnings until 7 a.m. The National Weather Service put McCaysville under a flash flood emergency until 9 a.m.
The Fannin County Emergency Management Agency advised residents to stay off the roads due to dangerous floodwaters.
“We still have numerous residents who need to be evacuated, including some in areas that emergency crews are currently unable to access or reach due to flooding and dangerous conditions,” the agency said.
Robert Poole, spokesperson for the Fannin County Emergency Management Agency on the Georgia side, estimated that about 20 people had been rescued, with no reported injuries or deaths. The water had begun receding by late Thursday morning, he said.
The downtown areas of McCaysville and Copperhill are a tourist destination for scenic railroad rides on the Blue Ridge Railway and Copperhill Special.

title: Aging Untold: How to choose a medical power of attorney
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we break down medical power of attorney, helping you choose a trusted healthcare proxy and ensure your wishes are honored.
Then, we examine the causes of chronic dry mouth and share simple ways to protect your oral health.
And, we explore the powerful physical and mental health benefits of the outdoors, showing how even a short daily dose of nature can ease anxiety and boost overall well-being.
If you cannot make health care decisions for yourself, who would do it for you?
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the person you name as your medical power of attorney holds a wide range of decision-making power.
“They can decide whether or not you’re going to go into a skilled facility in a rehab after a surgery. They can decide if you’re going to go into an assisted living. They can decide if you’re going to be at home, who your caregivers are going to be,” Cradduck said.
She said you need to know that this person can “advocate for your wishes, not for their heart’s desire.”
Dry mouth affects 40% of adults 80 and older and 30% of adults 65 and older, according to the American Dental Association. It can show up along with soreness, bad breath and trouble with dentures.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said there are several causes for dry mouth and finding that reason is the first step.
There are several possible causes, including dehydration, damage to nerves, cancer, underlying autoimmune disorders and medications, Rogers said.
Dry mouth can be an early sign in a person who is otherwise healthy, she added.
Dr. Nathaniel Mann, a Prisma Health emergency doctor, spent two years traveling the world, practicing medicine in remote environments.
Across his years in medicine, he has found that being outside is one of the most powerful treatments.
Mann, who also practices wilderness medicine, said he thinks people should be prescribed time outside the way they are prescribed medicine.
“I absolutely think we should,” he said.
Centuries worth of iron frame the city of New Orleans’ architecture, from balconies to fences and gates.
Darryl Reeves is one of the few blacksmiths who, like his grandfather before him, carry on the tradition.
“That’s what gives me joy,” Reeves said. “How many people get to beat on metal, especially if you’re frustrated with something and get it out? How many people do that?”

title: Bob Heinz, member of undefeated 1972 Dolphins’ 'No-Name Defense,' dies at 79
text:
Bob Heinz, member of undefeated 1972 Dolphins’ 'No-Name Defense,' dies at 79
Bob Heinz, a defensive tackle on the Miami Dolphins' undefeated 1972 team and a two-time Super Bowl champion, has died.
He was 79.
Heinz died Oct. 31, officials with the Dolphins announced earlier this week. A cause of death has not been released.
Related video above | Remembering those we lost in 2026
"We extend our deepest sympathies to his family, loved ones and former teammates," a statement from the Dolphins organization reads in part.
Heinz played nine seasons in the NFL, mostly with the Miami Dolphins.
The Dolphins selected him in the second round of the 1969 draft, 37th overall, out of the University of the Pacific.
He was a member of Miami’s “No-Name Defense” and a starter on the 1972 team that went 17-0, the only undefeated season in NFL history. Heinz also helped the Dolphins win Super Bowl VII and repeat as champions the following season in Super Bowl VIII.
He finished his career with the Washington Redskins in 1978.

title: JetBlue raises baggage fees again as jet fuel prices stay elevated
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(AP) - JetBlue has raised its checked baggage fees for the second time this year, making it more expensive for travelers to check luggage just as the busy holiday travel season gets underway.
The new fees for tickets purchased on or after Nov. 3 mean most economy passengers flying within the United States, Canada, Latin America and the Caribbean will pay at least $50 each way for their first checked bag, up from $39 previously.
The price climbs to $55 during peak travel periods, including Thanksgiving and the winter holidays, if passengers pay at least 24 hours before departure. Those who wait until the final 24 hours will pay $60 during off-peak periods and $70 during peak periods.
“We’re adjusting checked bag fees to help offset rising fuel and operating costs,” JetBlue said in an emailed statement. “This helps us keep our base fares competitive while giving customers the choice to pay for a checked bag only if they need one.”
At the start of the year, the first checked bag on most economy domestic JetBlue flights cost $35 during off-peak periods. But that was before the Iran war started in late February with U.S.-Israeli strikes and sent jet fuel prices swinging.
The fee for a second checked bag has also increased, starting at $70 each way during off-peak periods and $75 during peak travel. Passengers checking their bags at the airport can pay as much as $85 for a second bag.
JetBlue, which has its flagship terminal at New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport, previously raised its checked baggage fees in March. That increase helped set off a broader round of baggage fee hikes among major U.S. airlines, including Delta, United, American and Southwest.
The war with Iran remains unresolved, keeping traffic largely restricted through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical shipping route for global oil supplies. The disruption has kept jet fuel prices elevated.
JetBlue executives said last week during the airline’s third-quarter earnings call that demand has remained resilient even as fares have risen in response to higher jet fuel prices. JetBlue said its average fuel price reached $3.91 per gallon in the summer, up 57% from a year earlier, and is expected to climb to $4.64 during the final three months of the year, up 85% from the same time last year.
Some travelers, including eligible co-branded credit card holders and members of JetBlue’s loyalty program, can still check bags for free, the airline said.

title: 1 deputy dies and another not expected to survive after firefight with suspect at Washington home
text:
SPOKANE, Wash. (AP) — One of two sheriff’s deputies wounded in a firefight with a suspect in Washington state has died, and the other is not expected to survive, authorities said Wednesday.
Deputies responded to a home in Spangle, a small farming community south of Spokane, on Tuesday afternoon after a woman told her neighbor that she had been shot by her brother, the Spokane County Sheriff’s Office said.
They determined the suspect had a felony warrant and that there might be other victims, and SWAT team members and deputies tried to breach the door.
Gunfire erupted from the home, and the two deputies were struck. They were taken to a hospital in critical condition. One died that night, and the other was being kept on life support Wednesday, allowing for the donation of his organs, the sheriff’s office said in a written statement.
“He will continue to serve others with the gift of life,” the statement said.
Neither was identified, but Sheriff John Nowels described them as younger members of the SWAT team. The deputy who died had a wife and two children.
“Although we know our Deputies knew the risks, they bravely moved toward danger to protect others they did not know,” the sheriff’s office said. “They did this with honor and with an unwavering sense of duty.”
Other deputies returned fire and found the suspect dead inside, along with one other victim in the house and one in the yard, authorities said.
The names of the victims and the suspect have not been released.
Authorities are investigating the shooting and what may have led to it.
The woman who reported being shot by her brother was hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries.

title: Police seize 18 pounds of drugs worth more than $1 million in Maine bust
text:
Police seize 18 pounds of meth, crack, and fentanyl in Waterville drug bust
Police in Waterville say they seized 18 pounds of drugs when they searched a home on Western Avenue on Wednesday.
Police went to the home at about 12:30 p.m. to execute a search warrant related to alleged large-scale trafficking of illegal drugs.
During the search, police say they seized 13.5 pounds of methamphetamine, 3.5 pounds of crack cocaine, one pound of fentanyl, and about $30,000 in suspected drug money.
Police say the drugs are worth more than a million dollars on the street.
Tony Brown, 48, of New Haven, Connecticut, was arrested and charged with three counts of aggravated trafficking of scheduled drugs. He was being held on $750,000 bail and is due in court in March.
Police said more charges were possible.
“Unfortunately we are seeing more and more of these out of state actors coming into our community and setting up shop to sell their poison. Shutting down an operation of this size is a huge win for the citizens of Waterville," said Waterville Police Chief William Bonney.

title: Susan Collins had her Margaret Chase Smith moment. Just not the one she envisioned.
text:
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins has long admired Maine political icon Margaret Chase Smith, who famously broke with her Republican Party to denounce the red-baiting of Joseph McCarthy.
During Donald Trump’s two terms in the White House, Collins often was confronted with calls to have her own “Margaret Chase Smith moment.”
In an interview with The New York Times after her bruising loss to Democrat Troy Jackson, the Maine Republican argued she rose to that occasion many times.
Indeed, she broke with Trump, for example, on repealing the Affordable Care Act in 2017 and voted to convict him during his second impeachment after the 2021 U.S. Capitol riot.
When U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement surged here in January, Collins touted her influence in getting the agency to scale down its operations after just a few days. Then when an ICE agent shot and killed a 25-year-old Colombian immigrant in Biddeford in July, Collins took credit for pressuring the agency to pause “non-urgent” vehicle stops.
But it wasn’t enough to convince voters that Collins was willing to stand up to Trump, whose tariffs and Iran war are making everyday life more expensive.
“What bigger break could there be? It is never enough. I want results and they want angry rhetoric,” she told the paper of record.
So Collins got her “Margaret Chase Smith moment,” just not the one she envisioned.
“I would argue that I have, like Margaret Chase Smith, taken a lot of tough votes and stood up for what I believe in. But I think the best comparison is we each lost our last race for the Senate,” Collins told The Times, alluding to Smith’s failed 1972 reelection bid against Democrat Bill Hathaway.
On Tuesday, voters delivered a strong rebuke to Trump, handing control of the U.S. House and Senate to Democrats, including formerly safe Republican seats in deep red Texas and Kansas. Democrats reversed gains Republicans made with Hispanic, Black and young voters just two years ago.
It was seemingly Collins’ race to lose. Although she trailed in poll after poll after poll, Collins defied polls and expectations back in 2020 to secure a fifth term in the Senate. Those 2020 echoes drowned out the growing murmur of discontent as Trump governed with little regard to Republicans who, unlike the president, had to stand before voters.
“I was caught up in the Trump tsunami that swept away many incumbent Republican senators who have served their states well for many years and really care about our country,” Collins told The Times.
Then there was her 2018 vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the U.S. Supreme Court. At the time, Collins said that Kavanaugh assured her that he viewed Roe v. Wade as settled law. But Kavanaugh joined the Supreme Court majority in overturning that landmark abortion rights decision in 2022. That vote came back to haunt her on the campaign trail.
Her campaign, however, leaned heavily on the senator’s seniority and leadership on the powerful Appropriations Committee. That has allowed Collins to direct millions back home to Maine. Touring the state, Collins touted projects funded by those federal dollars, including $1 million for a new library in Kenduskeag and another $3.5 million for a future fire station in the small town just outside Bangor.
Collins told The Times she wanted voters to know what the choice was. Jackson, as a junior senator, won’t carry anywhere near the influence that Collins wields for now.
“Every town you go to, you see a project that was funded and work that needed to be done. That’s an opportunity that the state has walked away from,” Steve Abbott, Collins’ campaign manager, told The Times.

title: Portugal great Cristiano Ronaldo announces retirement from international soccer
text:
LISBON, Portugal (AP) — Cristiano Ronaldo announced on Thursday he won’t play for Portugal anymore, ending a career that spanned six World Cups and included a European title and the men’s all-time international scoring record.
The announcement marked the end of a lauded career that began more than two decades ago before Euro 2004 and finished with him walking out on the national team after falling out with coach Jorge Jesus.
“To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the No. 7 shirt of our national team,” the 41-year-old Ronaldo said in a long video message on social media. “I never felt it belonged to me alone but for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world.
“Today the time has come to pass it on to the future. It was not an easy decision because some decisions are not made with the mind alone. They are also made with the heart. A journey that began in August 2003 and changed my life forever has come to an end.”
Portugal plans tribute to ‘greatest of all time’
While long-time peer Lionel Messi finished his career with Argentina after a much anticipated farewell match last month, Ronaldo’s final appearance with Portugal has ended up being on Sept. 24 in a 1-0 win over Wales in the Nations League.
Jesus kept him on the bench for the following match and said he didn’t plan to start him in the next one, so Ronaldo decided to leave the team’s training camp. Jesus later said Ronaldo would be welcome back and the decision to return was up to him.
The Portuguese soccer federation released a statement expressing “deep gratitude and immense admiration” for Ronaldo’s service to the country.
“Cristiano Ronaldo has raised Portugal’s profile and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps; for many of us, he is the greatest player of all time!” the federation said.
It said it intends to organize a tribute to Ronaldo “in which the fans and the country can one more time applaud and celebrate a player who has given us so much.”
Like Messi, Ronaldo will keep playing at club level, and is expected to finish his club career at the end of this season with Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia.
He is in pursuit of his 1,000th career goal and sits on 985. Of those, a record 146 goals came in 234 appearances with Portugal.

title: Central Maine truck driver training program shifts into higher gear
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Two months after launching, a truck driver training program in central Maine is moving up a gear. Based in the Kennebec County town of Chelsea, the American Transportation Academy is joining forces with Augusta Adult and Community Education to expand commercial driver license opportunities.
“Through this collaboration, students will have the opportunity to develop the knowledge and hands-on skills needed to pursue their CDL and explore employment opportunities in an industry that plays a vital role in Maine’s economy,” said Trisha Watson, who established the academy with her husband, Toby Watson.
Combination vehicles
The goal is to help more adults access Class A training and pursue career opportunities in the transportation industry. A Class A commercial license allows drivers to operate combination vehicles such as tractor-trailers.
The academy provides a six-week training program combining classroom instruction, behind-the-wheel experience and practical skills development.
Augusta Adult and Community Education will support prospective students through academic preparation, career guidance and assistance identifying potential financial resources.
Kelli Gilzow Stowell, the organization’s workforce coordinator, will work with individuals to help them prepare for training, navigate resources and take the steps needed to succeed.
“CDL Class A training can open the door to meaningful career opportunities,” said Kayla Sikora, the organization’s director.
Commercial drivers support a wide range of industries, including transportation, construction, infrastructure and the delivery of goods and materials.
Growing demand
The Watsons, owners of Statewide Towing Inc. in Chelsea, previously told Mainebiz they started the academy to address growing demand for qualified commercial drivers across Maine and strengthen the industry’s workforce pipeline.
Entry-level driver training requirements are set by the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration. The academy was established through a combination of private funds and a business loan.
Earlier this year, the Maine Department of Labor and Maine Department of Transportation cited commercial driving as one of Maine’s most in-demand occupations.

title: Alleged drug dealers in Rockland arrested for a second time in as many months
text:
Alleged drug dealers in Rockland, Maine, arrested for a second time in as many months
Police in Rockland have arrested two people on drug trafficking charges after both were also arrested on drug-related charges last month.
Police say they have been investigating alleged drug trafficking out of 28-year-old Raven Meklin's home for months, and they have executed several search warrants there over the last few months.
In October, Meklin was charged with operating under the influence of drugs and Travis Griffin, 41, of Rockport, was charged with misdemeanor drug possession.
On Wednesday, police served both Meklin and Griffin with warrants charging them with felony drug trafficking.
When police were arresting Meklin, they say they found and seized more drugs and a semi-automatic shotgun. As a result of those discoveries, police added new charges of drug possession, illegal possession of a firearm by a prohibited person, and violation of conditions of release.
When police arrested Griffin, they seized more than 40 grams of crack cocaine and more than $4,000 in cash. That resulted in additional charges of drug trafficking and violation of conditions of release. Police say they also searched Griffin's home in Rockport and found more crack cocaine and evidence of drug distribution from that location.
As of Thursday morning, Meklin and Griffin were both being held at the Knox County Holding Facility on $25,000 cash bail each.

title: Midcoast Maine IEA Wins at Equestrian Show
text:
The Midcoast Maine IEA team won its second straight show on Sunday, Nov. 1 at Dove Hill Equestrian in Rowley, Mass., with six teams participating.
The team added another new member for this show, varsity intermediate rider Maddie Gundel.
This was the first show hosted by Dove Hill and the Midcoast team saw many new horses. In IEA competition, riders draw a random horse and must compete without first having a chance to ride and learn about their mount.

title: Gunman in Citibank shooting was angry over court case, drove to Tampa from Orlando
text:
Citibank office shooter targeted company over a $2,500 debt collection, Florida sheriff says
A gunman who killed a woman before being fatally shot by a security guard at Citibank’s sprawling office complex in Tampa targeted the campus because he was angry over a $2,500 debt collection, a sheriff said Thursday.
About three hours before Wednesday's shooting, Jacob Pearson called an attorney affiliated with Citibank and threatened violence, Hillsborough County Sheriff Chad Chronister said at a news conference on Thursday.
Pearson told the attorney's office to cancel the court case, saying, "Unless you want me to go over there with my AR-15, my bulletproof vest, and my insanity, you [expletive] cancel this court case. Do you understand me? They are only an hour and 3 minutes away ..."
The attorney's office called Citibank security, who determined it was a credible threat and called Orlando police for a welfare check on the suspect.
When the police arrived at Pearson's house, his wife told officers he was gone, but she didn't know where he went.
She told officers her husband was angry, got in his car, and left.
Pearson, 35, from Orlando, had no criminal record.
Police gave Citibank the update, contacted the Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office, and deputies headed to the bank campus.
Woman shot, killed
When deputies arrived, they heard gunshots, the sheriff's office said.
That's when Pearson crashed his car into a gate and exited with a rifle. He then shot one victim, returned to his car for his handgun and again shot the same victim, who was trying to crawl away. She was identified as 41-year-old Leanne Selman.
He then went into the cafeteria, the sheriff's office said, adding he appeared very calm.
The sheriff's office said Pearson had 90 rounds of ammunition.
Pearson was ultimately shot five times by a security guard and died at the hospital.
More than 360 deputies swarmed the campus.
Five others were hurt in the shooting.
The Citibank campus in suburban Tampa includes four three-story office buildings that house thousands of the banking giant’s employees.
911 calls
Radio traffic on Broadcastify.com from officers who responded to the Citibank complex described an exhaustive floor-by-floor search of the complex's buildings. Officers found people sheltering in locked rooms and closets, and carefully escorted them from the buildings and parking garage.
This is a developing story and will be updated.
The Associated Press contributed to this story.

title: New Jersey ticket holder wins $847M Powerball jackpot
text:
New Jersey ticket holder wins $847 million Powerball jackpot
A single Powerball ticket in New Jersey has won an estimated $847 million after matching all six numbers in Wednesday’s drawing, the company said Thursday.
The winning numbers were 15, 34, 41, 53, 56, and red Powerball 21, with a Power Play multiplier of 2x.
The winner has the option to take a one-time payment of $363.1 million or an annuity paid out over 29 years.
There were no winners for the $2 million and $1 million Match 5 prizes.
Wednesday’s jackpot was the ninth-largest prize in game history and the second-largest prize so far this year, according to game officials.
The last time the Powerball jackpot was won was Aug. 12, when a lucky player claimed a $1.04 billion jackpot in Illinois.
Powerball drawings take place three times a week, on Monday, Wednesday and Saturday, at 10:59 p.m. ET. The jackpot will reset to $20 million for Saturday’s drawing.
The odds of winning Wednesday’s jackpot were extremely slim, at an estimated 1 in 292.2 million, according to the lottery.
This jackpot cycle was the first in which players in the United Kingdom have participated from the beginning of the multi-drawing stretch, following the expansion of ticket sales to the country in July.
It also marks the first time a lottery outside of the U.S. has contributed to the Powerball jackpot, according to the lottery.

title: Maine men’s basketball hangs on to beat Sacred Heart
text:
Ace Flagg of Newport scored 14 points and grabbed 10 rebounds, and the Maine men’s basketball team held on for a 74-72 win over Sacred Heart on Thursday in Fairfield, Connecticut.
The Black Bears (1-1) led 72-69 when Killian Gribben blocked a shot by Sacred Heart’s Griffin Barrouk with 13 seconds left. Flagg grabbed the rebound, was fouled and made one of two free throws.
The Pioneers (1-1) pulled within one on a 3-pointer by Samon Reilly with six seconds remaining.
Maine’s Darius Lopes was fouled with five seconds left and made the first foul shot before missing the second, giving Sacred Heart a chance for a tie or win. Jaden Slaughter lost control of the ball, however, and was unable to get a shot off in time.
DeAndre Williams scored all of his team-high 16 points in the second half for Maine, which trailed 27-25 at the half. Yanis Bamba added 11 points and six rebounds, and Caleb Crawford finished with 10 points.
Reilly scored 18 points, while Jaylen Robinson and Slaughter each had 15 for Sacred Heart.

title: Newcastle Continues Safety Efforts for Halloween on Glidden Street
text:
Trick-or-treaters gathered for Halloween on Glidden Street in Newcastle on Saturday, Oct.31 with some new additions to improve safety.
According to Newcastle Town Manager Kevin Sutherland, last year was the first year the town decided to close the roads because of the amount of foot traffic. After feedback from 2025, the town decided to add “festive” purple and orange lights along the street to improve visibility.
“A big thank you to Ben Frey, Tor Glendinning, Seth Hagar, and our first responders for making this event such as success,” Sutherland said.

title: Wisconsin infant dies of measles, the third measles-related death this week in the US
text:
Wisconsin infant dies amid measles outbreak, the third measles-related death this week in the US
As of Tuesday, Wisconsin DHS reported 431 measles cases in 13 counties this year- the highest number of cases in more than 35 years
Wisconsin infant dies amid measles outbreak, the third measles-related death this week in the US
As of Tuesday, Wisconsin DHS reported 431 measles cases in 13 counties this year- the highest number of cases in more than 35 years
For the first time since 1990, an infant in Wisconsin has died from measles. This is the third measles-related death reported in the U.S. this week.
In a Thursday news release from the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, officials said the death is connected to an ongoing measles outbreak in the southwest part of the state.
Officials did not release information about the exact age, gender or location of the child who died.
"Any death of a child is a tragedy, and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease," DHS Secretary Kirsten Johnson said in the news release. "Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family."
As of Tuesday, Wisconsin DHS reported 431 measles cases in 13 counties this year — the highest number of cases in more than 35 years. Of those cases, 428 were in people who were not vaccinated.
The state encouraged people to get vaccinated to protect themselves, saying two doses are approximately 97% effective at preventing measles.
Health officials said the rate of MMR vaccination among kindergarteners in Wisconsin is at about 85%, well below the roughly 95% coverage needed to prevent measles from spreading through a population.
Wisconsin’s health department updated its guidance this week to recommend an early dose of MMR vaccine for certain infants between 6 and 11 months of age who are at increased risk of exposure during the outbreak. Typically, MMR vaccination doesn’t start until a child’s first birthday.
Until last year, there had been no measles deaths in the U.S. in decades. Three measles-related deaths have already been reported this week.
In Pennsylvania, an unvaccinated resident of rural Jefferson County, in the north-central part of the state, died after testing positive for measles, the Pennsylvania Department of Health said on Wednesday. They were the sixth person in Pennsylvania to die from measles this year.
On Monday, the New York State Department of Health announced that a child had died after contracting measles. The child lived in rural Lewis County, in the northern part of the state. The child’s death marked New York’s first in 30 years.
More than 4,800 measles cases have been reported across the U.S. this year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — the most since 1991, almost a decade before measles was declared eliminated in the U.S.
An international meeting to determine the status of measles elimination in the United States is scheduled to take place next week.
Jen Christensen from CNN contributed reporting.

title: How soon could Democrats try to carry out their affordability agenda?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
How soon could Democrats try to carry out affordability agenda?
House Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address gas prices, groceries, and health care, while President Trump signals openness to bipartisan cooperation.
How soon could Democrats try to carry out affordability agenda?
House Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address gas prices, groceries, and health care, while President Trump signals openness to bipartisan cooperation.
Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address key issues like gas prices, groceries, and healthcare following their midterm election victories.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Wednesday that the party will fight for an affordable America.
"The American people have chosen House Democrats because they want to see a dramatic change in direction, and that's exactly what House Democrats will deliver beginning on day one," Jeffries said.
Jeffries, who could make history as the nation's first Black speaker of the House, added that Democrats are committed to delivering dramatic change.
House Democrats are planning efforts to reinstate healthcare tax credits for the Affordable Care Act. The tax credits expired in 2025, leaving millions of Americans facing higher health insurance costs.
How soon could Democrats carry out their agenda?
Democrats will take control in January, when the new Congress is officially sworn in. Republicans maintain control of Congress for the next two months, and experts say little will likely happen. Analysts predict Democrats will continue to filibuster or stall any last-minute Republican bills.
Until the new members are sworn in, it will be some time before Democrats attempt to deliver on their promises.
President Trump signals willingness to work with Democrats
Despite the shift in power, President Donald Trump has signaled he will try to work with Democrats.
"I'll get along probably with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive, but I have the power of the veto," Trump said. "They've already called and they want to talk about things, and that's fine."
Some Democrats have floated the idea of filing motions to impeach Trump in the next session, but political analysts say the Senate lacks the two-thirds majority needed to convict him.

title: Non-juried, year-end show open to submissions at Damariscotta art gallery
text:
River Arts in Damariscotta announces a call to artists for a special year-end exhibition, “Celebration.” This non-juried show invites gallery visitors to shop locally for affordable art and fine craft during the holiday season, supporting Maine artists in the process.
All original fine art and fine craft will be accepted, including painting, drawing, printmaking, photography, sculpture, ceramics, jewelry, fiber, multimedia, pastel, glass, wood, collage, and more. There is no predetermined theme, and the exhibition is open to both River Arts members and non-members.
Artists may enter any number of pieces, with no size limits. The combined retail value of all entries may not exceed $500. Entry forms are available at the gallery or on the website at riverartsme.org. The entry fee is $15 for members and $30 for non-members. River Arts retains a 35% commission on sales.
Works may be delivered during gallery hours through the deadline of Saturday, Nov. 14, at 4 p.m.
The public is invited to an opening reception on Saturday, Nov. 21, from 2 to 4 p.m. “Celebration” will run through Dec. 31.
River Arts is located at 36 Elm St. in Damariscotta. Gallery hours are Tuesday through Saturday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. For more information, call 207-563-6868 or visit riverartsme.org.

title: Key federal panel approves Trump’s arch while it’s being challenged in court
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A key federal panel has given final approval to President Donald Trump’s proposed memorial arch near downtown Washington, clearing a key hurdle on the road to breaking ground.
The National Capital Planning Commission on Thursday approved the 250-foot (76-meter) project that Trump has sought as part of his efforts to remake the capital region. The 8-4 vote Thursday gives a green light to launch construction within a day.
The arch still faces legal challenges and a judge is expected to rule soon on whether to block it.
THIS IS A BREAKING NEWS UPDATE. Check back for updates. AP’s earlier story follows below.
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal panel was expected Thursday to approve President Donald Trump’s proposed memorial arch in Washington at the end of a meeting that drew dozens of opponents to a key part of the president’s push to leave his imprint on the nation’s capital.
The approval by the National Capital Planning Commission would clear a hurdle on the road to breaking ground on the project, and the administration has said it could launch construction within a day of the vote. But the proposed 250-foot (76-meter) tall gilded arch still faces legal challenges.
The remote, call-in hearing — which crashed repeatedly and was accompanied by a nearly universally negative comment section — drew witnesses who gave impassioned, three-minute comments opposing an arch they said will destroy the solemnity of the nearby Arlington National Cemetery. As of 6:30 p.m. Washington time, there were still dozens of people waiting to give testimonials.
The Trump-appointed chairman of the commission, however, launched into a gushing appraisal of the towering monument and lauded Trump for wanting to build it.
“President Trump understands as president and a superb builder that it’s important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments,” said Mark Paoletta, the commission’s chairman.
As Trump has often remarked, “the great cities around the world have arches: Paris, Rome, London,” said Paoletta, who also serves as general counsel for the White House Office of Management and Budget. In addition to Paoletta, the arch received support during the hearing from Republican lawmakers and a veteran who praised the administration’s efforts to build the monument.
The commission oversees construction on federal land in the city and began reviewing the arch plan in June.
Trump is working to remake Washington
The arch is one of several projects around Washington that the Republican president has undertaken as he alters the capital to his tastes — from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Those projects could soon face intense scrutiny after Democrats gained control of Congress in the midterm elections this week.
Many of the plans are being challenged in the courts, and three lawsuits have been filed opposing the arch. A judge has been asked to block the construction so long as lawsuits are still being litigated, and she could rule as early as Thursday.
Rep. Jared Huffman, a California Democrat who is set to chair the House Natural Resources Committee, called the project ill-advised and illegal.
“This arch would dishonor America,” Huffman told the commission. He called the proposed arch “a tribute to Donald Trump,” not veterans as Trump administration officials claim. The monument is similar to those built for emperors or kings, Huffman said, adding that Trump was using veterans as a pretext to build a memorial to himself.
A small group of protesters joined at the proposed site to oppose the arch. Julius Spain, a member of the Arlington County Board and veteran of Operation Iraqi Freedom, told the crowd it was their moment. “I’ve seen combat. I was prepared to give my life in defense of a grateful nation,“ he said. “And now in this moment, my friends, and residents, and citizens and everyone, this is our civil rights moment.”
Virginia Democratic Rep. James Walkinshaw told the protesters that if the arch is somehow built, “I’m not going to stop until we ensure it’s a temporary arch.”
Opponents argue that the arch is too big for the skyline and would disrupt carefully designed sight lines between landmarks in and around the capital — most prominently the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery — that were meant to symbolize the reunification of the North and the South after the Civil War.
But the opposition has done little to influence the members of the commission, which is led by some of Trump’s closest allies. Trump appointed Paoletta to chair the 12-member panel. Two other commissioners are also White House aides.
At one point, Arrington Dixon, who was appointed by District of Columbia Mayor Muriel Bowser, broke in during a period of relentless criticism of the panel to foreshadow what he called “the reality” of having the majority of the commission appointed directly by Trump, members of his administration or House committees currently chaired by Republicans.
Trump wants an arch, but it faces legal challenges
Still, a federal judge on Monday complicated Trump’s efforts to move quickly on the project.
U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan, who is overseeing a lawsuit challenging the Trump administration’s plans, said she must be told of any decision by the planning commission within an hour. The order set the same time limits for any decision by the National Park Service and the Department of the Interior.
Before Thursday’s hearing began, attorneys with the Justice Department filed a notice with Chutkan informing her that a contractor had already done site preparation work on Oct. 31, with what she said appeared to be no authorization from the National Park Service.
The plaintiffs in the three lawsuits are calling for a halt to work on a monument that is set to be built on a patch of grass off a bridge that spans the Potomac River and connects Washington with Arlington National Cemetery, in Arlington, Virginia. When complete, the monument would be 100 feet (30 meters) taller than the Statue of Liberty without its pedestal.
Critics, including the plaintiffs, argue that the Trump administration must seek congressional approval. The administration maintains that Congress cleared the way for a monument at Memorial Circle decades ago.
Paoletta said it was a “national disgrace” that a memorial arch had not been placed there, despite a 1925 law that designated such a memorial, he said.
Last week, the government submitted a 106-page plan for the arch that envisions a massive structure more than 12 stories high that includes a huge bronze statue of Lady Liberty with wings and carrying a torch with an eternal flame. The structure would include an observation deck and two mezzanines.
Inside the arch would be rooms for program space, offices, a staff lounge, circular staircases, multiple elevators and a fire command center. The project proposes significant traffic changes in the area, including rerouting traffic on nearby roads. Administration officials have said the arch also will have a national security function.
In a recent hearing, Chutkan asked why the Trump administration was so keen on moving ahead quickly with the arch despite the ongoing lawsuits, aside from Trump’s “desire to bedazzle the city.”
Administration lawyer Robert Stander said the arch was “absolutely a high-priority project” and that any ruling delaying construction would impede the work of the government.
___
Associated Press videographer Nathan Ellgren contributed to this story.
