title: Portland seafood eatery on OpenTable list of top 100 restaurants
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Portland seafood restaurant Scales is Maine’s only restaurant named to OpenTable’s 2026 Top 100 Restaurants in America list.
The waterfront restaurant earned a 4.9-star rating based on 1,348 diner reviews, according to the national restaurant reservation platform.
The annual list recognizes 100 restaurants across 21 states and Washington, D.C. It is based on more than 11 million reviews from verified OpenTable diners, along with dining and reservation data collected over the past year.
Scales’ selection puts Portland on a national list that includes restaurants in major dining markets as well as smaller communities. The recognition also marks a return for the restaurant, which appeared on OpenTable’s 2025 List alongside Portland’s Fore Street.
Both restaurants were founded by Portland restaurateur Dana Street, who also owns Street & Co. and Standard Baking Co. Street recently received the James Beard Foundation’s national award for Outstanding Restaurateur.
Maine was one of two New England states represented on this year’s list. Massachusetts had two honorees: LUNE in Dennis Port and Pammy’s in Cambridge.
California led this year’s list with 19 restaurants, followed by New York with 15 and Illinois with 12.
The announcement coincides with OpenTable’s release of its 2027 Dining Trends Report, which found that 68% of Americans expect to visit restaurants as often or more frequently than they do now.
“Diners have no shortage of places they can turn to for dining inspiration, but none quite like our Top 100, which casts a wide net across the country and reflects the restaurants Americans are truly loving,” said Amy Wei, COO at OpenTable.

title: These Maine towns flipped for Troy Jackson
text:
This story appears as part of a collaboration to strengthen investigative journalism in Maine between the BDN and The Maine Monitor. Read more about the partnership.
Future U.S. Sen. Troy Jackson did what no other Maine Democrat could for three decades: He took down Susan Collins.
Jackson did it in part by flipping the script on Collins in 45 municipalities that the formidable Republican incumbent won in 2020, based on a Maine Monitor analysis of data from The New York Times.
When Collins defied the polling in 2020 and held on to beat former Maine House Speaker Sara Gideon, that path to victory included wins in some of Maine’s largest communities such as Lewiston, Bangor and Auburn. This year, those three cities switched to support Jackson.
Jackson cruised to an 8-point victory in Lewiston, Maine’s second-largest city and home to nearly 24,000 registered voters, after Collins secured a 2-point win there six years ago. In neighboring Auburn, Jackson upended Collins’ 8-point victory from 2020 with a 5-point win of his own this week. And in Bangor, Maine’s third-largest city, where Collins had eked out a win by less than a percentage point in 2020, and where her campaign was hosting its watch party on Tuesday night, Jackson stormed to a 16-point victory.
But it wasn’t just the larger cities that flipped for Jackson. With 95% of votes reported Wednesday afternoon, Jackson also appeared to have won in smaller towns such as Tremont, Montville, Veazie, Bristol and others that previously voted for Collins.
Voters across the state, in both the large cities and small towns that flipped, provided some insight into their choices in the Senate race while leaving the polls on Tuesday.
John Cleveland, 76, is one of Auburn’s nearly 16,000 registered voters. He told The Monitor that he thought Jackson was a “competent candidate” after observing his work for decades as a state lawmaker, including a stint as president of the Maine Senate from 2018 to 2024.
“He’s focused on working citizens, working-class workers, and he certainly is willing to stand up to the president,” Cleveland said. “Susan Collins clearly has not been.”
In Stockton Springs, 84-year-old Bonnie-Jean Brooks said she has voted for Collins in the past but felt it’s been more difficult in recent years to meet with the five-term senator and have her listen to issues.
“I think that Troy Jackson brings a fresh face at a time when we need a fresh face,” Brooks said. “He is not going to be bought and sold. He’s going to bring new blood, and we need new blood in Congress. There’s no question about that.”
Lewiston voter Colby Hunter, 33, felt that both the Republican and Democratic parties “say the same general things are important,” but thought that Jackson and the Democrats “promote more access to housing and more affordability, which is important to me.”
And in Bangor, at least one couple liked Collins as a candidate but wanted their votes to stand as a repudiation of President Donald Trump.
Natalie Rhoads, 30, said both she and her husband voted for Jackson even though she thinks the Democratic Party has been producing some “really weak” candidates.
“I do think Susan Collins is a strong candidate,” Rhoads said. “But unfortunately, just what Trump is doing right now is something that I really can’t get on board with.”
Of the 45 flipped municipalities that The Monitor identified in the Times data, 10 have more than 5,000 registered voters as of 2025; nine have between 2,500 and 5,000 voters; and the others have fewer than 2,500 voters.
These cities and towns, from largest to smallest based on 2025 voter registration data, are Lewiston, Bangor, Auburn, Gorham, Windham, Augusta, Wells, Berwick, Old Town, Farmington, Gardiner, Raymond, Arundel, Durham, Sanford, Wiscasset, Boothbay, Bristol, Bowdoinham, Bethel, Thomaston, Searsport, Boothbay Harbor, West Bath, Nobleboro, Pownal, Veazie, Stockton Springs, Surrey, South Thomaston, Trenton, Tremont, Lubec, Appleton, Owl’s Head, Lovell, Penobscot, Wayne, Montville, Monroe, Greenwood, Westport Island, Southport, Stow and Stoneham.
The data from The Times did not yet include complete results for each of the municipalities as of Wednesday afternoon. Almost all of the 45 towns that flipped from Collins to Jackson had reported more than 95% of their results by 3 p.m. Wednesday, and one, Sanford, had reported 92%. If the remaining results yet to be included in The Times data were to be drastically different from the existing returns, that could impact Jackson’s final town-by-town win percentages slightly.
Of course, Jackson’s victory cannot be solely explained by the towns that he flipped from 2020. He also expanded on Gideon’s lead in Democratic strongholds such as Portland. And Collins saw her level of support slip even in some places that she still won comfortably.
Take the small Penobscot County town of Newburgh, where Collins enjoyed overwhelming support — just not as much as she did in 2020. The town of just over 1,000 registered voters supported her by a 40-point margin in 2020. That dipped to 33% this year.
Newburgh resident Chad Howland, 48, said that he has supported Collins in the past but voted for Jackson this time around. Howland’s top concerns this election were the war in Iran and escalating fuel prices, and he said he felt the country needs to shift in the last two years of the Trump presidency.
“It’s not that she hasn’t done right by Maine, but she’s been in the Senate for a very long time,” Howland said about Collins after voting at the Newburgh Town Office on Tuesday. “It may be time for some change.”

title: 4 Cornell lawsuit defendants join effort to oust Letitia James from criminal investigation
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Four men named in a former Cornell University student’s lawsuit are joining a co-defendant’s effort to block New York’s attorney general from leading a reopened criminal investigation into the woman’s gang rape allegations, according to court filings on Thursday.
The co-defendant’s lawyers said the men agreed to be added to a court petition that seeks Attorney General Letitia James’ removal from the case because of social media posts she made prior to her involvement in which she condemned the alleged assault and expressed support for the accuser.
The development comes a day after James appointed Jacqueline Kelly, a former federal prosecutor who oversaw sex crimes cases against music mogul Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs, as outside counsel for the investigation. She and a team of lawyers and investigators will be responsible for evidence gathering, witness interviews and other investigative steps. They will report to James.
A judge heard arguments last week on one of the accused men’s request to remove James but said he wouldn’t rule without knowing if the six other lawsuit defendants backed the effort. He gave the man’s lawyers until Thursday to try to get them to join.
Lawyers for one of the four men agreeing to join had separately filed court papers seeking to have James removed. Two other men named as defendants in the lawsuit didn’t have lawyers who could speak for them and did not provide a response, court filings said.
James’ office declined to comment.
A former Cornell student identified in court papers as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit in September alleging that several men raped her at a fraternity party in 2024. The woman said some of the men pressured her into using ketamine and marijuana and that she drank alcohol that left her too intoxicated to consent. Not all of the men named were accused of rape.
James, a Democrat, posted about the case on X and Facebook on Sept. 28, linking to a news article about the lawsuit. “I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you.”
On Oct. 1, Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed James as special prosecutor overseeing the criminal investigation, saying that she had lost faith in the local district attorney, who declined to bring charges in 2024 but had said he would restart the investigation following the former student’s lawsuit.
James initially declined to comment about her social media posts but addressed them at an Oct. 8 debate, saying: “Those comments demonstrate empathy, and what we need now more than ever in our body politic is more empathy.”
In court, the state’s lawyers argued that Hochul has wide latitude to appoint special prosecutors and said she picked James because of her track record handling sensitive cases in the national spotlight.
In a statement on Wednesday, James said she is confident that Kelly “will lead a fair and comprehensive investigation.”
Andrew Miltenberg, a lawyer for the man spearheading the removal effort, said in a court filing that Kelly’s appointment “changes the face of the investigation” but “does not establish any change in ultimate authority.”

title: Child dies of measles in Wisconsin's first such death since 1990
text:
MADISON, Wis. (AP) — An infant in southwestern Wisconsin has died after contracting measles, the state’s first death from the disease in 36 years, state officials announced Thursday.
The Wisconsin Department of Health Services did not specify where the death happened or provide any additional details to protect the privacy of the family.
The coroner listed the cause of death as measles, state health officials said.
“My heart is broken for the family,” said Kirsten Johnson, secretary of the state health department. “Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease.”
The U.S. stopped the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks of the viral disease.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed four measles-associated deaths in the U.S. this year, but state health departments have reported higher numbers. In Pennsylvania alone, health officials have reported five deaths this year and are investigating a possible sixth.
As of Thursday, Wisconsin reported 431 cases of measles, all but three in unvaccinated people. Nine people had been hospitalized.

title: Bangor And Brewer Veterans Day: Pancake Breakfast, Parade, Ceremonies
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Veterans Day is coming up next Wednesday November 11th, and there are a number of way the you can help to honor veterans along with many ways in which veterans are being celebrated by businesses across Maine.
Read More: When Will Bangor-Brewer's Chamberlain Bridge Return to Two Lanes?
In the Bangor/Brewer, there's everything from a pancake breakfast and parade to discounts at local shops and eateries.
What's Happening And When?
Breakfast:
Things kick off at Jeff's Catering in Brewer with the Bangor Breakfast Rotary Club's Annual "All-You-Can-Eat Veterans Day Pancake Breakfast. Veterans eat free, but for the rest of us it's just $10 for adults and $5 for kids 12 and under. The breakfast will run from 7 AM to 10 AM, and wraps up right in time for the Veterans Day Parade (more on that in a moment.) All the proceeds they collect from the breakfast go to Bangor Breakfast Rotary Charities.
Parades and Community Observances:
The Bangor High School JROTC will once again host a Veterans Day Parade the will travel from Vista Way in Brewer across the Joshua Chamberlain Bridge into Downtown Bangor. That will kick off at 10:15 AM and go till noon.
Following the Veterans Day Parade, there will be a ceremony to commemorate Maine's Korean War Veterans featuring the playing of Taps and the Marine Color Guard. This will take place at the Korean War Memorial at the Mt. Hope Cemetery in Bangor at 12:30 PM.
After that, at 1 PM at the Cole Land Transportation Museum (405 Perry Road in Bangor) they will have another ceremony to honor veterans. That will conclude at 2:30 PM.
Folks are welcome to make their way to St. John’s Episcopal Church (225 French Street, Bangor) for another veterans commemoration called "America at War in the 21 Century." It will feature music, poetry and guest speakers, that will take place at 3 PM.
Musical Tributes/ Concerts
There will be two special tributes to honor America and her veterans this weekend.
The Bangor Symphony Orchestra is teaming up the actor/author/champion for veterans, Gary Sinise, and the Lt. Dan Band will play two shows at the Collins Center for the Arts. The shows will include music and a book sale of Sinise's new book, with the proceeds going back into his foundation to help veterans.
Read More: Bangor Symphony Orchestra Honors Veterans With Gary Sinise
The shows will be at 7 PM Saturday 11/7 night and at 1 PM on Sunday 11/8 afternoon.
There will also be a concert at the Gracie Theater on the campus of Husson University in Bangor. Veterans can get into the "Bruce in the USA" Tribute for free with their military ID. That show will start at 7 PM as well/.
Free Meals & Discounts For Veterans
Many area local and national restaurants and stores will be offering veterans and active military discounts on food and sale items on Wednesday.
It's important that you call ahead to check if the offer is a dine-in or drive through only, if it requires a membership card or coupon, and what times the offer will run. The it's usually as easy as showing a military ID and you're good to go.
Some of the businesses offering specials or discounts include Dunkin, Starbucks, McDonalds, Burger King, Wendy's, Olive Garden, Buffalo Wild Wings, Denny's, Chili's, Chick-fil-et, Texas Roadhouse, Applebee's and Taco Bell.
Other companies such as FedEx, UPS, T-Mobile, AT&T, Verizon, Home Depot, Ace Hardware, Sports Clips and the Dollar General also offer discounts to veterans on Veterans Day.

If you're looking for more information about special Veterans Day meal specials and freebies, there is a list online. You can access it through this site by clicking here.
Make sure you stop to thank a veteran next Wednesday (and whenever you see them out and about).
To our veteran listeners and readers, we appreciate you. Thank you for your service.

title: Donald Trump dared voters to pretend he was on the ballot. They did, and Republicans lost big.
text:
The BDN Editorial Board operates independently from the newsroom, and does not set policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com.
President Donald Trump urged Americans to vote as if he was on the ballot Tuesday. They did.
Across the country, voters delivered a stunning rebuke to the president and the Republican Party. Voters were frustrated that Trump had not delivered on his promises, especially around rising costs, and felt he was more interested in growing his fortune than in their wellbeing.
In Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson, who had been in the race since only July, unseated five-term Republican senator Susan Collins.
Collins, the only Republican member of Congress in New England, could not overcome deep dissatisfaction with the president and frustration among many voters that she didn’t use her seniority and role as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee to hold Trump more accountable.
Her defeat should not diminish her long tenure in the Senate, which included a perfect voting streak, vital financial support for Maine’s communities and industries, and a long record as an important mediator and dealmaker between political parties that resulted in important bipartisan legislation and the continuing of the landmark Affordable Care Act.
In Kansas, a Democrat was elected to the U.S. Senate for the first time in nearly a century. It had been nearly four decades since there was a Democratic senator from Texas. On Tuesday, voters there elected Democrats to the open Senate seat and the state’s governorship. They also flipped several U.S. House seats to Democratic control despite Republican gerrymandering last year in an effort to make those seats safer for the GOP.
Democrats gained control of Congress by large margins in both the House and Senate.
After Tuesday’s big victories, Democrats must be careful not to overplay their hand. In many of these races, the Democratic victory was less a vote for liberal policies and more a repudiation of Republican actions and tactics. In Texas and South Carolina, for example, candidates who were essentially anointed by Trump were soundly defeated. More reasonable and seasoned Republicans, who Trump pushed aside, may have won those races.
Still, the sweeping Democratic victories across the country ushered in a new era of diversity in representation. Deb Haaland of New Mexico will be the country’s first Native American governor. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms will be the country’s first Black female governor. Chris Pappas in New Hampshire is the first openly gay man elected to the U.S. Senate.
In a late night interview with The New York Times Tuesday, Trump said he was “absolutely willing” to accept the results of the election, while blaming losses on Republicans. He also said he looked forward to working with Democrats and thought they could work some things out.
That is encouraging. However, the next two months before the new Congress is sworn in could be very dangerous, for the U.S. and the world, as a wounded and increasingly mentally unfit president and his allies seek to retain a grasp on power and to avoid accountability. Of course, those who have violated the law must be held accountable, but Congress — and the country — can’t become paralyzed by endless impeachments and investigations. At the same time, we must remember that targeted investigation of those who have run roughshod over the Constitution and laws of the country is different from the retribution of perceived enemies that Trump has promised and sought.
Trump has also threatened new attacks against Iran as he seemingly tries to end a war he never should have started. The war has driven up fuel and other prices, stressing Americans and prompting many to vote against Republicans.
To counter Trump’s record and to keep their power and influence, scores of billionaires (many of whom keep their identities hidden) donated heavily to Republican campaigns. Notably, Elon Musk, a Trump ally and the world’s richest man, spent nearly $500 million on Republican campaigns, including contributions to boost Susan Collins. More than $125 million was spent on ads to support Collins’ reelection campaign.
In the end, that looks like a bad investment as voters in Maine and across the country showed that the power of the people can overcome the power of money.

title: After funding cuts, Waterville genetics lab teams up with Canadian firm
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
GenoTyping Center of America, a genetic testing firm in Waterville, formed a partnership with Toronto-based data platform to expand the reach of both companies.
The partnership is with SoftMouse.NET, a cloud-based animal data platform.
“Researchers have long managed colony records and genotyping results in separate systems and workflows,” said Michael Greene, CEO and co-founder of the Waterville company. “This partnership brings those processes together in a way that improves efficiency, supports reproducibility and helps scientists focus more of their time on research rather than data management.”
Genetic testing
GenoTyping Center of America, founded in 2012, provides genetic testing and colony planning services to accelerate preclinical and drug discovery research. Genotyping is the process of extracting tissue in order to identify its DNA.
Through genotyping, testing and colony planning services, GTCA helps laboratories breed the animals with the genotype that’s needed for a particular study, protect the reproducibility of their results and reduce unnecessary animal use.
SoftMouse.NET, used by research laboratories worldwide, provides a centralized, mobile-friendly platform for managing animals, cages, matings, weaning schedules and protocol compliance, with automated alerts and audit trails.
The partnership addresses a longstanding challenge in biomedical research: colony records and genotyping results have traditionally lived in separate systems. Linking GTCA’s genetic data with SoftMouse.NET’s animal, breeding and study records could allow laboratories to maintain complete, auditable histories, strengthen compliance documentation and make better-informed breeding decisions with far less administrative work.
Lab space
GenoTyping Center of America was originally based in Ellsworth. Co-founders Greene, Todd Dehm and Kat Taylor moved the lab into 700 square feet at the Hathaway Creative Center in Waterville in 2018.
In 2023, the firm took additional space next to its lab and now has 1,870 square feet, also adding new laboratory equipment and hiring additional employees, bringing the workforce at that time to 12 full-time employees and one part-time.
But after the federal government cut funding for life science research, the company’s staff dropped to seven employees, two contractors and two interns from Thomas College.
“The freezing and slashing of federal research grants in early 2026, across agencies like the National Institutes of Health and the National Science Foundation, has required our customers to retract their research spending, which has had a direct, negative impact on GTCA,” Greene told Mainebiz. “Our revenues have dropped significantly year-over-year, forcing to reduce our workforce and cut costs wherever possible.”
The collaboration with SoftMouse.Net could provide advantages both to GTCA and its customers, he said.
“This reduces the time and potential error inherent in manually entering results,” said Greene.
He added, “This collaboration also helps broaden the reach and strengthen the value propositions of working with both companies.”
With enough growth, GTCA would look to expand its team, he said.
“Our current laboratory footprint is sufficient to absorb a substantial amount of growth before further expansion would be needed.”

title: Gorham elects Maine’s first openly nonbinary state lawmaker
text:
Seven Siegel will become Maine’s first openly nonbinary state lawmaker after winning the House District 109 seat in Gorham on Election Day. The Democrat received 3,229 votes, overcoming Republican Diana Kushnar’s 2,101 votes.
Siegel, a 37-year-old computer science teacher at Kennebunk High School serving their second term on the Gorham Town Council, moved to Maine six years ago. They ran for Maine House on reining in costs of living, modernizing technology policy and ending tax relief for corporations.
“I don’t make a big deal of (being nonbinary), because the policies and the work are more important,” Siegel said. “But I also think an important part is representation and having people see that nonbinary people exist, and they’re good policymakers, too.”
Siegel said the adult they would have needed as a kid would not be afraid to make their identity known and work hard. Now, they want to be that adult.
“I’m excited to work for the people of Maine,” they said, adding that they have found their long-term home in Gorham after living in multiple states. They and their wife, Becky Wartell, have a 3-year-old daughter.
Siegel will stay on the Gorham Town Council until their term ends in November 2028 because they want to help update the town’s comprehensive plan next year.
The Democrat was endorsed by Equality Maine, an organization that advocates for pro-LGBTQ+ legislation and policy reform in Maine.
“Seven will join the Maine Legislature at a time when LGBTQ+ rights are under attack here in Maine and nationwide — and their victory is a milestone moment for our community,” said Heide Lester, interim executive director at Equality Maine. “Elected officials like Seven are not only critical in the ongoing fight to protect the rights of all Mainers; they also inspire others to run and win.”
While Siegel will be the first openly nonbinary member of the Maine Legislature, Ambureen Rana is a Democrat representing House District 21 in Bangor who identifies as genderqueer. Siegel said they already spoke with Rana after being elected Tuesday.
WABI reported in 2023 that about 32 LGBTQ+ people have served in the Maine Legislature in the past 38 years.
This story was originally published by the Maine Trust for Local News. Madeleine Kaptein can be reached at mkaptein@metln.org.

title: LIV Golf is winding down operations, lawyer says in bankruptcy hearing
text:
LIV Golf is winding down operations, lawyer says in bankruptcy hearing
LIV Golf is shuttering after five years that fractured the sport's landscape, announcing Thursday in bankruptcy court it plans to wind down operations instead of launching a new version, because it didn't have enough support.
“The debtors are not currently proceeding with the LIV 2.0 plan,” attorney Matthew Williams of Gibson Dunn said in a hearing in New Jersey. “Instead, the debtors are toggling to a value-maximizing wind-down in their business."
LIV Golf, which launched in June 2022 by offering nine-figure signing bonuses to lure top names away from the PGA Tour, lost funding from Saudi Arabia in April after spending more than $5 billion.
Related video above: Ready to tee off: WTGL set for inaugural season
It filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on Sept. 8 and thought it had a lifeline in BC Partners Credit, which pledged a $300 million investment to pivot to a more financially sustainable “LIV 2.0.” But players like Jon Rahm, Sergio Garcia, Tyrrell Hatton and Louis Oosthuizen, weren't interested.
“BC Partners Credit supported a transaction that aligned the interests of players and investors, offering a credible path toward building a sustainable future for LIV Golf," BC Partners said in a statement. “While there was great support for the league, we are disappointed that mutually acceptable terms could not be reached among the various stakeholders.”
Instead of planning for a new version for 2027, LIV enters a liquidation phase.
Rahm already agreed to forfeit all claims against LIV — said to be worth some $100 million — to get out of his contract. He is back to playing the European tour, with hopes there will be a path back to the PGA Tour. The tour currently has a one-year ban dating to players' last LIV appearance.
LIV Golf paid $15.6 million to retain seven of its executives, including $6.375 million to CEO Scott O’Neil. Those payments are not unusual for a company trying to emerge from bankruptcy. The question now is whether those payments can be voided since LIV isn't going forward.
LIV suffered two big setbacks, before and after filing for bankruptcy.
The Asian Tour, which received financial support from LIV for an International Series, decided in July to renew an alliance with the PGA Tour and the commercially known DP World Tour in Europe.
Then, European tour CEO Guy Kinnings last month said anyone signing up for LIV 2.0 need not apply for membership on the European tour, which put European players at risk of having no part in the Ryder Cup.
Kinnings said in an interview with The Scotsman newspaper earlier this week, "But we also have to protect the tour against an entity which spent, so we are told, over $7 billion, with one of their aims being to ‘destroy the DP World Tour.’"
But the biggest setback was in April, two weeks after the Masters and two months after the start of the Iran war. PIF changed its investment strategy and said it would no longer pay for LIV Golf after the 2026 season.
LIV was originally run by Greg Norman, who tried unsuccessfully to start a world tour in 1994 only to have it quashed by Arnold Palmer and the PGA Tour. Norman had Saudi money at his disposal, and promoted LIV as “Golf, but louder” with its blaring music, 54-hole shotgun starts and $25 million in prize funds — individual and team — at each event.
But it had no broadcast deal the first year, meaning it had to cover production costs. It got the CW Network in 2023, and eventually got Fox Sports to sign on in 2025.
The year began with Brooks Koepka getting out of his LIV deal with one year remaining, and the PGA Tour created a path — with financial penalties — to return. Patrick Reed chose not to extend his deal and now is poised to return to the PGA Tour next year through his performance in Europe.
Rahm had said on Tuesday he would be willing to pay the same price as Koepka, though it was unlikely that same deal would be offered.
LIV 2.0 was pushing player equity and prize money that was more than half the $20 million purses for individuals when it began in 2022. LIV’s final event was in August in Indianapolis, won by Michael La Sasso. He failed to get through the second stage of European tour Q-school last week.

title: How Medicare for All would work in practice
text:
How Medicare for All would work in practice
Senator-elect Troy Jackson says establishing Medicare for All is one of his top goals in Congress
How Medicare for All would work in practice
Senator-elect Troy Jackson says establishing Medicare for All is one of his top goals in Congress
Senator-elect Troy Jackson said establishing Medicare for All is one of his top goals in Congress, but how would such a program work, and how much support would it have in Congress?
Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced a Medicare for All bill in 2025 that could serve as a framework. If enacted, it would create a single-payer healthcare system in which the government pays for covered care for U.S. residents of all ages.
People would be automatically enrolled at birth or when they establish U.S. residency. Coverage would include primary and preventive care, emergency services, mental health treatment, vision, dental and prescription drugs.
The bill would eliminate copays and coinsurance for covered services, though people above a certain income threshold could pay up to $200 a year for prescription drugs.
Private insurance would still exist, but insurers could only sell coverage for services not included in the national health insurance program.
"We're going to get more spending, more inefficiency and lower quality care, rather than what Medicare for All advocates are promising," said Michael Cannon, a health policy expert at the Cato Institute.
Some policy experts like Cannon argue Medicare for All is not the right path to universal coverage, saying private options create competition that pushes providers to offer higher-quality care.
"It would leave us with less freedom, less control over our health care," Cannon said. "It would enrich inefficient healthcare providers. It would reduce the quality of care."
An analysis by the Congressional Budget Office also outlined potential concerns about single-payer systems, though it noted that such a system would reduce the number of people who are uninsured and could encourage people to seek more frequent preventative care since they wouldn't have gaps in coverage.
Including Sanders, the bill had 19 cosponsors, and 18 are expected to return to Washington, D.C., next year.
They would be joined by at least four incoming senators who have expressed support for Medicare for All, including Jackson. Supporters would need to recruit dozens of other lawmakers in both chambers to pass the proposal.

title: Rush Announces Sphere Las Vegas Residency for 2027
text:
Rush Announces Sphere Las Vegas Residency for 2027
Rush announced they will take their ongoing reunion to the next level with a series of concerts at Sphere Las Vegas starting in May.
The Canadian rockers will settle down in Sin City for the Elevate From the Norm residency beginning May 21. Five dates total are booked so far throughout the month with the last night currently set for May 30.
Travel packages will be available on site beginning Friday (Nov. 6) at 1 PM ET. An artist presale will begin Wednesday (Nov. 11) at 1pm ET and the regular public sale starts Friday (Nov. 13) at 1pm ET. All details are available at the band’s official website and you can see all of the current dates below.
“When I first heard of Sphere, I thought to myself, ‘Wow, what a shame that Rush is no longer touring, because this venue sounds tailor made for the kind of visual attitude with which we have always designed our shows,’" Geddy Lee said in a press release. "Normally we spend months designing the visual effects for our shows and this scenario seemed like the cherry on top of the ice cream for our design team. But life is nothing if not surprising and now, here we are, living and touring in the present tense and we are able to make that particular dream come true."
"We are presently working hard to expand our touring concepts and concoct some new madness to suit this incredible venue and musically perform the kind of show we’ve been doing in some of our “one off” cities. Meaning playing all of 2112 and all of Moving Pictures along with an array of other songs," he detailed. "We are so effin’ excited to make use of this incredible opportunity to please our fans both visually and viscerally- from wherever they might fly in from. Gonna be so much fun!!”
The Story Behind the Residency’s Name
Hardcore Rush fans will recognize the name of the group’s 2027 residency as a lyrical nod to the song “Vital Signs” from Moving Pictures. The track is a longtime fan favorite when it comes to the deeper cuts in the Rush catalog.
It’s been the subject of debate over the years (let’s face it, that describes nearly every Rush song), with fans wondering what Geddy Lee is singing near the end of “Vital Signs” because of how he pronounces “elevate.”
"That was a hoot to write. We wrote it in about 5 minutes in the studio,” Lee told The Plain Dealer during a 2019 interview. “We just put it together quickly and had a lot of fun doing it. It's still fun to play. It's the quirkier side of Rush's sound, and I think there's always a need for that, to give your sound diversity."
READ MORE: What are the 'Big 4' of Rush Albums?
It Wasn't Easy Going Back to Rush
Many months removed now from the beginnings of the Fifty Something tour, which launched in June, the band -- with drummer Anika Nilles and keyboardist Loren Gold -- have settled into a groove which feels very authentic to the spirit of the Rush that fans have loved for so many years.
But as Lee shared during an interview before the tour hit the road, he and guitarist Alex Lifeson thought long and hard before they were able to find peace and move forward with the idea of bringing Rush back without the late Neil Peart, who passed away in 2020.
"We were twisting ourselves into a pretzel to try to avoid using the name that we have had for fifty years, and even before Neil came," he explained. "It just seems silly to go on as 'Lee and Lifeson Present The Music Of..."
"Let’s cut to the chase, shall we? Let’s just be who we are and have been for over fifty years.”
READ MORE: How Would Neil Peart Feel About the Rush Reunion?
The Fifty Something trek is in Hollywood, Florida tonight (Nov. 5) for the first of two shows at Seminole Hard Rock Live.
The group will take things overseas in the new year for a run of international concerts that will wrap up April 10 in Helsinki, Finland.
The end of that leg, on paper, works out nicely to give Lee and Lifeson a good break before the Sphere residency launches in late May.

title: Oklahoma man pleads guilty to social media threats to kill Trump
text:
Oklahoma man pleads guilty to social media threats to kill Trump
An Oklahoma man has pleaded guilty to threatening on social media to kill President Donald Trump, according to officials.
Howard Gimmey, 47, admitted to posting a message on social media on May 5 that said, "I'm going to kill the president," according to a news release from the U.S. Department of Justice.
On Oct. 6, a federal grand jury charged Gimmey with communicating a threat in interstate commerce. Gimmey could face up to five years in a federal prison and up to a $250,000 fine.
"This case is part of the nationwide National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 initiative, which is a White House directed, interagency effort to integrate federal, state, and local partners in protecting First Amendment rights while targeting individuals and organizations engaged in political violence," the DOJ news release said.
The initiative was a directive started by Trump in 2025 to stop domestic terrorism and organized political violence.

title: Letter: Maine needs fair trade agreements with Canada
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
Here’s something you don’t often hear in letters like this: Canada has not always played fair with Maine.
Ottawa protects its dairy farmers with over-quota tariffs above 200%. Canadian governments have also backed their lobster industry at every link in the chain, which is a big part of why so much of Maine’s catch is processed across the border. Those are real grievances.
But a 50% tariff on $20 billion of Canadian goods, answered by Canadian tariffs in return, doesn’t fix any of that. It just sends the bill to Maine.
No state is more tied to Canada than ours. In 2024, Canada supplied about 70% of Maine’s imports and bought roughly $1.3 billion of our exports.
I owned and ran the Union River Lobster Pot, and I served in the Maine Senate. Small-business owners can plan around a bad season or a jump in costs. What they can’t plan around is a rulebook that changes every few weeks.
I want more lobster processed in Maine. I want Canada to honor the dairy access it agreed to. Those goals are worth fighting for at the negotiating table with real enforcement. They aren’t won by blanket tariffs that tax Maine families and small businesses for problems they didn’t create.
Sen. Susan Collins has urged both governments to return to the table and reach a fair agreement. She’s right, and our delegation should keep pushing for the remainder of this Congress and in the next.
Maine businesses are ready to invest, grow and compete. Give them rules they can plan around.
Brian Langley
Ellsworth

title: Is a 90-day blackout coming? What the U.S. military’s new readiness initiative actually means
text:
JACKSON, Tenn. (WBBJ/Gray News) — Viral doomsday posts on social media are gaining traction, claiming the nation will soon face a 90-day blackout.
The rumor that the U.S. released a doomsday plan for a 90-day blackout began circulating after U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth unveiled a long-term strategic plan on Sept. 30.
Experts said, however, that people have been misinterpreting the FORTRESS America initiative in the strategic plan, which is essentially a plan to be prepared for modern-day attacks.
The initiative is not an announcement of an active blackout, power cut or impending attack. Rather, it is a prepared plan to ensure the U.S. military will have the ability to “fight and win under any circumstances,” including a cyberattack.
“We know that more nations are engaging in cyber attacks,” Sean Evans, chair and professor of political science at Union University, said. “We’re concerned about sabotage, so the whole idea is that if something happens that our military will be prepared. They’ll have a 90-day supply of energy. They’ll have back up ammunition.”
The FORTRESS America initiative is organized around five pillars: energy independence, supply-chain and defense-industrial base resilience, a strategic defense reserve, installation hardening and cyber resilience, and resilience in space and spectrum.
Under this initiative, every military department and defense agency will have the ability to operate independently for at least 90 days. This includes access to water, electricity, fuel and communications.

title: California Gov. Newsom says he will change all 548 death sentences in state to life without parole
text:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — California Gov. Gavin Newsom said Thursday that he’ll change more than 500 death sentences in the state to life in prison without the possibility of parole, though the state Supreme Court will have the final say in hundreds of those cases.
“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” Newsom said in a public letter.
Newsom’s decision comes as he prepares to leave office after eight years and considers a run for president. The Democrat, who’s long been opposed to the death penalty, placed a moratorium on executions in California in 2019.
His latest move came after he realized “the limits of what government can justly accomplish,” he said.
Newsom moved to grant clemency to 548 people currently sentenced to death in California, of whom 529 are men and 19 are women, according to numbers provided by his office.
The state constitution requires the California Supreme Court’s approval to grant clemency to anyone convicted of a felony more than once, which means the court would have to approve 382 of those commutations, or roughly 70%, according to Newsom’s office.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Newsom’s action represents the largest mass clemency in American history. If they are all approved, it would reduce the U.S. death row population by nearly 30%, the center said.
California voters upheld the death penalty
Americans have long been divided over the death penalty. Nearly half of U.S. states have banned capital punishment outright, but executions are still carried out routinely around the country. On Thursday alone, Florida, Alabama and Indiana were scheduled to perform lethal injections.
Californians voted to uphold the death penalty in 2012 and 2016 ballot measures. No one has been executed in the state since 2006 and California has the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.
Among the most notorious convicted killers on California’s death row are Richard Allen Davis, who kidnapped and murdered 12-year-old Polly Klaas in 1993, and Randy Kraft, the so-called “Scorecard Killer” who kept a list of his 16 victims in the 1970s and ’80s. Other prominent killers, including Scott Peterson and the Manson family members, received death sentences that were later commuted to life in prison.
Jess Nichol, Klaas’ sister, said she previously believed Davis deserved the death penalty, but her views evolved.
“The system tells survivors that execution matters to our healing,” Nichol said in a statement. “It doesn’t. It’s a distraction from what we actually need.”
Newsom said the decision was among the most difficult choices of his career because it will surface painful memories for crime victims’ families.
“As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution,” Newsom wrote.
The American Civil Liberties Union, which has said the implementation of the death penalty reflects racial bias, applauded the announcement.
“These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long,” Executive Director Anthony Romero said in a statement.
The ACLU is involved in an ongoing legal challenge to California’s death penalty statute, alleging it is racially discriminatory and unconstitutional.
Victims’ groups and prosecutors decry the decision
Patricia Wenskunas, founder of the California advocacy nonprofit Crime Survivors, which opposed the abolition of the death penalty, criticized Newsom’s decision.
“My heart hurts for every one of the victims and every one of their family members,” she said, calling the decision “offensive” and “outrageous.”
Steve Herr, whose son Sam Herr was murdered along with his friend Julie Kibuishi by Daniel Wozniak in 2010, said he was “absolutely disgusted” by the governor’s decision. He said the death of his son’s killer would have meant closure.
“When somebody commits such a heinous crime, they do not deserve to live,” Herr said. “To hear what Newsom just did … he’s just an outright coward.”
The California District Attorneys Association condemned the decision. Last month, the group sent a letter to Newsom expressing “grave concerns” about him considering the move and warning that such a sweeping action would inflict additional pain on victims’ relatives.
“With the stroke of a pen, Governor Newsom has disregarded the decisions of hundreds of jurors and judges, and the anguish of families who lost loved ones to the worst crimes imaginable,” CDAA President Jeannine M. Pacioni said in a statement. “The victims were never given a commutation. Their families were never given a choice. They deserve far better than this.”
San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow called the move a “sickening abuse of power.”
Dow referenced Rachel Newhouse and Aundria Crawford, two women who were kidnapped, raped and murdered by Rex Allan Krebs in 1999, and Kesha Gurke, a 19-month-old girl tortured and murdered by Michael Whisenhunt in 1995.
“San Luis Obispo County juries sentenced both men to death. A unanimous California Supreme Court affirmed both judgments. Their families have waited decades for the State of California to keep its word. Today, the Governor broke it,” Dow said.
Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer also condemned the decision, calling it “mercy for the wolves and while inflicting the ultimate act of cruelty on the sheep.”
Other governors have taken similar actions
Newsom has said in the past that it is wrong for the government to kill its citizens and that capital punishment in practice has discriminated against mentally ill people and people of color.
Other governors have granted broad clemency to all death row prisoners in their states, including Gov. Kate Brown in Oregon in 2022 and Gov. Jared Polis in Colorado in 2020. Both are Democrats.
In 2024, President Joe Biden also granted clemency to 37 out of 40 federal prisoners sentenced to death.
Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who will take over from Newsom in January, has said he will extend the state’s moratorium on the death penalty.
___
Ding and Weber reported from Los Angeles.

title: The Food Detective: Donut French Toast with Breakfast Sausage
The 2028 election begins as both parties navigate midterm fallout
text:
WASHINGTON — The final midterm votes are still being counted, but make no mistake: The next election season has already begun.
Presidential prospects in both parties jockeyed for position Wednesday, even as the political world was digesting the impact of the Democratic wave that crashed over American politics the night before. Democrats celebrated their party’s stunning success — and began promoting themselves — while dejected Republicans scrambled to distance themselves from President Donald Trump’s wreckage.
The Republican with the most at stake was likely Vice President JD Vance, who entered Tuesday night as the GOP’s leading presidential prospect and woke up Wednesday far more vulnerable — like any Republican who is close to Trump.
“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance said in a morning postmortem post on X. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.”
He added, “And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”
Vance has struggled to square his history of opposing foreign intervention with his defense of Trump’s war. He has said publicly that the conflict was necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon, but his private skepticism has been widely reported.
Trump did not dispute Vance’s assessment, even as he defended the war. But he also made no effort to help Vance’s potential prospects, telling reporters, “Maybe he won’t run.” Vance had said he would make a decision after the election.
Voters still processing an extraordinary midterm campaign may not welcome an immediate pivot to 2028. But for would-be candidates, there is real urgency to move toward a White House bid in what is expected to be a wide-open contest in both parties.
Possible 2028 contenders have been making moves
The first presidential primary votes will be cast in little more than a year. And some prospects, including Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, have already had preliminary conversations with potential presidential campaign staff.
Former vice president and 2024 Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris told The Associated Press on Wednesday that she was elated to see Democrats’ commanding performance — particularly across the South — and wants to play a role, regardless of whether she decides to run again.
“I believe I have a responsibility to contribute to the direction of the party, in particular around lifting up voices and issues that I have an experience with,” she said. “Whether I’m in office or not, that’s the role I feel compelled to play.”
Rahm Emanuel, who has spent much of the past year laying the groundwork for a potential presidential campaign, demurred when asked about his future plans.
“Don’t worry about the next election,” he said in an interview. “There’s a time and a season. And right now is the governing time.”
The Democrats, in particular, have a deep bench of high-profile leaders who strengthened their political brands Tuesday.
Blue-state governors like Maryland’s Wes Moore and Illinois’ JB Pritzker both scored decisive reelection wins and offered sweepy victory speeches. California’s outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom had worked to boost Democratic candidates all over, especially in the South. He also had a personal role in Democrats winning the House majority, having led Proposition 50, California’s response to the Texas Republican mid-decade gerrymander.
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro arguably had the most impressive performance with a commanding win in one of the nation’s most important swing states, while also helping his party win control of the state Legislature and flipping four congressional seats.
Shapiro faced immediate questions about his presidential ambitions during a round of interviews Wednesday morning on national television.
“The numbers were so big, I was wondering if you want to take this opportunity … to say, ‘You know what, I’m in for 2028.’ Or do you want to talk about something else?” CBS anchor Gayle King asked.
“I want to answer all your other questions, Gayle,” Shapiro laughed, before addressing his party’s future. “People want fundamental change, real reform. More importantly, they want their leaders to get stuff done, they want real results.”
And as the Democratic governors speak up, a fresh wave of Democrats will take the Senate majority, perhaps elevating the likes of Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff or even Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed from Michigan.
Progressives seized on El-Sayed’s victory in the Midwest as they quietly discussed who might take the progressive mantle from Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who at age 85 has ruled out another presidential bid. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez remains the dominant name in that conversation, but at 37, it’s unclear if she’ll take that step.
“This changes the 2028 presidential race,” Adam Green, co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, said of El-Sayed’s win. “A bold anti-establishment economic fighter can win battleground states. Period.”
GOP’s deep midterm losses may give some Republican hopefuls an opening
On the Republican side, the blowout could provide an opening to others in the party who had been wary about crossing Trump by beginning the process of moving on from his time at the helm.
Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich said the quiet part out loud in assessing Vance’s political strength.
“If the administration had won a big victory, Vice President JD Vance would have had an enormous argument to be the inevitable nominee,” Gingrich wrote on X. “Now … a good bit of the luster has come off the bloom.”
Gingrich listed a half dozen other Republicans who could compete with Vance: “The scale of the Republican defeat is so great that it makes the race for the GOP presidential nomination wide open.”
Former Trump rival Ron DeSantis, the outgoing Republican governor of Florida, was unsparing Wednesday in describing the scope of GOP losses, calling it “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country.” He held up his state, which elected Republicans to the governor’s office and U.S. Senate, as an exception and an example of “how you can deliver big results.”
Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, who invested significant time and resources trying to help Republicans who ended up losing, had already been openly weighing another White House run.
Trump’s fiercest critics were also vindicated. They include New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie, who has been mulling his own repeat bid.
Emboldened by the midterm results, however, the Democratic field is eager to move forward.
New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker, a former presidential candidate who begins the 2028 cycle with more than $20 million in his federal campaign account, offered an inspirational victory speech that left little doubt about his intentions.
“We have ended an election, but this has got to be the start of a movement,” Booker said. “America, tonight is the start of our comeback, baby.”
Story by Steve Peoples and Jill Colvin. Associated Press writers Bill Barrow, Steven Sloan and Linley Sanders contributed to this report.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: Near Record Warmth Thursday, Fog Tonight, and More Rain Heading Into the Weekend
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Wednesday. We finally managed to get a bit of a break from the wet weather today, following the widespread rainfall we’ve seen across the region over the last couple of days. Temperatures also managed to warm up considerably today, with many locations reaching the 50s and even lower 60s. The warmer temperatures are expected to stick around for the next couple of days, with Thursday and Friday potentially bringing near record warmth to the region. Before we get there, however, we’ll have to contend with some fog developing overnight tonight, which could make for some difficult travel conditions early tomorrow morning. More rain is also expected heading into the upcoming weekend, with the potential for additional drought relief across the region.
Temperatures across the region today were certainly a welcome change compared to the cooler weather we’ve experienced recently. Caribou managed to reach 55 degrees this afternoon, while Houlton climbed to 57 degrees. Some of our western and southern locations were even warmer, with Clayton Lake reaching 61 degrees and Millinocket topping out at 63 degrees. We also saw some impressive temperatures further south, with Bangor reaching 69 degrees and Augusta making it all the way to 74 degrees. The warmer air that’s been working its way into the region is expected to stick around through the end of the work week, with temperatures tomorrow expected to climb even higher.
Temperatures overnight tonight aren’t expected to cool off nearly as much as we’ve become accustomed to over the last several weeks. With plenty of moisture remaining in the atmosphere from our recent rainfall, along with mostly cloudy skies and light winds, temperatures should have no problem remaining in the mid 40s to lower 50s for most locations. Caribou and Presque Isle are both expected to see low temperatures around 50 degrees, while Houlton looks to fall back to around 46 degrees. For comparison, the average low temperature in Caribou for this time of year is around 30 degrees, meaning we’re looking at overnight temperatures running nearly 20 degrees above average.
One of my bigger concerns heading into tomorrow morning will be the potential for fog developing across the region overnight tonight. The combination of all the moisture we’ve received over the last couple of days, along with light winds and relatively mild temperatures, should provide favorable conditions for fog development. The latest high-resolution model guidance suggests that fog could become fairly widespread across portions of Aroostook County by the early morning hours of Thursday.
The National Weather Service in Caribou has issued a Dense Fog Advisory for northern portions of Aroostook County, which remains in effect until 8 AM Thursday. Some of the thickest fog is expected across the higher terrain, where visibility could be reduced to a quarter mile or less at times. If you’re going to be heading out early tomorrow morning, I would recommend giving yourself a little extra time to get where you’re going, especially if your travels take you through some of our higher elevations. Fog should gradually improve as we work our way through the morning hours.
Once we get through the morning fog, we’re looking at another unusually warm day across the region Thursday. I don’t expect a tremendous amount of sunshine during the day, with mostly cloudy skies expected for many locations. Despite the cloud coverage, southerly winds will continue to introduce warmer air into the region, allowing temperatures to climb into the lower to mid 60s for most towns. High temperatures are expected to reach around 64 degrees in Caribou and Presque Isle, while Houlton could climb to 66 degrees. Some of our western locations, including Allagash and Clayton Lake, could also reach the mid 60s.
To put those temperatures into perspective, the average high temperature in Caribou for this time of year is only around 45 degrees. That puts us nearly 20 degrees above average, and potentially close to some daily record high temperatures. I think the biggest factor in determining just how warm we get tomorrow will be the amount of cloud coverage we see. If we manage to see some breaks of sunshine during the day, I wouldn’t be surprised to see a few locations climb a little higher than currently forecast. We are also watching for another opportunity for rain showers Thursday afternoon, particularly across northern and western portions of Aroostook County. I don’t expect everyone to see rain, but scattered showers will become increasingly possible as we work our way through the afternoon and evening hours. Rain chances look a bit lower the further south you travel, with the best opportunity for showers remaining across the northern half of the region.
For more details on tomorrow’s unusually warm temperatures, the fog potential overnight tonight, and our increasing rainfall chances heading into the upcoming weekend, make sure to check out my First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening!

title: 8 more Maine towns adopt data center bans in lopsided elections
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Voters in at least eight Maine towns approved bans on new data centers Tuesday, including a permanent ban in one and temporary bans in seven.
The lopsided local votes come months after Gov. Janet Mills vetoed a statewide moratorium. They also come weeks before a Legislature with larger Democratic majorities convenes under Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree, a Democrat who has said she would sign a ban.
North Berwick went furthest, with 78% of voters approving a permanent ban on data center development. The other towns passed 180-day bans meant to give them time to weigh more comprehensive regulation.
Support ranged from 70% in Freedom to nearly 82% in Wells. More than 76% backed moratoriums in Eliot and Peru, according to WMTW, and almost 78% did in Brownfield.
The wave of local bans is the latest example of data center backlash that’s risen nationally. Stories about massive data centers driving up the costs of electricity and water elsewhere sparked broad concern among voters.
In most towns, data center moratoriums have been proposed preemptively, often in small towns that are unlikely to ever see large developments. Wiscasset is an exception. The town foiled an attempt to build a data center there in 2025, and two-thirds of voters there supported the moratorium.
In Sabattus, the proposal to ban data centers for 180 days also passed with support from two-thirds of voters. But many residents seemed only mildly interested in the topic outside the polls Tuesday.
“I’ve just been watching it through other towns … with the water and all that stuff,” Republican voter Jeff Plourde, 55, said outside Sabattus’ polling place Tuesday afternoon. “We don’t need it around here.”
Kim Reny, 61, said she voted against the ban, saying she thought data centers were “a good idea.”
Though data centers are broadly unpopular, several voters said they had not heard much discussion of the issue in town. Some voters told The Maine Monitor on Tuesday morning that they were not aware the town would be voting on the issue until they arrived at the polls.
The opposition crosses party lines. The Legislature passed what would have been a first-in-the-nation moratorium on data center projects in April. Mills vetoed that bill to save a data center project in Jay, which later fell through.
Wary of public backlash, developers are sometimes quiet about their plans to build centers until they’re well underway. In Jay, for example, local officials learned of the plan to build one in town only after reporting by the Bangor Daily News.
Environmental groups are already working on bills to regulate data centers statewide in the next legislative session, which begins in December.

title: Bar Harbor finds an ally off MDI in its push for a local option tax
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bar Harbor may have found some help in its quest for a local option tax, which can come in many forms, but which would could allow towns and cities to opt in to specific types of additional taxes (maybe on retail or lodging or something else) and a portion of that additional tax would go back to the local community where it was generated.
Bar Harbor, hoping to ease some of its infrastructure woes and ease the burden of residential property owners, has been discussing the possibility for years, often cyclically advocating for the possibility.
Last week Ellsworth City Manager Charlie Pearce went before the League of Towns and advocated for the local option sales tax as well. This time, though, it was for his city—and others who might need it.
The Bar Harbor Town Council recently reiterated its support for the town to lobby for this. It also has come up during its Sustainable Tourism Task Force discussions as a recommendation. One was also proposed by state Rep. Gary Friedmann in the Legislature. It did not go forward.
No local option tax initiatives have passed the Maine State Legislature, though different legislators have tried for decades. They’ve come in many forms with many formulas, sharing different percentages with the state, with different proposed requirements.
“Every time it comes up, the majority in the room is in favor of it,” Tremont Town Manager Jesse Dunbar told Pearce. “It does seem like it’s always when it gets to Augusta, that’s when it gets, you know, killed.”
Realtors, Dunbar said, have often been against it because of the potential impacts to short-term rental owners (if the tax was a local lodging tax on short-term rentals).
Pearce’s framing of growth quickly turned to how pressure impacts Mount Desert Island communities and its housing and traffic and tourism changes.
For Pearce, the problem is that service centers like Ellsworth and Bar Harbor bear a disproportionate infrastructure cost from people outside their communities. Ellsworth, which has a population of roughly 9,000 serves the regional population of roughly 80,000. Bar Harbor has a year-round population of approximately 5,200 and hosts many thousands of visitors each year, thanks to the popularity of Acadia National Park.
The financial impact to those towns, Pearce argued, could be decreased if they could find a way to keep some of the millions sent to the state that industries like lodging and retail generate. The state taxes those industries.
If towns have to raise taxes to fund services, Pearce said, then that creates frustration in some residents. However, all for-profit businesses do pay property taxes just as residential property owners do.
“How do we deal with those growth pressures?” he asked rhetorically at the beginning of his discussion.
He advocated for his city and service centers like it, saying that Ellsworth has thousands of people coming to work — or traveling through to work every day and there is no off season.
Last year, he said, Ellsworth had a net negative for full-time government employees. However, the budget still increased 6-7% on the municipal side.
“It’s a $600,000 increase to public safety, that’s off the top, no additional police or firefighters, it’s just 600 grand, another $400,000 employee benefits across the board, a good bulk of which goes to public safety pieces,” he explained.
Pearce continued, “Our finance director just noted, when you look at public safety, schools, and public works, and the infrastructure piece, you’re at like 90% of the government side of the thing, so there’s this kind of like dual dynamic with increased taxes too, where those are the biggest drivers and growing, but it’s like, hey, cut the economic development initiative, cut the $14,000 branding piece that’s, you know, so we can put up a welcome to Ellsworth sign, which we don’t have in Ellsworth right now.”
Those types of cuts, he said, don’t help citizens, but their taxes still increase.
“So, for me looking long term with our finance director, it’s like ‘OK, these are some pretty substantial costs. What’s going on here? And how do you dig into kind of like we’re seeing a lot of growth?’”
In the early 2000s, there were studies on service center economies—like Ellsworth’s—that he received from Twila Fisher.
“It has all the recommendations we’re still talking about now, local option tax, the inequitable service center aspect, the infrastructure demand,” he said.
Being a service center increases property taxes “and that manifests itself in really angry and aggressive town meetings, especially in service centers,” he told the others.
Retail tax revenue generated by stores in Ellsworth — much like Bar Harbor and all other towns — goes to the state. However, Ellsworth and Bar Harbor don’t receive much of that state money coming back to their communities to help lower the property tax burdens on its citizens.
“They ain’t sending that money back,” Pearce said. “Yes, we’re getting revenue sharing…. Yes, we’re getting school reimbursements, but a lot of that’s passed through money, especially with some of the infrastructure pieces.”
The Hilton Home2 Suites, he said, adds tens of thousands of dollars to Ellsworth’s tax base every year.
That, he asked “is a net positive from the infrastructure investment, right?”
The state receives 9% in lodging off every single stay at the Hilton Home2 Suites.
“We ain’t getting that,” he said. “We just passed three retail cannabis stores in Ellsworth. The state’s going to get 14% of the gross on that, essentially.”
The legal fees for licensing that Ellsworth has to pay for those stores, he said, is roughly $10,000.
He hoped Maine’s incoming new governor, Hannah Pingree, could be invited to meet with the League of Towns.
Pearce also focused on Bar Harbor’s moratorium on hotels. Ellsworth has one on RV parks, which means that those properties can’t be built to those uses currently.
“But you can kind of see this, like, shoot, if you’re getting 9% on the gross in Bar Harbor, and there’s a line item in your budget, when you add that hotel, and you can say, hey, I reduced your property — This tourism reduced your property taxes by X. You know, it makes it a lot more palatable to your residents,” Pearce said. “Like, what the value of having a tourism economy is locally to your property taxes, to your school systems, to your infrastructure. But when it’s ‘you know, hey, we’re going to add 300 more people here and we get, like, $25,000, $30,000 a year on the base of the property valuation.’“
This story was originally published by The Bar Harbor Story. To receive regular coverage from the Bar Harbor Story, sign up for a free subscription here.

title: Russell Brand Guilty of Rape and Sexual Assault
text:
Russell Brand Found Guilty of Rape and Sexual Assault
Actor and comedian Russell Brand has been found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, following a trial in London that lasted four weeks. Brand was found not guilty of two separate rape charges, as well as one count of attempted indecent assault.
Brand, once one of the most popular comedians in England and then a film star around the world in projects like Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him to the Greek, cultivated a comic persona as a wild (and often controversial) provocateur. In recent years, he had reinvented himself as a conservative YouTuber and podcaster.
In 2023, Channel 4 aired the documentary Russell Brand: In Plain Sight detailing allegations of Brand’s mistreatment of women. The police launched an investigation shortly thereafter, which eventually led to this trial and conviction.
READ MORE: The 10 Worst Comedies of the Last 10 Years
London’s Metropolitan Police said their detectives “gathered evidence from more than 100 witnesses and reviewed thousands of documents as part of the investigation” and “praised the women who reported Brand for their courage, resilience and determination, while encouraging any other potential victims who have not yet spoken to police to come forward.”
“Brand's offending,” they added “was between 2004 and 2009 and included one rape and three sexual assaults committed against four women. The offences took place in different locations, including a radio station, the set of a DVD recording and Brand's home address.” Brand had insisted on his innocence throughout the trial.
Brand will be sentenced on Monday, November 9. According to Variety, “in the U.K., a rape conviction can result in up to 19 years in prison and potentially even a life sentence, depending on the seriousness of the offense. The maximum sentence for sexual assault is 10 years.”

title: Trump signs proclamation he says will prevent future changes to the Oval Office and Cabinet Room
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday signed a proclamation that he said will prevent future changes to the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as he has redesigned them.
“We’re making it a national monument and it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
Trump’s proclamation signing comes two days after voters, dissatisfied with his economic policies, threw dozens of Republicans out of office, delivering control of Congress to Democrats.
It’s also the third day this week in which the president, a real estate mogul, delivered remarks fixated on his pet projects in Washington, D.C., including an opulent ballroom and the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
Since returning to the White House, Trump has overseen numerous design changes to various rooms, including the Oval Office, where he has filled the wall space with portraits, a copy of the Declaration of Independence and numerous golden accents.

title: Referendum vote for potential jail outside Bangor too close to call
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - There is still a razor-thin margin Wednesday night in Penobscot County, where voters are still waiting on the final outcome of Question One.
The referendum asks whether county commissioners can search outside of Bangor for a new potential jail site.
Right now, “yes” leads by just 149 votes—holding roughly 50-point-one percent to 49-point-nine percent.
Results from 10 municipalities are still outstanding.
County officials say towns have three days to submit their totals, but they hope to have a clearer picture by tomorrow or Friday.
Question One only authorizes a site search—any future plans to actually build a new jail would require another vote.
