title: Noble School District won’t pay for a new boiler. Lebanon is threatening legal action.
text:
NORTH BERWICK — Lebanon officials are weighing next steps with legal counsel after the Noble School District board voted Thursday night to initiate the closure of a partially shuttered elementary school where it had decided not to fund a replacement boiler.
Town officials hired an attorney after the school board’s Oct. 15 meeting, when the district also considered a winterization process for Lebanon Elementary School, specifically its water system.
The Select Board decided at an emergency meeting Saturday to pursue a cease-and-desist order with its attorney that would urge Maine School Administrative District 60 to not begin the winterization.
The school board voted 7-2 Thursday to begin closing the school, but Lebanon officials were granted a two-week delay on the winterization process to gather more information about the potential impacts it could have on the building. It’ll also give the town more time to decide whether it should fight to keep the building open.
Members of the Select Board have said they’re concerned that winterizing could cause costly or irrevocable damage to the 73-year-old school, such as burst pipes or mold, and that draining all water from the facility could create a significant fire hazard. With no heating source, and the risk of damage, it could result in the building being condemned without voter input, town officials have said.
Under state law, voters must approve a closed school’s use if it’s shuttered for lack of use.
“There’s so many things, and if they just mess up on one thing, that building will be ruined,” Select Board member Theresa Hartford said Saturday, adding that reopening the building if something goes wrong in freezing temperatures could be nearly impossible.
The district has been considering the future of the school for years and is just over a year into a drastic reorganization plan, which included ending classes at Lebanon Elementary. In the interim, roughly 135 children have been bused to other schools in the district, often with hourlong commutes.
The building has been used, however, for some after-school activities and adult education classes. That changed a few weeks ago, after the aging boiler failed.
Voters had decided in 2021 not to approve a series of MSAD 60 renovations that would have expanded nearby Hanson Elementary to make room for the students from Lebanon Elementary, which would have been demolished.
But that plan failed and no major upgrades were made. While Lebanon Elementary held students for a few more years, the building continued to age and the possibility of permanent closure became more likely.
The district’s attorney, Aga Dixon of Drummond Woodsum, said Thursday that when a school closes, the process is driven by state law. The initial decision is up to a vote by the school board, but needs to be approved by voters.
When a vote is eventually brought to residents — which Dixon said could happen as soon as June — they could decide not to approve its closure. In that case, the cost of keeping it open would fall solely on the town.
If voters support the closure, the district would retain the building and would have several options, Dixon said.
It could keep the building open under the Select Board’s control, lease it for temporary use to a third party for four years or transfer it to the town of Lebanon — which would incur any leftover debts on the facility. The building could also be sold or demolished.

title: Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 more years in prison
text:
Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 more years in prison
A Hong Kong court sentenced prominent activist Joshua Wong to 10 more years in prison Thursday under a Beijing-imposed national security law, in a case that critics say underscores the crackdown on the city’s once-thriving pro-democracy movement.
Wong, 30, first led student protests as a teenager and engaged in international advocacy efforts for Hong Kong's democracy movement. He was already serving a four-year, eight-month prison term after pleading guilty in the city's biggest national security case, and had been due to be freed in January.
But he was further charged in 2025 with conspiracy to collude with foreign forces to endanger national security, an offense under the security law imposed by Beijing in 2020.
Related video: Former Northern Arizona University fraternity leader sentenced in student’s hazing death
Judge William Tam said Wong and fellow activist Nathan Law colluded with foreign officials and other foreign actors and sought measures against China and Hong Kong.
The judge pointed to the U.S. revocation of the city’s preferential treatment as a special administrative region and U.S. sanctions imposed on Chinese and Hong Kong officials, saying these were the kinds of sanctions or hostile measures Wong and Law had called for.
“The punishment must fit the gravity of the crime committed,” Tam wrote. “It is also necessary for this court to express the community’s abhorrence of the defendant’s scheme and acts together with others to collude with foreign forces.”
Wong, who appeared at the High Court in a dark shirt and dark-framed glasses, appeared calm and nodded to his supporters and pro-democracy activists in the public gallery.
The United States strongly condemned the sentencing and called for Wong's immediate release.
The U.S. Consulate in Hong Kong said in a statement that Wong has been “unjustly imprisoned” since late 2020, showing that “Beijing will go to extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms in Hong Kong.”
Wong pleaded guilty to the offense earlier this year. Tam said he considered a 13-year prison sentence as a starting point but reduced it because of Wong’s guilty plea and mitigation.
Tam said Wong would serve the remaining two months of the sentence for his first national security conviction concurrently with the new sentence.
Wong looked calm during the sentencing
Wong appeared serious but calm as the judge read out his sentencing remarks. Before leaving the courtroom, his supporters waved to him. “Thank you all,” he said to them in Cantonese.
Tiffany Chin, a former member of the now-disbanded Scholarism movement once led by Wong, was in tears after the sentence was delivered.
With limited seating available, some took turns entering the courtroom. Dozens had lined up outside the court to secure a seat in the public gallery, some as early as Tuesday. One resident, ET Wong, said Wong walked a difficult path for Hong Kong’s future, human rights and the student movement. “He should not have spent a single day in wrongful imprisonment,” she said.
In a statement written in prison, Wong said he thought he was acting within the law and was not directly advocating for sanctions when he reposted others' social media posts or called on foreign companies to consider ceasing business with the Hong Kong police. He said he later realized his judgment was wrong.
He said during his nearly six years in prison, he enrolled in university courses and read many books. He said he devoted himself to becoming a better person, and he hoped he would regard the experience as having helped forge his character when he looks back one day.
Wong's convictions seen as discouraging dissent
Hong Kong once had a freewheeling civil society. But after huge anti-government protests rocked the city in 2019, authorities reduced public choice in elections and arrested many leading activists. Some news outlets known for reporting critical of the government shut down and dozens of civil society groups dissolved.
Observers say Wong's sentencing shows authorities' determination to keep prominent activists in prison for as long as possible.
Eric Lai, a research fellow at the Georgetown Center for Asian Law, said the national security law charges “can be repeatedly weaponized to keep a specific political prisoner in jail, if the government deems necessary.”
Beijing views Wong as an anti-China figure supporting Hong Kong independence, a stance that crosses its red line. Hong Kong authorities argue the security law is crucial for the city’s stability following the 2019 protests, maintaining that the city's law enforcement actions were evidence-based.
Prosecution highlights Wong’s lobbying and advocacy efforts
The prosecution alleged that Wong and Law had agreed in or around 2016 to lobby internationally to achieve their goal of democratic self-determination.
After the security law was enacted, Law, who left for the U.K., and others advanced their work abroad by meeting foreign politicians and launching petition drives, it said. Wong supported the effort from Hong Kong through foreign media outlets and social media to draw international attention and bolster the request for sanctions, a blockade or other hostile measures against China and Hong Kong, it said.
Wong's lawyer Derek Chan had urged the court to impose a sentence that would give his client some hope, adding that Wong wishes to take care of his parents after his release.
Chinese and Hong Kong authorities defend the ruling
Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing that Wong had pleaded guilty in the face of overwhelming facts and evidence and that the central government supports Hong Kong in upholding national security.
He said “relevant parties” should stop making irresponsible remarks about the city's judicial proceedings and stop interfering in its judiciary.
Hong Kong leader John Lee said Wong, Law and their accomplices are among the “primary culprits responsible for undermining Hong Kong’s prosperity and stability.”
Steve Li, chief superintendent of the police’s national security department, welcomed the court's ruling and said he hoped Wong would reflect on his wrongdoing.
To his supporters, Wong is a political star representing a younger generation born in the final years of Hong Kong's British colonial rule before the city's return to China in 1997.
Though he's held behind bars, Wong's influence appears to have remained a concern for the pro-Beijing camp.
In September, a pro-Beijing newspaper report criticized a 2017 documentary about Wong on Netflix for “beautifying” his crimes. The city’s security bureau told local media the government was taking follow-up action.
The documentary then topped Netflix’s most-watched list in Hong Kong.

title: These toys are worth buying for your kids, according to Good Housekeeping experts and kid testers
text:
Good Housekeeping reveals 2026 Toy Award winners kids could not stop playing with
Kids and experts tested 160 toys for safety, at-home feedback and real-world play.
Good Housekeeping reveals 2026 Toy Award winners kids could not stop playing with
Kids and experts tested 160 toys for safety, at-home feedback and real-world play.
Hundreds of new toys hit shelves each year, but which ones are actually worth bringing home?
Good Housekeeping has revealed the winners of the 2026 Toy Awards, showcasing the best toys tested by about 370 children and evaluated by experts through hands-on play, at-home testing and an in-person day of play.
Alec Scherma, the Good Housekeeping Institute's senior mechanical engineer, said around a dozen children visited the institute to test the newest toys while experts observed which ones caught their attention.
In the lab, each toy goes through several kinds of tests.
"We need to make sure that there's nothing too small for kids to eat, we always check on durability," Scherma said. "In terms of actual play, we always want to make sure that the toy is fun, right?"
Here are some of the standouts:
Connetix 32-piece Mini Travel Pack
Parents loved the Connetix 32-piece Mini Travel Pack for its portable magnetic tin, which doubles as a building surface. Scherma said the mini magnetic tiles stick together and to the tin, making it a safe and mess-free travel option for airplane and car rides.
Melissa & Doug Swirl & Serve Set
Kids let their imaginations run wild with the Melissa & Doug Swirl and Serve Set, which offers four soft-serve flavors and mix-and-match swirl combinations.
Scherma said parents loved how compact it was and how much imaginative play it inspired.
Monster Jam Chomping Megalodon RC
This remote-controlled Monster Jam toy was a favorite during Good Housekeeping's in-person testing day.
With the press of a button on the remote control, the megalodon goes into "beast mode," breaking free from its chain. The shark is speedy and can gnash its teeth, pop wheelies and spin in circles.
With so many toys on the market, Scherma says parents should always verify they're buying from a reputable brand and that toys are third-party tested.
"We make sure when we're testing them here every single toy brand they send us their safety papers which we review to make sure they follow everything that they're supposed to, that they're third-party tested," Scherma said.

title: Google says it will cut off search engine access for students at schools that reject AI
text:
(AP) - Students using Google software in the classroom will not be allowed to access the company’s search engine unless their school system also opts in to using artificial intelligence, the tech giant said Tuesday.
The Mountain View, California, company has been facing pushback from educators, child development experts and parents over the use of its technology in schools, with the backlash heating up since it announced in August that it had turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students who use Google Classroom.
On Tuesday, the company said that practice would no longer be the default option for school administrators. Instead, K-12 schools will be able to individually turn each Google tool on or off — including Gemini, Gemini Notebook and search, with each being off by default until administrators turn it on. But because search is integrated with AI, schools that opt out of AI altogether would also lose access to Google search.
“We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach,” Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post.
The company also said it is updating its search tools to make them “better for learning,” including offering step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don’t get quick answers to schoolwork."
But turning off AI altogether is not possible if schools want to use Google products.
Google is by far the dominant provider of education technology for U.S. schools. Worldwide, the company says 150 million students and teachers use its Google Classroom platform, and many students use school-provided Chromebook computers.
Google faced an outcry in August when it switched on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students. Until August, Google had only allowed Gemini to be turned on for students 18 or older.
Tuesday’s announcement was met with swift criticism from educators and policymakers.
“Google is using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI. This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service,” wrote Lina Khan, former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, on social media. “As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line.”
New York City and Los Angeles, home to the nation’s biggest school districts, have issued temporary bans on generative AI tools in elementary and middle schools as they assess AI use and safety and develop policies on its use.
Many students already use AI to help with school and homework, but the technology has also made it easier to cheat and find quick, easy answers to questions instead of thinking critically. And experts have raised questions about how access to AI is affecting children’s brain development.
Josh Golin, executive director of children’s advocacy group Fairplay, said Google’s attempt to “strong-arm schools into using its AI products is likely to backfire.” He said Google’s technology in schools is not about learning but about “developing lifetime brand loyalty” for its products.
“Because AI isn’t safe for kids and undermines education and critical thinking, schools should turn off Google’s AI tools the minute that option becomes available,” Golin said in a statement.
Rather than fret about losing access to search, Golin urged schools to turn off not just AI but also Google, and “use this opportunity to help students find more privacy-protective alternatives for search, as well as ways to do more substantive research beyond search and click.”

title: Residents force review of school cost-sharing between Cumberland-North Yarmouth
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
After the Cumberland-North Yarmouth school board decided not to review the district’s cost-sharing agreement last spring — following opposing requests from each town about whether to do so — a petition will now force talks about the decades-old agreement.
“When you explained it to people, it wasn’t hard to get their signature,” said Shirley Storey-King, a Cumberland resident who organized the petition.
The cost-sharing formula for Maine School Administrative District 51 calculates how much each town contributes. The agreement has been a topic of discussion in recent years as both towns consider what would account for a fair financial distribution of the school’s growing budget and look to reduce residents’ rising tax burdens.
The current formula, created in 1966, is based on the overall property taxes each town generates. Currently, Cumberland pays for 73% of the municipal contribution to the school budget and North Yarmouth pays 27%.
Advocates for reconsidering the agreement say it should be more dependent on how many students each town sends to the district. In recent years, 68% of MSAD 51 students have come from Cumberland and 32% from North Yarmouth. Others argue that a 60-year-old formula should be regularly reviewed as a matter of practice.
In February, the Cumberland Town Council unanimously requested that the MSAD 51 Board of Directors examine and potentially revise the formula. Less than a month later, the North Yarmouth Select Board asked that the school board ignore the request, saying it was not a good time to alter the agreement and changes could disproportionately impact North Yarmouth taxpayers, since the town has less than half of the population of Cumberland.
Caught between the towns, in the spring the School Board decided not to discuss the agreement. Storey-King, who brought the idea of revisiting the formula to the Cumberland Town Council when she was a councilor in 2023, decided to force the issue through a petition drive.
“It matters to me because I started it, and when I left the council I promised I’d finish it,” said Storey-King. “Even if (the agreement) was just revisited every five years, that would be worth my effort.”
The petition required at least 1,095 signatures, or 10% of all district voters in the last gubernatorial election. Working with eight other volunteers, Storey-King stood outside the polls in June, at the post office and farmers market and brush dump, gathering 1,139 Cumberland signatures, as well as a handful from North Yarmouth residents. She submitted the names last week.
Cumberland leaders were not surprised the petition resonated with residents.
“Cost is a big driver. A lot of folks are feeling the pinch right now,” wrote Cumberland Councilor Tig Filson in an email. “Every dollar matters.”
Under state statute, the petition requires a meeting where each town sends two selected representatives and a school committee member. A state-approved facilitator will then present data about the sharing of district costs, hear concerns from representatives and develop a plan accordingly.
Paul Whitmarsh, chair of the North Yarmouth Select Board, said he’s concerned that revisiting the cost-sharing agreement may increase tensions between the towns, which share services including a recreation department and a library.
“I think trying to pass (the cost) on to a neighboring town rather than actually going to the root of the problem of the school budget growth is just not the way to go,” said Whitmarsh.
Cumberland Council Chair Michael Edes said the review shouldn’t be seen as town against town.
“This was never about lowering our tax burden at the expense of another town. It is about fundamental fairness in funding the schools, which both towns are very proud of,” said Edes in an email.
In anticipation of the petition’s completion, earlier this fall the school board asked Cumberland and North Yarmouth to create a joint steering committee with representatives from both the towns and the school board. The small group is intended to delve into the issue that arise at the MSAD 51 Tri-Community Meetings, which gathers the school board and leaders of both towns several times a year.
MSAD 51 board Chair Kim Vine said she hopes that those conversations — and even some of those same representatives — will inform the required discussion.
“It’s why we formed the committee in the first place,” said Vine. “It was getting very uncomfortable to be stuck in the middle like that, so this is meant to restore some of that relationship.”
The district is in the process of finding a facilitator for the meeting, said MSAD 51 Superintendent Jeff Porter. Any change to the cost-sharing agreement would need approval from the majority of representatives at the meeting. Depending on the change, it would also have to be approved by voters.
“Hopefully, as the process really gets underway, we’re already at a level of understanding that, ‘Hey, this is just this is just something that we need to do, and no hard feelings, right?’” said Vine.

title: California Gov. Newsom says he will change all 548 death sentences in state to life without parole
text:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — California Gov. Gavin Newsom said Thursday that he’ll change more than 500 death sentences in the state to life in prison without the possibility of parole, though the state Supreme Court will have the final say in hundreds of those cases.
“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” Newsom said in a public letter.
Newsom’s decision comes as he prepares to leave office after eight years and considers a run for president. The Democrat, who’s long been opposed to the death penalty, placed a moratorium on executions in California in 2019.
His latest move came after he realized “the limits of what government can justly accomplish,” he said.
Newsom moved to grant clemency to 548 people currently sentenced to death in California, of whom 529 are men and 19 are women, according to numbers provided by his office.
The state constitution requires the California Supreme Court’s approval to grant clemency to anyone convicted of a felony more than once, which means the court would have to approve 382 of those commutations, or roughly 70%, according to Newsom’s office.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Newsom’s action represents the largest mass clemency in American history. If they are all approved, it would reduce the U.S. death row population by nearly 30%, the center said.
California voters upheld the death penalty
Americans have long been divided over the death penalty. Nearly half of U.S. states have banned capital punishment outright, but executions are still carried out routinely around the country. On Thursday alone, Florida, Alabama and Indiana were scheduled to perform lethal injections.
Californians voted to uphold the death penalty in 2012 and 2016 ballot measures. No one has been executed in the state since 2006 and California has the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.
Among the most notorious convicted killers on California’s death row are Richard Allen Davis, who kidnapped and murdered 12-year-old Polly Klaas in 1993, and Randy Kraft, the so-called “Scorecard Killer” who kept a list of his 16 victims in the 1970s and ’80s. Other prominent killers, including Scott Peterson and the Manson family members, received death sentences that were later commuted to life in prison.
Jess Nichol, Klaas’ sister, said she previously believed Davis deserved the death penalty, but her views evolved.
“The system tells survivors that execution matters to our healing,” Nichol said in a statement. “It doesn’t. It’s a distraction from what we actually need.”
The American Civil Liberties Union, which has said the implementation of the death penalty reflects racial bias, applauded the announcement.
“These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long,” Executive Director Anthony Romero said in a statement.
Victims’ groups and prosecutors decry the decision
Patricia Wenskunas, founder of the California advocacy nonprofit Crime Survivors, which opposed the abolition of the death penalty, criticized Newsom’s decision.
“My heart hurts for every one of the victims and every one of their family members,” she said, calling the decision “offensive” and “outrageous.”
Steve Herr, whose son Sam Herr was murdered along with his friend Julie Kibuishi by Daniel Wozniak in 2010, said he was “absolutely disgusted” by the governor’s decision. He said the death of his son’s killer would have meant closure.
“When somebody commits such a heinous crime, they do not deserve to live,” Herr said. “To hear what Newsom just did … he’s just an outright coward.”
The California District Attorneys Association condemned the decision. Last month, the group sent a letter to Newsom expressing “grave concerns” about him considering the move and warning that such a sweeping action would inflict additional pain on victims’ relatives.
“With the stroke of a pen, Governor Newsom has disregarded the decisions of hundreds of jurors and judges, and the anguish of families who lost loved ones to the worst crimes imaginable,” CDAA President Jeannine M. Pacioni said in a statement. “The victims were never given a commutation. Their families were never given a choice. They deserve far better than this.”
San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow called the move a “sickening abuse of power.”
Dow referenced Rachel Newhouse and Aundria Crawford, two women who were kidnapped, raped and murdered by Rex Allan Krebs in 1999, and Kesha Gurke, a 19-month-old girl tortured and murdered by Michael Whisenhunt in 1995.
“San Luis Obispo County juries sentenced both men to death. A unanimous California Supreme Court affirmed both judgments. Their families have waited decades for the State of California to keep its word. Today, the Governor broke it,” Dow said.
Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer also condemned the decision, calling it “mercy for the wolves and while inflicting the ultimate act of cruelty on the sheep.”
Other governors have taken similar actions
Other governors have granted broad clemency to all death row prisoners in their states, including Gov. Kate Brown in Oregon in 2022 and Gov. Jared Polis in Colorado in 2020. Both are Democrats.
In 2024, President Joe Biden also granted clemency to 37 out of 40 federal prisoners sentenced to death.
Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who will take over from Newsom in January, has said he will extend the state’s moratorium on the death penalty.
___
Ding and Weber reported from Los Angeles.

title: Maine's 2nd District race is heading toward a ranked-choice runoff
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
The contest between Republican Paul LePage and Democrat Matt Dunlap for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District is heading toward a ranked-choice runoff.
A ranked-choice tabulation will be held starting 10 a.m. Monday, the Maine secretary of state’s office said Thursday morning.
That comes a day after LePage declared victory in the neck-and-neck race at the Sea Dog in Bangor.
Former Gov. LePage’s 5,400-vote first-choice lead over State Auditor Dunlap is more than double the edge that Democrat U.S. Rep. Jared Golden held when the Bangor Daily News and Decision Desk HQ called the 2nd District race in 2024. Golden won that runoff against Republican state Rep. Austin Theriault and a recount confirmed it.
To overtake LePage, Dunlap would need to net more than 5,418 votes from the 6,140 ballots that were blank or went to write-ins. But in the 2024 runoff, nearly 91 percent of ballots like those were set aside, and only 380 of more than 10,000 blanks moved to one of the candidates.
If 2024’s patterns hold, less than 300 blank ballots will transfer in the count. Even if Dunlap won all of them, he would still trail by more than 5,000 votes and would likely fall short of the 1.5-point margin needed for a state-funded recount.
It’s the third ranked-choice runoff for the 2nd District since Maine adopted the voting method for primary elections and general election contests for federal offices.
In 2018, Golden came from behind during the ranked-choice runoff to unseat Republican U.S. Rep. Bruce Poliquin. Poliquin sued to overturn the results, but Trump-appointed U.S. District Court Judge Lance Walker rejected his arguments. A day later, Poliquin dropped his request for a recount.
A ranked-choice runoff is triggered whenever there isn’t a candidate who secures more than 50% of the vote.
BDN writer Michael Shepherd contributed to this report.

title: In MSAD 58, Kingfield leaves and Strong stays
Is it legal to add water to a drinking-water well in Maine without authorization?
text:
No.
Maine law prohibits adding water to a drinking-water well, even one on your property. The ban took effect in 2002 as part of broader environmental legislation.
Exceptions allow licensed well drillers and authorized water transporters to add water that meets applicable standards. State-authorized injections into certain wells known as “Class V,” including aquifer recharge wells, are also permitted. The prohibition also excludes monitoring wells and wells used for temporary dewatering or extracting oil, gas or brine.
The Maine Emergency Management Agency warns that pouring water into a dry well can introduce bacteria, viruses or other contaminants. And the water will likely seep into the surrounding aquifer, offering little relief.
The agency recommends contacting a well driller about options, including lowering the pump or replacing the well.
As of Oct. 15, Maine had received 156 reports of dry wells this year amid a drought expected to persist into 2027.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.

title: Midcoast middle school temporarily closed after bedbugs found
text:
WALDOBORO, Maine — “Out of an abundance of caution,” RSU 40 decided to arrange for a comprehensive professional pest treatment at Medomak Middle School after several bed bugs were discovered.
“While we understand that this news may be unsettling, we want to reassure families that there is currently no indication of an infestation at our school,” said a letter sent to families from Superintendent Daniel Welch and Principal Joshua Snyder.
“Out of an abundance of caution, we have also made the decision to arrange for a comprehensive professional treatment of the entire school. Although there is no evidence of a larger problem, we feel this proactive approach is the best way to provide peace of mind to our students, staff, and families,” the letter stated.
Maine regulations require advanced notification before certain treatments can be performed in schools.
“This will, unfortunately, have an impact on schools days this week and early next week.
For Nov. 5, there is no school for MMS students. Teachers and support staff will spend the day creating online lessons and activities.
Friday, Nov. 6, Monday, Nov. 9, and Tuesday, Nov. 10 will be remote learning days for the middle school students.
The district encouraged families to take a few simple precautions:
Check belongings: Look over your child’s backpack, coat, and other personal items.
Know what to look for: Bed bugs are small, reddish-brown insects, about the size of an apple seed when fully grown. Small dark spots on bedding or fabric can also be a sign.
Keep an eye out at home: If you have concerns, check bedding, mattress seams, and areas where belongings are stored.
Reach out: If you discover bed bugs or have questions, please contact the school.
“It’s important to remember that bed bugs can travel on clothing and personal belongings, and their presence is not a reflection of anyone’s cleanliness or housekeeping. They are a nuisance but are not known to spread disease,” the letter stated.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: Alaskans wait for more votes in US Senate, governor’s races. Both could go to ranked tabulations
text:
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — Alaskans settled in Wednesday to await more results from key races on the general election ballot, including a bitterly fought U.S. Senate campaign and an open seat for governor.
A ballot measure seeking to repeal Alaska’s unique system of open primaries and ranked vote general elections also was too early to call.
If no candidate wins more than 50% of first-choice votes, rankings will come into play. Alaska accepts ballots from overseas voters for up to 15 days after the election, making Nov. 18 the date targeted by state elections officials to tabulate under the ranked vote system.
The major candidates in the Senate race are two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola.
In the governor’s race, former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is trying to become the first Democrat elected to the office in a generation. He faces three other Republicans, including business owner Bernadette Wilson, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump.
Litigation and allegations of partisan tricks rocked the Senate race
The contest dominated headlines ahead of Tuesday’s election and attracted the attention of the U.S. Department of Justice.
With less than two weeks before Election Day, the agency sued at President Donald Trump’s direction seeking to block certification of the race if Sullivan loses. The lawsuit cited potential confusion with another Sullivan on the ballot, retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan.
A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit, but the department has appealed.
Suspicions long held by the senator and his supporters that the lesser-known Sullivan was running to sow confusion gained new life last week, when The New York Times reported that top political aides to Peltola appeared to be involved in recruiting him.
The report was based on interviews with a former Peltola campaign manager, who was fired shortly before the August primary. It also cited text messages and campaign finance documents indicating that an operative trying to recruit candidates was paid by a group backing Peltola.
Federal authorities have confirmed the existence of a criminal investigation in the matter.
Peltola denied any involvement. Dan J. Sullivan, who has denied running at the behest of Democrats, has not responded to messages seeking comment in the last week.
The senator elevated the issue in his closing argument to voters and questioned Peltola’s denials.
On Wednesday his campaign expressed confidence in Sullivan’s chances, “despite the biggest election cheating scandal in the history of Alaska” and “despite a bloodbath for Republicans everywhere else in the country.”
Sullivan and Peltola say the vote count will take time
Both campaigns urged patience as the ballot count continues.
Peltola addressed supporters Tuesday night after news broke that Democrats had won enough seats to gain control of the Senate. She was joyful — even taking a selfie with the crowd — but said it will take time for the state to count ballots.
Alaska allows up to 10 days to receive absentee ballots sent from within the U.S., a timeline that can be critical for ballots from rural Alaska communities that are often accessible only by air or water and rely on air service for mail delivery.
“It’s going to take a long time to make sure we’re counting every vote from every far-flung hinterland community, from every tiny outpost, from all of our service members serving overseas, our young people going to colleges,” Peltola said.
Democrat seeks to reclaim governor’s office
Kreiss-Tomkins expressed excitement about the early vote results when speaking to supporters on election night, saying, “What a night this is for the future of our state.”
He cast himself as a consensus builder in the race to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy and said he would work across party lines to address the state’s challenges.
State Republican leaders urged their voters to rank the three GOP candidates in the race to maximize the party’s chances of success.
But Trump, speaking at a rally in support of Republican candidates including Sullivan and Wilson last month in Wasilla, called ranked voting a “scam.” And he railed on social media against the other two Republican gubernatorial candidates, former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson and former state Attorney General Treg Taylor.
Wilson said in a statement Wednesday that she was “cautiously optimistic for the days ahead.”
Alaska’s last Democratic governor was Tony Knowles, who had back-to-back terms from 1994 to 2002. The state had an independent governor from 2014 to 2018.
Ballot measure seeks to repeal unique elections process
Alaskans were asked to decide for the second time in two years on a ballot measure seeking to repeal the open primary and ranked vote general election system.
Voters approved the system in 2020, and it took effect for elections in 2022. Voters narrowly rejected a repeal effort two years ago.

title: UMaine Political Science chair calls Jackson campaign ‘impressive’ even with ‘blue wave’ help
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - WABI spoke to University of Maine Political Science Chair Mark Brewer on Wednesday to get his take on how the national environment played a role in deciding Maine’s senate race.
He said that the “Blue Wave” does serve as an indictment on the Trump Presidency and that perhaps being lost in the mix is the 101 day sprint to the finish of the Troy Jackson campaign.
Jackson became the Democratic nominee when Graham Platner’s scandal plagued campaign came to an end following an allegation of sexual assault, which Platner denies.
“It was an impressive piece of organizing starting with what they did to get the nomination at that convention. They had that thing locked up days in advance. Even the competitors were like wow I can’t believe that just happened to us. They followed that up raising $20 million in that short period of time. He was on message. He rarely had any gaffs on the trail. They got him ready for debates where he held his own. I think that their campaign was incredibly impressive but all that being said obviously Trump plays a big role here not just for Collins but there’s lots of Republican losers today Who are grumbling over their morning coffee or cereal about Donald Trump,” said Brewer.

title: Matt Dunlap conceded to Paul LePage, but they’re headed to a ranked-choice runoff anyway
text:
The tight race for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District will head to a ranked-choice runoff after neither candidate secured more than 50% of the vote, Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows announced Thursday.
But the process is unlikely to swing the election. Former Republican Gov. LePage, who holds a 5,400-vote lead with all municipalities reporting, is very likely to win the race. He declared victory at a news conference Wednesday — though The Associated Press has not yet called the race.
And on Thursday afternoon, shortly after Bellows’ announcement, Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap, LePage’s opponent, conceded the race.
“This isn’t the result we were hoping for, and I’m disappointed that we came short. Congratulations to Paul LePage, I wish him the best,” Dunlap said in a news release.
Some voters might be confused by this set of circumstances: Dunlap’s concession, the ranked-choice runoff, the lack of a call from the AP. Let’s break each down in turn.
Why is the race headed to a ranked-choice runoff?
While the AP’s incomplete results initially showed LePage with more than 50% of the tally, that didn’t include the 6,017 blank ballots cast. The state includes those blank ballots when it determines the 50% threshold necessary to avoid a ranked-choice runoff. LePage is just 316 votes short of the winning threshold.
“If no candidate has been assigned ranking number one on more than 50% of the ballots cast for that particular office, the ranked‑choice voting count must proceed in rounds,” state law reads.
That means that starting Monday in Augusta, the secretary of state will begin the ranked-choice voting process with a confirmation of the accuracy of the votes cast — a process that’s very similar to a full recount, Bellows said Thursday in an interview with the Portland Press Herald.
Then, tabulators will eliminate truly blank ballots — the ones with no bubbles filled — from the total. It’s entirely possible that, with just a couple hundred blank ballots removed, LePage will reach the 50% threshold.
Ballots with no first choice but with a filled-in second choice are next up.
And then the state will count second-choice votes from ballots that initially ranked a write-in over either LePage or Dunlap. That’ll include the 123 votes for the declared write-in, Gregory A. Ward, and some as-yet unknown number of ballots with other write-ins.
It’s unknown how many of the blank ballots fall into each category, nor is it known how many voters who wrote in a candidate chose LePage or Dunlap as their second choice.
If a ranked-choice runoff is happening, why did Dunlap concede?
Political concessions have little bearing on the legal process of counting votes, and Bellows confirmed Thursday that the ranked-choice runoff will go forward.
The state is following precedent: In 2018, when Dunlap was secretary of state, the Republican gubernatorial primary went to a ranked-choice runoff despite the losing candidates conceding and the party saying the runoff was unnecessary.
In congratulating LePage on his likely victory, Dunlap was merely expressing that he didn’t see a path to victory — runoff or no runoff.
That analysis is likely accurate. With LePage just hundreds of votes short, he could cross the 50% threshold in the first round of tabulation.
LePage senior adviser Brent Littlefield backed up his team’s decision to declare victory, saying it is “very clear … that Paul LePage is the congressman-elect.”
Why hasn’t the AP called the race for LePage?
The AP is typically cautious about calling races for candidates, deciding to do so only when the trailing candidate has no path to victory.
“Can the trailing candidates catch the leader? Only when the answer is an unquestionable ‘no’ is the race ready to be called,” the news organization wrote in an FAQ on its website.
The AP does consider candidate concessions when making race calls, but the math is the more important factor. With the race headed to a ranked-choice runoff, and with uncertainty about what those 6,017 blank ballots contain, the news organization must still see a theoretical path for Dunlap.
Has ranked-choice voting decided Maine races before?
Ranked-choice tabulation was also used two years ago in this same district’s election. In 2024, the 2nd District race between incumbent Democratic Rep. Jared Golden and Republican Austin Theriault went to a runoff after 3% of voters did not select either candidate.
That runoff began a week after the election and finished three days later, with Golden declared the winner. A subsequent recount confirmed his win.
After first-round votes were counted, Golden had a 2,159-vote lead out of nearly 400,000 votes, with about 48.65% of the total ballots cast. Golden even contested the need for a recount, saying that he had secured the majority of first-choice votes — but Bellows maintained that blank ballots are counted toward the total needed to avoid a runoff.
LePage, though, is much closer to the 50% threshold than Golden was, and holds a larger lead over his opponent. It’s almost certain he will emerge as the eventual winner.
If the results bear out as his team expects, the former governor’s return to elected office is remarkable in the context of this election cycle: LePage would become the only Republican so far in this “blue wave” midterm to flip a Democratic-held U.S. House seat.
All of Maine’s other elections heavily favored Democrats, with Troy Jackson defeating Sen. Susan Collins and Hannah Pingree easily winning the governor’s race. By running up the margins in deep-red, rural areas, LePage seems to have completed his latest political comeback.
When he likely wins next week’s automatic runoff, the 78-year-old will be one of the oldest freshman congressmen in American history — a back-bencher with little individual lawmaking power in a heavily Democratic Congress.
What does Golden have to say?
Golden acknowledged LePage’s against-the-grain win Thursday afternoon in a statement on social media.
“I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances,” he said on X. “So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami. I stand ready to work with him to ensure the smooth transition that Mainers deserve.”

title: Democrats set to take power as midterm voter data shows shift among young men
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - With Democrats set to take power on Capitol Hill, data on who voted in the midterm elections shows changes in the electorate.
President Donald Trump’s failure to deliver on key campaign promises from 2024 is a main reason a wide range of voters participated this midterm cycle, with some crossing party lines to send a message to lawmakers. Trump says he is still favored.
“I mean our speeches were really, the speeches made at the 30 rallies. And those speeches were, that was tremendous love. It was it was pretty amazing,” Trump told reporters Wednesday.
Two years ago, young people turned out to vote for Trump, especially young men (ages 18-29).
Data from Tufts University shows that has changed. Fifty-six percent of young men supported Trump two years ago. Tuesday, 58% favored a Democratic House candidate.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Republicans must choose how to proceed.
“Americans hate the direction our country is going in right now,” he said. “So now, Republicans are going to have to choose whether to keep listening to the nonsense that’s coming out of 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue or start acting in the interests of the American people. If they continue to embrace Trump, they’re going to be following him right over the cliff, as this election has shown, and it’ll get even worse for them.”
The Associated Press Voter Poll found concerns about inflation, tariffs, the war in Iran and other unfulfilled campaign promises by Trump were driving choices at polling places.
Education levels remain a strong indicator of whether Americans vote Democratic or Republican, the data shows.

title: UMaine men’s hockey looking to bounce back against visiting UMass this weekend
text:
Two teams stuck at .500 will try to jumpstart their seasons when the University of Maine men’s hockey team will entertain the University of Massachusetts for a two-game series at Alfond Arena on Friday and Saturday nights beginning at 7 p.m.
UMaine is 4-4 and is coming off 7-2 and 3-2 (overtime) losses at Boston University in its Hockey East openers.
UMass is 4-4-1 and 1-0 in Hockey East and is coming off a non-conference split with ECAC team Harvard, losing 2-1 and winning 4-2.
UMaine is 3-1 at Alfond Arena and UMass is looking for its first road win after three losses.
UMaine sixth-year head coach Ben Barr spent five seasons at UMass as an assistant and then as the associate head coach before landing the UMaine job. He has gone 6-5-1 against UMass coach and mentor Greg Carvel.
The teams split a pair in Amherst, Massachusetts, a year ago with UMaine unleashing a 54-shot barrage en route to a 6-2 victory in the opener before the Minutemen responded with a 4-0 triumph in the second game behind Jackson Irving’s 37-save gem.
Barr said the Minutemen are very similar to BU.
“They have a lot of really good high-end players,” Barr said. “They have some veteran defensemen who are really good players in this league. They have three to four lines of high-end guys. We’re going to have to win the energy and physical battles.”
The UMaine coach said it is important to get off to a good start. In Friday night’s loss, BU scored three goals in the game’s first 1:31 and never looked back.
He also said he needs more from his veteran players.
“We have players who can get better for us right now. It’s never about how many goals and assists you have. We need some of our veteran guys to chip in a little bit,” Barr said. “Are we just going to throw the puck all over the place and run around or are we going to forecheck, shrink the game a little and try to grind?”
The veteran line of senior center and alternate captain Sully Scholle between graduate student left wing and captain Owen Fowler and senior right wing Charlie Russell has combined for just two assists between them over the past four games.
Junior right wing Thomas Pichette and junior center and linemate Oskar Komarov have each played in just four of the eight games. Pichette has an assist but Komarov has yet to produce a point.
Fowler said it is important for the team to execute minor things, like passing.
“The puck shouldn’t be bouncing off your stick or anything like that,” he said. “The tiny details add up to wins or losses and whether or not the puck goes into the net for you.”
Right wing Lee Parks had his five-game goal-scoring streak snapped last weekend but he extended his points streak to seven games with an assist each night. He leads UMaine with five goals and three assists. Senior center and linemate Max Scott (2 & 6), an alternate captain, and senior left wing Tanner Klimpke (4 & 3) are next.
Isa Parekh (2 & 3) and Lukas Peterson (0 & 5) head up the defense corps in front of goalies Albin Boija (3-2 record, 2.03 goals-against average and .914 save percentage) and Petter Wickstrom Stumer (1-2, 3.32, .875).
UMass has been led by left wing Jack Musa (2 & 10) and linemates Vaclav Nestrasil (5 & 2) and Jack Galanek (3 & 2) along with Egor Barabanov (2 & 3) and Maxim Masse (1 & 4). Francesco Dell’Elce (2 & 2) is the top point-producer among the defense corps and Ethan Eskit has appeared in six of eight games between the pipes and is 2-3-1 with a 1.67 GAA and a .944 save percentage.

title: Vikings sit Murray with hamstring strain, will start Wentz at QB against the Bills on Monday night
text:
EAGAN, Minn. (AP) — Minnesota Vikings quarterback Kyler Murray will miss at least the next game because of a hamstring strain, coach Kevin O’Connell announced on Thursday.
Carson Wentz will start instead against Buffalo on Monday, with Max Brosmer serving as the backup. Murray’s status will be evaluated week to week, O’Connell said, with the hope he can be ready to play by Nov. 15 when the Vikings (6-1) visit Green Bay. Murray is not under consideration for injured reserve, O’Connell said, which would require a minimum four-game absence.
“We do feel like we’d be putting him at risk by possibly turning this into a more significant injury than it already is,” O’Connell said.
Murray was forced out of the season opener after 11 snaps because of a concussion that also kept him out of the following game. Wentz threw three touchdown passes in the rally to beat Green Bay and started the rainy victory at Chicago, going 23 for 39 for 276 yards with six sacks and no turnovers while Murray was out.
Wentz, the second overall pick in the 2016 draft, went 2-3 as the starter last year while J.J. McCarthy was sidelined. O’Connell sidestepped a question about whether Wentz could keep the job with a strong performance even after Murray is cleared.
“There’s a ton of confidence in Carson,” O’Connell said. “He’s already helped us.”
Murray was hurt on a read-option run in the fourth quarter at Detroit last week when he turned the corner past star defensive end Aidan Hutchinson for a 9-yard gain. Murray remained in the game as the Vikings took their first loss, but an MRI exam on Monday confirmed the strain after he had reported soreness.
O’Connell, who declined to specify the severity of the injury, stressed the importance of a cautious approach with an injury that can linger if it’s not fully healed. Wide receiver Justin Jefferson wound up missing seven games with a hamstring strain in 2023. With Murray struggling to find a rhythm throwing the ball, the Vikings will be wary to send him out if he can’t run at full speed.
“Just knowing that Kyler needs his mobility, it’s a big huge part of what makes him an effective player,” O’Connell said.
Since Kirk Cousins tore his Achilles tendon at Green Bay on Oct. 29, 2023, O’Connell and the Vikings over a span of 52 games will have switched starting quarterbacks for injury or performance 17 different times, including 14 in-season changes and five in-game.

title: Cyberattack on blood bank freezers thwarted, follows supermarket fridge hacks
text:
PARIS (AP) — A cyberattack on several blood banks tried to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but was thwarted before it could do any damage to blood products or samples, French authorities said.
The incident comes after supermarkets in a number of European countries reported this week that their fridges and freezers warmed up after they were remotely taken over, resulting in tons of spoiled food at a total cost of millions of dollars (euros).
The French Blood Establishment, or EFS, said “temperature and defrosting thresholds were raised to extremely high levels” on Monday at three of its cold-storage sites for plasma, in a statement released late Tuesday. Monitoring systems quickly detected the problem, allowing staff to take action in time so that “no blood products or samples were compromised,” it said.
French weekly newspaper Le Canard Enchaîné, which first reported the cyberattack, said that the attack had attempted to reset temperatures that normally are at minus 30 Celsius (minus 22 Fahrenheit) to as high as 110 C (230 F).
The cyberattack hit a supplier of refrigeration equipment at three EFS sites. The products stored were bags of plasma intended for transfusions and plasma used to manufacture medicines, and were either transferred or secured, the EFS statement said.
“No health consequences have been identified, and no blood products were lost,” the blood bank said.
The EFS said blood collection and distribution operations remain uninterrupted, ensuring continued services for patients at hospitals and other healthcare.
The company supplying the refrigeration equipment, Coolworld, said in a statement it “is aware” of the cybersecurity incident.
“The vulnerability currently being reported in the media relates to a component from a third-party supplier and was outside Coolworld’s direct control,” the statement said. The company said only a limited number of units were affected and it was taking “appropriate measures.”
France’s national cybersecurity agency and the Health Ministry are investigating the incident.
This week’s cyberattacks on refrigeration systems mirrored an episode in mid-October that targeted fridges and freezers at hundreds of supermarkets and independent stores across France, Belgium and the Netherlands.
One of the chains hit in that earlier incident, Dutch supermarket chain Ahold Delhaize, said Wednesday that it expected the cyberattack to reduce its sales in the fourth quarter by as much as 250 million euros ($281 million), and crimp its operating income for the period by up to 100 million euros.
“While most of the disruption was contained within two weeks, work continues to fully restore our normal operations,” CEO Franz Muller said. “As we all recognize, cyber threats are an increasingly harsh reality of doing business today,” he said in a statement released with Delhaize’s quarterly earnings.
The company had earlier blamed “malicious actions by others” and proactively took some of its systems offline, including websites and apps for its various brands in Europe as well as in the United States.

AP journalist Kelvin Chan in London contributed to the story

title: The Most Popular Movies on Streaming This Week
text:
The Most Popular Movies on Streaming This Week
The world of streaming provides a near-infinite array of viewing possibilities. There are now countless streaming services, each with their own libraries containing hundreds or thousands of movies to watch. (Did you know there’s a streaming service called Howdy? Well, there is. And I have heard its selection is the rootin’ and tootin’-est in all the land.)
With all those choices and with all those services, it’s hard to know what people are actually watching. Most streaming services do not share their data, and those who publish “most viewed” lists often do so using arcane mathematical formulas that can’t be fact checked. (Do we really think the obscure 2009 family film Aliens in the Attic had 2.1 million views on Netflix last week? I have no proof that it didn’t. Maybe it did!)
One way I like to investigate this topic is by looking at streaming films’ popularity on the movie-based social media app Letterboxd. As we have outlined previously, popularity on Letterboxd is determined by “a mix of member activity, including reviews, comments, watches, logs, watchlists, etc.” The more people are reviewing, watching (and saying they want to watch), logging, and writing about something, the higher it rates on the site in terms of “popularity.”
But Letterboxd also allows you to filter results in their database according to where movies are available, either in theaters or on VOD or streaming. And when you weed out the popular films that are exclusively available in theaters, you wind up with a list of the most popular titles of the moment on streaming — and here they are (and where to currently stream them)...

title: Postal employee shot 2 coworkers at an Iowa post office before being captured, police say
text:
DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — A female postal worker shot two female co-workers at the main post office in Iowa’s capital city Thursday before being captured nearby and faces attempted murder charges, authorities said.
Jennifer Christine Pledger, 39, of West Des Moines stood above one woman who she had shot and fired again, police said, and continued firing as she fled the building.
A male employee was injured in a fall while trying to escape. None of the injuries were believed to be life-threatening, according to police.
“They’re all at the hospital. They are being cared for right now,” Des Moines police Sgt. Paul Parizek said of the victims, who included two women, 45 and 53, and a 55-year-old man. All were in stable condition.
Pledger is being charged with two counts of attempted murder, two counts of willful injury causing serious injury and intimidation. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach possible relatives were unsuccessful and information was not immediately available on an attorney who could speak on her behalf.
The shooting happened on the facility’s second floor, in an area not accessible to the public. Witnesses reported hearing 10 to 12 shots, he said.
Parizek said officers responded within three minutes and quickly captured Pledger, who was detained along a nearby bike path without resistance. A 9 mm handgun was recovered where she was detained.
Police began receiving calls about the shooting around 9:10 a.m., and the suspect was detained at 9:21 a.m., Parizek said.
The post office is just north of downtown Des Moines and across the street from one of the city’s main hospitals.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Postal Inspection Service said in an email that it was investigating the shooting along with local, state and federal law enforcement.
Gov. Kim Reynolds said she was in contact with the Department of Public Safety regarding the shooting.
“We are monitoring the situation and our prayers are with everyone involved,” she posted online. “Grateful for the immediate response by law enforcement.”
Des Moines Public Schools said the district’s nearby elementary school, welcome center and nutrition center temporarily barred anyone from entering or leaving the facilities due to the shooting. Those restrictions were lifted after police told them the suspect was in custody.
Past shootings at postal facilities have prompted the Postal Service to study employee safety.
In 1986, a disgruntled postal worker went on a deadly rampage at a post office in Edmond, Oklahoma, shooting 14 fellow workers before killing himself. In 1991, a fired postal worker killed four former co-workers at his former post office in Royal Oak, Michigan, before killing himself. After those and other shootings, postal officials commissioned a study released in 2000 to examine workplace violence around the time that the term “going postal” was becoming conversational.
The report issued several recommendations to flag violent tendencies while concluding that “going postal” was a myth and that postal employees are less violent than the national workforce.
Other attacks have occurred since the report, including a 2006 shooting in Goleta, California, where a former postal worker stormed into a sorting facility and fatally shot six workers before killing himself.
___

title: Maine’s 2nd Congressional District race will proceed to ranked choice tabulation
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WAGM) - The Maine Department of the Secretary of State announced Thursday that the 2nd Congressional District race will proceed to ranked choice voting tabulation after no candidate received a majority of first-choice votes cast on Election Day.
First-choice vote totals
Maine’s 487 municipalities reported 341,248 total ballots cast in the race, according to the Secretary of State’s Office.
Paul LePage (R) received 170,263 votes (49.894%). Matthew Dunlap (D) received 164,845 votes (48.307%). Declared write-in candidates received 123 votes (0.036%), and there were 6,017 blank votes (1.763%).
Because no candidate received more than 50% of the total ballots cast, the ranked choice tabulation will begin Monday, Nov. 9, at 10 a.m. at the Maine Department of Public Safety Headquarters building at 45 Commerce Drive in Augusta.
The process is open to the public and will be livestreamed on the Secretary of State’s YouTube page.
What happens next
“The first step in the process will be to verify the vote totals from every municipality to ensure accuracy,” said Secretary of State Shenna Bellows. “Once the election night totals are verified, assuming neither candidate received a majority of the votes, which is what we are observing now, we will proceed to the ranked choice voting tabulation.”
How ranked choice voting works in Maine
In ranked choice voting races, a candidate must receive more than 50% of the first-choice votes counted on Election Day to win the race outright.
If no candidate appears to have reached that threshold based on initial unofficial results from the municipalities, the Secretary of State’s Office determines whether to proceed with ranked choice tabulation.
Votes are tabulated in rounds. The lowest-ranked candidate is eliminated in each round until two candidates remain. The candidate who receives more than 50% of the votes in the final round is declared the winner.
More information is available on the RCV Resources webpage on the Secretary of State’s website.
About the district
The 2nd Congressional District includes all municipalities and unorganized territories in Androscoggin, Aroostook, Franklin, Hancock, Oxford, Penobscot, Piscataquis, Somerset, Waldo and Washington counties.
It also includes the Kennebec County municipalities of Augusta, Belgrade, Chelsea, Farmingdale, Fayette, Gardiner, Hallowell, Manchester, Monmouth, Mount Vernon, Oakland, Randolph, Readfield, Rome, Sidney, Vienna, Wayne and Winthrop.
At more than 27,000 square miles, it is the largest district east of the Mississippi River, according to the Secretary of State’s Office.
Recount process
Maine has no mandatory recounts. Maine statute Title 21-A, §737-A lays out a specific plan, process and any related costs for votes to be recounted.
After the ranked choice tabulation, the losing candidate may request a hand recount.

title: Obituary: Charlotte L. (Lilly) Bickford
text:
WEBSTER, Mass. / CUMBERLAND FORESIDE – Charlotte L. (Lilly) Bickford, 85, of Thompson Road, passed away following a brief illness on Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026, at UMass Memorial Health – Harrington Hospital – Webster Campus.
Ms. Bickford was born in Quakertown, Pa., daughter of the late Elmer and Mae (Martin) Lilly, and graduated from Allentown High School, Muhlenberg College, and Andover College, earning both associate’s and bachelor’s degrees. She lived in Cumberland Foreside, Maine, for most of her life and moved to Webster, Mass. in 2023.
Charlotte was a lifelong lab technician and previously worked at the Worcester Foundation for Experimental Biology in Shrewsbury, Mass., and Maine Medical Center before retiring. She spent two decades in Shrewsbury, Mass., helping her sister to raise her three children. She was a member and flutist in her community choir in Maine. She was an independent woman who enjoyed reading and had an extensive collection of owl-related items, as well as anything to do with lighthouses.
She is survived by her brother, William Lilly of Lorana, Texas; and many beloved nieces and nephews.
She was predeceased by her husband of 51 years, William L. Bickford; two brothers, Bruce A. Lilly and Martin Lilly, and two sisters, Myrtle Olson and Virginia Mae Cioppa.
Charlotte’s family would like to thank the staff at Christopher Heights for their wonderful care over the past three years, and especially thank her private aides, Margaret Mutahi, Magdalene Mbogori, Emma Maina, Teresa Berry, and Margaret Nganju, for their dedication to Charlotte during the past year.
A burial will be held privately at the family’s convenience. Paradis-Givner Funeral Home in Oxford, Mass. is directing the arrangements.
In lieu of flowers, you may make memorial contributions to The National Multiple Sclerosis Society or a nonprofit of your choice.

title: Why this attorney has been putting up positive billboards
text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (InvestigateTV) - Sam Aguiar has been a personal injury lawyer since 2008.
“It’s a tough field, but it’s a rewarding field,” Aguiar said.
In December 2024, he decided to go beyond the courtroom and put up billboards around town with motivational messages.
“I designed them myself,” Aguiar said. He sent them to his billboard representative and told them to get the billboards up before he changed his mind.
“I know it sounds a little crazy,” he said.
Simple messages for difficult times
Aguiar said the plan was to make the messages simple so they would resonate with people.
“I remember there was ‘Believe in yourself.’ There was ‘Good vibes only today.’ There was ‘Stay strong’—very short messages, you know—hoping to speak to different people who may be going through different times,” he said.
Since December, Aguiar has put up about 60 billboards in high-traffic areas around Louisville.
The response was immediate. More than 2,000 people have reached out through phone calls, emails, texts, and social media.
“I was getting messages from trauma nurses who said they saw some by the hospitals that really braced them for what they knew was going to be another tough shift. We’d gotten a great message from a cancer patient who was driving up from E-town a few days a week to go through chemo, and she said that when those messages popped up, it gave her a little bit of a boost. We had EMTs reach out. We had some teachers reach out. We had single moms reach out. It was awesome,” Aguiar said.
Aguiar has also had fun with the campaign. One billboard near the fairgrounds references a social media trend his 13-year-old would recognize.
“I figured if you can’t beat them, join them,” he said. “Maybe Mom and Dad up front will, you know, like being reminded that they’re a 10. And then maybe their kiddos in the back will see six, seven and start doing whatever that little motion is at six, seven.”
Not about business
Aguiar said the goal was never about generating business, though some new clients have come his way.
“It’s not hard to remind people that they’re important, that they’re loved, that they’re making a difference, um, and that they make the world a better place,” he said.
Aguiar has spent more than half a million dollars on the campaign and wants to continue it.

title: Hundreds place ‘I voted’ stickers at memorials of Alex Pretti, Renee Good
text:
MINNEAPOLIS, Minn. (KARE) — Hundreds of people placed “I Voted” stickers at the memorials of Alex Pretti and Renee Good to mark Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Pretti and Good were fatally shot in Minneapolis by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents earlier this year during Operation Metro Surge.
Stickers at Pretti’s memorial
“We can’t change what happened, but we’ll keep fighting,” Caitlyn Hren-Borger said.
Hren-Borger, a Minneapolis resident, visits Pretti’s memorial often. This time, she left an “I Voted” sticker.
“Because Alex couldn’t vote, and it’s really important to be able to make our voices heard,” Hren-Borger said.
Hren-Borger said the memorial was “just really beautiful” as more stickers were placed.
Dan Weston, a visitor to the Pretti memorial, was among the hundreds who placed stickers there.
“It still feels like we have power,” Weston said. “It felt like we paid homage to change, and we won’t forget him or Renee or anyone else.”
Stickers at Good’s memorial
Peg Baier, a visitor to the Good memorial, wanted her sticker to be near Good’s.
“She can’t vote, but we can,” Baier said. “It’s one meaningful thing that we can do in her name.”
Carol Ohana, another visitor to the Good memorial, said the stickers give her hope.
“It gives me hope because it shows the good side of people,” Ohana said.
Baier said, “There’s so much hope and so much diversity coming back, and at the same time, this is Minnesota, and we’re still grieving. I want to think that her life wasn’t for nothing, that at least she became a focal point to galvanize people and get us out to vote.”
Visits to both memorials
“This is the best I’ve felt in a very long time today,” Jonathan Fondell said.
Fondell, a Minneapolis resident, visited both memorials.
“It seemed like the best way to memorialize them is to just sort of come and visit and say, ‘Hey, this is what I’m voting against, things like this happening,’” he said.
For those who placed them, the stickers represent hope.
“Our community is never going to be the same, but we’re here together,” Hren-Borger said.

title: Judge grants injunction to temporarily halt removal of beloved York tree
text:
A York County Superior Court judge has issued a restraining order against the town of York, temporarily halting the removal of a tree that some residents want to save.
The honey locust tree, located on a traffic island in York Village Square, has been at the center of a weekslong debate over whether it should be saved as work begins on a long-awaited revitalization plan.
Town officials say voters approved the plan in 2015, including the removal of the tree and a monument next to it. But many residents say they don’t remember that being a condition of the improvement.
On Oct. 27, resident Kiki Tidwell filed a lawsuit and requested a temporary restraining order to stop construction.
Justice James Martemucci issued the temporary restraining order — which remains pending ahead of oral arguments — on Monday, one day after another resident, James Kences, filed a request for emergency intervention.
Crews have been ordered not to touch the tree during ongoing construction at the intersection. It had been scheduled for removal Tuesday or Wednesday.
Tidwell, a former member of the town’s climate action committee, said Thursday that the town’s decision to remove the tree was a violation of a climate action plan approved by voters in 2022, and that it was never properly disclosed that the tree would come down.
“We could never get the town to hear anything,” Tidwell said of her time on the committee. “(The town) has basically done nothing on the climate action plan.”
In her complaint, Tidwell cites a state law protecting public shade trees — or trees located on public right-of-ways like highways and local roads. Removing it, she said, is a violation of that law, though it grants trimming, cutting and removal of shade trees if a public road needs to be altered.
“The removal of the Existing Tree is part of a project to both alter the town way, and improve the safety of the subject intersection,” reads the town’s response to the lawsuit, citing Town Manager Peter Joseph.
Joseph did not respond to requests for comment Thursday.
Tidwell also says the tree prevents the area from becoming a “heat island,” or an area that could become 10-15 degrees hotter without shade. The town’s response states the revitalization plan includes planting new trees. But removing the honey locust could spell decades of unregulated heat for residents in York Village while they wait for saplings to grow, Tidwell said.
Tidwell also cited a York land use ordinance that prioritizes the preservation of natural landscapes. She wrote that the town’s actions constitute an abuse of discretion because it did not use available tree planting funds to preserve or relocate the tree.
Martemucci has yet to make a final decision on the pending restraining order, but a hearing is scheduled for Friday afternoon, which will include oral arguments from the town and Tidwell.

title: Trump signs proclamation he says will prevent future changes to the Oval Office and Cabinet Room
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday signed a proclamation that he said will prevent future changes to the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as he has redesigned them.
“We’re making it a national monument and it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
Trump’s proclamation signing comes two days after voters, dissatisfied with his economic policies, threw dozens of Republicans out of office, delivering control of Congress to Democrats.
It’s also the third day this week in which the president, a real estate mogul, delivered remarks fixated on his pet projects in Washington, D.C., including an opulent ballroom and the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
Since returning to the White House, Trump has overseen numerous design changes to various rooms, including the Oval Office, where he has filled the wall space with portraits, a copy of the Declaration of Independence and numerous golden accents.

title: JetBlue raises baggage fees again as jet fuel prices stay elevated
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(AP) - JetBlue has raised its checked baggage fees for the second time this year, making it more expensive for travelers to check luggage just as the busy holiday travel season gets underway.
The new fees for tickets purchased on or after Nov. 3 mean most economy passengers flying within the United States, Canada, Latin America and the Caribbean will pay at least $50 each way for their first checked bag, up from $39 previously.
The price climbs to $55 during peak travel periods, including Thanksgiving and the winter holidays, if passengers pay at least 24 hours before departure. Those who wait until the final 24 hours will pay $60 during off-peak periods and $70 during peak periods.
“We’re adjusting checked bag fees to help offset rising fuel and operating costs,” JetBlue said in an emailed statement. “This helps us keep our base fares competitive while giving customers the choice to pay for a checked bag only if they need one.”
At the start of the year, the first checked bag on most economy domestic JetBlue flights cost $35 during off-peak periods. But that was before the Iran war started in late February with U.S.-Israeli strikes and sent jet fuel prices swinging.
The fee for a second checked bag has also increased, starting at $70 each way during off-peak periods and $75 during peak travel. Passengers checking their bags at the airport can pay as much as $85 for a second bag.
JetBlue, which has its flagship terminal at New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport, previously raised its checked baggage fees in March. That increase helped set off a broader round of baggage fee hikes among major U.S. airlines, including Delta, United, American and Southwest.
The war with Iran remains unresolved, keeping traffic largely restricted through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical shipping route for global oil supplies. The disruption has kept jet fuel prices elevated.
JetBlue executives said last week during the airline’s third-quarter earnings call that demand has remained resilient even as fares have risen in response to higher jet fuel prices. JetBlue said its average fuel price reached $3.91 per gallon in the summer, up 57% from a year earlier, and is expected to climb to $4.64 during the final three months of the year, up 85% from the same time last year.
Some travelers, including eligible co-branded credit card holders and members of JetBlue’s loyalty program, can still check bags for free, the airline said.
