title: UMaine women’s soccer advances to America East semis with win over Albany
text:
ORONO, Maine — The defending three-time America East tournament champion University of Maine women’s soccer team received an early first-half goal from leading scorer Isabella Meadows and a late second-half goal from Sandrine Brault to beat Albany 2-0 in their league quarterfinal series at the New Balance Soccer Complex in Orono.
Third seed UMaine, now 8-5-4, will travel to take on second seed Bryant, 6-6-4, in Sunday’s 4:30 semifinal.
Bryant (Rhode Island) received a first-round bye.
Sixth seed Albany finished at 5-8-3 and had its four-game unbeaten streak (2-0-2) snapped.
It was UMaine’s sixth consecutive win over Albany and the Great Danes have been shut out in all six.
All-America East first team striker and UConn transfer Meadows opened the scoring just 7:42 into the game.
Back Audrey Palmer collected the ball 30 yards from goal along the left hand side and maneuvered past a Great Dane defender and sprinted into the penalty area before sliding a pass across the front of the goal where the open Meadows steered past Albany goalie Claudia Volino. It was her team-leading eighth goal of the campaign.
Each team attempted four shots in the first half with Albany have a slight edge in play over the final 20 minutes.
The Great Danes pressed for the equalizer in the second half and had an 11-5 edge in shot attempts along with a 5-3 advantage in corner kicks.
But the Black Bears defended well and Brault gave them some valuable breathing room when she pounced on a loose ball off a Britta Denny cross and shot it off the body of Volino and into the net for her third goal of the season.
The ball popped in the air and dropped behind the unfortunate goalie.
Albany finished with a 15-9 edge in shot attempts.
UMaine goalie Elena Barenberg and Albany’s Volino each finished with five saves.

title: Hannah Pingree taps former Republican and tribal leader to build her Cabinet
text:
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree on Thursday named a former Republican state senator who once co-hosted a TV talk show with her and a Penobscot Nation leader to co-chair the committee that will help pick her Cabinet.
Roger Katz, a lawyer who served four terms as a state senator and was Augusta’s mayor, and Maulian Bryant, the executive director of the Wabanaki Alliance and former ambassador for the Penobscot Nation, will lead a volunteer Transition Committee whose full membership will be announced in the coming days, Pingree’s team said.
The picks pair a Republican with long ties to the Democrat and a tribal leader at the center of a policy fight Pingree has promised to take on early. She pledged during the campaign to pass a tribal sovereignty bill within her first 100 days, an issue that divided Gov. Janet Mills and Wabanaki leaders through both of Mills’ terms.
Katz, a centrist lawmaker who has often criticized President Donald Trump and former Gov. Paul LePage, now chairs the University of Maine System’s board of trustees. He and Pingree, a former House speaker and top aide to Mills, co-hosted “The Maine Event,” a public affairs talk show that began on public access in 2014 and later aired on Maine Public.
“Roger Katz and Maulian Bryant bring the experience and judgment I want at the table as we build this administration,” Pingree said in a statement.
Scott Ogden, a former deputy chief of staff to Mills who also worked for U.S. Sens. Angus King and Olympia Snowe and for Pingree’s mother, U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, will co-direct the paid transition staff. Former Portland Mayor Karen Geraghty will plan the Jan. 6 inauguration.
The state gives a governor-elect $5,000 for the transition and inauguration. State law requires separate transition and inaugural committees to raise the rest.

title: Multiple flights in Europe diverted because of bomb threats after ‘malicious’ hoaxes
text:
MILAN (AP) — Bomb threats targeted more than a dozen flights in Europe on Thursday, leading to a slew of emergency landings and military escorts in some cases, authorities said. No hazardous or suspicious materials have been found in what a British official called “malicious” hoaxes.
Several similar threats targeted planes earlier this week, prompting searches and diversions, with at least 25 flights targeted, officials said. Europe has experienced a slew of other disruptions recently, such as attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems, drone incursions and mysterious triggers to alert apps.
While fake bomb threats are relatively common, it is unusual to see so many in a single day. They come at a time of increased geopolitical tensions and warnings from authorities that Russia may be ramping up so-called hybrid threats in Europe.
It wasn’t known whether this week’s threats were linked, who sent them or what they hoped to achieve.
An email containing the threat to Rome-bound planes was sent on behalf of a group that described itself as anti-feminist, according to a copy provided by an airport official and reviewed by The Associated Press. An official from another European airport said the threat they received also came from a group calling itself anti-feminist, and used some of the same language. It wasn’t clear if the same group sent the two threats. Both officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to share the information.
Travelers weren’t too frightened
At Rome’s airport, travelers whose flights weren’t affected seemed to take the threats in stride.
“As of now, I am not scared of being in an airport or getting on board a plane,” said Alessia Strada, a 19-year-old Italian returning from Kenya. ”Probably this idea I have about traveling in Europe will change in the near future, but let’s see how it goes.”
Alex Langenkamper, a 38-year-old German headed to Munich, said “crazy people” exist and will in the future.
Meanwhile, Michael Romano, a 54-year-old traveler headed to Colombia, expressed concern about the world moving toward war.
“These things never used to happen here in Europe,” he said. “This is all new, so it is a little bit scary.”
‘Stress-testing’ governments and driving up costs
Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, senior fellow at the Bruegel think tank in Brussels, said the threats were “stress-testing” how European governments and airport officials respond, and whether their responses were coordinated.
The idea behind the threats “appears to be to sow chaos, uncertainty, about the reliability of air traffic across Europe” and could have “cascading effects” — like economic damage and costs related to inspection, investigation and cleaning aircraft.
Joji Waites, who heads flight safety at the British Airline Pilots’ Association, said the industry has put in place “proved mechanisms” for dealing with such threats, including a team of assessors to grade the level of threat in a red-amber-green color-coding system, quick notification of flight crews, and the evacuation of planes on the ground.
Each flight disruption could cost airlines as much as $250,000, on a par with the possible costs of dealing with an unruly passenger, said Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England.
“And that’s because you might end up with the crew going out of hours. You might need replacement crew. You have got passengers that miss their flight connections,” Baum said. ”It knocks everything out of sync for the rest of the day for the airline in question.”
Military escorts cost money, too, which would be borne by governments rather than airlines, he added.
Officials decry the hoaxes
Britain’s transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, told British broadcasters that flights across Europe have been hit by “malicious hoax threats.”
European Union Transport Commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas told reporters in Dublin that it was “too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked.”
“National investigations remain ongoing,” he said, adding that an EU information-sharing mechanism on aviation security had been activated.
French air base goes on high alert
An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a military air base in France after receiving a threat, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s office said. The flight landed safely at the base in Evreux, which was under high alert, and military bomb disposal teams were examining the plane, the office said.
Lecornu ordered warplanes to intercept the plane because the pilot “didn’t cooperate as expected with the authorities,” his office said. It declined to comment further.
Hours after the flight landed, the plane was sitting on the tarmac with a Red Cross vehicle nearby while explosive experts with dogs examined it.
An investigation was opened by French aviation security authorities. The regional prosecutor, Remi Coutin, said in a statement that the pilot and co-pilot were questioned about what happened.
Aer Lingus later said its pilots fully cooperated with the French authorities and “the engagement of the pilots with the authorities has now concluded.”
Italian and Croatian air force jets escort a Finnair flight
Italian air force fighter jets escorted a Finnair flight that departed Helsinki bound for Rome after a threat was received by email, the air force said in a statement. Croatia’s defense ministry said one of its fighter planes first intercepted the commercial jet in Croatian airspace before handing it off to the Italians.
Finnair said that two of its flights, including the one that received the military escort and landed safely in Rome, “faced unfounded hoax bomb scares.” The other flight, operated by Jettime from Helsinki to Vienna, landed safely at its destination, and was expected to return to service after an inspection, Finnair said.
Three Ryanair flights bound for Sofia, Bulgaria, meanwhile, also received military escorts and made emergency landings after bomb threats, officials said. Two of the flights — one from Copenhagen, Denmark, and the other from Madrid — landed safely in Sofia, airport officials said. The third, from London, was diverted and landed safely in Plovdiv, Bulgaria’s Plovdiv Airport, CEO Krassimir Peshev said.
Hoaxes prompted similar searches earlier this week
Several flights across Europe received bomb threats earlier this week, officials said.
The flights included ones operated by Polish airline LOT, Scandinavian Airlines, Wizz Air and Ryanair. The hoax threats came after a plane headed for Bulgaria was diverted to Hungary upon receiving a similar bomb threat while in the air. No one was injured.
A slew of other flights were disrupted Thursday. Among those incidents:
— Czech police said searches of four planes that landed in Prague after being targeted by bomb threats turned up nothing. They haven’t given details on where the flights originated, and said they took precautions despite not finding the threats credible.
— A LOT Polish Airlines flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed at its destination, where inspections found no hazardous or suspicious items, the airline said.
— A Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest landed safely in the Romanian capital following a bomb threat, airport spokesman Teo Postelnicu said. Checks turned up no bomb.
— A flight to Warsaw landed in Vienna after Polish authorities received a threatening email, said Stefan Loidl, a police spokesperson in the Lower Austria province. Nothing was found and the plane continued to Warsaw. He said there was also an abstract threat to Vienna Airport concerning four other flights, which he declined to identify, but operations weren’t disrupted.
——-
Charlton reported from Paris and Biller from Rome. Associated Press writers throughout Europe contributed.

title: Graduation ceremony held for new loggers from KVCC logging program
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
HINCKLEY, Maine (WABI) - After the conclusion of a 20-week program, students from the KVCC logging program will soon be entering their new “office” in the woods.
The 10th graduation ceremony was held near the Harold Alfond campus farm Thursday afternoon, recognizing 15 new graduates from Kennebec Valley Community College’s Mechanized Logging and Forestry Trucking Program.
The program, now in its 10th year, runs from June to November. The program is designed to help students operate mechanized logging equipment, identify commercial wood, and prepare contract work in the logging industry.
“We’re going to be half a million-dollar machines all the time. Being able to understand what you’re going to do with them all the time and when you go into the real workforce. You help keep contractors going,” said graduate Jackson Newton.
Throughout the course, students trained on nearly $5 million worth of forestry equipment loaned by regional equipment dealers, helping prepare students in managing both old and state-of-the-art machinery for contract workers.
“People who want to hop in one of these machines, you can’t do. Like people just don’t want. some random person running their multi-million dollar or half a million-dollar machine with no experience,” said graduate Samuel Armstrong.
Instructors say that generous support gives young operators invaluable seat time in modern machinery before entering the workforce.
“We love to see them come in the first day, not really sure about what they were doing and what they know. Some of them didn’t know the difference between hardwood and softwood. We’ve taken them from there to merchandising some of the big money wood,” said Program Coordinator Donald Burr.
Graduates are now preparing to take their commercial driver’s license (CDL) exams before beginning full-time jobs with logging contractors across the state.
“I bet when we get into the real world it’ll be a lot more different, a lot faster pace,” said Newton, “I’ve learned a lot and I’m ready.”

Madawaska Heads to States as Northern Maine Soccer Championships Wrap Up
The Northern Maine regional soccer championships are complete, and five Aroostook County teams are heading to Saturday's state championship games.
Madawaska's boys added their name to that list Wednesday afternoon, defeating Fort Fairfield 2-0 in the Class D North championship at Presque Isle High School.
It was the third consecutive year the Owls and Tigers met for the regional title, and this time Madawaska took control early with two first-half goals.
Meanwhile, Presque Isle's girls saw their Class B championship hopes end against John Bapst, while Fort Fairfield's girls battled Penobscot Valley in a close Class D final before the Lady Howlers pulled away in the second half.
Here's how Wednesday's three championship games played out.
Girls Soccer
Class B North: John Bapst Ends Presque Isle's Championship Run
(1) John Bapst 3, (3) Presque Isle 0
Presque Isle's girls came into Wednesday's Class B North championship looking to knock off top-seeded John Bapst and earn a trip to the state finals.
But the Crusaders brought the Lady Wildcats' tournament run to an end with a 3-0 victory at Hampden Academy.
Presque Isle had put together an impressive postseason to reach the championship game.
The third-seeded Lady Wildcats defeated Skowhegan 3-1 in the quarterfinals before rolling past seventh-seeded Cony 4-0 in Saturday's semifinals.
Hailey Plant, Carrlyn Buck, Bridgid Schupbach and Willow Bugbee each scored in that semifinal victory, showing the offensive balance that helped Presque Isle reach the regional final.
Wednesday brought a tougher challenge against a John Bapst team that entered the game undefeated.
The Crusaders came away with the shutout and the Class B North championship, advancing to Saturday's state final.
For Presque Isle, the loss brings an end to a strong fall season that included a run to the Northern Maine championship game.
Class D North: Penobscot Valley Wins Fifth Straight Regional Championship
(1) Penobscot Valley 2, (2) Fort Fairfield 0
For the first 40 minutes Wednesday evening, there wasn't much separating Fort Fairfield and Penobscot Valley.
The top two seeds in Class D North battled through a scoreless first half at Presque Isle High School, with both teams making it difficult for the other to generate scoring opportunities.
But the Lady Howlers found the breakthrough in the 49th minute.
Charlotte Brochu scored to give Penobscot Valley a 1-0 lead, putting Fort Fairfield in a position where the Tigers needed to find an equalizer.
The game remained close until the 73rd minute, when McKenna Ireland added an insurance goal to make it 2-0.
Goalkeeper Brooklyn Raymond recorded another shutout for Penobscot Valley, securing the victory and the program's fifth consecutive Class D North regional championship.
Fort Fairfield entered Wednesday after consecutive tournament shutouts, defeating Washburn 4-0 in the quarterfinals and Central Aroostook 1-0 in the semifinals.
The Tigers had earned their place in the regional final with strong defensive performances of their own.
Although Wednesday's result didn't go their way, reaching the Class D North championship capped another successful postseason for Fort Fairfield.
For Penobscot Valley, the victory means another opportunity to compete for a state championship after five straight regional titles.
Boys Soccer
Class D North: Madawaska Scores Twice in First Half to Claim Regional Championship
(1) Madawaska 2, (3) Fort Fairfield 0
For the third consecutive season, Madawaska and Fort Fairfield met with the Class D North boys championship on the line.
And Wednesday afternoon, the top-seeded Owls made sure they would be the ones heading to states.
Madawaska scored twice in the opening 25 minutes and held Fort Fairfield scoreless the rest of the way, earning a 2-0 victory at Presque Isle High School.
Aiden Gagnon opened the scoring in the 13th minute, giving the Owls an early 1-0 advantage.
Just 12 minutes later, Josh Querze added another goal in the 25th minute to double Madawaska's lead.
Those two first-half goals would be all the Owls needed.
Goalkeeper Aleck Gendreau recorded the shutout, helping Madawaska secure the regional championship and a place in Saturday's Class D state final.
It was another strong postseason performance for the Owls, who reached Wednesday's championship after shutting out Hodgdon 2-0 in the semifinals.
Fort Fairfield had also earned its way into the final with a strong tournament run, including a 3-1 semifinal victory over second-seeded Central Aroostook.
But Madawaska's early scoring and defensive effort proved to be the difference Wednesday.
The Owls will now travel to Messalonskee High School on Saturday to face Class D South champion Monmouth.
The top-seeded Mustangs advanced with an 8-0 victory over Narraguagus in the Southern Maine regional championship.
That sets up a state championship matchup between two regional champions, with Madawaska looking to finish its season with one more victory.

title: Susan Collins will be remembered for her service – and her shortcomings
text:
As a high school senior in Caribou, 18-year-old Sue Collins boarded a plane for the first time to fly to the nation’s capital as one of two young Mainers offered a chance to get a close-up view of the U.S. Senate.
It was the start of a journey that would last a lifetime.
Though Sen. Susan Collins is no doubt reeling from her rejection by Maine voters this week, I am sure she will come to appreciate that her three decades of admirable Senate service cements her place in history. Her home state will recognize it, too.
Come 2027, I hope Sen. Collins will carry on her public service in new ways. It would be helpful both to historians and the public today if one of the things she chooses to do is to write a memoir — ideally with an openness that she isn’t famous for.
I’m sure I’m not the only person who would like insight into the myriad choices and sacrifices Collins made along the way – and perhaps, in that way, could come to better appreciate her long career in D.C.
Though Sen. Collins’ family had deep roots in local politics, she told me years ago that she had never been to Washington before that Nixon-era trip and had, like many young people, never met a senator.
On Capitol Hill in 1971, Collins had the opportunity to chat for a couple of hours with Sen. Margaret Chase Smith, the only woman serving in the chamber with 99 men, and already a Maine legend.
Sen. Collins recalled talking with Sen. Smith about everything from the armed services to the definition of full employment – serious, adult issues.
Sen. Collins came away from the session in Sen. Smith’s private office with an understanding of the importance of “standing tall for what you believe in.”
“That pivotal meeting was the beginning of my journey to the Senate,” Sen. Collins said in 2017.
Since her election to the U.S. Senate in 1996, Sen. Collins has become both one of the nation’s most experienced senators and one admired for her willingness to set aside partisanship on occasion.
More than half a century after she met Sen. Smith, Collins now joins her as one of the great senators in Maine history, second in longevity only to William Frye of Lewiston, who died five months into his sixth term in 1911.
Like Sen. Smith in 1972, Sen. Collins’ Senate career ended before she was ready for it to end.
Her 2026 campaign boasts about bringing a lot of federal money to Maine weren’t inaccurate. But in the sweep of recent history, that’s not destined to matter much. Firehouses can crumble away. Heroic stands are not forgotten.
Think about Sen. Smith. What do we in Maine recall about her? One highlight of her career still mentioned frequently is the courageous, eloquent speech she gave, early on, denouncing the excesses of Sen. Joseph McCarthy.
Sen. Collins said she learned about the need to stand tall for what you believe in from Sen. Smith. When the time came for her to exhibit similar leadership and courage, however, I and many others believe Sen. Collins faltered.
Though she would express concern as President Trump ran amok, Collins never truly risked her status to stand firm for this great republic in a new, alarming hour of need.
Yes, she once voted to convict him after an impeachment trial, but Collins spent his second term avoiding any serious confrontation with him — while making nice with even Trump’s most extreme supporters in Maine. I would like to understand why.

title: Indiana carries out first of 3 US executions taking place on single day
text:
(AP) - An Indiana man who admitted killing his girlfriend’s two children was executed early Thursday in the first of three lethal injections scheduled for the same day in the U.S.
Jeffrey Weisheit killed the children, ages 8 and 5, by setting fire to his girlfriend’s house in the Evansville area in 2010.
Weisheit died at the Indiana State Prison in Michigan City. The lethal injection started just after midnight and he was pronounced dead at 12:45 a.m., according to Noelle Russell, Indiana Department of Correction chief communications officer.
She said Weisheit’s final meal was barbecue ribs and he had no final words.
Florida and Alabama were also set to carry out executions Thursday, which would mark the second time this year that three people in the U.S. would be put to death on the same day.
It will be Florida’s 19th execution this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis — matching a record set by the state in 2025 — but the first this year in Indiana.
The death penalty has faced renewed scrutiny following the September failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee, although courts have rejected efforts to halt other executions since she survived two lethal doses of pentobarbital.
Lawyers had asked for a life sentence for Weisheit
Lawyers wanted Indiana Republican Gov. Mike Braun to allow Weisheit, 50, to undergo brain scans in an effort to reinforce their argument that he has a history of head injuries and mental health problems. Braun declined, and he also turned down a request to reduce the sentence to life in prison.
Weisheit’s latest objection centered on the state’s planned use of lethal drugs purchased from a pharmacy that is facing a disciplinary hearing next week at the Indiana Pharmacy Board. The Indiana Department of Correction said that it’s confident “in our ability to humanely carry out” the execution.
Following the execution, Braun issued a brief statement noting Weisheit’s case was reviewed many times by state and federal courts.
“These reviews have never resulted in an overturned sentence,” he said. “Today, Weisheit’s sentence has been carried out as ordered by the court.”
Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said that the execution provided “long-awaited justice for Alyssa Lynch and her brother Caleb, two innocent children whose lives were stolen in an act of unspeakable cruelty.”
Florida on the verge of tying last year’s execution record
In Florida, Jesse Guardado confessed and quickly pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing a 75-year-old woman inside her Walton County home in 2004 before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other valuables to support his drug habit. She had helped him get a job and housing.
A federal appeals court in 2024 said that Guardado, now 64, had received a “full and fair” hearing during the death penalty phase of his case.
Florida has carried out more than half the 32 total executions in the U.S. so far this year. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said that his goal is to bring justice to families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out.
Alabama man convicted of killings when he was 19
Michael Taylor, 54, faces execution in Alabama, 35 years after fatally beating an older couple with a metal bar during a robbery in their Gadsden home. Police arrested the 19-year-old Taylor with the victims’ Cadillac, an hour away in Birmingham. The execution would be the state’s third this year.
Death penalty opponents had urged Republican Gov. Kay Ivey to reduce Taylor’s sentence to life in prison, noting his age and immaturity at the time of the killings. She declined.
“If the state kills Michael, it is not the 19-year-old who made the worst mistake of his life who it kills. But the mature, well-respected, God-fearing man sitting in that cell today,” said Esther Brown of Project Hope to Abolish the Death Penalty.
The state plans to execute Taylor by lethal injection after a judge declared a nitrogen gas method unconstitutional. His attorneys objected to the last-minute switch to lethal injection since he selected nitrogen gas as his method several years ago, but a judge ruled against Taylor.
____
Fischer reported from Fort Lauderdale, Florida and Chandler from Montgomery, Alabama. Associated Press reporter Ed White contributed from Detroit.

title: Machias fire chief arrested on OUI charge while responding to emergency call
text:
The Machias fire chief was arrested Halloween night after allegedly responding to an emergency call while intoxicated.
Fire Chief Joseph Thompson Sr., 68, was placed on paid administrative leave Sunday following the incident, according to Town Manager Sarah Craighead-Dedmon.
Thompson was booked in Washington County Jail late Saturday evening on one charge of operating under the influence, according to a jail dispatcher. He paid $60 to be bonded out just after 3 a.m. Sunday.
Thompson, who has been a member of the town’s fire department since 2004, is also an EMT and previously served as fire chief of the Jonesboro-Roque Bluffs volunteer fire department, according to the Machias ambulance service’s Facebook page.
Thompson was promoted to fire chief in June 2025 after longtime Chief Joey Dennison resigned, according to a town Facebook post.
Thompson responded to a vehicle-pedestrian crash Halloween evening along Dublin Street in Machias, according to Washington County sheriff’s Chief Deputy Mike Crabtree.
It was not clear on Thursday why Thompson was suspected of being under the influence of alcohol after he arrived at the crash scene. Crabtree said he did not have information on that part of the investigation.
The crash Thompson was responding to, which is under investigation by Maine State Police, left a 56-year-old man with serious injuries, requiring a LifeFlight transport to Bangor. The man is now stable, according to a Machias police dispatcher.
The Washington County Sheriff’s Office arrested Thompson so as not to involve town personnel, Crabtree said, adding that he assumed officers breathalyzed Thompson at the scene.
The case against Thompson is now with the Washington County district attorney’s office, Crabtree said.
The arrest and administrative leave comes days after the Machias Select Board approved three new EMT positions, ensuring the town’s ambulance station is fully staffed, according to The Maine Monitor. Demand on Machias ambulances is expected to jump after the recent shuttering of the volunteer-run ambulance service roughly 25 miles away in Dennysville.
The Machias Fire Department will be overseen by three firefighters during Thompson’s leave, which has no specified end date, according to Craighead-Dedmon, who wouldn’t comment further on the reason for Thompson’s paid leave, adding it was a “personnel matter.” The town manager confirmed that Thompson is still fire chief.
Thompson did not immediately respond to a Facebook message Thursday morning from the Bangor Daily News.

title: More than one in three Americans think debt for the latest phone is worth it
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — More than one in three Americans think it is worth putting a new phone on a credit card and taking on debt to get the latest model, according to a new WalletHub survey.
The same survey found almost nine out of 10 people say new phones are overpriced. Nearly half say they would feel inferior using a budget cell phone plan.
John Kiernan, managing editor of WalletHub, said the conflicting results show the phone is still seen as a status symbol.
“A lot of it has to do with keeping up with appearances and presenting a certain image to others,” Kiernan said. “For example, 32% of people say someone who always has the latest iPhone is quote unquote rich, and a lot of us want to give off that impression whether or not it’s true.”
Kiernan also said that because phones can do so much, having the latest model is sometimes more about keeping up with technology for work.
For people trying to save, Kiernan’s first suggestion is to shop around.
“Look into what kind of option you have from phone carriers and phone plans,” Kiernan said. “A lot of times if you switch from one carrier to another you can get a new phone and maybe a bunch of other devices as well.”
Kiernan also said buyers can choose the model behind the latest phone. It will not be the newest, but it could be more affordable. He said researching bundled services may also lead to a good deal on a new phone.

title: Artemis II punched holes in atmosphere and affected GPS systems, study says
text:
Artemis II punched holes in atmosphere and affected GPS systems, study says
A study says that NASA's Artemis II mission ripped through the upper atmosphere so fast that it punched a hole in the ionosphere, affecting GPS monitoring systems.
Related video above: Recovery team welcomes Artemis II crew back to Earth
The new study from the Department of Earth Sciences at National Cheng Kung University in Taiwan studied Artemis II's takeoff for disruptions to the atmosphere.
The researchers say that Artemis II's rocket and Orion capsule actually produced three different disturbances to the ionosphere. The ionosphere is part of Earth's upper atmosphere and is mostly made up of charged particles, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. It's where many satellites used for communication orbit the Earth, because the ionosphere reflects and modifies radio waves used for communication. The ionosphere is also the layer of our atmosphere where auroras form.
The study says the three disturbances occurred due to the rocket launch and later the Orion capsule's orbital maneuver engines.
"This is the first time a single space mission produced such multiple ionospheric disturbances over the same region," the researchers wrote.
The scientists studied samples of Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) and Global Positioning System (GPS) observations around the time of the launch. It's known that any effect on the ionosphere can affect these systems, which are relied on by everything from basic GPS to self-driving cars.
The study also noted that this has been known to happen before.
"The ionosphere is often disturbed during rocket or missile launches, causing anthropogenic or human-made space weather," the researchers wrote. The disturbances were noted as far back as the 1970s, after the Apollo missions and the 1973 launch of the Skylab space station.
The discovery of how specifically a new mission like Artemis II, which sent humans into space farther than ever before, affects the ionosphere and GPS satellites is valuable knowledge to space agencies like NASA. Further study of human-made space weather would assist space agencies and astronauts if they plan to return to the moon, and beyond.
The study still requires peer review and was published preliminarily in the journal Geophysical Research Letters.

title: US Department of Justice must be reorganized
text:
In 1870, Congress created the Department of Justice and organized it under the executive branch. The department received general direction from the president, but developed its own norms and procedures and functioned somewhat independently, and to a large degree, apolitically.
Through a series of disastrous appointments of attorneys general and Supreme Court decisions favoring executive power, the Justice Department is now the political prosecution arm of the chief executive. It has been claimed to be so by both political parties. It does not matter whether one party is more at fault, here, than the other. The breaking of the norms of non-political behavior and rational jurisprudence will be extremely corrosive to our republic.
Since Congress organized the Justice Department, it can reorganize it — with a presidential signature or an overridden veto. I suggest the department be reorganized to report to an evenly balanced, bipartisan congressional committee with statutory guardrails solidifying its historical norms and procedures. I believe this will discourage the department’s use by either party to harass political opponents. This is only one step toward setting our democracy on track for the future, and I believe it is one that both political parties can get behind.
Joel Lee
Belfast

title: Trump's lawyers to appear before appeals court as he fights hush money conviction
text:
Court weighs Trump's appeal in the Stormy Daniels hush money case
New York appeals judges grilled President Donald Trump’s lawyers and prosecutors Thursday about his bid to erase his historic hush money conviction, but the court didn’t signal how or when it would rule.
The judges delved into legal theory, presidential immunity and some evidence in Trump's 2024 trial. Convicted of 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to obscure a $130,000 payment to adult film performer Stormy Daniels, Trump denies any wrongdoing. He has turned to state and federal courts in hopes of unwinding the verdict.
Trump, who denounced the case on social media as recently as September, didn't attend Thursday's court session.
Much of the back-and-forth focused on prosecutors' theory that the hush money was meant to keep unflattering information about Trump away from the electorate before the 2016 vote, and that it amounted to an illegal campaign contribution under the Federal Election Campaign Act.
Trump lawyer Robert Giuffra Jr. told the judges that Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg's office has no place tying a case to a federal election law.
“We think it’s the most obvious ground for reversal,” he said.
Prosecutors argued that they weren’t prosecuting an alleged federal campaign finance offense, but rather presenting it as a factor underlying what they claim was a Trump-orchestrated conspiracy.
“So are you relying upon FECA in order to prove your falsifying business records (charge)?” Justice Troy Webber asked.
“Only partially,” replied Bragg's appeals chief, Steven Wu, adding that it was “important only to show that the purpose for the falsifying business records here was to conceal that conspiracy.”
Judges drill down on question about White House conversations
The appeal also concerns whether jurors should have been allowed to hear testimony about supposed White House workflow and conversations — some with then-Communications Director Hope Hicks — and even Trump social media posts during his first term. His lawyers cite presidential immunity for official acts, and they argue his official conduct included responding to the Daniels drama once it became public in 2018.
“Ms. Hicks was serving as a White House official,” talking with the president about how to respond to press inquiries that implicitly concerned his fitness for office, Giuffra told the appeals judges.
Wu countered later: “In this conversation, they were not speaking about a press response. ... The president was talking to her about his private opinion.”
The appeals judges pressed both sides about the matter and the specifics of Hicks' testimony. She told jurors that she asked Trump how he wanted to respond, but as for what he said, she testified only that he expressed relief that the Daniels story hadn't emerged during the campaign.
Bragg's office contends that all the White House-related evidence was fair game. The conversations were “unofficial conduct,” some of the other evidence was public record, and some was a general description of office practices, prosecutors say. They maintain that even if some of the evidence should have been excluded, its admission was a “harmless error” that doesn't warrant overturning a conviction that rested on “a mountain” of other proof against Trump.
Justice Bahaati E. Pitt-Burke wondered aloud about that.
“If you take all of those things cumulatively, right, and there’s a problem with this evidence, there’s a problem with this evidence, at what point ... does it stop being harmless error and turn into something else?” she asked.
“It would have to be a lot more than there was in this case,” Wu responded.
Trump's lawyers also have argued the case was political
While the appeal turns on complex legal disputes, political overtones aren’t hard to find. The very first paragraph of one of the Trump team’s court filings contended that the case was the flimsy product of “immense political pressure” on a Democratic prosecutor to go after Trump — rhetoric that echoes the Republican president’s own oft-repeated claims in the court of public opinion.
The trial involved $130,000 that Daniels got from Trump's then-fixer and lawyer, Michael Cohen, weeks before the 2016 election. The money bought, for a time, her silence about an alleged sexual encounter with the married Trump a decade earlier. He says that nothing sexual happened between them.
Trump's company reimbursed Cohen in 2017, logging those payments as legal expenses.
Trump's lawyers argue there’s only “weak” evidence that he even knew about Cohen’s dealings at the time. His trial attorneys also said that payments to Cohen were indeed legal expenses, and that any hush money expended on Trump's behalf wasn't hidden campaign spending, just an effort to avoid embarrassing his family.
The distinction matters because, under New York law, falsifying business records isn't a felony unless it's done with an intent to commit or conceal a separate crime.
While pursuing his state appeal, Trump also has been trying to shift the case to federal court and have it dismissed on immunity grounds. A federal judge said no — for the third time — in August. Trump's attorneys are appealing that decision, with arguments set for Nov. 16.

title: Rockland Man Arrested in Connection to Damariscotta Hit-and-Run
text:
The Damariscotta Police Department arrested a person in connection with a hit-and-run crash that seriously injured a 65-year-old female bicyclist at the intersection of Main Street and Biscay Road in Damariscotta on the morning of Wednesday, Nov. 4.
In a Thursday, Nov. 5 press release, Damariscotta Police Chief Erik Josephson identified John Barczak, 67, of Rockland, as the driver. Barczak was arrested without incident at approximately 4 p.m. on Nov. 4 and transported to Two Bridges Regional Jail in Wiscasset.
Barczak was charged with elevated aggravated assault, reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon, and leaving the scene of an accident involving serious bodily injury.
The vehicle, later found at a local business, was identified as a red Toyota Tacoma by Damariscotta Police Officer William Smith using physical evidence, surveillance footage, and vehicle-related information. Smith then identified Barczak as the driver.
According to a Nov. 4 Facebook post from the Damariscotta Police Department, a 911 call was made to the Lincoln County Communications Center at approximately 5:26 a.m. advising that a woman on a bicycle had been struck by a vehicle, which had then fled the scene by the time emergency responders arrived.
The woman was transported by Central Lincoln County Ambulance Service to MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital in Damariscotta for treatment. Due to the severity of her injuries, she was later transported Maine Medical Center in Portland for further treatment.
The Damariscotta Police Department was assisted by the Damariscotta Fire Department, Lincoln County District Attorney’s Office, and Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office responded to the scene.
This is an ongoing story and will be updated as more information is provided.

title: UMaine offers retirement incentives to faculty to help reduce budget shortfall
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - The University of Maine is offering voluntary retirement incentives to eligible faculty members to help close a projected $19 million budget shortfall for Fiscal Year 2028.
This week, UMaine notified 158 faculty members at the university’s flagship and Machias campuses that they are eligible for a special retirement incentive. The incentive includes a one-time payment equal to 100% of the faculty member’s base annual salary if they retire on Sept. 1, 2027.
Faculty members must be at least 55 years old as of Nov. 1 and have provided at least 10 years of full-time equivalent service to the university to be eligible.
The deadline to sign up is Jan. 2, 2027.
The payouts will be funded through a $6 million commitment made by the UMaine System. Some of those funds will go to a separate retirement incentive being offered to faculty at the University of Maine at Farmington.
Effect on the budget
The university said the number of staffers who accept the buyout will determine what its draft fiscal year 2028 budget looks like, and what additional cuts need to be made to close the gap. The university has previously announced plans to cut $10 million from the academic budget, and an additional $6 million from the non-academic budget.
UMaine officials said at a Monday budget meeting that it is their top priority for the coming weeks to come up with a plan to resolve the outstanding $3 million deficit.
In the announcement, the university stressed that they are one of many higher education institutions in the country that are grappling with funding gaps, citing major layoffs at University of Oregon and University of Utah.

title: Harmeet Dhillon exits after radical overhaul of Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Harmeet Dhillon, a conservative attorney who oversaw a radical reshaping of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, celebrated the mass departures of career lawyers and spearheaded sweeping investigations into elite universities, said Thursday that she had resigned from her post.
Dhillon had been a powerful and divisive figure inside President Donald Trump’s Justice Department since her confirmation last year as assistant attorney general, where she dramatically changed the direction of a division created during the country’s Civil Rights Movement to protect the rights of minorities.
“We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women and girls’ sports, and so much more,” Dhillon said in a social media post announcing her departure, using the acronym for diversity, equity and inclusion. She called serving in the position “the honor of a lifetime.”
Though the resignation was announced on the heels of midterm elections in which Democrats swept the House and Senate in a startling rebuke of Trump, Dhillon said in an interview with Fox News Digital that she had made the decision to depart weeks earlier but was asked by the White House to remain in her post until after the elections. She said she wanted to return to the private sector and had not been asked to resign.
“My decision, my choice,” she said.
As leader of the division, Dhillon drew fierce criticism from former Justice Department attorneys who accused her of abandoning its traditional civil rights enforcement mission in favor of conservative causes. More than three quarters of the unit’s workforce at the beginning of Trump’s second term have left — a move Dhillon has called the “biggest single personnel self-purge in DOJ history.”
She accused the past administration of pursuing a misguided liberal agenda and welcomed the departures of attorneys not aligned with the Trump administration’s priorities, saying in an interview last year with conservative pundit Glenn Beck that “the job here is to enforce the federal civil rights laws — not woke ideology.”
During her tenure, the Civil Rights Division scrapped police reform settlements and investigations and launched probes into universities the Trump administration saw as improperly prioritizing diversity and inclusion, discriminating against white applicants in the admissions process and failing to crack down on antisemitic conduct on campus.
Her pressure campaign against schools led to numerous settlements, and in one case, the resignation of the president of the University of Virginia. She also led an effort to pressure states to turn over detailed voter records despite repeated court losses.
Attorney General Todd Blanche wrote in a social media post announcing Dhillon’s departure that she had led the division with “conviction” and “defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor.”
“The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors,” Blanche wrote.
But Stacey Young, a former Civil Rights Division attorney who now leads a network of Justice Department alumni, called her “the most destructive, lawless and hateful” head of the division in department history.
“Americans’ civil rights don’t enforce themselves. For almost 70 years, the Civil Rights Division brought to fruition the civil rights laws that Americans demanded,” Young said in an emailed statement Thursday. ”Dhillon decimated it.”
Dhillon, who was born in India and immigrated with her Sikh family to the United States as a child, was a prominent figure in conservative legal and political circles well before being tapped to her Justice Department position.
As a California lawyer, she was involved in numerous high-profile causes and legal fights, including challenging that state’s stay-at-home order during the coronavirus pandemic and filing a lawsuit that accused the state of failing to verify citizenship for voter registration.
She launched a bid to become chair of the Republican National Committee but lost in January 2023 to Ronna McDaniel in a race that exposed fierce internal divisions in the party.
Dhillon and her law firm also represented Trump himself as a House committee investigating the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol issued a subpoena for his testimony. The panel ultimately abandoned that effort and wrapped up its work without forcing the issue, prompting Dhillon to boast on the social media platform X that the committee had “waved the white flag.”

title: Founder Michael Curless returns to Acadia Fire, launches soccer academy
text:
ELLSWORTH — Michael Curless, the founder of Acadia Fire Football Club, has returned as the club’s chief executive officer and a member of its board of directors. Mark Hudhammer will continue as the Director of Coaching. Curless will oversee the club’s soccer philosophy and launch Curless Soccer Academy, a developmental program open to all children ages 6-11, beginning Jan. 4 at Acadia Fire Soccer Center.
The Academy is built to offer the highest level of soccer training with the lowest level of pressure and travel. Children attend two professionally coached training sessions each week and a Saturday practice game, with few tournaments and no regular league standings. Training focuses on ball skills, athletic movement, and positional soccer tactics taught through small-sided games. Every child is welcome. There is no tryout, and financial assistance is available.

title: Columnist and Filmmaker Complete Guest Lineup for ‘An Addition of One’
text:
“Waldoboro Voices” creator Rebecca Cooney and documentary filmmaker Ian Cheney will join playwright and performer Shannon A. Mullen onstage after performances of “An Addition of One” at The Waldo Theatre, completing the lineup of guests for postshow discussions.

title: 'She was disappointed': Sen. Collins campaign manager details election loss
text:
'She was disappointed': Sen. Collins campaign manager details election loss
Democrat Troy Jackson will head to Washington next year as Maine’s next senator, securing a major win for his party but an upset for Republicans.
Sen. Collins’ campaign manager and longtime chief of staff detailed the behind-the-scenes of Tuesday night’s loss to WMTW's media partner, WABI.
“She was disappointed, but she was proud of everything that she had done and proud of everything the staff had done, and just told us to hold our heads high.” Steve Abbott said.
Collins did not address the crowd after conceding Tuesday, but did release a statement.
“It has been the honor of my life to serve the people of Maine in the United States Senate. I'm proud of all I have been able to accomplish for our state and for our country in the past 30 years,” Collins said.
The results sent shockwaves through the state, with Democrats thrilled for a victory and Republicans devastated to lose a longtime senator.
"I was very shocked, actually, that Sen. Collins didn't win," said moderate Democrat Joe Carroll. "I kind of expected her tenure to kind of pull her through."
Jackson defeated Collins with just about three months to campaign. Jackson was quickly chosen as the democratic nominee after Graham Platner dropped out due to a sexual assault allegation he denies.
In his victory speech in Portland, Jackson told supporters what he wants to accomplish once he’s sworn in, including Medicare for All and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Jackson also addressed voters who did not get the election results they wanted.
"To every Mainer who voted for (Collins), you know you can count on me to be your senator now,” Jackson said.
The senator leaves Washington with a plethora of accomplishments to show for it. Collins secured federal funding for hundreds of projects in Maine as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee.
Jackson said during the debate on Maine’s Total Coverage that he’s looking to get on as many committees as possible and wants to sit on the same powerful appropriations committee Collins currently chairs.
“I'm sure that he'll be able to bring some resources to the state,” UMaine political science professor Mark Brewer said. “Will it be at the level that Susan Collins was able to bring immediately? Probably not.”
Collins has made it clear she will work to ensure a smooth transition for Jackson’s team.
With a major win under his belt, Jackson is set to attend orientation to familiarize himself with Senate procedures and traditions.

title: Man who allegedly threatened Maine university gets 10 months on separate federal charge
text:
A Cornish man who allegedly said he had the urge to set off an explosive at the University of New England was sentenced on Wednesday to 10 months in prison for a separate incident involving a threatening social media post.
Blake Tibbetts, 24, pleaded guilty on April 27 to a federal charge of transmitting a threatening interstate communication.
That charge stemmed from a post Tibbetts made on the social platform X, “in which he used a racial epithet in an angry exchange with another X user and threatened to pay ‘a visit VERY soon’ to the user’s ‘kind,’ sending ‘them’ his ‘condolences.’” according to court records.
The exchange happened in the replies to a post by political analyst Chuck Todd, who wrote: “Being angry and staying angry is a choice. Giving grace is a choice. Choose wisely. Don’t let the algorithms fool you, in the real world, folks choose grace,” according to a screenshot in court records.
On Sept. 14, 2025, Tibbetts was at a restaurant in Cornish when he said he had the urge to initiate an explosive device with the intent to harm others, specifically on a university campus, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office.
The next day, Maine State Police found Tibbetts in Biddeford. Tibbetts allegedly confirmed that he made threatening statements while he was at the restaurant. In a statement he said that he “started having unstable emotions and confided in [name redacted] about having an unshakable desire to hurt people,” according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office.
State police said at the time that Tibbetts was charged with terrorizing, criminal use of explosives and criminal attempt to cause a catastrophe.
Federal and state law enforcement used warrants to search Tibbetts’ home and phones and were able to connect him to the threatening social media post that was the basis for the federal charge.

title: Wildfire response enters new phase in White Mountain National Forest
text:
Firefighters are transitioning to the offensive in their fight against a wildfire in White Mountain National Forest.
By midmorning Thursday, the U.S. Forest Service estimated that the Wild River Fire encompassed 856 acres.
The Forest Service first responded to the blaze roughly 7 miles southeast of Gorham, New Hampshire, on Sunday afternoon. It’s located on the northwest side of the Wild River in Coos County, New Hampshire, just west of Mount Hastings in Maine’s Oxford County.
The fire’s easternmost edge was roughly a half-mile from the state line as of Thursday. Its northern edge is about 3 miles from Shelburne, New Hampshire, where a public meeting on the fire was held Thursday night.
Officials initially estimated the fire, which is primarily burning leaves and other forest litter, at nearly 300 acres on Monday and more than 375 acres on Tuesday. After a rapid overnight spread, which the Forest Service largely blamed on ongoing drought conditions, officials estimated the fire grew to nearly 1,000 acres by Wednesday morning.
But the response grew alongside it, from 40 assigned personnel on Monday to nearly 90 by Wednesday night. The increased manpower and uptick in air support, which includes helicopters and drones, have helped firefighters make some progress and more precisely map what they’re up against, resulting in the revised estimate of 856 acres.
The source of the wildfire is still under investigation, but the Forest Service believes it was likely human-caused. The area of the fire was officially closed to the public on Wednesday.
‘CRITICAL PHASE’
Firefighters started on the defensive while mounting resources throughout the week.
Crews initially focused on setting up fire lines and cutting vegetation to limit the fire’s spread, Sarah Hankens, a spokesperson for the Forest Service at White Mountain National Forest, said earlier this week. The leap from fewer than 400 acres Tuesday to nearly 1,000 acres Wednesday was through mostly inaccessible terrain, she said.
But since Wednesday, the Forest Service and assisting agencies have been shifting to the offensive, and the plan for Thursday was to suppress the blaze by air and follow through on the ground.
“Multiple aviation assets will be utilized to moderate fire spread near the head of the fire and suppress any known or potential fire spots,” Hankens said in an update Thursday. “During periods of higher humidity and favorable weather, firefighters may take advantage of opportunities to conduct direct attack operations, working directly along the fire’s edge to strengthen containment and extinguish active fire.”
Maine is also lending a hand. The Maine Forest Rangers said in a social media post Thursday that several rangers and one helicopter have assisted in suppression efforts.
Hankens Thursday did not provide an updated containment percentage, which had been at 11% since Monday. However, she indicated progress has been made on that front, noting “containment objectives have been achieved” in some areas, allowing “mop-up activities” to move forward.
“This critical phase of suppression helps secure fire perimeters, reduce the likelihood of flare-ups, and move the incident closer to full containment,” Hankens said.
However, she noted that crews still face an uphill battle through steep and rocky terrain, and that persisting drought conditions in the region have also posed a challenge.
‘TURNING POINT’
Forest Service officials explained the response for community members at Thursday’s public meeting in Shelburne.
They said resources have come from near and far: The response has included local fire departments and state agencies, as well as rangers and apparatus from across the country.
Ryan Hughes, a wildfire prevention specialist with the Forest Service and the Wild River Fire’s incident commander, said “this is a hard time of year” to fight a wildfire because the agency’s seasonal employees are off until next year.
“Good news is, it’s not fire season out West anymore, so the resources that are still working are available to us,” he said.
Hughes said the main challenge for firefighters has been access. Working along the Wild River and adjacent brooks, firefighters have been forced to make river crossings and have since created an “improvised bridge.”
Hughes noted that the area went about three weeks without rain prior to the fire. Some precipitation in the past few days has helped, he said, but it was relatively light.
Officials also recognized the concern the fire has created for residents in the region.
“I grew up here in Shelburne,” said Josh Sjostrom, district ranger for the national forest’s Androscoggin Ranger District, noting he recognized people in the audience. He said a wildfire of this size in the area and the reciprocal response “can be jarring.”
However, officials expressed confidence in getting the fire contained soon, and said the lack of spread in recent days is a promising sign. Hughes called the transition to offense a “turning point.”
Officials also said they’ve been focusing their efforts on the north and west edges — the direction it most recently spread — and have long-term suppression and monitoring plans in place.

title: Hundreds place ‘I voted’ stickers at memorials of Alex Pretti, Renee Good
text:
MINNEAPOLIS, Minn. (KARE) — Hundreds of people placed “I Voted” stickers at the memorials of Alex Pretti and Renee Good to mark Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Pretti and Good were fatally shot in Minneapolis by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents earlier this year during Operation Metro Surge.
Stickers at Pretti’s memorial
“We can’t change what happened, but we’ll keep fighting,” Caitlyn Hren-Borger said.
Hren-Borger, a Minneapolis resident, visits Pretti’s memorial often. This time, she left an “I Voted” sticker.
“Because Alex couldn’t vote, and it’s really important to be able to make our voices heard,” Hren-Borger said.
Hren-Borger said the memorial was “just really beautiful” as more stickers were placed.
Dan Weston, a visitor to the Pretti memorial, was among the hundreds who placed stickers there.
“It still feels like we have power,” Weston said. “It felt like we paid homage to change, and we won’t forget him or Renee or anyone else.”
Stickers at Good’s memorial
Peg Baier, a visitor to the Good memorial, wanted her sticker to be near Good’s.
“She can’t vote, but we can,” Baier said. “It’s one meaningful thing that we can do in her name.”
Carol Ohana, another visitor to the Good memorial, said the stickers give her hope.
“It gives me hope because it shows the good side of people,” Ohana said.
Baier said, “There’s so much hope and so much diversity coming back, and at the same time, this is Minnesota, and we’re still grieving. I want to think that her life wasn’t for nothing, that at least she became a focal point to galvanize people and get us out to vote.”
Visits to both memorials
“This is the best I’ve felt in a very long time today,” Jonathan Fondell said.
Fondell, a Minneapolis resident, visited both memorials.
“It seemed like the best way to memorialize them is to just sort of come and visit and say, ‘Hey, this is what I’m voting against, things like this happening,’” he said.
For those who placed them, the stickers represent hope.
“Our community is never going to be the same, but we’re here together,” Hren-Borger said.

title: Celebrating 50 Years of Early Bird History
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
For around five decades, shoppers have donned pajamas and mingled in downtown Damariscotta before the sun rises.
The Early Bird Sale, a staple of the Twin Villages area, has grown and changed since its roots in a handful of Bath stores.
Renys was opened in Damariscotta in October 1949 by Robert “Bob” Reny. It expanded to 19 stores in Maine, including one in Bath.
John Reny, R.H. Reny’s son and the current president of Renys, said the idea for the Damariscotta early bird sale came from the store’s Bath location. Three Bath stores held a yearly sale from 6-9 a.m. on the first Saturday of November, also the first day of hunting season. Reny said he thinks this was a purposeful choice.

title: A day of honor
Melania Trump to bring Russian and Ukrainian representatives to White House this week
text:
Melania Trump to bring Russian and Ukrainian representatives to White House this week
First lady Melania Trump will bring representatives from Russia and Ukraine to the White House on Thursday, after announcing a ceasefire in the city of Oleshky last month.
“First lady Melania Trump will personally bring representatives of Russia and Ukraine, two nations actively at war, together at the White House,” the first lady’s office said on Tuesday, touting the limited ceasefire as an “unprecedented diplomatic initiative by an American first lady.”
Trump will host Ukraine’s ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova, according to Ukrainian and Russian authorities.
Lubinets and Lantratova have met before, most recently during the Oleshky ceasefire last week. Neither has been involved in top-level negotiations with the U.S. delegations before, but they are expected to be accompanied by officials who have.
The Kremlin announced on Wednesday that Lantratova would be accompanied by Russian President Vladimir Putin’s special envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who is an experienced negotiator. Ukrainian media reported that the lawmaker and negotiator David Arakhamia would be joining Lubinets for the meeting.
Speaking to CNN while en route to Washington DC, Dmitriev said that a key motivating factor in his work as an interlocutor was his “deep belief in cooperation between the US and Russia.”
“I’m focused on US-Russia relations in general and if there’s a humanitarian situation to solve, I’m always trying to help,” he said.
Most recently, Marc Beckman, senior adviser to the first lady, thanked Dmitriev for his “leadership in establishing and sustaining the ceasefire in Oleshky.” Last month, US special envoy Steve Witkoff introduced Dmitriev to the freed US citizen Stephen Hubbard — classified by the US State Department as “wrongfully detained” — saying that Dmitriev “had a lot to do with [the release] happening.”
Trump, who will also deliver remarks on the limited ceasefire, has kept a much lower profile during her husband’s second term. But while she’s eschewed some of the more traditional roles of the job, she’s engaged behind the scenes in more substantive policy work.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Wednesday that he’d awarded the first lady the Order of Princess Olga, a Ukrainian civil decoration. It celebrates her “significant personal contributions” to humanitarian support for Ukraine, and her “active human rights and charitable work aimed at rescuing Ukrainian children and citizens.”
Trump announced on Oct. 23 that she had secured a localized ceasefire to facilitate the humane evacuation of elderly residents from Oleshky. The limited ceasefire began on Oct. 27 and concluded on Sunday. Hundreds of people were evacuated from Oleshky and returned to Ukraine, including one man who hadn’t seen his wife for 1,711 days.
The humanitarian situation had become so dire in Oleshky that some residents were forced to eat grass and weeds without access to medicine, clean water or electricity, Andrii Sybiha, Ukraine’s foreign minister, said last month.
Trump’s office said that she worked directly with Ukrainian and Russian leadership as the “exclusive intermediary” through channels she previously established while working to reunite children separated from their families during the war.
“The mission was a success, delivering critical aid to the region and enabling the evacuation of nearly 800 people,” Trump posted on X, adding that she hoped Oleshky “serves as a foundation for lasting peace between both nations.”
The first lady’s office said last month that the circumstances of Oleshky came to her attention during a private discussion at the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York.
CNN previously reported that Pope Leo discussed the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky on a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin earlier in October while in the hospital recovering from lung cancer surgery, according to the Vatican. The Kremlin said that Putin “supported” the Vatican’s intention to help alleviate the conditions.

title: South Portland residents rejected a new police station. What happens to the land now?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
South Portland voters on Tuesday defeated a measure calling for constructing new public safety buildings to replace the aging police and fire stations, but it’s now unclear what happens to the Cash Corner property purchased by the city for the new police station.
The city hasn’t made a decision about alternative uses or next steps for the parcel at 279 Main St. according to Shara Dee, the city’s communications officer.
It would need to be used for a police related purpose because a significant portion of the funding — $1.5 million of the $2.5 million purchase — came from police asset forfeiture funds, according to City Manager Scott Morelli. If the city opts to sell the property, it would need to return a portion of the proceeds back to that designated account.
“We anticipate those discussions will take place with the City Council as we consider the most responsible way to move forward,” Dee said.
Mayor Elyse Tipton announced that the city entered into a contract to acquire the old Walgreens on Main Street at a council meeting in early March. The purchase was finalized in May. The rejected bond included a new $44.35 million police station.
The purchase of the property did not increase property taxes, instead drawing upon the police asset forfeiture funds and $1 million from Tax Increment Financing funds.
City staff thought the 2.9 acre parcel would be the optimal spot for a new station.
A new police station would require 2.5 to 3 acres, according to a site fit analysis conducted by Colliers, a design team. The Cash Corner location would place law enforcement closer to the city’s west end.
The City Council previously planned to build the new police station on the field outside the old Mahoney Middle School, but when site work cost estimates came back higher than expected, councilors opted to look into other options. The site work at Mahoney alone would have cost more than $5 million.

title: Future voter arrives early: Woman goes into labor at polling place
text:
TOPEKA, Kan. (WIBW/Gray News) — Tessa Von Fange went into labor after a trip to the Shawnee County Elections Office in Kansas, where she went to vote.
Tessa Von Fange is a longtime voter. She said she has missed very few elections.
“I don’t think there are too many elections that I’ve missed,” Tessa Von Fange said. “So, especially as I’ve gotten older, I don’t miss them at all really.”
Labor begins during the trip
Tessa Von Fange thought her baby would be born after Election Day.
“I’m going to make it to that induction. I had already really thought I wasn’t going to have her before then,” Tessa Von Fange said.
Her husband, Chris Von Fange, said an election worker told him his wife was in labor.
“Shocked, I was overwhelmed,” Chris Von Fange said. “Just to hear from the election worker that your wife is in labor is like millions of questions.”
“I was 100% in denial until my water broke,” Tessa Von Fange added.
Baby’s name
The couple had already chosen the baby’s name before the trip.
“We had her name picked out already,” Tessa Von Fange said. “Her name is Morgan, but it did make me think, what would that be? If she were a boy, Chad. I thought that was funny.”
Message to voters
The Von Fanges said everyone should make time to vote.
“No matter what you have going on, there’s always a half-hour of your time that can be spent to go to a polling place to have your vote cast,” Chris Von Fange said.
Tessa Von Fange received a future voter sticker at the elections office.
“That was the only sticker I got, but I stuck it right on my belly and came to the hospital with it on,” she said.
Morgan was born at 1:16 a.m. on Nov. 3. She weighed 8 pounds, 1 ounce.

title: A lasting salute to veterans & military K-9s
text:
WRITTEN BY JOSHUA ARCHER
Over the summer, a young man from Aroostook County set out to earn Eagle Scout status by completing a community project to honor local veterans and the often overlooked K-9s who served.
After several years of hard work and with most of the necessary boxes ticked — merit badges, examples of leadership, etc. — Luke Gordon of Caribou had one final task to complete before he could submit to counsel that he was ready to earn the rank of Eagle Scout. All the 17-year-old scout had left was to organize and execute a community service project.
He set his sights on a small memorial park in Washburn, just outside where his troop, Troop 177, holds their regular meetings.
“I thought that it’d be beneficial and helpful because, Washburn, they might not have a lot, but what they do have is special,” Gordon said.
Gordon’s goal was to adorn Washburn’s Veterans Memorial Park with two new flag poles. One flag to honor Vietnam veterans and the other military working dogs.
“The Vietnam War was very big and controversial, and when I was looking at who I wanted to honor I saw the need to represent them at the park,” Gordon said. “And I think that the K-9s don’t get enough recognition for the tremendous amount of work they do.”
After multiple fundraisers, the three-month project pulled in upwards of $3,000 in donations and materials, thanks to the help of local businesses, fellow scouts, community members, family, and friends.
As Gordon worked on his service project, folks from around town who had either seen posts on social media about what he was up to or heard about it from loved ones were eager to walk right up to him and show their appreciation with words of thanks or by handing him cash.
“Family members of soldiers would walk up to me and be like, ‘Hey, I saw you on Facebook! My grandfather served and I wanna give you money! Thank you for what you’re doing!’ and they would hand me a $20 or a $50,” Gordon said.
He finished raising money, digging holes, pouring cement, and erecting the poles just days before Washburn’s annual August Festival, a time when folks come to celebrate the local area.
At the festival, in front of a large crowd of veterans and their families, Gordon raised the flags, and then stood before his accomplishment to read the names of 38 Aroostook County service members who died in the Vietnam war.
“I always thought Veterans Day was a time to appreciate the soldiers, but looking at it from the point I’m at today, after my project, it’s more than that. It’s a time of remembrance of all who served and what they sacrificed. All the people who died and even the ones who lived. They fought for our country, they fought for our freedom, and it’s good that they’re not being forgotten. And that years after, we’re still doing things like raising flags, holding dedications to remember their sacrifice, and the oath they gave to protect our country,” Gordon said.
With his Eagle Scout service project now complete, Gordon has submitted the final results to a district advancement committee. He said it could take some time to hear back while his efforts are under review, but he’s confident he’ll achieve Eagle Scout status before his 18th birthday next year.
“I just have to wait and be patient,” he said. “And after this project I’ll remember most of all the people who helped me and the impact it gave me, watching people during the festival look at the flags, talk about it, holding hands, that’s what I’ll remember.”

title: New Orleans blacksmith preserves centuries-old ironwork tradition
text:
NEW ORLEANS (Aging Untold) — In New Orleans, the city’s architecture is often framed in iron. Centuries of old balconies, fences and gates have survived fires and hurricanes.
At Andrew’s Welding and Blacksmith Shop, Darryl Reeves is one of the few who still carry on the tradition. His grandfather was a blacksmith as well.
Reeves remembers being shooed away as a boy from his grandfather’s shop, but the memory of the blacksmith stuck with him.
“We used to just pass through and just watch these guys beat on this metal with the sparks and all,” Reeves said. “I think that had a lot of influence with me enjoying to work with metal.”
Crafting iron by hand
Reeves said he loves taking a raw piece of metal and transforming it.
From iron hinges to hand-forged designs like metal leaves, Reeves makes what he needs, including his ironworking tools.
Reeves has restored historic ironwork throughout New Orleans, including the fence in front of the Cabildo, using plans dating back to the 1790s.
“That’s learning from the past. That’s given a conversation with the person that actually fabricated it,” Reeves said.
Training the next generation
A younger generation is now learning from Reeves.
His apprentice, Karina Roca, moved to New Orleans from Boston.
“Well, I’ve always secretly wanted to be an iron worker,” Roca said. “And then I saw a PBS program on Darryl Reeves over 10 years ago at this point, and I was like, ‘Yep, I’m going to study under that guy.’”
Roca, who is working on a master’s degree in historic preservation at Tulane, has been working in the blacksmith shop for five years.
“It works in so many ways to kind of keep this aesthetic of New Orleans alive,” Roca said. “It’s very Spanish. It’s very West African. It’s very French. So it’s sort of this symbol, this beacon of a space where all of these cultures have come together for centuries now.”
For Reeves, blacksmithing is more than bending metal. It’s preserving history, culture and the spirit of New Orleans, one hand-forged piece at a time.

title: House could vote next week to impeach Hegseth as GOP support wavers
text:
(CNN) - The House of Representatives could vote as soon as next week to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, weeks before the Democratic majority is sworn in.
The possible vote follows Republican losses in Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky) told CNN he plans to trigger a vote to impeach Hegseth when Congress returns next week.
Multiple GOP sources told CNN they expect it to pass.
Republicans point to Iran decision
Many Republicans want to blame Hegseth for convincing President Donald Trump to attack Iran with no exit strategy.
Republican strategists privately acknowledge the party’s problems extend beyond the war. Trump also is commander-in-chief, and the decision to attack was ultimately his.
Trump’s position
Many Republican lawmakers remain reluctant to break from Trump despite the message of disapproval voters sent to Washington.
White House insiders said Trump is supporting Hegseth and wants him to fight against impeachment.

title: Woman assaulted by home intruder defends her fiance, accused of planning the attack
text:
BUCKEYE, AZ (AZFamily/Gray News) — A woman who was attacked in Arizona last month defended her partner in court on Wednesday against accusations that he planned the attack online.
Police said the woman’s fiancé, 23-year-old Zarian Dyer, plotted the Oct. 16 attack with Adrian Ayala, 20, over Reddit.
She told a judge that it’s not true, despite police saying they have messages and other evidence tying Dyer to the plot.
“My partner was forced to deal with false accusations fabricated by the defendant during his frantic attempt to make excuses,” she told the court, referring to claims by Ayala that her partner sent him.
Court documents say Dyer told Ayala when to come, where to park and how to get inside. A prosecutor alleged Dyer wanted Ayala to FaceTime him during the attack. Police said the woman did not consent.
During the hearing, the victim broke down in tears, explaining what happened during the attack.
“My security sensor alerted me that my front door was opening,” she said. “Assuming it was my partner returning from bringing in groceries, my daughter and I walked to the door to assist him. Instead, I found a stranger at my door.”
She said Ayala asked to use her restroom. After she refused, she said he barged into her home and attacked her.
Ayala is also accused of kicking the woman’s 17-month-old daughter.
Ayala, who was arrested Oct. 17, is out of custody. A judge entered not guilty pleas on his behalf on five counts and kept his release conditions in place, including no contact with the victims.
The woman also described losing income and facing eviction since the arrests.
Dyer is still in custody with a bond set at $500,000.
