title: Once feared extinct, venomous primate found alive and well
text:
Once feared extinct, venomous primate found alive and well
A venomous primate — once feared extinct — is alive an well, a new study states.
The Bangka slow loris, a small primate once classified as possibly extinct, is still living on Indonesia’s Bangka Island, researchers report.
The species had not been recorded in scientific literature for decades, and the International Union for Conservation of Nature lists 1937 as the year it was last seen.
Related video above | ARCHIVE: Kentucky family adopts monkey in 1997
But new evidence from records kept by the Alobi Wildlife Rescue Center shows that the center rescued more than 90 Bangka slow lorises since 2015.
Researchers say 86 of the animals were later released on the island.
The rescue reports also show how often lorises turn up around people: among 43 animals rescued since 2021, 16 were found in houses or gardens, six were recovered from roads, and seven had burns consistent with electric shock.
They were hiding in plain site, officials said.
The findings provide strong evidence that the species is not extinct, but they do not establish how many remain or whether released animals survived.
The Bangka slow loris is critically endangered, and much of its forest habitat has been damaged or destroyed by tin mining, palm oil plantations and settlements, the new report states
Researchers recommend protecting habitat, monitoring releases and establishing a breeding program.
Like other slow lorises, the primate species is venomous. It can mix a secretion from glands near its elbows with saliva and deliver it through a bite.
The study’s authors recommend reassessing the species’ “possibly extinct” listing in light of the new evidence.

title: After taking control of Congress, Democrats vow major probes into Trump’s ‘tentacles of corruption’
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Corruption topped the list of concerns for voters who ousted Republicans and handed Democrats control of Congress in the midterm elections. Now, the newly empowered Democratic Party is putting the issue front and center as its leaders chart their course for investigations and policymaking.
Senior Democrats in both chambers of Congress have vowed to marshal the subpoena powers and larger investigative staffs that come with their soon-to-be majorities to probe what they say is the self-enrichment that President Donald Trump and people in his orbit have done at the public’s expense. The Republican president and his White House have long denied any wrongdoing.
House Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda to look at how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office — and Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who’s in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Trump for a third time.
Months ago, Jeffries tasked the ranking Democrats on the Oversight and Judiciary committees, Rep. Robert Garcia of California and Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, with leading the effort, as Democrats work to link the costs of public corruption to the affordability concerns hitting Americans’ pocketbooks.
“Lawyer up,” Garcia posted on X as election results favoring Democrats began coming in on Tuesday night.
The Senate is expected to conduct similar investigations.
“Americans want us to clean up corruption in government,” said Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., who is poised to return as Senate majority leader next year. “No American should have to make tradeoffs at the supermarket while Trump is making inside trades on the stock market.”
Investigation targets could include ICE raids, Epstein and DOGE
Garcia, the top Democrat on the Oversight and Government Reform Committee, has outlined five priorities, including Trump family business dealings, the administration’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations. Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the ranking Democrat on the Natural Resources Committee, said he wants to dig into Trump’s White House ballroom and other construction projects, as well as the Trump family’s role in mineral deals.
With the House majority comes an infusion of congressional committee staff and resources, and the effort is expected to be sprawling, involving House committees with authority to conduct oversight on Cabinet officials and the agencies they lead.
In the Senate, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., who is expected to become the chairman of the Homeland Security Committee’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, said his panel will want to look into Trump’s real estate projects around the nation’s capital and his crypto dealings with special envoy Steve Witkoff. Witkoff is a longtime ally who partnered with Trump on the president’s family cryptocurrency venture, World Liberty Financial.
“The tentacles of corruption reach deep in this administration, and they have added costs to everyday Americans,” Blumenthal said in an interview with The Associated Press on Wednesday. The senator added that he also wants hearings on ICE raids, the actions of the Department of Government Efficiency and Medicare plans he says are too restrictive and have cost some patients care.
Meanwhile, Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, who is in line to become Senate Finance Committee chairman, ticked off several investigative targets that he describes as part of an “accountability” agenda, including banks that he contends ignored red flags about the financial dealings of Epstein and pharmaceutical companies that have profited from their ties to the Trump administration.
“When I am chair, they will be forced to answer to the Senate Finance Committee for their role in hurting the American people and enabling Trump’s corruption,” Wyden said in a statement Wednesday.
The issue of corruption resonated for voters, The AP Voter Poll shows
Many U.S. voters in Tuesday’s elections expressed deep concerns about government corruption and the state of democracy, according to The AP Voter Poll, which surveyed more than 100,000 voters nationwide.
While roughly 4 in 10 voters said the economy was the top issue facing the country, about 3 in 10 said that “the state of democracy” was the top issue. About half of U.S. voters said government corruption was “crucial” to their vote for Congress, and most of those voters supported the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race, while about one-third said they voted for the Republican.
About 8 in 10 voters who said “the state of democracy” was the top issue facing the country supported the Democrat, while about 2 in 10 supported the Republican.
Older voters, those age 65 or older, were more likely than voters under 65 to say “the state of democracy” was the most important issue facing the country. About 4 in 10 older voters pointed to this as the nation’s top problem, compared with about 3 in 10 who said the economy. That view was reversed with younger voters, who were more likely to call the economy the top issue.
That explains why anti-corruption played such a central role in Democratic campaigns this cycle, with candidates accusing their Republican opponents of looking out for themselves or their donors rather than a broader constituency. They embraced stock trading bans and bans on former members of Congress becoming lobbyists and promised to be part of an effort to root out corruption.
Democrats’ challenge: Focusing on corruption without ignoring cost-of-living issues
In his public comments since his party lost the elections, Trump has taken a conciliatory tone toward Democrats, conceding that they “did a good job” in their campaigns as he’s tried to skirt personal blame for the GOP’s midterm thrashing. That could change as investigations ramp up.
“As the president has said, he’s willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said Wednesday. “If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people.”
Schumer insisted that congressional Democrats will be able to balance legislating on key issues, such as affordability, while launching investigations to target “rampant corruption.”
In a letter to Democratic lawmakers announcing his candidacy for House speaker, Jeffries said the “days of the House functioning like a wholly owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over.”
“The massive corruption the country has experienced from the Trump Cartel explains why very little is getting done to help everyday Americans,” Jeffries wrote as he promised to target price gouging and push for a stock trading ban for lawmakers. “That changes immediately.”
The challenge for Democrats will be to continue to tie corruption to the affordability issues that topped the list of concerns for voters.
The Congressional Integrity Project, an advocacy group initially created to combat Republican investigations into President Joe Biden’s Democratic administration, is now shifting its focus to help Democratic lawmakers make that connection. In a memo, the group urged congressional Democrats to trace the Trump administration’s actions to people in and outside government, as well as corporations, who may be profiting from those moves.
“Corruption is not just corruption,” said the group’s senior adviser, Jack Miller. “It is costing taxpayers and costing Americans in their everyday lives.”
Some Democratic lawmakers are already stressing that congressional investigations have to be directly tied to affordability issues, while urging restraint.
Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt., said that Democrats need to earn voters’ trust, and while investigations are an important part of the Democratic agenda, “we can’t turn this into just a vengeance tour.”
“We have to be careful, cautious and judicious about that,” Welch said.

title: Penobscot County taxes on track to increase under proposed 2027 budget
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Property taxes are on track to increase again in Penobscot County under a proposed 2027 county budget that saw no reductions following hours of review.
The county budget committee met for more than four hours in Bangor on Wednesday night, reviewing the proposed spending plan line-by-line without making any cuts.
A committee member told WABI that “there’s just no fat to cut.” Committee members identified operating the county jail in its current form as a major financial burden driving expenses.
The proposed $41.6 million budget represents an increase of approximately $6 million over last year. That difference equates to an estimated 23% tax hike for the county, following an increase of more than 15% last year.
Penobscot County commissioners are scheduled to take a final vote on the budget later this month.

title: Throwback Thursday
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - For 90 year old Bessie Higgins, age was never a reason to stop learning or creating. It’s the focus of this week’s Throwback Thursday with Brian Bouchard.
There’s an old saying that you’re never too old to learn something new, and Bessie Higgins was living proof of that. In this week’s Throwback Thursday, we dial the time machine back to 1987 where WAGM reporter Joe Prescott met Higgins, who was still taking art classes at the University of Maine at Presque Isle.
This is Bessie Higgins. At 90 years old, she is by far the senior student in this art class at the University of Maine in Presque Isle. She’s lived and worked in Aroostook County since 1928 and during that time has become well known for her paintings. When not taking classes at the college, she still paints and sells her works.
Bessie Higgins - Artist
“Almost everybody that paints at all likes to sell. If you don’t like to sell, you don’t paint. I really think that’s true because It was something about having them and then selling them to somebody who likes them.”
While she considers painting her real talent, she enjoys being involved in all forms of art and being around other artists.
Bessie Higgins - Artist
“Painting is more my forte than sculpture, let us say. When I had a chance to come over, we lived. And it’s always nice to just see people.”
Art instructor Cliff Budman has had the pleasure of having Bessie Higgins in many of his classes over the years and says she’s an inspiration to the students and to him.
Cliff Budman – Art Instructor
“She likes to be with young people. Well, it’s good for our soul and her soul as a person doing imagery. She’s just a joy to have in our classes and she’s been in so many of them that she’s just one of us here and she always has been.”
Bessie Higgins will be 91 years old in January, and despite her age, she shows no signs of slowing down anytime soon.

title: Scarborough Town Council approves immigration enforcement ordinance
text:
Scarborough Town Council approves immigration enforcement ordinance
The council voted Wednesday night to approve an ordinance addressing the town's involvement in federal immigration enforcement
Scarborough Town Council approves immigration enforcement ordinance
The council voted Wednesday night to approve an ordinance addressing the town's involvement in federal immigration enforcement
The Scarborough Town Council voted 6-1 Wednesday night to approve an ordinance addressing the town's involvement in federal immigration enforcement.
The ordinance limits the voluntary use of town employees, property and equipment to assist with federal civil immigration enforcement, except where cooperation is required by law or a judicial order.
The ordinance follows months of discussion about federal immigration enforcement in Scarborough, which is home to an Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility on Manson Libby Road.
Councilor Scott Doherty cast the lone dissenting vote, saying he had previously supported the measure but felt a speaker during public comment was trying to bait him into a response.
Doherty said he supported people exercising their right to protest peacefully but that the comments made during Wednesday's meeting influenced his decision to vote against the ordinance.

title: Hall Funeral Homes to Host Lunch & Learn About Loss
text:
Hall Funeral Homes & Cremation Services invites community members to a Lunch & Learn event, “What Happens After a Loss? A Practical Guide to the First Steps,” at 11:30 a.m. Tuesday, Nov. 17 at Hall’s of Waldoboro.
The loss of a loved one can be an overwhelming experience, leaving families with questions about what happens next, who to contact, and what decisions need to be made. title: Maine voters turned out in record numbers, preliminary data shows
text:
Maine voters turned out in record numbers for 2026 midterm election, preliminary data shows
The official numbers are still being tallied, but Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said there were a record number of voters who turned out for the 2026 midterm election.
Bellows said that based on unofficial returns, more than 730,000 people voted in Maine, which she said is the most Maine voters who turned out for a midterm.
Data from the Secretary of State's Office showed that, as of 2 p.m. on Election Day, more than 311,000 of the 325,000-plus absentee ballots that were issued had already been returned and accepted.
Many Maine municipalities were reporting total voter turnout of 70% to 80%.
Maine's previous record for voter turnout during a midterm election was in 2022, when about 61.8% of eligible voters cast a ballot, a total of 680,909 people.
In the presidential election in 2024, voter turnout in Maine was 842,447 — which was just over 74% of citizens who were of voting age.
Maine consistently has a significantly higher voter turnout than the national average, and usually has one of the highest voter participation rates in the country.

title: Plan a visit to a Maine monument honoring our veterans
text:
WRITTEN BY RICHARD SHAW
Maine has to be among the most patriotic of all the 50 states. Every community seems to have a veterans’ roll of honor or monument from all wars, dating back to the American Revolution. The grave sites of those who served are sacred ground, decorated with flowers and U.S. flags by volunteers. Civil War historian Brian Swartz claims Bangor alone may enjoy the honor of having more veterans’ memorials than any other place in the state. Monuments and graves at Mount Hope Cemetery, the Cole Land Transportation Museum, and in downtown parks remember sons and daughters from another time. Following is a sampling of some noteworthy examples. Why not spend a day, or longer, gratefully visiting every one of them?
Civil War Monuments
Maine’s nearly 200 monuments honoring Union Army veterans who served are scattered from Kittery to Presque Isle. Many date to the 19th century, and another, Bangor’s modern 2nd Maine memorial in Mount Hope Cemetery, erected in 1962, depicts an angel carrying a wounded soldier. Nearby is the 1864 soldiers’ monument, possibly the nation’s first civilian-funded memorial, bordered by veterans’ graves. The book, “Silent Sentinels — Maine’s Civil War Monuments,” coming out in 2027, will feature, in words and photos, backgrounds on all the memorials. It was co-written by Swartz, Earle Shettleworth, and Ford Reiche. Numerous websites help guide visitors to each site.
World Wars I and II
Probably because the isolationist United States didn’t enter World War I until April 1917, three years after the conflict began, state memorials recalling The War to End All Wars are not plentiful. But at least two — Lincoln’s exceptional doughboy statue (doughboy was a popular nickname for a United States infantryman during World War I) and Farmington’s impressive memorial arch — are worth the visit.
World War II monuments are easier to find. New Sweden’s Memorial Gate is at Thomas Park. And the Cole museum is home to a “man in a jeep” monument, dedicated in 1997, honoring casualty Charlie Flanagan of Bangor, the city’s other 4,914 citizens who served in that war, and the 110 who lost their lives. An adjacent granite monument lists all of their names. And a Portland memorial honors the 255 area service members who were killed in the Second World War.
Korea and Vietnam
Two post-World War II conflicts are also remembered in a number of Maine monuments. The State of Maine Korean War Memorial, dedicated on July 29, 1995, inside Mount Hope Cemetery, honors veterans who served and the nearly 250 who died in the three-year conflict (1950-1953). The state’s three Medal of Honor recipients’ names are inscribed on the monument, alongside those of fallen and missing service members. Vietnam War veterans are remembered at several Cole museum monuments. Augusta’s Capital Park is home to the Maine Vietnam Veterans Memorial, which features a metal sculpture of three soldiers who cast an image that moves with the sun’s transit.
Other Notable Memorials
Spanish-American War sailors and casualties are remembered at Bangor’s Davenport Park, which features a monument containing the shield and scrollwork of the USS Maine, sunk in Havana Harbor on Feb. 15, 1898. Other memorials of note are located throughout the state. Who knew that a Confederate soldier was the model for a monument in York? Or, that the state’s shortest Civil War statue depicts a soldier in Vienna? Augusta’s Maine Veterans Cemetery and the Acadia National Cemetery near Columbia Falls are also noteworthy.
In the words of Cole Land Transportation Museum executive director Jennifer Munson, “Our freedoms were secured through courage, duty, and extraordinary sacrifice. These memorials ensure that personal stories remain visible, personal, and meaningful for the generations to follow.”

Aging & driving
As people age and their health changes, families can face the question of when a loved one should stop driving.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports older drivers are more likely than younger drivers to be involved in a car accident. Defective pipes
For more than a dozen homeowners outside Atlanta their dream home came with a costly surprise.
They’re blaming one of the nation’s biggest home builders for selling them houses with defective plumbing. Homeowners say the pipes began leaking about four years after they moved in.
Beau’s Bags
Sabrina and Brenden Miller walked through the doors of Oak Lawn Hospital with 17 bags full of comfort items, a delivery they make each year on their son’s birthday.
Positive billboards
Sam Aguiar has been a personal injury lawyer since 2008.
“It’s a tough field, but it’s a rewarding field,” Aguiar said.
In December 2024, he decided to go beyond the courtroom and put up billboards around town with motivational messages. He’s up to 60 total billboards so far.

title: Blue Dog Democrats have a plan to reduce the debt and fix our broken budget process
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Jared Golden of Lewiston represents Maine’s 2nd Congressional District in the U.S. House of Representatives. This piece was originally published on Oct. 30 in “ Dear Mainer,” Golden’s Substack. It is reposted here in its entirety, with permission.
For years, our country has been running a live experiment in out-of-balance budgets. We all know that when you spend more than you can afford, the bill eventually comes due. Our nation is now at that inflection point.
Washington has spent years cutting taxes while increasing spending, and the bill is catching up with us: Our record-breaking $40 trillion debt is driving up interest rates, making it more expensive for Americans to own a home, buy a car or start a small business.
Debt payments have grown so large that they eclipse nearly every other line item in the budget. They are crowding out investments in education, national security and other priorities — and threatening the future of Social Security and Medicare.
Alarm bells about our dangerous fiscal situation are growing louder and louder. But Congress’ budgetmaking process is so thoroughly broken that it’s unlikely we can respond as necessary without major reforms.
Consider these facts: Congress has not passed a complete budget on time for 30 years. Government shutdowns are growing longer and becoming more frequent. Trillion-dollar deficits have become the norm as neither party seems willing to make difficult choices or tradeoffs to improve our financial health. And a breakdown in our system of checks and balances has undermined Congress’ spending authority and made it harder for the parties to negotiate budget bills in good faith.
Congress needs to get serious about the debt, reform the broken budget process that got us into this mess, and start making responsible choices again. Recently, I joined two of my fellow Blue Dogs — Reps. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington and Adam Gray of California — to introduce the Congressional Budget Reform Act of 2026 to get us back on track.
Our bill would tackle rising costs by getting the debt under control, end harmful government shutdowns and restore critical checks and balances in federal spending. I’m using this [column] to go over the details of the bill with you, and to explain why I think these nine reforms are crucial to getting our fiscal house in order.
Fixing the broken budget process
The last time Congress passed a complete budget on-time, “Macarena” was an international dance craze and most people connected to the internet through a dial-up modem — if they were connected at all.
At the same time that regular order has collapsed, government shutdowns have become routine and are getting longer, dragging out the pain for Americans affected by furloughs and lapses in critical programs. And President Donald Trump has exposed a loophole in our system of checks and balances that makes it too easy for a chief executive to roll back congressionally approved spending, undermining the ability of budget negotiators to bargain in good faith.
The Congressional Budget Reform Act of 2026 makes four key improvements to fix the broken budget process:
Bundle the 12 appropriations bills into four “minibuses”: Bundling will streamline the budget process, reduce bottlenecks and encourage on-time enactment of appropriations.
No more government shutdowns: This reform would enact the Prevent Government Shutdowns Act, which would implement automatic, 14-day continuing resolutions in the event of any lapse in government funding. It would also require Congress to stay in session until all appropriations bills are completed.
End the fast track for impoundments in the Senate: The expedited rescission, which allows federal funding to be canceled with a simple majority rather than the 60-vote threshold required to enact it, was never used until recently. In 2025, President Trump successfully used it to rescind $9.4 billion in congressionally approved spending on a party-line vote, threatening future efforts to pass bipartisan spending bills. The Congressional Budget Reform Act of 2026 would strengthen checks and balances by requiring rescissions to achieve the same 60-vote threshold as appropriations.
Explicitly prohibit the “pocket rescission”: The “pocket rescission” is an executive maneuver in which a president waits to request a rescission until near the end of the fiscal year, causing the authorization to expire and the funding to be withheld before the congressional review period ends. In the latest example, President Trump in September used a pocket rescission to unilaterally undo $810 million in congressionally authorized spending. The legality of this move has been questioned, and Congress can clarify the law to prevent it. The Congressional Budget Reform Act of 2026 would prohibit a president from submitting rescission requests or withholding funding within 90 days of an appropriation expiring.
Strengthening fiscal guardrails
According to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, the United States’ debt-to-GDP ratio is nearly 100%, with interest payments on the debt exceeding spending on education, defense, Medicaid or total non-defense discretionary spending. This level of debt, driven by tax cuts for the wealthy and increased spending, is unsustainable, threatening Social Security, Medicare and the country’s ability to respond to future crises.
The Congressional Budget Reform Act of 2026 contains three provisions to help restore fiscal stability:
Enforceable debt targets: The bill would require Congress to set debt reduction targets in the annual budget resolution and create a special reconciliation process to enforce the target if it is exceeded.
Strengthen PAYGO: Congress enacted the Statutory Pay-As-You-Go Act in 2010 to require offsets to new spending or tax cuts. The president’s Office of Management and Budget (OMB) keeps two scorecards to track the deficit impact of spending over five- and 10-year periods. Debits on either scorecard are meant to trigger automatic spending cuts, but Congress has never allowed this to happen. The Congressional Budget Reform Act of 2026 would require the House to take a recorded vote before exempting legislation from the PAYGO Scorecard, delaying debits to future years or wiping the scorecard to zero.
Deficit Reduction Accounts: This provision would require deficit reduction accounts in appropriations bills, which would allow savings to go toward reducing the deficit, automatically lowering applicable spending allocations so those savings cannot be repurposed for other spending.
Improving information and data available to Congress
Congress is responsible for crafting fiscally responsible budgets that deliver for the American people today and build a strong foundation for a safe, prosperous future. To do that, lawmakers need the best, most up-to-date information available.
The Congressional Budget Reform Act of 2026 contains two provisions to increase transparency about the fiscal state of the nation and provide Congress with the information it needs to keep America on track:
Fiscal State of the Nation: This provision would require an annual, nonpartisan briefing in a joint hearing of the House and Senate Budget committees from the comptroller general.
Report on Fiscal Contingency Preparedness: This provision would require the Treasury Department and OMB to conduct and publish an annual assessment of the government’s fiscal resilience to major emergencies, subject to independent Government Accountability Office review.
We can turn this ship around
Congress has been off course for far too long, ignoring the warning signs of our skyrocketing deficits and debt and allowing the collapse of a budgetmaking process that could make us truly reckon with the tradeoffs necessary to get back on a path toward fiscal stability.
The House and Senate should implement these reforms before passing the next budget. By reforming the appropriations process, strengthening fiscal guardrails and improving the information and fiscal analysis available to members of Congress, I believe we can start turning this ship around.

title: NASA space telescope plunges to Earth after two decades studying cosmic explosions
text:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — One of NASA’s premier space telescopes plunged to Earth on Wednesday, ending its 22-year investigation of the universe’s biggest explosions.
The Swift Observatory’s demise came less than three months after a long-shot rescue mission failed.
The U.S. Space Force confirmed Swift’s reentry near Indonesia after tracking its sinking orbit, the result of intense solar activity the past few years.
NASA hired a private company to whip together an orbit-boosting effort, but Katalyst Space’s three-armed robotic craft ran into trouble following its July launch and came crashing down in September.
It was not immediately known how much of the 1 ½-ton spacecraft burned up in the atmosphere. NASA anticipated some of the denser pieces surviving.
Swift rocketed into orbit in 2004 on what was expected to be a two-year study of gamma ray bursts and exploding stars. It observed thousands of them over a mission that lasted 11 times longer than planned, serving as a first responder for other telescopes that could probe deeper.
NASA is gauging industry’s interest in mounting a rescue mission for another observatory whose orbit is being chipped away by solar storms: the Hubble Space Telescope. Launched in 1990, Hubble is expected to come crashing down by the mid-2030s, according to recent analyses.
The space agency is looking for input from private companies on whether and how they might boost Hubble’s orbit, upgrade its systems or guide it to a controlled reentry — or all three. Any such mission would need to happen by 2032.
Unlike the rush job with Swift, the space agency has more time to explore options for saving Hubble, said Nicky Fox, NASA’s science mission chief.
“Hubble still has important science ahead of it,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a statement, “and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible.”

title: After years of declines, drug overdose deaths in Maine have leveled off in 2026
text:
After years of steep declines, Maine’s drug overdose deaths have plateaued in 2026. Through September, fatal overdoses are occurring at nearly the same rate as last year.
Maine recorded 285 fatal overdoses from January to September this year, compared to 289 during the same period in 2025, according to data released by the state on Thursday.
Fueled by the opioid crisis, overdose deaths in Maine mostly climbed from the 2010s through 2022. They peaked at 723 that year and have dropped by double-digit percentages every year since, including by 20% in 2025, when Maine reported 390 deaths.
Gordon Smith, director of opioid response for the state, said in an interview Thursday that the reasons why people use drugs are complex and change over time. He said that makes it difficult to pinpoint why the decline in overdose deaths has flattened this year.
“We knew that we would not be able to sustain declines of those levels, like the 20% we saw last year, until we got to zero,” Smith said. “That’s not how this works.”
Through September, there had been 5,609 nonfatal overdoses in Maine, up from 5,478 during the same period in 2025, according to the data.
Courtney Gary-Allen, executive director of the Maine Recovery Action/Access Project nonprofit, said overdoses spiked during and after the pandemic, due to people feeling isolated and the temporary closure of healthcare services. Isolation is a risk factor for drug use, she said.
Gary-Allen said it took years to rebuild recovery services while people were dying of overdoses. She said services have stabilized since last year, and that could be one reason why the decline slowed down.
“It’s taken us five years to right the ship, and now overdose deaths are back to 2019 numbers,” Gary-Allen said.
Maine had 380 overdose deaths in 2019, slightly fewer than in 2025.
Smith said high inflation, and cuts to food assistance and Medicaid may also be contributing to drug deaths flattening this year. Smith said stressful life conditions, such as not being able to afford heating fuel or groceries, may cause some to turn to drugs.
“We’ve done a lot to help people, but we’re always looking at what is it that we haven’t done that could have saved the people we’ve lost this year already,” he said.
Smith said that after years of investing in capacity, the state now has about 650-700 residential recovery beds, with another 250 set to open in the next several months. Residential programs include a blend of detox, and short-term and long-term treatment programs.
“The most significant investment we’ve made is to make treatment more available,” Smith said. “You want to create an ecosystem of treatment and recovery support so that when people are ready, there’s enough treatment available.”
Kerry MacDonald, executive director of Guardian Recovery Pine Tree in Westbrook, said the state has made a “huge investment to expand our residential capacity across the state.”
MacDonald said Guardian Recovery Pine Tree’s residential programs, including detox and 30-day in patient, are expanding from 41 beds to 76 at its new facility in Westbrook.
She said that expansion should go a long way toward eliminating waiting lists for their longer-term programs.
“More than anything, we just wanted to be able to provide services to people who need them, instead of turning people away,” MacDonald said.

title: Inflation, tariffs and a voter revolt: The midterm verdict on Trump's economy
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump was publicly humbled by inflation in Tuesday’s midterm elections, as rising prices provoked a blistering set of losses for Republicans in House, Senate and gubernatorial races.
Most voters said that Trump’s own policies had smothered growth and drove costs even higher, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of roughly 100,000 midterm voters. The president’s message that the fault lay with his predecessor, Democrat Joe Biden, didn’t land. Americans saw prices start to climb with Trump’s chaotic rash of tariffs last year, and energy costs spiked after he launched a war with Iran in February.
About two-thirds of voters said Trump’s own policies had fueled inflation. By contrast, only about half of 2022 midterm voters said this about Biden’s policies, according to AP VoteCast.
Voters in states from California to Mississippi were broadly in agreement that Trump’s taxes on foreign imports have done more harm than good.
The election results matched what voters had been telling pollsters for months, but Trump had campaigned with a decidedly deaf ear.
“I’ve done a great job,” Trump said at one of his final midterm rallies in Iowa. “Prices are coming way down.”
Voters have buyer’s remorse with Trump
Democratic victories in Tuesday’s midterms signaled that most voters don’t believe the economy or Trump is working for them.
Consumer prices are up 3.7% over the past 12 months, compared to an inflation rate of 3% when Trump began his second term. The president told reporters on Wednesday that the Iran war “drove the gasoline up a little bit short-term,” but he felt the choice to fight Iran was worth it because of its push for nuclear weapons. “If I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again,” he said.
There is no guarantee that a House and Senate with a Democratic majority can fix an economy pestered by uncomfortably high inflation. Trump and Congress would likely need to work on a bipartisan basis, or simply keep the economy stable enough to allow the Federal Reserve to ratchet down inflation through its setting of interest rates.
But voters did prefer Democrats to the status quo of a president who could govern with little to no congressional pushback from Republicans.
About 9 in 10 voters said the cost of living was a “crucial” or “major” factor in their vote for Congress. And about 6 in 10 of this group backed Democratic candidates in their local House races.
The economy is still growing, but AI is a source of fear instead of hope
The underlying economy is stronger than many Americans think, with the S&P 500 stock index up more than 10% so far this year and the unemployment rate at a healthy 4.2%. Investors greeted the news of Democratic wins as a positive with stocks up on Wednesday.
Still, the major driver of growth has been the buildout of artificial intelligence — a boom that Trump has actively stoked by refusing to codify more aggressive federal oversight.
Voters don’t share Trump’s optimism about AI, which he has renamed “super intelligence” in federal documents.
Instead of buying the arguments that AI would increase productivity and accelerate growth, about 6 in 10 voters said AI will do more to hurt society.
The technology could displace workers as jobs get automated or it could be a financial bubble that if popped could wreak havoc on retirement savings. Despite the anxiety, only about one-quarter of voters said AI was a “crucial” factor.
Wealth isn’t trickling down to the middle class
Tech billionaires such as Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Elon Musk have become frequent guests of Trump, attending state dinners or jetting aboard with the president. But the growing concentration of wealth has been disconcerting for voters.
Nationwide, about 7 in 10 voters said the economy favors the wealthy, while only about 3 in 10 said it’s fair to everyday Americans. The wealth gap has become so extreme that even a majority of voters with a 2025 household income of $300,000 or more in the tech-heavy state of California felt the economy was tilted toward the rich.
Still, a slight majority of voters across the country had a “somewhat” or “very” favorable impression of capitalism, compared to about one-third who “strongly” or “somewhat” favor socialism.
But the election suggested that voters believe the government should use its heft to help reduce the cost of healthcare. About 6 in 10 said they wanted the government to play a “bigger role” in addressing medical expenses. Most voters said Trump’s policies have made healthcare costs worse.
Trump caught in a trap with voters
How voters felt about the overall economy generally depended on the size of their paychecks. While Trump campaigned on stats suggesting record low poverty, the working poor saw their own finances as crumbling.
For those earning less than $50,000 a year, about 6 in 10 said they were worse off now than they were two years ago before Trump became president.
People with higher incomes felt better about the economy, but that created a different problem for Trump. Higher-income voters were more concerned about the state of American democracy, and voters focused on democracy overwhelmingly broke for Democrats. Without congressional approval, Trump laid off thousands of federal workers, altered federal spending and imposed hundreds of billions of dollars in new tariffs that the Supreme Court earlier this year ruled were illegal.
About 4 in 10 households with 2025 household incomes above $200,000 said that democracy was their top issue, putting the issue about even with the economy. Voters in most lower-income categories, on the other hand, clearly prioritized the economy.
Overall, a slim majority of voters said government corruption was a crucial factor for their vote, while about half said this about high prices. Higher-income voters were much less likely than lower-income voters to see high prices as a key factor.
What most voters took away from the past 22 months of Trump’s presidency was that he brokered deals, took government stakes in private companies and acted in ways that put him at the center of the economy instead of America’s workers.
Most voters — about 6 in 10 — said Trump’s priorities were misplaced.
When voters were asked if Trump fought for people like them, most said he didn’t.
___
The AP Voter Poll is a survey of more than 100,000 voters conducted by SSRS for The Associated Press, ABC News, CBS News, CNN, FOX News Media, NBC News and Versant. The survey blends probability-based and non-probability-based interviews with registered voters in all 50 states conducted from Oct. 19 to Nov. 3 in Alaska and Oct. 22 to Nov. 3 in all other states. A detailed methodology statement is available here. The margin of sampling error is plus or minus 0.6 percentage points for the full sample.

title: Rockers That Didn't Get a Chance to Perform on 'Saturday Night Live'
text:
21 Rock Artists That Never Got a Chance to Play ‘Saturday Night Live’
After decades on air, we're used to seeing rock 'n' roll artists on Saturday Night Live, but when the show first launched in 1975, there were obstacles to overcome.
"Rock and roll people did not do television because they sounded terrible. So we had to figure that out, and that was a big, big fight over the first season," SNL's creator Lorne Michaels said to Entertainment Weekly in 2025.
"If you look at, say, Elvis Presley on The Ed Sullivan Show [in 1956], or the Beatles [in 1964] for that matter, it's all on a boom [microphone], you know, and the sound was more than good enough for that period for them to catch fire and all that," he explained. "But by the time we came on, the music was recorded in a completely different way, and television was still using a boom. So that was the biggest sort of fight at the beginning."
The very first episode of SNL featured musical performances by Billy Preston and Janis Ian, but even then, Michaels was focused on how the sound could be improved for episode two and all other future episodes.
"When Paul Simon did the second show, I brought [producer] Phil Ramone in, who was working with him that summer on Still Crazy [After All These Years]. And the television audio guy was not thrilled about that," Michaels continued. "Just the idea that we were gonna mic it differently. Remember, Elvis is him and the Jordanaires, and a boom is covering all their music. And now it was different."
READ MORE: 20 Rock Artists Who've Never Played 'SNL'...But Still Could
Clearly, the kinks were figured out so that bands and solo artists that appeared on SNL could sound, well, good on TV, something viewers came to expect more and more as broadcast technology developed over the years.
Many seasons of SNL later, the musical guests on the show have run the gamut of musical genres and there's no sign of slowing down. But there are, of course, some acts that would have made excellent guests who simply never got the opportunity, some for reasons we may never know. In the below gallery, we've rounded up 21 examples of such artists that unfortunately won't ever get this chance.

title: Google says it will cut off search engine access for students at schools that reject AI
text:
(AP) - Students using Google software in the classroom will not be allowed to access the company’s search engine unless their school system also opts in to using artificial intelligence, the tech giant said Tuesday.
The Mountain View, California, company has been facing pushback from educators, child development experts and parents over the use of its technology in schools, with the backlash heating up since it announced in August that it had turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students who use Google Classroom.
On Tuesday, the company said that practice would no longer be the default option for school administrators. Instead, K-12 schools will be able to individually turn each Google tool on or off — including Gemini, Gemini Notebook and search, with each being off by default until administrators turn it on. But because search is integrated with AI, schools that opt out of AI altogether would also lose access to Google search.
“We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach,” Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post.
The company also said it is updating its search tools to make them “better for learning,” including offering step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don’t get quick answers to schoolwork."
But turning off AI altogether is not possible if schools want to use Google products.
Google is by far the dominant provider of education technology for U.S. schools. Worldwide, the company says 150 million students and teachers use its Google Classroom platform, and many students use school-provided Chromebook computers.
Google faced an outcry in August when it switched on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students. Until August, Google had only allowed Gemini to be turned on for students 18 or older.
Tuesday’s announcement was met with swift criticism from educators and policymakers.
“Google is using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI. This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service,” wrote Lina Khan, former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, on social media. “As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line.”
New York City and Los Angeles, home to the nation’s biggest school districts, have issued temporary bans on generative AI tools in elementary and middle schools as they assess AI use and safety and develop policies on its use.
Many students already use AI to help with school and homework, but the technology has also made it easier to cheat and find quick, easy answers to questions instead of thinking critically. And experts have raised questions about how access to AI is affecting children’s brain development.
Josh Golin, executive director of children’s advocacy group Fairplay, said Google’s attempt to “strong-arm schools into using its AI products is likely to backfire.” He said Google’s technology in schools is not about learning but about “developing lifetime brand loyalty” for its products.
“Because AI isn’t safe for kids and undermines education and critical thinking, schools should turn off Google’s AI tools the minute that option becomes available,” Golin said in a statement.
Rather than fret about losing access to search, Golin urged schools to turn off not just AI but also Google, and “use this opportunity to help students find more privacy-protective alternatives for search, as well as ways to do more substantive research beyond search and click.”

title: Boothbay’s Crocker Earns Ninth in Class C Boys Championship XC Race
text:
Boothbay senior A.J. Crocker raced to a ninth place finish at the Class C boys cross country state championship on Saturday, Oct. 31 at Cony High School in Augusta. Crocker set a personal record during the race with a time of 17:20.83, 12 seconds faster than his prior best. According to Boothbay head coach Nick Scott, it is the first time a Seahawks runner has earned a top 10 finish at states since 2019.
“What an incredible ending to an incredible season,” said Scott. “It’s amazing that three of our runners set all-time personal records at the state championship on what is arguably the hardest course they faced all season.”
In addition to Crocker, the Seahawks that set new personal records included John Cooper (eight seconds) and Miles Hyson (19 seconds).
Crocker’s top 10 result boosted the Seahawk boys to a team score of 193 points, which placed the squad ninth among the 13 schools competing at the event. Winthrop won the boys Class C championship with a score of 47, Houlton was second (66), George Stevens took third (105), Maranacook was fourth (127), and Dirigo rounded out the top five with 161 points.
Also scoring points for the Boothbay boys team score were junior Jackson Zehm (31st, 19:00.39), sophomore John Cooper (44th, 19:24.86), sophomore Miles Hyson (63rd, 20:37.54), and junior Alex Ross (75th, 21:11.33). Junior Louie Caidoc (81st, 21:34.48) and junior Ben Gapski (89th, 23:13.50) also competed for Boothbay.
Dirigo’s William Morris won the meet with a time of 16:18.47, Alfie Cognata, of Winthrop, was second in 16:51.20 and Waynflete’s Tadhg Lake was close behind in third with a time of 16:57.26.
Girls Results
Freshman Polly Nadeau led the Boothbay girls team to a sixth place finish among nine teams competing at the Class C state championship meet. Nadeau placed 11th in the race with a time of 22:20.23.
Also scoring points for the Lady Seahawks were sophomore Maggie McCarthy (31st, 23:52.46), senior Olivia Rittal (42nd, 24:26:34), sophomore Audrey Robinson (45th, 24:41.85), and freshman Emma Scott (61st, 26:20.31). Senior Lexi Hughes also competed in the race (64th, 26:41.84).
Maine Coast Waldorf tallied a low score of 58 to win the Class C girls championship. North Yarmouth Academy was the runner-up with 85 points, George Stevens took third (103), Maranacook was fourth (112), and Orono placed fifth (130).
Reagan Mattson, a freshman at Maranacook Community High School, won the girls race with a time of 19:52.73. Dirigo’s McKenzie Boyle earned second (20:33.64), and Winthrop’s Kylie Van Tassel was third (20:56.06).
